upsert.boundary: The Atlantic era, 1500 to 1880
upsert.description: Portuguese ships trade along the coasts from the 1400s; the Atlantic slave trade carries about 12.5 million people to the Americas, most between 1700 and 1850, while the Saharan and Indian Ocean trades carry millions more north and east. States that trade in captives grow (Asante, Dahomey, Oyo) and others are torn apart (Kongo); Morocco destroys Songhay (1591); the Ottomans rule Egypt and the Maghreb's coast; the Dutch settle the Cape (1652). In the 1800s come the Sokoto caliphate, the Zulu kingdom, Muhammad Ali's Egypt, the Suez Canal, and diamonds and gold in the south.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; slave trade numbers from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database as recalled
sources to check: Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); Lovejoy, Transformations in Slavery (3rd ed. 2012); slavevoyages.org

upsert.boundary: Colonial conquest and rule, 1880 to 1957
upsert.description: European powers partition almost all of Africa within a generation; only Ethiopia, victorious at Adwa (1896), and Liberia stay independent. Wars of conquest, rinderpest, sleeping sickness and forced labour, worst in the Congo Free State, kill millions. Railways run from mines and plantations to ports; Africans fight in both world wars; Egypt becomes independent in 1922 and apartheid begins in South Africa in 1948; independence movements grow after 1945.
provenance: sources to check: Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa (1991); Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: Herders, the first farmers and the Pharaohs, 5000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Herding spreads across the green Sahara; as it dries after about 4000 BCE herders move south into the Sahel and east to the Nile, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE and its Old, Middle and New Kingdoms follow; Kerma and Kush rise upriver. Pearl millet, sorghum, African rice and yams are domesticated in the Sahel and West Africa; herders reach East Africa; Bantu-speaking farmers begin to move out of the borderlands of Cameroon and Nigeria.
provenance: sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000); Fuller and Hildebrand, in The Oxford Handbook of African Archaeology (2013)

upsert.boundary: Independent Africa, 1957 to 2025
upsert.description: Ghana in 1957, then most of the continent by 1965, the Portuguese colonies in 1975, Zimbabwe in 1980, Namibia in 1990 and South Africa's democracy in 1994. One-party states and coups; wars in Nigeria, Angola, Mozambique, Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia and the Congo; famine in the Sahel and Ethiopia; HIV/AIDS; the Rwandan genocide; growth after 2000, mobile phones and cities. Africa's people grow from about 285 million (1960) to about 1.5 billion (2025), a fifth of humanity.
provenance: inferred: populations from UN World Population Prospects as recalled
sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019); Meredith, The State of Africa (2011); UN World Population Prospects 2024

upsert.boundary: Iron, Kush, Carthage and the Bantu expansion, 1000 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Iron is smelted in West and Central Africa by about 800 to 500 BCE (Nok); Bantu-speaking farmers carry iron and farming through Central, Eastern and Southern Africa, reaching the Limpopo by about 300 CE. Kush rules Egypt as its twenty-fifth dynasty, then Meroë flourishes; Phoenicians found Carthage, which Rome destroys in 146 BCE; Egypt falls to Persia, Alexander, the Ptolemies and Rome. Aksum rises in Ethiopia and becomes Christian about 330; camels make the Sahara crossable by about 300.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; whether West African iron is an independent invention is debated
sources to check: Vansina, How Societies Are Born (2004); Ehret, The Civilizations of Africa (2002); Grillo et al. 2020, PNAS (Bantu expansion phylogeography)

upsert.boundary: Kingdoms of gold, faith and trade, 500 to 1500
upsert.description: The Arab conquest brings Islam to North Africa from the 640s. Caravans across the Sahara carry gold north and salt, cloth, books and Islam south, under Ghana (Wagadu), then Mali and Songhay. The Swahili towns trade with Arabia, India and China; Great Zimbabwe rules the gold of the plateau; Ife and Benin cast bronze; Kongo forms; Ethiopia's Zagwe and Solomonic kings build churches; the Fatimids, Almoravids, Almohads and Mamluks rule the north. Madagascar is settled from Borneo.
provenance: sources to check: Fauvelle, The Golden Rhinoceros (2018); Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973); UNESCO General History of Africa, vols. 3 and 4

upsert.boundary: The Later Stone Age and the green Sahara, about 52,000 years ago to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: Microlithic tools, bows and poisoned arrows, ostrich-eggshell beads exchanged across hundreds of kilometres, and rock art; foragers everywhere. From about 12,500 years ago the African Humid Period turns the Sahara into grassland, lakes and rivers: fishing and hunting peoples make some of the world's earliest pottery there (Ounjougou, about 9400 BCE), and by about 6000 BCE some herd cattle in the eastern Sahara.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date and place of African cattle domestication are contested
sources to check: Huysecom et al. 2009, Antiquity 83 (Ounjougou pottery); Kuper and Kröpelin 2006, Science 313 (Holocene Sahara)

upsert.boundary: Africa's Middle Stone Age, about 300,000 to 52,000 years ago
upsert.description: Homo sapiens forms across the continent from populations joined and divided by deserts, lakes and forests that grow and shrink with each swing of climate. People make prepared-core flakes and points, use fire and ochre, and from about 100,000 years ago leave engraved ochre, shell beads and pigment workshops at Blombos, Pinnacle Point and Taforalt. The lineages that lead to the Khoe-San separate from the others about 250,000 years ago or more.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; divergence dates from genomes vary by method
sources to check: Schlebusch et al. 2017, Science 358 (southern African genomes); Scerri et al. 2018, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 33; Henshilwood et al. 2011, Science 334 (Blombos ochre workshop)

upsert.boundary: The Archaic and the first American farmers, 8000 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers settle into regional ways of life. Squash is domesticated in Oaxaca by about 8000 BCE and maize from teosinte in the Balsas valley by about 7000 BCE; beans, manioc, chili and cotton follow, and the Andes domesticate potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas. Monumental towns rise at Caral and the Norte Chico of Peru from about 3000 BCE, and mounds at Watson Brake in Louisiana about 3500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS 106 (early maize); Shady Solís et al. 2001, Science 292 (Caral)

upsert.boundary: The Americas before the main peopling, to about 16,000 years ago
upsert.description: For almost all of this span no people live in the Americas. Mammoths, mastodons, horses, camels, giant ground sloths and sabre-toothed cats roam; when sea level falls, Beringia joins Siberia to Alaska. Footprints at White Sands in New Mexico, dated about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would put people south of the ice during the glacial maximum, if their dates hold.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; any presence before about 16,000 years ago is contested
sources to check: Bennett et al. 2021, Science 373, and Pigati et al. 2023, Science 382 (White Sands); Braje et al. 2017, Science 357

upsert.boundary: The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya, Moche, Tiwanaku and Wari, 250 to 900
upsert.description: Teotihuacan holds perhaps 100,000 people until about 550; the Classic Maya city-states (Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán) have writing, calendars and divine kings; the Moche rule the north coast of Peru, Tiwanaku and Wari the highlands. The southern Maya lowlands empty between about 800 and 950 amid drought and war.
provenance: sources to check: Martin, Ancient Maya Politics (2020); Douglas et al. 2015, PNAS (Maya drought)

upsert.boundary: Conquest and colonies, 1492 to 1776
upsert.description: Columbus's landfall brings epidemics and conquest; the Aztec state falls in 1521 and the Inca in 1532 to 1572; Potosí's silver (from 1545) and Zacatecas's fund Spain and flow to China. Brazil's sugar, and the Caribbean's after the 1640s, are worked by enslaved Africans; English, French and Dutch colonies take the Atlantic coast of North America from Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608); Native nations fight, trade furs and ally; the Seven Years' War gives Britain Canada (1763).
provenance: sources to check: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006); Taylor, American Colonies (2001)

upsert.boundary: The Formative: villages, temples and the first American states, 2000 BCE to 250 CE
upsert.description: Village farming spreads; the Olmec of the Gulf coast (about 1600 to 400 BCE) and Chavín in the Andes (about 900 to 200 BCE) build temple centres and art styles that reach far; early Maya cities such as El Mirador and the Zapotec capital of Monte Albán become states; Paracas and Nazca flourish on the Peruvian coast, Adena and Hopewell in the Ohio valley; Teotihuacan begins to grow about 100 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Coe and Koontz, Mexico (7th ed. 2013); Moseley, The Incas and Their Ancestors (2001)

upsert.boundary: Independence and nations, 1776 to 1914
upsert.description: The United States (1776 to 1783), Haiti (1791 to 1804), Spanish America (1810 to 1825) and Brazil (1822) become independent. The United States expands west, removing and defeating Native nations, and takes half of Mexico (1846 to 1848); slavery ends in the US in 1865 and in Brazil in 1888. Railways carry wheat, beef, coffee, rubber and nitrates to world markets, and about forty million immigrants arrive, most from Europe.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; immigration total from Hatton and Williamson as recalled
sources to check: Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. 3; Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Americas since 1914
upsert.description: The United States becomes the largest economy and a world power; the Depression and the New Deal; the Second World War; populism and import substitution in Latin America (Vargas, Perón); the Cuban revolution (1959); the civil rights movement; military dictatorships from 1964 to about 1990 and their end; the debt crisis of 1982; NAFTA (1994); by 2025 about a billion people live in the Americas.
provenance: sources to check: Skidmore, Smith and Green, Modern Latin America (9th ed. 2018); Kennedy, Freedom from Fear (1999)

upsert.boundary: Paleo-Indian hunters, about 16,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: People move down the Pacific coast and later through an ice-free corridor; Monte Verde in Chile is occupied about 14,500 years ago, and Clovis points spread across North America between about 13,050 and 12,750 years ago. Mammoths, horses, camels and giant sloths go extinct by about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago, with hunting and climate both blamed.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE (Monte Verde); Waters and Stafford 2007, Science 315 (Clovis dates); Meltzer, First Peoples in a New World (2nd ed. 2021)

upsert.boundary: The Postclassic: Toltecs, Cahokia, the Aztecs and the Inca, 900 to 1492
upsert.description: Tula and Chichén Itzá; Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde in the Southwest; Mississippian towns, with Cahokia at perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people; the Norse at L'Anse aux Meadows about 1000 and in Greenland until about 1450; the Thule Inuit spread across the Arctic; Chimú on the Peruvian coast. Tenochtitlan is founded in 1325 and the Aztec Triple Alliance formed in 1428; the Inca expand from Cusco from about 1438 to rule perhaps ten million people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Cahokia's size is debated
sources to check: Pauketat, Cahokia (2009); D'Altroy, The Incas (2nd ed. 2014); Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012)

upsert.boundary: Discovery and exploration of Antarctica, 1820 to 1959
upsert.description: The continent is first sighted in 1820 (Bellingshausen, Bransfield, Palmer); sealers nearly exterminate the fur seals; Ross charts the ice shelf (1841); the heroic age of exploration (1897 to 1922); Amundsen reaches the South Pole in December 1911 and Scott a month later; whaling peaks in the 1930s; seven states claim territory; the International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958).
provenance: sources to check: Fogg, A History of Antarctic Science (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Antarctic Treaty, 1959 to 2025
upsert.description: The Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force 1961) sets the continent aside for peace and science and freezes territorial claims; the ozone hole is found above it (1985); the Madrid Protocol bans mining (1991); ice shelves collapse (Larsen B, 2002) and the ice sheets' losses add to rising seas.
provenance: sources to check: Antarctic Treaty Secretariat (ats.aq); Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin 1985, Nature 315 (ozone)

upsert.boundary: Antarctica untouched, to 1820
upsert.description: The ice sheets grow and shrink with the glacial cycles; no person sees the continent. Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle in 1773 without sighting land.
provenance: sources to check: Pyne, The Ice (1986)

upsert.boundary: Iron kingdoms, empires and the Axial age in Asia, 1000 to 321 BCE
upsert.description: The Neo-Assyrian empire (911 to 609 BCE); the Babylonian exile (587 BCE); Cyrus founds the Achaemenid empire (550 BCE), the largest yet; Zoroastrianism spreads; the Upanishads, the Buddha and Mahavira teach in the Ganges valley; Confucius, Laozi and the Warring States in China; the Hebrew Bible takes shape; Alexander conquers Persia (334 to 323 BCE).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Buddha's dates are contested by a century
sources to check: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002); Lewis, in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)

upsert.boundary: Cities, writing and the Bronze Age states of Asia, 3500 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Uruk and the Sumerian cities; cuneiform writing about 3200 BCE; Akkad's empire about 2334 BCE; the Indus cities from about 2600 to 1900 BCE; Ur III; Hammurabi of Babylon about 1792 to 1750 BCE; the Hittites; Erlitou and the Shang, with oracle-bone writing about 1250 BCE; Indo-Aryan speakers and the Vedas in north India about 1500 BCE; the Bronze Age collapse in Anatolia and the Levant about 1200 BCE; the Zhou conquest of the Shang in 1046 BCE.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Mesopotamian dates on the middle chronology
sources to check: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (3rd ed. 2016); Liu and Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

upsert.boundary: Caliphates, Tang and Song, 600 to 1200
upsert.description: Muhammad (about 610 to 632) and the Arab conquests (632 to 750); the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, Baghdad founded in 762; the Tang (618 to 907) and the An Lushan rebellion; the Song (960 to 1279) and their commercial revolution, printing, paper money and gunpowder; the Chola in south India; Angkor; Srivijaya; Heian Japan; Goryeo Korea; the Seljuk Turks; the Crusader states.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed. 2016); Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule (2009)

upsert.boundary: The classical empires of Asia, 321 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: Chandragupta's Maurya empire and Ashoka; Qin unifies China (221 BCE) and the Han rule it for four centuries; the Silk Roads join China to Iran and Rome; the Parthians and then the Sasanians rival Rome; the Kushans rule from Bactria to the Ganges; Buddhism reaches China; the Guptas preside over India's classical age; Korea's Three Kingdoms and Japan's Kofun state form; the Sui reunify China (589).
provenance: sources to check: Twitchett and Loewe (eds.), The Cambridge History of China, vol. 1 (1986); Thapar, Early India (2002)

upsert.boundary: Western dominance, reform and revolution in Asia, 1800 to 1945
upsert.description: Britain rules India after 1818 and directly after the rebellion of 1857; the Opium Wars open China, the Taiping war devastates it, and the Qing fall in 1911; Japan's Meiji Restoration (1868) industrializes it and builds an empire; the Ottoman empire is partitioned after 1918 and Turkey becomes a republic (1923); Gandhi leads India's mass movements; Japan invades Manchuria (1931) and China (1937), and the Pacific war ends with the atomic bombs.
provenance: sources to check: Bose and Jalal, Modern South Asia (4th ed. 2017); Spence, The Search for Modern China (3rd ed. 2013); Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan (2000)

upsert.boundary: Archaic humans and the first Homo sapiens in Asia, to about 62,000 years ago
upsert.description: Homo erectus lingers in Java; Neanderthals live in the west and Central Asia, Denisovans in the east and on the Tibetan plateau, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis on the islands. Homo sapiens reaches the Levant at Misliya (about 180,000 years ago) and Skhul and Qafzeh (about 120,000 to 90,000), and perhaps Arabia and India, but these groups leave few descendants. Toba erupts in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; early dates in Arabia, India and China are contested
sources to check: Hershkovitz et al. 2018, Science 359 (Misliya); Petraglia et al. 2007, Science 317 (Jwalapuram and Toba)

upsert.boundary: The first farmers of Asia, 9700 to 3500 BCE
upsert.description: Wheat, barley, lentils, sheep, goats, cattle and pigs are domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, with Göbekli Tepe's enclosures, Jericho and Çatalhöyük; millet in north China by about 8000 BCE and rice in the Yangtze valley by 7000 to 5000 BCE; Mehrgarh in Baluchistan by about 7000 BCE; Ubaid villages canal the Mesopotamian plain.
provenance: sources to check: Zeder 2011, Current Anthropology 52 (Near Eastern domestication); Fuller et al. 2009, Science 323 (rice)

upsert.boundary: Foragers settle Asia, about 62,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: The dispersal passes through South and South-east Asia, mixing with Denisovans; people reach Sahul, the Tibetan plateau, Siberia and Japan; figurative cave art appears in Sulawesi and Borneo by about 45,000 years ago; pottery is made in China and Japan (Jōmon) from about 20,000 to 16,000 years ago; at the end the Natufians of the Levant settle in villages.
provenance: sources to check: Aubert et al. 2019, Nature 576; Wu et al. 2012, Science 336

upsert.boundary: Gunpowder empires and the oceanic trade, 1400 to 1800
upsert.description: The Ming voyages (1405 to 1433); the Ottomans take Constantinople (1453); the Safavids make Iran Shi'ite (1501); the Mughals rule most of India (from 1526); the Portuguese reach Calicut (1498) and the Dutch East India Company (1602) the spice islands; Tokugawa Japan (1603) closes itself to most foreigners; the Qing conquer China (1644 to 1683) and double its territory; Britain wins Bengal at Plassey (1757). Asia still makes most of the world's manufactures.
provenance: sources to check: Streusand, Islamic Gunpowder Empires (2011); Rowe, China's Last Empire (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Mongol era in Asia, 1200 to 1400
upsert.description: The Mongols conquer from Korea to Iran, sack Baghdad (1258) and rule China as the Yuan (1271 to 1368); the Mamluks stop them at Ain Jalut (1260) and the Delhi Sultanate holds them off India; the routes they join carry the plague west; the Ming expel the Yuan (1368); Timur rebuilds an empire from Samarkand (1370 to 1405).
provenance: sources to check: May, The Mongol Conquests in World History (2012); Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia (2001)

upsert.boundary: Independence and Asia's rise, 1945 to 2025
upsert.description: India and Pakistan (1947), Indonesia, Burma and Ceylon become independent; the Chinese revolution (1949); the Korean and Vietnam wars; Israel and the Arab–Israeli wars; Japan's, then the tigers', then China's and India's growth; the Great Leap and the Cultural Revolution; Iran's revolution (1979); the Iran–Iraq and Gulf wars; the wars in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. By 2025 Asia holds about 59% of humanity and makes about half of the world's output.
provenance: inferred: shares as recalled from UN and IMF figures
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024; IMF World Economic Outlook database

upsert.boundary: Steppe migrations and Europe's Bronze Age, 3000 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Yamnaya herders from the Pontic steppe spread west (the Corded Ware culture, from about 2900 BCE), bringing much of Europe's later ancestry and probably its Indo-European languages; Bell Beakers spread metal across the west; Stonehenge's sarsens rise about 2500 BCE; Minoan Crete's palaces (from about 2000 BCE) and Mycenaean Greece (1600 to 1100 BCE) write Linear A and B; the palaces fall about 1200 BCE; Urnfield cultures follow.
provenance: sources to check: Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522; Kristiansen and Larsson, The Rise of Bronze Age Society (2005)

upsert.boundary: Classical antiquity, 800 BCE to 476 CE
upsert.description: Greek city-states and colonies around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea; Athens' democracy (508 BCE), its philosophy and drama; the Persian wars; Alexander's conquests; the Roman republic conquers the Mediterranean (264 to 146 BCE) and Augustus makes it an empire (27 BCE); two centuries of peace; Christianity spreads and becomes the religion of the state (380); Goths, Huns and Vandals; the western empire ends in 476.
provenance: sources to check: Osborne, Greece in the Making (2nd ed. 2009); Beard, SPQR (2015); Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

upsert.boundary: The early Middle Ages, 476 to 1000
upsert.description: Germanic kingdoms in the west, the Eastern Roman empire in the east; the Justinianic plague (541); Slavs settle the east and the Balkans; the Arabs conquer Iberia (711); Charlemagne is crowned emperor (800); Vikings raid, trade and settle from Rus to Iceland and Normandy; Christianity reaches Bulgaria, Rus (988), Poland and Scandinavia; manors and serfdom take hold.
provenance: sources to check: Wickham, The Inheritance of Rome (2009)

upsert.boundary: Europe's early modern era, 1500 to 1789
upsert.description: The oceanic empires of Spain, Portugal, the Dutch, England and France; the Reformation and the wars of religion; the Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) and the Peace of Westphalia; the scientific revolution; the Dutch Republic's golden age; the Glorious Revolution; Russia reaches the Pacific (1639) and Peter the Great builds St Petersburg; the Enlightenment; Britain's coal and steam.
provenance: sources to check: Cameron (ed.), Early Modern Europe (1999); Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)

upsert.boundary: The High and Late Middle Ages, 1000 to 1500
upsert.description: Europe's people double; towns, fairs, guilds and universities grow; the Great Schism (1054); the Norman conquest of England (1066); the Crusades (1096 to 1291); Magna Carta (1215); the Mongols take Rus (1237 to 1240); the Great Famine (1315) and the Black Death (1347 to 1351); the Hundred Years' War; the Ottomans take Constantinople (1453); the Renaissance begins in Italy; printing; the Reconquista ends (1492).
provenance: sources to check: Bartlett, The Making of Europe (1993); Jordan, Europe in the High Middle Ages (2001)

upsert.boundary: Revolution, industry and nations in Europe, 1789 to 1914
upsert.description: The French Revolution and Napoleon; the Congress of Vienna (1815); industry spreads from Britain to Belgium, France and Germany; the revolutions of 1848; the Irish famine; the Crimean war; Russia frees its serfs (1861); Italy (1861) and Germany (1871) unify; tens of millions emigrate; Europe holds about a quarter of humanity at its peak around 1900, Russia included.
provenance: sources to check: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016); Blanning, The Pursuit of Glory (2007)

upsert.boundary: Neanderthal Europe, to about 47,000 years ago
upsert.description: Neanderthals, descended from Europe's earlier humans, live through two glacial cycles, hunting large game and making Mousterian tools; a Homo sapiens skull at Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, marks an earlier venture that did not last. Hippos swim in the Thames during the Last Interglacial.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Apidima identification is contested
sources to check: Harvati et al. 2019, Nature 571 (Apidima); Papagianni and Morse, The Neanderthals Rediscovered (2013)

upsert.boundary: Mesolithic foragers and Europe's first farmers, 9700 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers live in the Holocene forests and along coasts and lakes. Farmers from Anatolia reach Greece about 6500 BCE, spread up the Danube (the Linear Pottery culture, about 5500 BCE) and along the Mediterranean, and reach Britain and Scandinavia about 4000 BCE, largely replacing the foragers; megaliths are raised along the Atlantic; Varna's graves hold the world's oldest worked gold (about 4500 BCE).
provenance: sources to check: Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522; Whittle, Europe in the Neolithic (1996)

upsert.boundary: Division and union, 1945 to 2025
upsert.description: An iron curtain divides Europe; the Marshall Plan and welfare states in the west, Soviet rule in the east; Western Europe integrates (1951, 1957) and grows fast; 1968; the Berlin Wall falls (1989) and the Soviet Union dissolves (1991); wars in Yugoslavia; the European Union enlarges east (2004) and adopts the euro; the euro crisis; Brexit; Russia's wars on Ukraine (2014, 2022).

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens in Europe: the Upper Palaeolithic, about 47,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: Homo sapiens arrives from about 45,000 years ago (Bacho Kiro) and the Neanderthals disappear about 40,000 years ago. Aurignacian people carve ivory figurines and play bone flutes (about 40,000 years ago) and paint Chauvet (about 36,000); the Gravettian follows; the glacial maximum drives people to refugia in Iberia, southern France and Ukraine; the Magdalenians paint Lascaux (about 17,000 years ago) and resettle the north as the ice retreats.
provenance: sources to check: Hublin et al. 2020, Nature 581 (Bacho Kiro); Higham et al. 2014, Nature 512; Conard et al. 2009, Nature 460 (flutes)

upsert.boundary: The world wars in Europe, 1914 to 1945
upsert.description: The First World War; the Russian revolutions (1917) and civil war; the influenza; new nation-states from the fallen empires; Mussolini, Stalin and Hitler; collectivization and the Ukrainian famine; the Great Terror; the Second World War and the Holocaust.
provenance: sources to check: Kershaw, To Hell and Back (2015); Snyder, Bloodlands (2010)

upsert.boundary: Ancient Sahul and Near Oceania, about 65,000 to 3,500 years ago
upsert.description: People cross from Wallacea to Sahul at least 50,000 and perhaps 65,000 years ago, spread across the continent, reach Tasmania, the New Guinea highlands and the Bismarck and Solomon islands; most of the megafauna vanish by about 40,000 years ago; the Lake Mungo burials, about 42,000 years old, are among the oldest ritual burials known. Rising seas cut off Tasmania and then New Guinea; New Guineans drain the Kuk swamp to grow taro and bananas from about 10,000 to 7,000 years ago.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first arrival is contested
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547 (Madjedebe); O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115 (a later arrival); Denham et al. 2003, Science 301 (Kuk)

upsert.boundary: Sahul and the Pacific before people, to about 65,000 years ago
upsert.description: At low sea level Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania form one continent, Sahul, never joined to Asia; giant marsupials such as Diprotodon, giant birds and reptiles live there; the Pacific islands are empty of people.
provenance: sources to check: Hiscock, Archaeology of Ancient Australia (2nd ed. 2024)

upsert.boundary: Contact and colonization in Oceania, 1768 to 1901
upsert.description: Cook's voyages (1768 to 1779); the First Fleet at Sydney (1788), smallpox (1789) and the frontier wars; the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872); gold rushes (from 1851); Kamehameha unites Hawai'i (1810) and the United States annexes it (1898); missionaries; islanders recruited or kidnapped for plantation labour; epidemics halve many island populations.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (5th ed. 2020); Belich, Making Peoples (1996)

upsert.boundary: Island kingdoms and the continent before contact, 1300 to 1768
upsert.description: Māori iwi spread through Aotearoa; the Tu'i Tonga's maritime state; Rapa Nui's moai; Hawai'i's chiefdoms; Aboriginal Australia's hundreds of nations with their trade routes, songlines and burning of the land. Magellan crosses the Pacific (1521), Spain takes Guam (1668), Dutch ships chart western Australia and Tasman sights Tasmania and New Zealand (1642), and Makassan fishermen visit Arnhem Land.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon (ed.), The Cambridge History of the Pacific Islanders (1997)

upsert.boundary: Federation, war and the island nations, 1901 to 2025
upsert.description: Australia federates (1901) under the White Australia policy; Gallipoli (1915); the Pacific war (1941 to 1945); nuclear tests in the Marshall Islands, Australia and French Polynesia (1946 to 1996); the Stolen Generations; Samoa (1962), Nauru (1968), Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975) and others become independent; Australia's 1967 referendum and the Mabo judgment (1992); rising seas threaten the atolls.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (5th ed. 2020); Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Lapita and the settling of Remote Oceania, about 1500 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking voyagers with pottery, pigs, chickens and outrigger canoes, the Lapita culture, reach the Bismarcks about 1350 BCE, then Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE; Micronesia is settled from the Philippines and from Melanesia; the dingo arrives in Australia. After a long pause East Polynesia is settled in a burst from about 1000 CE: the Society Islands, Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa last, about 1280; Polynesians reach South America and bring back the sweet potato.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108 (East Polynesian chronology); Ioannidis et al. 2020, Nature 583 (contact with the Americas)

value: exploring: each region's eras follow the conventional periodization of its own historiography, so their boundaries differ from the world's and from each other's

changes.value: The Events pass, step 3: every region its own history. Each M49 region's lifecycle is opened into eras of its own periodization, the one its historians use, rather than the world's: Africa's Middle and Later Stone Age, herders and Pharaohs, iron and the Bantu expansion, kingdoms of gold and trade, the Atlantic era, colonial rule and independence; the Americas' Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Formative, Classic and Postclassic periods, conquest, independence and the century since 1914; Asia's from its archaic humans to its rise since 1945; Europe's from Neanderthal Europe to division and union; Oceania's from Sahul before people to the island nations; and Antarctica's three. The existing regional Events (the Natufian, Mesopotamian irrigation, the fall of the Han, the late Ming crisis and the Ming–Qing transition, the Taiping war, India's 1918 drought, India's democracy, the Great Leap and the famine, China's and India's reforms, the Great Famine of 1315, the Reformation, the Glorious Revolution, Britain's turn to coal, the Crimean war, Russia's emancipation, the Spanish conquest, the US Civil War, the Still Bay and Howiesons Poort toolkits, and the Americas' isolation) move into their region's eras.

upsert.boundary: Africa's own crops domesticated, about 3000 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Sorghum in the eastern Sahel, pearl millet in the western Sahel (by about 2500 BCE), African rice in the inner Niger delta, and yams and the oil palm at the forest's edge: crops that later carry farming across the continent and, sorghum and millet, to India.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the dates of sorghum and of African rice are uncertain
sources to check: Manning et al. 2011, Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (pearl millet); Fuller and Hildebrand, in The Oxford Handbook of African Archaeology (2013)

upsert.boundary: Akhenaten's worship of the Aten, about 1353 to 1336 BCE
upsert.description: The king closes the temples of Amun, builds a new capital at Amarna and has the sun-disc, the Aten, worshipped above all gods: the first known attempt to impose one god on a state, undone after his death.
provenance: sources to check: Hornung, Akhenaten and the Religion of Light (1999)

upsert.boundary: The kingdom of Aksum, about 100 to 940
upsert.description: From the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea, Aksum trades ivory and gold through the Red Sea with Rome, Arabia and India, mints its own coins from about 270, raises great stelae and conquers Meroë; a Persian writer of the third century counts it among the four great kingdoms of the world.
provenance: sources to check: Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation (2012)

upsert.boundary: Ezana of Aksum becomes Christian, about 330
upsert.description: King Ezana's coins change from the crescent and disc to the cross; Ethiopia's church, linked to Alexandria, becomes one of the oldest continuous Christian churches.
provenance: sources to check: Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation (2012)

upsert.boundary: The Almohads, 1121 to 1269
upsert.description: A Berber reform movement from the High Atlas rules the Maghreb and al-Andalus; Averroes writes under them; defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) opens Spain to the Christian kingdoms.
provenance: sources to check: Bennison, The Almoravid and Almohad Empires (2016)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa; Southern Europe (Spain, Portugal)

upsert.boundary: The Almoravids, about 1040 to 1147
upsert.description: Saharan Berber reformers found Marrakesh (about 1070), conquer the Maghreb and, after the battle of Sagrajas (1086), al-Andalus, uniting both shores of the strait until the Almohads overthrow them.
provenance: sources to check: Bennison, The Almoravid and Almohad Empires (2016)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Morocco), Western Africa (Mauritania); Southern Europe (Spain)

upsert.boundary: The Arab conquest of North Africa, 640 to 709
upsert.description: Arab armies take Egypt (641), Libya and Ifriqiya, destroy Byzantine Carthage (698) and reach Morocco by about 709, against Berber resistance led by Kusaila and the queen called al-Kahina. Islam and Arabic spread over the following centuries, and Berber armies carry the conquest into Spain.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Bantu expansion, about 2500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Farmers speaking Bantu languages move out of the borderlands of Cameroon and Nigeria, through the rainforest to the Great Lakes by about 500 BCE, and on to the Limpopo and Natal by about 300 to 500 CE, with yams and oil palm, then cereals, cattle and iron. They absorb or displace most foragers. Some 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages today.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its routes are argued from languages, archaeology and genomes together
sources to check: Vansina 1995, Journal of African History 36; Grollemund et al. 2015, PNAS 112; Patin et al. 2017, Science 356
upsert.region: Africa: Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa, from Western Africa

upsert.boundary: Bantu-speaking farmers reach southern Africa, about 200 to 500
upsert.description: Iron-using farmers with sorghum, millet and cattle settle the eastern side of southern Africa to the Limpopo and Natal; Khoe herders and San foragers keep the drier west.
provenance: sources to check: Huffman, Handbook to the Iron Age (2007)

upsert.boundary: Oba Ewuare builds Benin into a kingdom and city, about 1440 to 1473
upsert.description: Ewuare rebuilds Benin City within great earthworks, expands the kingdom and the guilds of bronze-casters whose plaques and heads record its court; the kingdom lasts until Britain sacks the city in 1897.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates from oral tradition
sources to check: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995)

upsert.boundary: Shell beads in North Africa, about 150,000 to 82,000 years ago
upsert.description: Pierced Tritia shells, some coloured with ochre, at Bizmoune in Morocco (about 142,000 to 150,000 years old) and Taforalt (about 82,000): the oldest known ornaments, worn perhaps to show who belonged to whom.
provenance: sources to check: Sehasseh et al. 2021, Science Advances 7 (Bizmoune); Bouzouggar et al. 2007, PNAS 104 (Taforalt)

upsert.boundary: Ochre workshop, engravings and beads at Blombos Cave, about 100,000 to 72,000 years ago
upsert.description: A kit for mixing ochre paint in abalone shells (about 100,000 years ago), ochre slabs engraved with cross-hatching and shell beads (about 75,000), and the oldest known drawing, a cross-hatched line in ochre (about 73,000): symbolic culture in southern Africa long before the dispersal.
provenance: sources to check: Henshilwood et al. 2002, Science 295; Henshilwood et al. 2011, Science 334; Henshilwood et al. 2018, Nature 562

upsert.boundary: A San-like toolkit at Border Cave, about 44,000 years ago
upsert.description: Digging-stick weights, a poison applicator, beeswax hafting, bone arrowheads and ostrich-eggshell beads like those San foragers used in the twentieth century: a way of life that lasted more than forty thousand years.
provenance: sources to check: d'Errico et al. 2012, PNAS 109

upsert.boundary: Camels make the Sahara crossable, about 100 BCE to 300 CE
upsert.description: Dromedaries, spreading west from Egypt and the Horn, let traders cross the desert in caravans, which later carry the gold trade.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the timing is uncertain
sources to check: Bulliet, The Camel and the Wheel (1975)

upsert.boundary: Carthage, from its founding about 814 BCE to its destruction in 146 BCE
upsert.description: A Phoenician colony becomes the naval and trading power of the western Mediterranean, ruling Sicily, Sardinia and southern Spain; in three wars with Rome (264 to 146 BCE), Hannibal's among them, it loses everything, and Rome razes the city.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the founding date is traditional
sources to check: Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Tunisia); Southern Europe (Sicily, Sardinia, Spain)

upsert.boundary: Christian monasticism in the Egyptian desert, about 270 to 451
upsert.description: Antony withdraws to the desert and Pachomius founds the first communal monasteries (about 320); the practice spreads to Syria, Byzantium and the West. At Chalcedon (451) Egypt's church parts from Rome and Constantinople, becoming the Coptic church.
provenance: sources to check: Brown, The Rise of Western Christendom (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Early Homo sapiens across Africa, about 300,000 to 230,000 years ago
upsert.description: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (about 315,000 years old, just before this account's span), Florisbad in South Africa (about 260,000) and Omo Kibish in Ethiopia (about 233,000) show modern faces with longer, lower braincases, at three corners of the continent. The species formed across Africa as a web of populations that split and rejoined, not in one valley.
provenance: inferred: fossil ages as recalled, each uncertain by tens of thousands of years
sources to check: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546; Grun et al. 1996, Nature 382 (Florisbad); Vidal et al. 2022, Nature 601 (Omo Kibish)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Morocco), Southern Africa, Eastern Africa (Ethiopia)

upsert.boundary: Egypt unified under its first kings, about 3100 BCE
upsert.description: Rulers from Upper Egypt, remembered as Narmer and Menes, unite the Nile valley and delta under one crown, with a capital at Memphis, a court, taxes and hieroglyphic writing: one of the first states.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; radiocarbon places it about 3200 to 3000 BCE
sources to check: Dee et al. 2013, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 469; Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Fatimid caliphate, 909 to 1171
upsert.description: Ismaili Shi'ite caliphs rise in Ifriqiya, conquer Egypt (969), found Cairo and the al-Azhar mosque, and rule as rivals of Baghdad's Abbasids until Saladin ends the dynasty.
provenance: sources to check: Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa; Western Asia (Syria, the Hejaz)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's First Intermediate Period, about 2181 to 2055 BCE
upsert.description: Central rule fails and provincial governors rule for themselves; texts speak of low Nile floods and famine. Rulers from Thebes reunite the country.
provenance: sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

upsert.boundary: The empire of Ghana (Wagadu), about 700 to 1200
upsert.description: Soninke kings between the Senegal and Niger rivers tax the gold that comes from Bambuk to the desert's edge; Arab writers describe it from about 770, and al-Bakri in 1068 describes its twin capital, one of whose towns is probably Koumbi Saleh. It weakens after the Almoravid wars and is absorbed by Mali.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its origins may be centuries earlier
sources to check: Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)

upsert.boundary: Great Zimbabwe, about 1220 to 1450
upsert.description: A Shona capital of dry-stone walls and towers, with perhaps 10,000 or more people at its height, controls the gold of the plateau and trades it through Sofala and Kilwa; it declines as trade moves north to Mutapa.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; colonial-era claims of foreign builders are long refuted
sources to check: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture (2001)

upsert.boundary: Fishers and hunters of the green Sahara, about 9000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: Communities along the Sahara's lakes and rivers fish with bone harpoons, make wavy-line pottery and bury their dead in cemeteries such as Gobero in Niger and early Khartoum: a settled foraging life that the drying later ends.
provenance: sources to check: Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE 3 (Gobero)

upsert.boundary: Herding spreads across the Sahara and into the Sahel, about 5000 to 2500 BCE
upsert.description: Cattle, sheep and goat herders move across the Sahara; as it dries after about 4000 BCE they follow the retreating grass south into the Sahel and east to the Nile.
provenance: sources to check: Marshall and Hildebrand 2002, Journal of World Prehistory 16

upsert.boundary: Ibn Battuta's travels, 1325 to 1354
upsert.description: A scholar from Tangier travels about 120,000 kilometres through the Islamic world and beyond, from Mecca to India, China, the Swahili coast and Mali, and dictates the Rihla: a portrait of a connected Afro-Eurasia before and during the Black Death.
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta (1986)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Morocco), Western Africa (Mali), Eastern Africa; Asia; Southern Europe (al-Andalus)

upsert.boundary: Ibn Khaldun writes the Muqaddimah, 1377
upsert.description: In Algeria the Tunisian scholar writes an introduction to history that explains the rise and fall of dynasties by group solidarity, taxation and the life of cities, an early theory of how societies change.
provenance: sources to check: Irwin, Ibn Khaldun: An Intellectual Biography (2018)

upsert.boundary: Ife's bronze and terracotta heads, about 1100 to 1450
upsert.description: The Yoruba city of Ile-Ife, sacred as the place of creation, casts naturalistic heads in copper alloy and terracotta of a skill that astonished the Europeans who first saw them in 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Blier, Art and Risk in Ancient Yoruba (2015)

upsert.boundary: The bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu, about 850 to 950
upsert.description: Intricate cast bronzes, beads from as far as Egypt or India, and a burial of a titled man in south-eastern Nigeria show wealth, craft and long-distance trade in the forest centuries before Benin.
provenance: sources to check: Shaw, Unearthing Igbo-Ukwu (1977)

upsert.boundary: The Ishango bone, about 20,000 to 25,000 years ago
upsert.description: A baboon fibula from the upper Semliki in the Congo, notched in groups that some read as counting or a lunar record: one of the oldest objects that may hold numbers.
provenance: exploring: its date and its reading as numbers are both contested
sources to check: Brooks and Smith 1987, African Archaeological Review 5
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo)

upsert.boundary: Kanem and Bornu, about 700 to 1893
upsert.description: The Sayfawa kings rule around Lake Chad for about a thousand years, Muslim from about 1085, trading captives and horses across the Sahara to Libya; Bornu's musketeers make it a power in the 1500s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the dynasty's start is traditional
sources to check: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Chad), Western Africa (Nigeria, Niger)

upsert.boundary: The kingdom of Kerma in Nubia, about 2500 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Africa's first state south of Egypt rules the middle Nile from its capital at Kerma, with great mud-brick temples and royal tombs with hundreds of sacrificed retainers, until Egypt's New Kingdom conquers it.
provenance: sources to check: Bonnet, The Black Kingdom of the Nile (2019)

upsert.boundary: The Khoe-San lineages branch off, about 300,000 to 200,000 years ago, as genomes date it
upsert.description: The ancestors of the Khoe and San peoples of southern Africa separate from the lineages that lead to all other living people, the deepest split among living humans. Later mixing blurs it, and the date depends on the mutation rate assumed.
provenance: exploring: genomic divergence dates as recalled, from about 350,000 to 200,000 years by method
sources to check: Schlebusch et al. 2017, Science 358; Ragsdale et al. 2023, Nature 617 (weakly structured stem)

upsert.boundary: The kingdom of Kongo, about 1390 to 1914
upsert.description: A kingdom south of the lower Congo river with its capital at Mbanza Kongo; its king Nzinga a Nkuwu is baptized in 1491 and his son Afonso I makes Kongo a Christian kingdom that writes to Lisbon and Rome. The slave trade, Portuguese Angola and the defeat at Mbwila (1665) break it into rival lines; it is absorbed into Portuguese Angola in 1914.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the founding date is traditional
sources to check: Thornton, A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)

upsert.boundary: Kush rules Egypt as its twenty-fifth dynasty, about 747 to 656 BCE
upsert.description: Kings from Napata on the middle Nile, Piye and Taharqa among them, conquer and rule Egypt and revive its old styles, until Assyria drives them south; they keep building pyramids at el-Kurru and Nuri.
provenance: sources to check: Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000)

upsert.boundary: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, about 1181 to 1221
upsert.description: Under the Zagwe king Lalibela, eleven churches are carved down into the volcanic rock as a New Jerusalem, at a time when Jerusalem itself had fallen to Saladin.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the churches may have been cut over a longer span
sources to check: Phillipson, Ancient Churches of Ethiopia (2009)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers from Borneo settle Madagascar, about 500 to 900
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking seafarers from south-east Borneo reach the uninhabited island and later mix with Bantu-speaking Africans: Malagasy is an Austronesian language, and Malagasy genomes are about half Asian and half African.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; earlier human traces on the island are debated
sources to check: Pierron et al. 2017, PNAS 114; Adelaar, in The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar (2005)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Madagascar); from South-eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The empire of Mali, about 1235 to 1460
upsert.description: Sundiata Keita's victory at Kirina (about 1235) founds an empire that controls the gold of Bambuk and Bure and the cities of the Niger, Timbuktu and Djenné among them, larger than any in western Europe of its time; it declines after about 1400 as Songhay and the Tuareg take its towns.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the epic of Sundiata is oral tradition
sources to check: Gomez, African Dominion (2018); Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)

upsert.boundary: The Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria, 1250 to 1517
upsert.description: Slave soldiers seize power in Cairo, stop the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260), expel the last Crusaders (1291) and rule Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz, with Cairo the largest city west of China, until the Ottomans conquer them.
provenance: sources to check: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Egypt); Western Asia (Syria, the Hejaz)

upsert.boundary: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca, 1324 to 1325
upsert.description: Mali's king crosses the Sahara with thousands of followers and so much gold that its value falls in Cairo for years; Mali appears on European maps, the Catalan Atlas (1375) showing him holding a gold nugget, and scholars and architects return with him.
provenance: inferred: as recalled from al-Umari's account
sources to check: Levtzion and Hopkins (eds.), Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (Mali), Northern Africa (Egypt); Western Asia (Mecca)

upsert.boundary: Mapungubwe, southern Africa's first state, about 1075 to 1220
upsert.description: On a hill at the Limpopo, rulers set apart from commoners trade gold and ivory to the coast for glass beads; the gold rhinoceros from its royal graves is its emblem. Its people move north as the climate dries, and Great Zimbabwe takes its place.
provenance: sources to check: Huffman 2009, Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 28

upsert.boundary: The kingdom of Meroë, about 300 BCE to 350 CE
upsert.description: Kush's southern capital becomes a centre of iron smelting and trade with its own script (still undeciphered) and powerful queens, the Kandakes, until it declines and Aksum overruns it.
provenance: sources to check: Edwards, The Nubian Past (2004)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's Middle Kingdom, about 2055 to 1650 BCE
upsert.description: Theban kings reunite Egypt, reclaim the Faiyum, fortify Nubia's cataracts and write the classics of Egyptian literature; the Hyksos from the Levant then rule the delta.
provenance: sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Mutapa state, about 1430 to 1760
upsert.description: Shona rulers north of Great Zimbabwe control the gold trade to the Zambezi; the Portuguese trade with, fight and finally dominate them in the 1600s before the Rozvi take the plateau.
provenance: sources to check: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture (2001)

upsert.boundary: The Naqada culture and the making of Upper Egypt, about 4000 to 3150 BCE
upsert.description: Farming villages along the upper Nile grow into chiefdoms with elite tombs at Hierakonpolis, Naqada and Abydos; at Abydos tomb U-j (about 3250 BCE) holds labels with the earliest Egyptian signs.
provenance: sources to check: Wengrow, The Archaeology of Early Egypt (2006)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's New Kingdom empire, about 1550 to 1070 BCE
upsert.description: Theban kings expel the Hyksos and build an empire from Nubia to Syria: Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II, who fights the Hittites at Kadesh (1274 BCE) and later makes the first known peace treaty with them. The empire fades with the Bronze Age collapse.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; regnal dates conventional
sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Egypt, Sudan); Western Asia (the Levant)

upsert.boundary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, about 900 BCE to 1 CE
upsert.description: Farmers on the Jos plateau make life-size terracotta heads and figures, the oldest large sculpture south of the Sahara, and smelt iron from about 500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Breunig and Rupp 2016, Journal of African Archaeology 14

upsert.boundary: Egypt's Old Kingdom and the pyramids, about 2686 to 2181 BCE
upsert.description: Kings of a strong central state build the step pyramid of Djoser and the pyramids of Giza (about 2560 BCE), organizing tens of thousands of workers with rations, scribes and boats; Egypt has perhaps one to two million people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; regnal dates conventional
sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

upsert.boundary: Ostrich-eggshell beads exchanged across eastern and southern Africa, about 50,000 to 33,000 years ago
upsert.description: Bead styles shared over about 3,000 kilometres show that groups in eastern and southern Africa were linked by exchange, as San hxaro gift-giving later linked camps; the link breaks after about 33,000 years ago as climate shifts the rains.
provenance: sources to check: Miller and Wang 2022, Nature 601

upsert.boundary: Herders reach East Africa, about 3000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Herders from the north build monumental pillar cemeteries around Lake Turkana (about 3000 to 2400 BCE) and spread into the highlands of Kenya and Tanzania; genomes show them mixing with local foragers.
provenance: sources to check: Hildebrand et al. 2018, PNAS 115 (Lothagam North); Prendergast et al. 2019, Science 365

upsert.boundary: Shellfish and ochre at Pinnacle Point, about 164,000 years ago
upsert.description: In a cave on South Africa's south coast, people living through the cold of the penultimate glacial collect shellfish and use ground ochre: the oldest known systematic use of the sea's foods, on a coast that may have been a refuge for a shrunken population.
provenance: sources to check: Marean et al. 2007, Nature 449

upsert.boundary: Portugal explores Africa's Atlantic coast, 1415 to 1488
upsert.description: Portugal takes Ceuta (1415), passes Cape Bojador (1434), ships the first African captives to Lisbon (1441 to 1444), trades gold at Elmina (1482) and reaches Kongo (1483); Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope (1488). The sea route bypasses the Sahara's caravans.
provenance: sources to check: Russell, Prince Henry 'the Navigator' (2000)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern, Western, Middle and Southern Africa; Southern Europe (Portugal)

upsert.boundary: Greek Egypt: Alexander and the Ptolemies, 332 to 30 BCE
upsert.description: Alexander takes Egypt and founds Alexandria; his general Ptolemy's dynasty rules for three centuries from it, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse the centre of Greek learning, until Cleopatra's defeat makes Egypt Roman.
provenance: sources to check: Manning, The Last Pharaohs (2010)

upsert.boundary: The rock art of the central Sahara, about 8000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: At Tassili n'Ajjer and the Acacus, painted and engraved scenes record wild animals, 'round-head' figures, then cattle herds and herders' camps, and at last horses and chariots: a picture of the green Sahara and its drying.
provenance: exploring: rock-art dating is mostly by style and is uncertain
sources to check: di Lernia and Gallinaro, in The Oxford Handbook of African Archaeology (2013)

upsert.boundary: Egypt and North Africa under Rome and Byzantium, 30 BCE to 641
upsert.description: Egypt and the province of Africa ship grain to Rome and later Constantinople; Christianity spreads early and deep, from Alexandria's theologians to Augustine of Hippo; the Vandals take the Maghreb's coast for a century; the Arab conquest ends Roman rule.
provenance: sources to check: Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993)

upsert.boundary: Cattle herding in the eastern Sahara, about 6500 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: At Nabta Playa and elsewhere in Egypt's Western Desert people keep cattle, with sheep and goats from south-west Asia; whether Africans also tamed local aurochs is debated. Cattle become wealth, ritual and food across the green Sahara.
provenance: exploring: an earlier, independent domestication about 9000 BCE is argued but not accepted
sources to check: Wendorf and Schild 1998, Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 17; Pfeiffer et al. on cattle genomes

upsert.boundary: The trans-Saharan gold trade, about 750 to 1600
upsert.description: Caravans of thousands of camels carry West African gold, the main source of gold for the Mediterranean and the Islamic world for centuries, north to Sijilmasa, Tunis and Cairo, with ivory and captives; salt, copper, cloth, horses, books and Islam go south.
provenance: sources to check: Gomez, African Dominion (2018); Austen, Trans-Saharan Africa in World History (2010)

upsert.boundary: Africa's first pottery, at Ounjougou in Mali, about 9400 BCE
upsert.description: Hunters and gatherers in the green Sahara's south make pots to cook and store wild grasses, independently of the pottery of East Asia.
provenance: sources to check: Huysecom et al. 2009, Antiquity 83

upsert.boundary: The Solomonic dynasty takes Ethiopia's throne, 1270
upsert.description: Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe and claims descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a claim told in the Kebra Nagast; his line rules, with interruptions, until 1974.
provenance: sources to check: Marcus, A History of Ethiopia (1994)

upsert.boundary: The Songhay empire, 1464 to 1591
upsert.description: Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu (1468) and Djenné; Askia Muhammad makes Songhay the largest empire in West African history, with Timbuktu a centre of Islamic scholarship, until a Moroccan army with firearms wins at Tondibi (1591).
provenance: sources to check: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire (1999)

upsert.boundary: The Swahili coast's towns, about 800 to 1500
upsert.description: Bantu-speaking traders build towns of coral stone along the coast from Mogadishu to Sofala, Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu and Zanzibar among them; Muslim since the 9th to 12th centuries, they trade the interior's gold, ivory and captives across the Indian Ocean for Indian cloth and Chinese porcelain, and speak Kiswahili.
provenance: sources to check: Horton and Middleton, The Swahili (2000); Brielle et al. 2023, Nature 615 (Swahili genomes)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Somalia)

upsert.boundary: The Vandal kingdom in Africa, 429 to 534
upsert.description: Vandals and Alans cross from Spain, take Carthage (439) and rule Roman Africa as a naval power that sacks Rome in 455, until Justinian's army destroys them.
provenance: sources to check: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)

upsert.boundary: Iron smelting begins in West and Central Africa, about 800 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: Furnaces at Taruga and Nok in Nigeria, in Cameroon, and at Urewe sites around Lake Victoria smelt iron, perhaps invented in Africa, perhaps learned from the north; iron hoes and axes later open the forests and savannas to farming.
provenance: exploring: whether African iron-working was invented independently is debated
sources to check: Alpern 2005, History in Africa 32; Holl 2009, Journal of World Prehistory 22
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle and Eastern Africa

upsert.boundary: The African Humid Period, about 12,500 to 6,000 years ago
upsert.description: As northern summer sunlight peaks, the monsoon moves north: the Sahara and Arabia become grassland and savanna with lakes as large as Mega-Chad, and hippos, crocodiles, fishers and later herders live where there is now desert. It ends as the monsoon retreats again (ev.aridification).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its end was abrupt in some places and gradual in others
sources to check: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews 19; Kuper and Kröpelin 2006, Science 313
upsert.region: Northern, Western and Eastern Africa; Western Asia (Arabia)

upsert.boundary: The 4.2-kiloyear drought, about 2200 to 1900 BCE
upsert.description: A centuries-long dry spell in the Mediterranean, south-west Asia and South Asia, seen in lake, cave and sea records. Whether it brought down Akkad, Egypt's Old Kingdom and the Indus cities, or only strained them, is debated.
provenance: exploring: its extent and its effects on states are contested
sources to check: Weiss et al. 1993, Science 261; Staubwasser and Weiss 2006, Quaternary Research 66; Middleton 2018, Journal of Archaeological Research 26
upsert.region: Northern Africa; Western and Southern Asia; Southern Europe

changes.value: Africa's own history to 1500, filled inside its eras from the long to the short: the Middle Stone Age's signs of symbolic culture, the Later Stone Age's exchange networks, the green Sahara and its herders, Egypt from the Naqada chiefdoms to the New Kingdom, Kerma and Kush, the domestication of Africa's own crops, the Bantu expansion, iron, Carthage, Meroë, Aksum, the camel and the gold trade of the Sahara, the Arab conquest of the north, and the kingdoms and towns of 500 to 1500 from Ghana and the Swahili coast to Great Zimbabwe, Mali, Benin and Kongo. Two Events of the Earth come with them: the African Humid Period and the drought of about 2200 BCE. Each is placed in its M49 region and subregion, filed by dimension with a Realization, contained in the era or longer Event it is part of, and linked to what it led to.
