upsert.boundary: The Adal–Ethiopian war, 1529 to 1543
upsert.description: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of Adal, with Ottoman muskets, conquers most of the Christian highlands; Portuguese musketeers help Ethiopia defeat and kill him at Wayna Daga (1543). Oromo migrations then reshape the highlands.
provenance: sources to check: Marcus, A History of Ethiopia (1994)

upsert.boundary: Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa, March 1896
upsert.description: Menelik II's army of about 100,000 destroys an Italian invading force, the greatest defeat of a European army in Africa; Ethiopia stays independent and becomes a symbol for African and diaspora nationalists.
provenance: sources to check: Jonas, The Battle of Adwa (2011)

upsert.boundary: The African Continental Free Trade Area, from 2021
upsert.description: Trading begins under an agreement signed by 54 of the 55 African Union states to remove most tariffs between them, where trade among African countries is a small share of their trade.
provenance: sources to check: African Union, AfCFTA Secretariat

upsert.boundary: France conquers Algeria, 1830 to 1847
upsert.description: France takes Algiers (1830) and, against Abd al-Qadir's long resistance, the interior by 1847, with razzias, burned villages and famine; settlers follow, and Algeria becomes part of France.
provenance: sources to check: McDougall, A History of Algeria (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Algerian war of independence, 1954 to 1962
upsert.description: The FLN's insurrection against French rule and a million settlers; torture, massacres and some two million Algerians moved into camps; perhaps 300,000 or more Algerians die. Independence (1962) is followed by the flight of the settlers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is contested, from about 300,000 to over a million
sources to check: Horne, A Savage War of Peace (1977); Evans, Algeria: France's Undeclared War (2012)

upsert.boundary: Angola's civil war, 1975 to 2002
upsert.description: The MPLA government, backed by Cuba and the Soviet Union, fights UNITA, backed by South Africa and the United States; the battle of Cuito Cuanavale (1987 to 1988) leads to Namibia's independence; the war ends with Savimbi's death. Perhaps half a million die.
provenance: sources to check: Gleijeses, Visions of Freedom (2013)

upsert.boundary: Apartheid in South Africa, 1948 to 1994
upsert.description: The National Party classifies every person by race and separates them by law: pass laws, forced removals of about 3.5 million people, homelands, Bantu education, and the banning of the ANC and PAC after Sharpeville (1960). Resistance, sanctions and economic decline bring negotiations from 1990.
provenance: sources to check: Clark and Worger, South Africa: The Rise and Fall of Apartheid (3rd ed. 2016)

upsert.boundary: The Arab Spring, December 2010 to 2012
upsert.description: A street vendor's self-immolation in Tunisia sets off protests that topple Ben Ali (January 2011) and Mubarak (February 2011) and start wars in Libya, Syria and Yemen; only Tunisia keeps a democracy, and it too reverts after 2021.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The New Arab Wars (2016)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Tunisia, Egypt, Libya); Western Asia (Syria, Yemen, Bahrain)

upsert.boundary: The Asante empire, 1701 to 1901
upsert.description: Osei Tutu and the priest Okomfo Anokye unite the Akan states under the Golden Stool; Asante grows rich on gold, kola and captives and rules most of modern Ghana, until Britain annexes it after the War of the Golden Stool (1900).
provenance: sources to check: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

upsert.boundary: Britain sacks Benin City, 1897
upsert.description: A punitive expedition burns Benin City, exiles the oba and carries off thousands of bronzes and ivories to London, now argued over in claims for their return.
provenance: sources to check: Hicks, The Brutish Museums (2020)

upsert.boundary: The Berlin conference, November 1884 to February 1885
upsert.description: Fourteen states, no African among them, agree how claims to African coasts will be recognized and give the Congo basin to King Leopold's association.
provenance: sources to check: Förster, Mommsen and Robinson (eds.), Bismarck, Europe and Africa (1988)

upsert.boundary: The Nigerian civil war, 1967 to 1970
upsert.description: The Eastern Region secedes as Biafra after massacres of Igbo in the north; the federal blockade starves the enclave, and about one to three million die, most of hunger, before Biafra surrenders.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Heerten, The Biafran War and Postcolonial Humanitarianism (2017)

upsert.boundary: The South African War, 1899 to 1902
upsert.description: Britain conquers the Boer republics of the Transvaal and Orange Free State and their gold; about 26,000 Boer women and children and at least 20,000 Black Africans die in British camps. The peace leaves Black South Africans' rights to the white settlers.
provenance: sources to check: Nasson, The South African War 1899–1902 (1999)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch Cape Colony, 1652 to 1806
upsert.description: The Dutch East India Company's supply station at the Cape grows into a colony of settlers and enslaved people from Asia and Africa; the Khoekhoe lose their land and, in the smallpox of 1713, most of their people; trekboer herders push the frontier east until it meets the Xhosa. Britain takes the colony in 1806.
provenance: sources to check: Ross, A Concise History of South Africa (2nd ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Cash crops, mines and migrant labour: the colonial economy, about 1900 to 1950
upsert.description: Railways from ports to mines and plantations; head and hut taxes payable in coin push men into wage work far from home; the Gold Coast becomes the world's largest cocoa grower by 1911, Nigeria and Senegal export groundnuts, the Copperbelt opens in the 1920s; forced labour persists in many colonies into the 1940s.
provenance: sources to check: Austin, African Economic History (1987, 2nd ed.); Frankema and van Waijenburg 2012, Journal of Economic History 72
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa

upsert.boundary: The Congo crisis, 1960 to 1965
upsert.description: The army mutinies days after independence, Katanga secedes, Prime Minister Lumumba is overthrown and murdered (1961) with Belgian and American complicity, UN troops intervene, and Mobutu takes power in 1965 to rule for 32 years.
provenance: sources to check: Reybrouck, Congo: The Epic History of a People (2014)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo)

upsert.boundary: Leopold II's Congo Free State, 1885 to 1908
upsert.description: The Belgian king rules the Congo basin as his own property; to meet rubber quotas his agents and the Force Publique take hostages, burn villages and cut off hands. Violence, flight, famine and sleeping sickness kill perhaps millions; an international campaign forces Belgium to annex it (1908).
provenance: exploring: the death toll is contested; Hochschild's ten million is not well founded, and demographers give wide ranges
sources to check: Hochschild, King Leopold's Ghost (1998); Vansina, Being Colonized (2010)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo)

upsert.boundary: The Congo wars, 1996 to 2003
upsert.description: Rwanda and Uganda invade to pursue the génocidaires and overthrow Mobutu (1997); in the second war, from 1998, nine African states and many militias fight over the Congo and its minerals. Excess deaths are counted in millions, mostly from disease and hunger, though the highest estimates are disputed.
provenance: exploring: the International Rescue Committee's 5.4 million excess deaths to 2007 is contested by the Human Security Report
sources to check: Prunier, Africa's World War (2009); Stearns, Dancing in the Glory of Monsters (2011)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo), Eastern Africa (Rwanda, Uganda)

upsert.boundary: Dahomey takes the slave ports of Allada and Ouidah, 1724 to 1727
upsert.description: King Agaja conquers the coast so that Dahomey, not its neighbours, sells captives to European ships; the kingdom, with its army of women soldiers, remains a major supplier until the trade's end and falls to France in 1894.

upsert.boundary: The war in Darfur, 2003 to 2010
upsert.description: The Sudanese government and Janjaweed militias answer a rebellion with massacres of Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa villagers; perhaps 200,000 to 300,000 die and two million flee.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Flint and de Waal, Darfur: A New History of a Long War (2008)

upsert.boundary: Africa's share of humanity falls from 12% to 8%, 1750 to 1910
upsert.description: Africa holds about an eighth of humanity from 1500 to 1750, then falls to about 8% by 1890 to 1910, its lowest. The slave trades remove millions of young people at their peak, wars of capture and colonial conquest kill more, rinderpest and sleeping sickness follow; and the denominator grows, as Europe's and the Americas' numbers rise fast. Africa's share turns upward only after about 1920.
provenance: inferred: shares from this model's h.region-africa, built on Our World in Data's country populations; Africa's numbers before 1900 are poorly known (Durand's and McEvedy's ranges differ widely)
sources to check: Manning, Slavery and African Life (1990); Our World in Data, population by world region; Frankema and Jerven 2014, Economic History Review 67 (African population 1850–1960)

upsert.boundary: The Derg and Ethiopia's wars, 1974 to 1991
upsert.description: A Marxist military council deposes Haile Selassie, wages the Red Terror, fights Somalia (1977 to 1978) and Eritrean and Tigrayan rebels, and falls in 1991; Eritrea becomes independent in 1993.
provenance: sources to check: Tareke, The Ethiopian Revolution: War in the Horn of Africa (2009)

upsert.boundary: The West African Ebola epidemic, 2013 to 2016
upsert.description: The largest Ebola outbreak known infects about 28,600 people in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone and kills about 11,300, overwhelming health systems already weakened by war.
provenance: sources to check: WHO, Ebola Situation Report, 10 June 2016
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's revolution of 1919 and independence, 1919 to 1922
upsert.description: Mass protests against British rule after the exile of Saad Zaghlul lead Britain to declare Egypt independent in 1922, keeping control of defence and the canal.
provenance: sources to check: Fahmy, Ordinary Egyptians (2011)

upsert.boundary: Apartheid ends, 1990 to 1994
upsert.description: F.W. de Klerk unbans the ANC and frees Nelson Mandela (February 1990); after negotiations and violence, South Africans of every race vote in April 1994 and Mandela becomes president.
provenance: sources to check: Sparks, Tomorrow Is Another Country (1995)

upsert.boundary: Ethiopia's famine, 1983 to 1985
upsert.description: Drought, war and the government's grain policies and resettlement kill perhaps 400,000 to a million in the north; televised pictures bring the largest relief effort of its time.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: de Waal, Evil Days (Africa Watch, 1991)

upsert.boundary: Italy invades and occupies Ethiopia, 1935 to 1941
upsert.description: Mussolini's army, using poison gas, conquers Ethiopia (1936); the League of Nations' sanctions fail; British and Ethiopian forces restore Haile Selassie in 1941.
provenance: sources to check: Mockler, Haile Selassie's War (1984)

upsert.boundary: Ghana becomes independent, March 1957
upsert.description: Kwame Nkrumah's Gold Coast becomes Ghana, the first colony south of the Sahara to win independence, and its capital Accra hosts the pan-African conferences that follow.
provenance: sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: Africa's growth and cities after 2000
upsert.description: Commodity prices, debt relief, peace in Angola, Mozambique and Sierra Leone, and mobile phones lift growth to about 5% a year; Lagos, Kinshasa, Luanda and Addis Ababa grow fast. The share of Africans in extreme poverty falls, but their number rises, so by 2025 most of the world's extreme poor live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024

upsert.boundary: The genocide of the Herero and Nama, 1904 to 1908
upsert.description: After the Herero and Nama rise against German South West Africa, General von Trotha orders the Herero driven into the desert; perhaps 80% of the Herero and half of the Nama die in the desert and in camps. Germany acknowledged it as genocide in 2021.
provenance: sources to check: Olusoga and Erichsen, The Kaiser's Holocaust (2010)

upsert.boundary: Liberia founded and independent, 1822 to 1847
upsert.description: The American Colonization Society settles freed Black Americans at Monrovia (1822); Liberia declares independence in 1847, ruled by the settlers' descendants over the indigenous majority.
provenance: sources to check: Clegg, The Price of Liberty (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Mahdist state in Sudan, 1881 to 1898
upsert.description: Muhammad Ahmad proclaims himself the Mahdi, defeats Egyptian armies and takes Khartoum (1885); his successor rules until Kitchener's army, with machine guns, kills about 10,000 at Omdurman in a morning (1898).
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The Mahdist State in the Sudan (2nd ed. 1970)

upsert.boundary: The Maji Maji war in German East Africa, 1905 to 1907
upsert.description: Peoples of southern Tanzania rise against forced cotton growing, trusting a sacred water to turn bullets; German scorched-earth tactics and the famine after them kill perhaps 100,000 to 300,000.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Iliffe, A Modern History of Tanganyika (1979)

upsert.boundary: The Mau Mau war in Kenya, 1952 to 1960
upsert.description: Kikuyu fighters rise over land taken by settlers; Britain declares an emergency, hangs over a thousand, and detains perhaps 80,000 or more in camps where many are tortured. Kenya becomes independent in 1963.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; detention numbers are debated
sources to check: Anderson, Histories of the Hanged (2005); Elkins, Imperial Reckoning (2005)

upsert.boundary: Portugal defeats Kongo at Mbwila, 1665
upsert.description: Portuguese Angola's army kills Kongo's king António I; rival claimants fight over the kingdom for forty years, and the wars feed the slave trade.
provenance: sources to check: Thornton, A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)

upsert.boundary: Diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand, 1867 to 1899
upsert.description: Diamonds found in 1867 and the world's richest gold reef in 1886 turn southern Africa into a mining economy: Johannesburg grows from nothing to 100,000 people in a decade, migrant workers from across the region live in compounds under pass laws, and by the late 1890s the Rand produces about a quarter of the world's gold.
provenance: sources to check: Feinstein, An Economic History of South Africa (2005)

upsert.boundary: Mozambique's civil war, 1977 to 1992
upsert.description: RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and then South Africa, fights the FRELIMO government; about a million die, mostly of hunger, until the Rome accord (1992).
provenance: sources to check: Newitt, A History of Mozambique (1995)

upsert.boundary: Mobile money in Africa, from M-Pesa in 2007
upsert.description: Kenya's M-Pesa lets people send money by text message; within a decade most Kenyan households use it, and mobile money spreads across Africa ahead of the rest of the world.
provenance: sources to check: Suri and Jack 2016, Science 354
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Kenya), and across Sub-Saharan Africa

upsert.boundary: Muhammad Ali's Egypt, 1805 to 1848
upsert.description: An Ottoman officer seizes Egypt, destroys the Mamluks, builds a conscript army, state factories and a cotton economy, conquers Sudan and twice nearly topples the sultan; his dynasty rules until 1952.
provenance: sources to check: Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's revolution of 1952 and Nasser's rule, 1952 to 1970
upsert.description: Free Officers overthrow the king; Nasser nationalizes the Suez Canal (1956), survives the British, French and Israeli attack, builds the Aswan High Dam, redistributes land and leads Arab nationalism until the defeat of 1967.
provenance: sources to check: Gordon, Nasser's Blessed Movement (1992)

upsert.boundary: Queen Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba, 1624 to 1663
upsert.description: Njinga resists Portuguese Angola for four decades by war, diplomacy, alliance with the Dutch and her own trade in captives, and dies ruling an independent Matamba.
provenance: sources to check: Heywood, Njinga of Angola (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Organisation of African Unity, 1963, and the African Union, 2002
upsert.description: Independent states found the OAU at Addis Ababa, pledging to keep the colonial borders; it supports the liberation movements in the south, and in 2002 becomes the African Union, with a right to intervene against genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: The Ottomans take Egypt and the Maghreb's coast, 1517 to 1574
upsert.description: Selim I conquers Mamluk Egypt (1517); Ottoman corsair governors take Algiers, Tripoli and finally Tunis (1574). Morocco alone stays outside the empire.
provenance: sources to check: Abun-Nasr, A History of the Maghrib in the Islamic Period (1987)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria)

upsert.boundary: The Oyo empire at its height and its collapse, about 1650 to 1836
upsert.description: A Yoruba cavalry state rules the savanna between the forest and the Niger and sells captives through the coast; it breaks up in civil war and under the Sokoto jihad in the 1820s and 1830s, and the Yoruba wars that follow send many to Brazil and Cuba.
provenance: sources to check: Law, The Oyo Empire c.1600–c.1836 (1977)

upsert.boundary: Africa's share of humanity rises from 9% to 18.9%, 1950 to 2025
upsert.description: Africa's people grow from about 230 million in 1950 to about 1.5 billion in 2025: deaths fall with vaccines, antibiotics, cheaper food and clean water, while births fall later and more slowly than anywhere before them, from about 6.5 children per woman in 1950 to about 4 in 2025. Africa adds more than a fifth of the people added to the world since 1900, and most of them since 1980.
provenance: inferred: shares from this model's h.region-africa; numbers from UN World Population Prospects as recalled
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024; Bongaarts and Casterline 2013, Population and Development Review 38 (Africa's slow fertility decline)

upsert.boundary: The Portuguese colonies become independent, 1974 to 1975
upsert.description: After wars of liberation since 1961 and the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon, Guinea-Bissau, Cabo Verde, São Tomé, Mozambique and Angola become independent; Angola and Mozambique fall at once into civil wars fed by the Cold War and South Africa.
provenance: sources to check: Newitt, Portugal in Africa (1981)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Angola), Eastern Africa (Mozambique), Western Africa (Guinea-Bissau, Cabo Verde)

upsert.boundary: The rinderpest panzootic, 1888 to 1897
upsert.description: A cattle plague arriving with Italian army cattle in the Horn sweeps to the Cape, killing perhaps nine in ten cattle and many wild buffalo and antelope; herding peoples starve, Ethiopia's great famine of 1888 to 1892 kills perhaps a third of its people, and bush and tsetse fly spread over the empty grazing lands.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Ethiopian toll is uncertain
sources to check: Phoofolo 1993, Past and Present 138; Pankhurst, The Great Ethiopian Famine of 1888–1892 (1964)

upsert.boundary: The genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, April to July 1994
upsert.description: After the president's plane is shot down, Hutu Power militias and soldiers kill about 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about a hundred days, while the UN withdraws; the Rwandan Patriotic Front's victory ends it, and a million and more Hutu flee into the Congo.
provenance: sources to check: Des Forges, Leave None to Tell the Story (Human Rights Watch, 1999)

upsert.boundary: The Sahel drought and famine, 1968 to 1974
upsert.description: Years of failed rains across Mauritania, Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad kill herds and crops; perhaps 100,000 or more die, and the drought, later linked partly to aerosol pollution of the northern hemisphere, lasts into the 1980s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Giannini et al. 2003, Science 302 (Sahel drought and ocean temperatures)
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (the Sahel), Middle Africa (Chad)

upsert.boundary: Jihadist insurgencies in the Sahel and the Lake Chad basin, from 2009
upsert.description: Boko Haram's rising in north-east Nigeria (2009), the fall of northern Mali to Tuareg and jihadist rebels (2012) and the spread of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates across Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger; French and UN forces leave after coups from 2020.
provenance: sources to check: Thurston, Jihadists of North Africa and the Sahel (2020)
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (Nigeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger), Middle Africa (Chad, Cameroon)

upsert.boundary: The Scramble for Africa, 1881 to 1914
upsert.description: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain Egypt (1882); the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) sets rules for claiming the rest; with machine guns, quinine and African soldiers, Britain, France, Germany, Belgium's king, Portugal, Italy and Spain partition almost the whole continent by 1914. Peoples who had lived without states, perhaps a third or more of Africans, come under colonial governments.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the share of Africans living without states before conquest is a rough guess
sources to check: Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa (1991); Vansina, Being Colonized (2010)

upsert.boundary: The Sokoto caliphate, 1804 to 1903
upsert.description: Usman dan Fodio's jihad against the Hausa kings (1804 to 1808) founds the largest state in nineteenth-century West Africa, a federation of emirates that spreads Islamic learning and keeps a vast plantation slavery, until Britain conquers it.
provenance: sources to check: Last, The Sokoto Caliphate (1967); Lovejoy, Jihad in West Africa (2016)

upsert.boundary: The Soweto uprising, June 1976
upsert.description: Schoolchildren march against teaching in Afrikaans; police open fire, and protests spread across the country; hundreds die, and a generation of young activists joins the ANC in exile.
provenance: sources to check: Clark and Worger, South Africa: The Rise and Fall of Apartheid (3rd ed. 2016)

upsert.boundary: Debt and structural adjustment, 1980 to 2000
upsert.description: After the oil shocks and falling commodity prices, African states borrow, default and accept IMF and World Bank programmes that cut spending and open markets; income per person in Sub-Saharan Africa falls through the 1980s and early 1990s, and the period is remembered as lost decades.
provenance: sources to check: van de Walle, African Economies and the Politics of Permanent Crisis (2001)

upsert.boundary: Sudan's civil war, from April 2023
upsert.description: The army and the Rapid Support Forces fight for power; Khartoum is devastated, the RSF commits mass killings in Darfur, and by 2025 about twelve million people have fled their homes, the largest displacement in the world, with famine declared in parts of the country.
provenance: sources to check: UNHCR and OCHA Sudan updates 2025; IPC famine classification (2024)

upsert.boundary: The Suez Canal is built and opened, 1859 to 1869
upsert.description: Dug largely by Egyptian corvée labour, the canal joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and cuts the sea route from Britain to India by about 40%; the debts it and the khedive's projects leave lead to European control of Egypt's finances (1876) and British occupation (1882).
provenance: sources to check: Karabell, Parting the Desert (2003)

upsert.boundary: Tewodros II reunites Ethiopia, 1855 to 1868
upsert.description: A frontier warlord ends the Era of the Princes, reunites the highlands and tries to modernize the army; a British expedition storms Magdala and he kills himself (1868).
provenance: sources to check: Marcus, A History of Ethiopia (1994)

upsert.boundary: The Tigray war, November 2020 to November 2022
upsert.description: Ethiopia's federal army, with Eritrean troops and regional militias, fights the Tigray People's Liberation Front; siege, massacres and famine kill perhaps hundreds of thousands, one of the deadliest wars of the century so far.
provenance: exploring: the death toll is highly uncertain
sources to check: International Crisis Group reports; Ghent University estimates (2022)

upsert.boundary: Morocco defeats Songhay at Tondibi, 1591
upsert.description: Ahmad al-Mansur's army of a few thousand with arquebuses crosses the Sahara and routs Songhay's much larger army; Timbuktu falls, its scholars are deported, and the Sahel splits into smaller states.
provenance: sources to check: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire (1999)

upsert.boundary: The Union of South Africa and the Natives Land Act, 1910 to 1913
upsert.description: The four colonies unite as a self-governing dominion ruled by white men; the Land Act of 1913 confines African ownership to reserves of about 7% of the land.
provenance: sources to check: Ross, A Concise History of South Africa (2nd ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Britain occupies Egypt, 1882
upsert.description: Colonel Urabi's revolt against foreign control of Egypt's finances ends at Tel el-Kebir; Britain occupies Egypt, nominally for a short time, and stays until 1956.
provenance: sources to check: Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East (1993)

upsert.boundary: The First World War in Africa, 1914 to 1918
upsert.description: Allied forces take Togoland, Kamerun and South West Africa; in East Africa Lettow-Vorbeck's German force is chased for four years, and about a million African porters are conscripted, of whom perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 die of disease, hunger and exhaustion.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; carrier deaths are uncertain
sources to check: Paice, Tip and Run (2007); Strachan, The First World War in Africa (2004)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern, Western, Middle and Southern Africa

upsert.boundary: The Second World War in Africa, 1940 to 1943
upsert.description: British, Commonwealth and Free French forces defeat Italy in East Africa (1941) and, after the campaigns of the Western Desert and El Alamein (1942) and the Anglo-American landings, the Axis in North Africa (May 1943); hundreds of thousands of African soldiers serve, and colonial economies are mobilized for the war.
provenance: sources to check: Killingray, Fighting for Britain (2010)

upsert.boundary: The year of Africa, 1960
upsert.description: Seventeen countries become independent in one year, fourteen of them French colonies, with Nigeria and the Congo; by 1965 most of the continent is independent.
provenance: sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: Zanzibar's plantations and the East African slave and ivory trade, about 1820 to 1873
upsert.description: The Omani sultan moves his capital to Zanzibar (1840), which grows most of the world's cloves with enslaved labour; Swahili and Arab caravans push to the Great Lakes and the Congo for ivory and captives, until British pressure closes Zanzibar's slave market (1873).
provenance: sources to check: Sheriff, Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar (1987)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Tanzania), Middle Africa (eastern Congo)

upsert.boundary: The Zulu kingdom and the wars of the 1820s, 1816 to 1840
upsert.description: Shaka builds a centralized Zulu kingdom with regiments and short stabbing spears; the wars and migrations of the time (the Mfecane, a term historians now contest) form new states among the Ndebele, Sotho, Swazi and Gaza, and empty some areas that Boer trekkers then enter.
provenance: exploring: the scale and causes of the Mfecane are debated
sources to check: Hamilton (ed.), The Mfecane Aftermath (1995)
upsert.region: Africa: Southern Africa (South Africa, Lesotho, Eswatini)

upsert.boundary: The HIV/AIDS pandemic, from 1981
upsert.description: A virus that crossed from chimpanzees to people in central Africa, probably around Kinshasa in the 1920s, is recognized in 1981. It kills about 40 million people by 2025, two thirds of them in Sub-Saharan Africa, where life expectancy in southern Africa falls by ten years or more in the 1990s; antiretroviral drugs, widely available from about 2004, turn it into a chronic illness.
provenance: sources to check: UNAIDS Global AIDS Update 2024; Faria et al. 2014, Science 346 (origin in Kinshasa)
upsert.region: Africa (Eastern, Southern and Middle Africa above all); the Americas; Asia; Europe

changes.value: Africa's own history from 1500 to 2025: the Atlantic era's states and wars, the Cape Colony, the Sokoto caliphate, Muhammad Ali's Egypt, the Zulu kingdom, the conquest of Algeria, Zanzibar's slave economy, the Suez Canal and the mineral revolution; the Scramble and colonial rule, from the Congo Free State, rinderpest, Adwa and the genocide of the Herero and Nama to apartheid; and independent Africa, from Ghana to the Tigray and Sudan wars, with HIV/AIDS as a world Event located mostly here. Two Events name the measure they turn, Africa's share of humanity: its fall from 12% to 8% between 1750 and 1910, and its rise from 9% to 18.9% since 1950. The Scramble names the share of people living under a state, which it raises.

upsert.boundary: Potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas domesticated in the Andes, about 6000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Highland farmers domesticate the potato and quinoa and herd llamas and alpacas, the only large domestic animals of the Americas; coastal peoples grow cotton and squash and fish the rich Pacific upwelling.
provenance: sources to check: Pearsall, in Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Aztec Triple Alliance, 1428 to 1521
upsert.description: Mexica migrants found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco (1325); in 1428 they ally with Texcoco and Tlacopan and build a tribute empire over central Mexico. Tenochtitlan, with perhaps 200,000 people, is larger than any city in Spain when Cortés arrives.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012); Townsend, Fifth Sun (2019)

upsert.boundary: Cahokia and the Mississippian world, about 1050 to 1350
upsert.description: Near modern St Louis, maize farmers build a city of perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 around Monks Mound, the largest earthwork in the Americas; Mississippian chiefdoms spread across the south-east, many still living when Spanish expeditions arrive in the 1540s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Cahokia's population is debated

upsert.boundary: Caral and the Norte Chico, about 3000 to 1800 BCE
upsert.description: In the dry valleys north of Lima, people who fish, grow cotton and irrigate build pyramids, sunken plazas and towns; Caral is among the oldest cities of the Americas, as old as Egypt's pyramids, with no pottery and perhaps no war.
provenance: sources to check: Shady Solís et al. 2001, Science 292; Haas et al. 2004, Nature 432

upsert.boundary: Chaco Canyon and the Ancestral Puebloans, about 850 to 1150
upsert.description: In the desert of New Mexico, Ancestral Puebloans build great houses of several hundred rooms, straight roads and astronomical alignments, at the centre of a network that trades turquoise and macaws; drought ends it, and later Mesa Verde too is abandoned (about 1280).
provenance: sources to check: Lekson, The Chaco Meridian (2nd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: Chavín de Huántar, about 900 to 200 BCE
upsert.description: A temple in the Peruvian highlands, with underground galleries and carved jaguar-and-serpent gods, becomes a pilgrimage centre whose art style spreads along the Andes.
provenance: sources to check: Burger, Chavín and the Origins of Andean Civilization (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Chimú kingdom, about 900 to 1470
upsert.description: From its adobe capital Chan Chan, the largest city of the pre-Columbian Andes, Chimú rules the north coast of Peru with vast irrigation canals, until the Inca conquer it.
provenance: sources to check: Moseley and Cordy-Collins (eds.), The Northern Dynasties (1990)

upsert.boundary: The Classic Maya, about 250 to 900
upsert.description: Dozens of city-states, Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán and Caracol among them, ruled by divine kings who record their wars and dynasties in a full writing system and track time with the Long Count calendar; the lowlands hold perhaps several million people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; lidar surveys since 2018 suggest larger populations
sources to check: Martin and Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2nd ed. 2008); Canuto et al. 2018, Science 361
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, Belize, Honduras)

upsert.boundary: Clovis hunters, about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago
upsert.description: Fluted stone spear points made in the same way appear across North America within a few centuries, often with mammoth and mastodon kills; the Anzick child's genome links Clovis people to most later Native Americans.
provenance: sources to check: Waters and Stafford 2007, Science 315; Rasmussen et al. 2014, Nature 506
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America, Central America

upsert.boundary: The Haudenosaunee confederacy, by about 1450 to 1600
upsert.description: Five Iroquoian nations south of Lake Ontario unite under the Great Law of Peace, with a council of chiefs chosen by clan mothers; the confederacy becomes a major power of the colonial wars.
provenance: exploring: its founding date is debated, from about 1142 to about 1600
sources to check: Fenton, The Great Law and the Longhouse (1998)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (United States, Canada)

upsert.boundary: Adena and Hopewell, about 500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Peoples of the Ohio valley build burial mounds and great geometric earthworks and trade obsidian from the Rockies, copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf across half a continent.
provenance: sources to check: Milner, The Moundbuilders (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Inca empire, about 1438 to 1533
upsert.description: From Cusco, Pachacuti and his successors conquer the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile in under a century, ruling perhaps ten million people with roads of 40,000 kilometres, storehouses, labour taxes and knotted-cord records; a succession war between Atahualpa and Huascar is ending when Pizarro arrives.
provenance: sources to check: D'Altroy, The Incas (2nd ed. 2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina)

upsert.boundary: The Classic Maya collapse, about 800 to 950
upsert.description: The southern lowland cities stop raising monuments and empty, one after another, as wars multiply and a series of droughts strikes; the north, at Chichén Itzá, carries on.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weight of drought among the causes is debated
sources to check: Kennett et al. 2012, Science 338; Douglas et al. 2015, PNAS 112

upsert.boundary: The Americas' large animals die out, about 13,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: Mammoths, mastodons, horses, camels, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts and sabre-toothed cats disappear, about three quarters of the large mammal genera; new hunters and the rapid climate swings of the deglaciation are both blamed, and the loss leaves the Americas with few animals to domesticate.
provenance: exploring: the weight of hunting against climate is debated
sources to check: Koch and Barnosky 2006, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 37; Faith and Surovell 2009, PNAS 106

upsert.boundary: The Moche, about 100 to 800
upsert.description: On Peru's north coast, lords buried with gold, as at Sipán, rule irrigated valleys, build adobe pyramids and make portrait vessels; floods and droughts linked to El Niño weaken them.
provenance: sources to check: Bawden, The Moche (1996)

upsert.boundary: Monte Albán and the Zapotec state, about 500 BCE to 750 CE
upsert.description: Zapotec rulers found a hilltop capital over the valley of Oaxaca, conquer neighbouring valleys and carve some of the earliest Mesoamerican writing.
provenance: sources to check: Marcus and Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996)

upsert.boundary: Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago
upsert.description: A camp of wooden huts by a creek, with mastodon meat, seaweed and medicinal plants, preserved under peat: the site that broke the 'Clovis first' account.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2008, Science 320; Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10

upsert.boundary: Paracas and Nazca, about 800 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: On Peru's south coast, Paracas weavers make some of the finest textiles of antiquity and Nazca people draw the giant lines and figures on the desert floor and tap groundwater with spiral wells.
provenance: sources to check: Silverman and Proulx, The Nasca (2002)

upsert.boundary: The Norse in Greenland and Vinland, about 985 to 1450
upsert.description: Norse farmers settle south-west Greenland (about 985) and reach Newfoundland, where L'Anse aux Meadows is occupied in 1021; the Greenland colonies die out by about 1450 as the climate cools and trade with Norway fails.
provenance: sources to check: Kuitems et al. 2022, Nature 601 (L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021); Arneborg, in The Viking World (2008)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Greenland, Canada); Europe (Northern Europe)

upsert.boundary: The Olmec, about 1600 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: On the Gulf coast of Mexico, at San Lorenzo and La Venta, rulers carve colossal stone heads and jade figures; Olmec symbols, the ballgame and perhaps the calendar spread across Mesoamerica.
provenance: sources to check: Pool, Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (2007)

upsert.boundary: People spread through the Americas, about 16,000 to 13,000 years ago
upsert.description: Descendants of a population that lived isolated in Beringia move south, probably along the Pacific coast first, then through an ice-free corridor; within a few thousand years they reach Tierra del Fuego. Genomes show one main founding population, splitting early into northern and southern branches.
provenance: sources to check: Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018, Science 362; Braje et al. 2017, Science 357

upsert.boundary: The Preclassic Maya cities, about 1000 BCE to 150 CE
upsert.description: In the lowlands of Guatemala the Maya build El Mirador's huge pyramids, causeways and the first Maya writing; the San Bartolo murals show their gods and kings; many centres collapse about 150 CE.
provenance: sources to check: Estrada-Belli, The First Maya Civilization (2011)

upsert.boundary: Squash and maize domesticated in Mexico, about 8000 to 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Squash is grown in Oaxaca by about 8000 BCE; teosinte, a wild grass with a few hard seeds, is turned into maize in the Balsas valley from about 7000 BCE, and over thousands of years its cobs grow large enough to feed cities. Beans, chili and cotton follow.
provenance: sources to check: Smith 1997, Science 276 (squash); Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS 106 (maize)

upsert.boundary: Teotihuacan, about 100 BCE to 550 CE
upsert.description: A planned city of perhaps 100,000 people grows around the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon in the valley of Mexico, among the largest cities in the world in its time; its influence reaches the Maya, whose Tikal it may have conquered in 378. It is burned and abandoned about 550.
provenance: sources to check: Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Thule spread across the Arctic, about 1200 to 1300
upsert.description: Ancestors of the Inuit, with dog sleds, kayaks and umiaks for whaling, move from Alaska across Arctic Canada to Greenland in a few generations, replacing the Dorset people.
provenance: sources to check: Friesen and Arnold 2008, American Antiquity 73
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Alaska, Canada, Greenland)

upsert.boundary: Tiwanaku and Wari, about 500 to 1000
upsert.description: Tiwanaku, by Lake Titicaca, farms raised fields and spreads its religion; Wari, near Ayacucho, builds the first Andean empire with roads, administrative centres and knotted-cord records. Both fall apart by about 1000, perhaps in drought.
provenance: sources to check: Janusek, Ancient Tiwanaku (2008); Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

upsert.boundary: Tula and Chichén Itzá, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: The Toltec capital Tula dominates central Mexico and later Aztecs remember it as the source of civilization; Chichén Itzá, sharing its style, rules much of the Yucatán.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012)

upsert.boundary: Mound building at Watson Brake, about 3500 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers in Louisiana raise a ring of earth mounds, the oldest monumental earthworks in North America, two thousand years before Poverty Point.
provenance: sources to check: Saunders et al. 2005, American Antiquity 70

upsert.boundary: Footprints at White Sands, about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago
upsert.description: Human footprints in the dried lake beds of New Mexico, beside those of mammoths and giant sloths, dated by seeds, pollen and quartz to the height of the last glacial: if the dates hold, people lived south of the ice sheets thousands of years before Clovis.
provenance: exploring: the dates are contested but have held up to repeated testing
sources to check: Bennett et al. 2021, Science 373; Pigati et al. 2023, Science 382

changes.value: The Americas' own history to 1492, inside its eras: the White Sands footprints, the peopling and Monte Verde, Clovis, the megafaunal extinctions, the domestication of squash, maize, potatoes and llamas, Caral, Watson Brake, the Olmec, Chavín, the Zapotec and early Maya states, Paracas and Nazca, Hopewell, Teotihuacan, the Classic Maya and their collapse, Moche, Tiwanaku and Wari, Chaco, Cahokia, the Norse, the Thule, Chimú, the Aztec Triple Alliance and the Inca. With them, each region scale names a concept, the history of its region, so it is a category scale: only the Events that concern a region need a level on it.

upsert.boundary: The fall of Tenochtitlan, 1519 to 1521
upsert.description: Cortés lands with about 500 men, wins Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Mexica as allies with tens of thousands of warriors, and after smallpox kills Cuitláhuac and much of the city, takes Tenochtitlan by siege in August 1521.
provenance: sources to check: Restall, When Montezuma Met Cortés (2018); Townsend, Fifth Sun (2019)

upsert.boundary: Brazil abolishes slavery, May 1888
upsert.description: The Golden Law frees the last enslaved people in the Americas, about 700,000; the empire falls to a republic the next year.
provenance: sources to check: Conrad, The Destruction of Brazilian Slavery 1850–1888 (1972)

upsert.boundary: Brazil's gold rush, 1695 to 1760
upsert.description: Gold and then diamonds in Minas Gerais draw hundreds of thousands of Portuguese and many more enslaved Africans inland; Rio de Janeiro becomes the colony's capital (1763), and Brazilian gold flows through Lisbon to Britain.
provenance: sources to check: Boxer, The Golden Age of Brazil (1962)

upsert.boundary: Sugar and slavery in Brazil, about 1530 to 1650
upsert.description: Portuguese planters in Pernambuco and Bahia grow sugar on mills worked first by enslaved Native people, then by Africans; by 1600 Brazil is the world's largest sugar producer and the main destination of the Atlantic slave trade.
provenance: sources to check: Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society (1985)

upsert.boundary: The sugar revolution in the Caribbean, about 1640 to 1800
upsert.description: Barbados, then Jamaica, Saint-Domingue and the other islands turn to sugar on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who die faster than they are born and are replaced by new captives; by the 1780s Saint-Domingue produces about a third of the world's sugar and is the richest colony on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, Sugar and Slaves (1972); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985)

upsert.boundary: Civil wars in Central America, 1979 to 1996
upsert.description: The Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua (1979) and the American-backed Contra war, El Salvador's civil war, and Guatemala's war, in which the army's campaigns against Maya villages are judged genocide; about 300,000 die in all.
provenance: sources to check: Commission for Historical Clarification, Guatemala: Memory of Silence (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala)

upsert.boundary: Missions convert the peoples of the Americas, 1524 to 1650
upsert.description: Franciscans arrive in Mexico in 1524, then Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits; millions are baptized, temples are destroyed and churches built on them, and an Indigenous Catholicism forms around saints and the Virgin of Guadalupe. By 1650 most surviving Native people of Spanish and Portuguese America are Christian.
provenance: sources to check: Lockhart, The Nahuas After the Conquest (1992); MacCormack, Religion in the Andes (1991)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America, the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: The civil rights movement, 1954 to 1968
upsert.description: From Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and the Montgomery bus boycott (1955) to the Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Voting Rights Act (1965), Black Americans and their allies end legal segregation and disenfranchisement in the South; Martin Luther King Jr. is murdered in 1968.
provenance: sources to check: Branch, Parting the Waters (1988)

upsert.boundary: Columbus reaches the Caribbean, October 1492
upsert.description: Sailing west for Castile to reach Asia, Columbus lands in the Bahamas, then Cuba and Hispaniola, and returns with captives and a little gold; his second voyage (1493) brings settlers, horses, pigs and sugarcane. The hemispheres are joined.
provenance: sources to check: Phillips and Phillips, The Worlds of Christopher Columbus (1992)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean; Europe (Southern Europe: Castile)

upsert.boundary: The Cuban revolution, 1953 to 1962
upsert.description: From the Moncada attack (1953) to Batista's flight (January 1959), Fidel Castro's guerrillas take Cuba; the new state nationalizes property, allies with the Soviet Union, defeats the Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) and becomes the first communist state in the Americas.
provenance: sources to check: Pérez, Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution (5th ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The Latin American debt crisis, 1982 to 1990
upsert.description: Mexico's default (August 1982) sets off a crisis across the region: with American interest rates high, governments cut spending, inflation soars and income per person falls through the 'lost decade'; the crisis ends with the Brady bonds and a turn to open markets.
provenance: sources to check: Bulmer-Thomas, The Economic History of Latin America since Independence (3rd ed. 2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: Military dictatorships in Latin America, 1964 to 1990
upsert.description: Coups in Brazil (1964), Chile (1973), Uruguay and Argentina (1976) bring juntas that torture and disappear tens of thousands, often with American support, under the doctrine of national security; most fall in the 1980s, Chile's last, in 1990.
provenance: sources to check: Grandin, The Last Colonial Massacre (2004)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America, Central America

upsert.boundary: English colonies on North America's Atlantic coast, 1607 to 1733
upsert.description: From Jamestown (1607), where tobacco and, from 1619, enslaved Africans take root, and Plymouth (1620) and Massachusetts Bay (1630), to Georgia (1733): thirteen colonies of farmers, planters and merchants, with elected assemblies, grow by migration and high fertility to about 2.5 million people by 1775, pushing Native nations west.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, American Colonies (2001)

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: The Haitian Revolution, 1791 to 1804
upsert.description: The enslaved of Saint-Domingue rise in August 1791; under Toussaint Louverture and then Dessalines they defeat French, Spanish and British armies, end slavery, and declare Haiti independent on 1 January 1804: the only slave revolt to found a state.
provenance: sources to check: Dubois, Avengers of the New World (2004)

upsert.boundary: Pizarro takes the Inca empire, 1532 to 1533
upsert.description: Arriving as Atahualpa wins a war of succession against Huascar, after epidemics have killed the previous emperor, Pizarro's 168 men capture Atahualpa at Cajamarca, take a room of gold as ransom, execute him, and enter Cusco; Inca resistance from Vilcabamba lasts until 1572.
provenance: sources to check: Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas (1970)

upsert.boundary: Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears, 1830 to 1850
upsert.description: Under the Indian Removal Act, the United States forces about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people west of the Mississippi; thousands die on the way.
provenance: sources to check: Saunt, Unworthy Republic (2020)

upsert.boundary: Latin America's wars of independence, 1808 to 1826
upsert.description: After Napoleon seizes Spain (1808), juntas and armies across Spanish America fight for independence: Hidalgo's rising in Mexico (1810), Bolívar in the north and San Martín in the south, until Ayacucho (1824) and the fall of Callao (1826); Brazil separates from Portugal peacefully as an empire (1822). About eighteen new states emerge.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions 1808–1826 (2nd ed. 1986)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The Louisiana Purchase, 1803
upsert.description: Napoleon, having lost Saint-Domingue, sells France's claim to the Mississippi basin to the United States, doubling its territory.
provenance: sources to check: Kastor, The Nation's Crucible (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Mexican Revolution, 1910 to 1920
upsert.description: Madero's revolt against Díaz opens a decade of civil war (Villa, Zapata, Carranza, Obregón); perhaps one to two million die or flee, and the 1917 constitution promises land reform and national control of oil and minerals.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is contested
sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution (1986)

upsert.boundary: The Mexican–American War, 1846 to 1848
upsert.description: The United States invades Mexico and takes about half its territory, from Texas to California, in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
provenance: sources to check: Greenberg, A Wicked War (2012)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (United States), Central America (Mexico)

upsert.boundary: NAFTA, 1994 to 2020
upsert.description: Canada, the United States and Mexico remove most tariffs between them; trade within North America roughly triples and supply chains cross the borders, until the agreement is renegotiated as the USMCA (2020).
provenance: sources to check: Hufbauer and Schott, NAFTA Revisited (2005)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America, Central America (Mexico)

upsert.boundary: The New Deal, 1933 to 1939
upsert.description: Roosevelt's government answers the Depression with relief, public works, bank regulation, union rights and the Social Security Act (1935); federal spending and the reach of the state grow for good.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, Freedom from Fear (1999)

upsert.boundary: New France and the fur trade, 1608 to 1763
upsert.description: Champlain founds Quebec (1608); a thin French colony along the St Lawrence and down the Mississippi lives by trading furs with Native allies, Huron, Algonquin and later many others, and fights the Haudenosaunee and the English, until Britain takes Canada in 1763.
provenance: sources to check: White, The Middle Ground (1991)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Canada, United States)

upsert.boundary: The New Laws and the Valladolid debate, 1542 to 1551
upsert.description: Pressed by Bartolomé de las Casas, Spain bans the enslavement of Native Americans and limits the encomienda; at Valladolid Las Casas and Sepúlveda debate whether conquest is just: an early argument over universal rights, followed by forced labour under other names.
provenance: sources to check: Hanke, All Mankind Is One (1974)

upsert.boundary: The Panama Canal, 1904 to 1914
upsert.description: After the United States backs Panama's secession from Colombia (1903), it builds the canal across the isthmus, at the cost of about 5,600 workers' lives, cutting the sea route from New York to San Francisco by more than half.
provenance: sources to check: McCullough, The Path Between the Seas (1977)

upsert.boundary: The War of the Triple Alliance, 1864 to 1870
upsert.description: Paraguay fights Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay and is destroyed: it loses perhaps a quarter to over half of its people, most of its men, the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history.
provenance: sources to check: Whigham and Potthast 1999, Latin American Research Review 34
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Paraguay, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay)

upsert.boundary: The conquest of the Plains and the West, 1862 to 1890
upsert.description: From the Dakota war (1862) to Wounded Knee (1890), the US Army and settlers defeat the Plains and western nations, confine them to reservations, and the bison, perhaps 30 million in 1800, are shot to fewer than a thousand by 1889.
provenance: sources to check: Hämäläinen, Lakota America (2019); Isenberg, The Destruction of the Bison (2000)

upsert.boundary: Populist states in Latin America: Vargas and Perón, 1930 to 1955
upsert.description: Getúlio Vargas in Brazil (from 1930) and Juan Perón in Argentina (from 1946) build states that court urban workers, nationalize industries and protect them behind tariffs, setting the pattern of import substitution and mass politics that lasts into the 1980s.
provenance: sources to check: Skidmore, Smith and Green, Modern Latin America (9th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: The silver of Potosí, 1545 to 1650
upsert.description: A mountain of silver found in the Andes in 1545 makes Potosí one of the largest cities of the world by 1600; after 1573 the mita forces Andean villages to send men to its mines, where mercury refining kills many. Its silver pays Spain's wars and, through Manila, buys China's goods.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Lane, Potosí (2019)

upsert.boundary: The Pueblo Revolt, 1680 to 1692
upsert.description: Led by Popé, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico rise together, kill about 400 colonists and missionaries, and drive the Spanish out for twelve years.
provenance: sources to check: Knaut, The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 (1995)

upsert.boundary: Railways cross North America, 1863 to 1885
upsert.description: The first transcontinental railroad (1869), built largely by Chinese and Irish workers, and the Canadian Pacific (1885) cut the crossing from months to a week, open the plains to farming and ranching and bind the continent's markets.
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (United States, Canada)

upsert.boundary: Reconstruction and its end, 1865 to 1877
upsert.description: The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments give freed people citizenship and Black men the vote; Black Southerners hold office for a decade, until white terror and the withdrawal of federal troops (1877) restore white rule and Jim Crow.

upsert.boundary: The Americas' share of humanity grows from 2.6% to 13.9%, 1800 to 1960
upsert.description: From its low after the Columbian collapse, the Americas' share of the world's people rises fivefold: about forty million immigrants from Europe and millions from Asia and Africa (most of the latter enslaved, before 1867), the high fertility of frontier families with cheap land, and earlier falls in mortality than Asia or Africa. After 1960 it eases as Latin American fertility falls.
provenance: inferred: shares from this model's h.region-americas
sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998); Our World in Data, population by world region

upsert.boundary: The Taíno of the Greater Antilles destroyed, 1493 to 1520
upsert.description: Forced into gold mining and farm labour under the encomienda, hit by war, famine and, from 1518, smallpox, the Taíno of Hispaniola fall from perhaps several hundred thousand to a few thousand within a generation; the Spanish raid the Bahamas and the mainland for slaves to replace them.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Hispaniola's 1492 population is estimated from about 100,000 to several million
sources to check: Reséndez, The Other Slavery (2016); Livi Bacci 2003, Hispanic American Historical Review 83
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica)

upsert.boundary: The rebellion of Túpac Amaru II, 1780 to 1783
upsert.description: A descendant of the Inca leads the largest Indigenous rising of colonial Spanish America in the Andes against forced sales and labour; it is crushed, and perhaps 100,000 die.
provenance: sources to check: Walker, The Tupac Amaru Rebellion (2014)

upsert.boundary: The United States Constitution and Bill of Rights, 1787 to 1791
upsert.description: A written constitution with separated powers, federalism and an amendment process, and the first ten amendments' guarantees of speech, religion and due process; it counts an enslaved person as three fifths and leaves slavery in place.
provenance: sources to check: Klarman, The Framers' Coup (2016)

upsert.boundary: The American Revolution, 1775 to 1783
upsert.description: Thirteen colonies rebel against British taxation and rule, declare independence (July 1776) and, with French help, win at Saratoga and Yorktown; the Treaty of Paris (1783) recognizes the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Wood, The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1992)

upsert.boundary: Venezuela's collapse and exodus, from 2013
upsert.description: Falling oil prices, price controls and Maduro's authoritarian rule shrink Venezuela's economy by about three quarters; nearly eight million people, about a quarter of the population, leave, the largest displacement in the Americas' modern history.
provenance: sources to check: R4V Inter-Agency Coordination Platform reports (2024)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Peru)

upsert.boundary: The Spanish–American War, 1898
upsert.description: The United States intervenes in Cuba's war of independence, defeats Spain and takes Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines; Cuba becomes independent under American oversight.
provenance: sources to check: Pérez, The War of 1898 (1998)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Cuba, Puerto Rico); Asia (South-eastern Asia: the Philippines); Oceania (Micronesia: Guam)

upsert.boundary: The Atlantic revolutions, 1775 to 1826
upsert.description: Revolutions in British North America, France, Saint-Domingue and Spanish America overthrow monarchies and colonial rule in the name of popular sovereignty and rights, found the United States, Haiti and the Latin American republics, and spread the idea that rulers answer to the governed.
provenance: sources to check: Palmer, The Age of the Democratic Revolution (1959–64, new ed. 2014); Polasky, Revolutions without Borders (2015)

changes.value: The Americas' own history from 1492 to 2025: Columbus and the destruction of the Taíno, the fall of the Aztec and Inca states, Potosí, the missions, Brazil's and the Caribbean's sugar and slavery, the English and French colonies, the Pueblo Revolt, Brazil's gold; the Atlantic revolutions (a world Event, added here as the parent of the American, Haitian and Spanish American revolutions), the Louisiana Purchase, Indian Removal, the Mexican–American war, the gold rush, Reconstruction, the railways, the conquest of the Plains, the Paraguayan war, Brazil's abolition, 1898, the Panama Canal and the Mexican Revolution; then the New Deal, Vargas and Perón, the Cuban revolution, civil rights, the dictatorships, Central America's wars, the debt crisis, NAFTA and Venezuela's exodus. One Event names the measure it turns: the Americas' share of humanity, from 2.6% in 1800 to 13.9% by 1960. Also corrected: a relation that cited WaveOfAdvance by a wrong stub now cites WaveOfAdvance#4cec, resolved; and four relations whose ids misnamed their kind or parent are replaced by correctly named ones.
