Checked 2026-10-11 against the usual estimate of about 117 billion (Population Reference Bureau). That estimate counts 46 billion births between 8000 BCE and 1 CE and 26 billion between 1 and 1200 by assuming 80 and 60 births per 1,000 a year; in a population that barely grows that means a life expectancy of about 12.5 and 17 years. This model's life expectancy is 25 to 30 in those periods, as palaeodemography and ancient censuses put it, which gives 35 to 40 births per 1,000 and about 22 billion by 1 CE. After 1650 the two accounts agree within a few billion. Raising this value to 117 would contradict the model's own life expectancy before 1650; so it stays, with both accounts inside the band.

upsert.reason: Integral of humanity times a crude birth rate consistent with the model's life expectancy; the upper band holds the Population Reference Bureau's account (about 117 billion by 2022).

upsert.boundary: The Archaic: Mesoamerica's first farmers, 8000 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: Foraging bands in the highland valleys begin to grow squash (Guilá Naquitz, Oaxaca, by about 8000 BCE), turn teosinte into maize in the Balsas valley from about 7000 BCE, and add beans, chili, avocado and cotton; for thousands of years these crops supplement foraging, until maize cobs grow large enough, after about 2500 BCE, to support settled villages.
provenance: sources to check: Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS 106; Smith 1997, Science 276

upsert.boundary: The Classic: Teotihuacan and the Maya kingdoms, 250 to 900
upsert.description: Teotihuacan, with perhaps 100,000 people, dominates central Mexico and reaches deep into the Maya world until it is burned about 550; Monte Albán rules Oaxaca; dozens of Maya kingdoms, led by Tikal and Calakmul in rival alliances, record their kings and wars in a full script and the Long Count. From about 800 the southern lowland kingdoms fail one after another amid war and repeated droughts.
provenance: sources to check: Martin and Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2nd ed. 2008); Evans (2013)

upsert.boundary: Wars, open markets and the drug wars, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: The Sandinista revolution (1979) opens a decade of civil wars in Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala, ended by peace accords from 1990 to 1996. Mexico defaults (1982), opens its economy and joins NAFTA (1994), the year of the Zapatista rising and the peso crisis; the party of the revolution loses the presidency in 2000. From 2006 the army's war on the cartels and the cartels' wars with each other drive homicides to the highest numbers in Mexico's modern history, and millions from Mexico and the northern isthmus migrate north.
provenance: sources to check: Meyer, Sherman and Deeds (2018); INEGI homicide statistics

upsert.boundary: New Spain, 1521 to 1821
upsert.description: The Viceroyalty of New Spain rules from Mexico City, built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Epidemics, the cocoliztli above all, cut central Mexico's Indigenous population from perhaps 15 to 25 million to about a million by 1620 on Borah and Cook's widely cited figures, which others think too high; Indigenous towns keep their lands and councils under Spanish rule and the Church. Silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato makes New Spain Spain's richest colony, the Manila galleons link Acapulco with Asia, and a mixed population grows. The Maya highlands and the isthmus form the Captaincy General of Guatemala.
provenance: sources to check: Gibson, The Aztecs under Spanish Rule (1964); Borah and Cook, The Aboriginal Population of Central Mexico on the Eve of the Spanish Conquest (1963)

upsert.boundary: Paleo-Indian Mexico and the isthmus, about 16,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: The people who reached Monte Verde in Chile by 14,500 years ago must have passed through, but the earliest securely dated sites here are later: at El Fin del Mundo in Sonora, Clovis hunters kill gomphotheres about 13,400 years ago. Claims of people at Chiquihuite Cave in Zacatecas 26,000 years ago rest on stone flakes whose human making is disputed.
provenance: sources to check: Sanchez et al. 2014, PNAS 111 (El Fin del Mundo); Ardelean et al. 2020, Nature 584 (Chiquihuite)

upsert.boundary: The Postclassic: Toltecs, Mixtecs, Maya city-states and the Aztecs, 900 to 1521
upsert.description: Tula and Chichén Itzá rise as the southern Maya cities empty; Mixtec kingdoms record their dynasties in painted books; the northern Maya are ruled from Mayapán until about 1441, then by small rival states. In the valley of Mexico the Mexica found Tenochtitlan (1325) and with Texcoco and Tlacopan build the Triple Alliance's tribute empire (1428), checked in the west by the Tarascan state. The era ends with the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan (1519 to 1521).
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012); Evans (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Preclassic: villages, the Olmec and the first states, 2000 BCE to 250 CE
upsert.description: Villages with pottery spread from the Pacific coast of Chiapas, where the earliest known ball court is built about 1650 BCE; the Olmec of the Gulf coast (San Lorenzo, La Venta) carve colossal heads and spread a shared art and religion; writing and the 260-day calendar appear by about 600 BCE; Zapotec Monte Albán and Maya El Mirador become cities and states, and Teotihuacan begins to grow about 100 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Pool, Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (2007); Evans, Ancient Mexico and Central America (3rd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Independent Mexico and the isthmus republics, 1821 to 1910
upsert.description: Mexico and Central America leave Spain in 1821, and the Central American federation breaks into five republics by 1841. Mexico's decades of coups, Texas's secession and the war with the United States (1846 to 1848) cost it half its territory; La Reforma separates church and state, and Juárez defeats the French-backed Maximilian (1867). The Maya of Yucatán rise in the Caste War (1847). Díaz's long rule (1876 to 1911) brings railways, foreign capital and order while haciendas take village lands; coffee and then bananas tie the isthmus to foreign markets and firms.
provenance: sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution vol. 1 (1986); Woodward, Central America: A Nation Divided (3rd ed. 1999)

upsert.boundary: Revolution, banana republics and the one-party state, 1910 to 1979
upsert.description: The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) kills or drives out one to two million people and leaves a constitution of land reform and national resources; its party rules from 1929, distributes land under Cárdenas, nationalizes oil (1938) and presides over the growth of 1940 to 1970. On the isthmus, United Fruit and coffee planters back dictators such as Ubico and Somoza; Costa Rica abolishes its army (1948); a CIA-backed coup ends Guatemala's land reform (1954). Mexico's wheat programme begins the Green Revolution.
provenance: sources to check: Knight (1986); Woodward (1999); Meyer, Sherman and Deeds, The Course of Mexican History (11th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: The American century in the Caribbean, 1898 to 1962
upsert.description: The United States takes Puerto Rico, oversees Cuba under the Platt Amendment and occupies Haiti (1915 to 1934) and the Dominican Republic (1916 to 1924); Trujillo and Batista rise from the forces it trained or tolerated. Sugar booms and busts; the British islands' labour rebellions of 1934 to 1939 bring unions, parties and universal suffrage; West Indians migrate to Panama, Cuba, the United States and, after 1948, Britain. The Cuban revolution (1959) and the end of the West Indies Federation (1962) close the era.
provenance: sources to check: Higman (2011); Pérez, Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution (5th ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The first islanders, about 6000 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers from South America reach Trinidad, then all but joined to the mainland, by about 6000 BCE (Banwari Trace); by about 4000 BCE people cross open sea to Cuba and Hispaniola, from Central America or from South America (their stone tools fit both), and later Archaic peoples settle Puerto Rico and the northern Lesser Antilles. They fish, gather shellfish and tend some plants; ancient genomes show them to be a population distinct from the farmers who come after them.
provenance: sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590

upsert.boundary: Emancipation and its limits, 1804 to 1898
upsert.description: Independent Haiti pays France an indemnity for recognition (1825) and is shunned by the slaveholding powers. Britain frees about 670,000 enslaved people in its islands (1834 to 1838) after the Baptist War in Jamaica, France and Denmark in 1848 and the Netherlands in 1863, while Cuba's sugar boom draws hundreds of thousands more Africans until the 1860s and slavery lasts there until 1886. Freed people seek land of their own; planters bring indentured labourers from India and China. Cuba fights two wars for independence (1868 to 1878 and 1895 to 1898), the second ended by the United States' intervention.
provenance: sources to check: Higman (2011); Scott, Slave Emancipation in Cuba (1985)

upsert.boundary: Independent and dependent islands, 1962 to 2025
upsert.description: Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent in 1962 and most British islands follow by 1983, while Puerto Rico, the French departments, the Dutch islands and others stay tied to their metropoles. Cuba becomes a Soviet ally whose missiles bring the world to the brink of nuclear war (1962), then endures the Special Period after 1991; Haiti passes from the Duvaliers to coups, an earthquake (2010) and gang rule. Tourism, offshore finance and remittances replace sugar.

upsert.boundary: Saladoid farmers and potters, about 500 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: Arawak-speaking farmers from the lower Orinoco sail up the Lesser Antilles to Puerto Rico with manioc, clay griddles for cassava bread and white-on-red painted pottery; ancient DNA shows a new population from South America that largely replaces or absorbs the Archaic islanders of the eastern islands. Villages are built around plazas with burials at their centre.
provenance: sources to check: Keegan and Hofman (2017); Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590

upsert.boundary: Conquest and the Spanish Caribbean, 1492 to 1640
upsert.description: Columbus's landfall begins the conquest of the Greater Antilles; within a generation the Taíno are destroyed by forced labour, war, famine and disease, and the first enslaved Africans and sugar mills arrive on Hispaniola. As Spain's interest moves to Mexico and Peru, the islands become ports and forts for the treasure fleets, with Havana their meeting point, raided by French, English and Dutch privateers; from the 1620s England, France and the Netherlands settle the smaller islands Spain had left.
provenance: sources to check: Elliott (2006); Higman, A Concise History of the Caribbean (2011)

upsert.boundary: The sugar islands, 1640 to 1804
upsert.description: Barbados turns to sugar in the 1640s and the model spreads to Jamaica (English from 1655), the French islands and Saint-Domingue: plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who die faster than they are born and are replaced by new captives. Over the whole slave trade the Caribbean receives almost half the Africans landed in the Americas, most of them in this era; on the sugar islands nine people in ten are enslaved, and maroons hold the mountains of Jamaica. The era ends with the Haitian Revolution, which destroys the richest colony on Earth and founds the first state built by the formerly enslaved (1804).
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, Sugar and Slaves (1972); Higman (2011); Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)

upsert.boundary: Ostionoid and Taíno chiefdoms, about 600 to 1492
upsert.description: Farming villages spread west into Hispaniola, Jamaica and Cuba and north into the Bahamas, home of the Lucayans; by about 1200 the Taíno of the Greater Antilles live in chiefdoms (cacicazgos) with ball courts, stone-lined plazas, carved zemí figures and cassava grown in mounded fields, while the Kalinago hold the Lesser Antilles. How many people lived on Hispaniola in 1492 is disputed, from about 100,000 to several million.
provenance: sources to check: Rouse, The Tainos (1992); Keegan and Hofman (2017)

upsert.boundary: Iberian America, 1492 to 1808
upsert.description: Castile and Portugal divide the hemisphere at Tordesillas (1494). Spain conquers the Caribbean, the Aztec and Inca states and much else by 1572 and rules through viceroyalties, courts, the Church and the labour drafts of Indigenous towns; Portugal settles Brazil's coast with sugar mills worked by enslaved Africans. Epidemics, war and forced labour cut the Indigenous population by perhaps nine tenths by 1650, and the society that follows ranks people by descent as Spaniards, Indians, mestizos, mulattos and Africans. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas flows to Europe and China. The Bourbon and Pombaline reforms of the 1700s tighten taxes and control, and the resentment of American-born elites grows.
provenance: sources to check: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006); Burkholder and Johnson, Colonial Latin America (10th ed. 2019)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: Debt, democracy and open markets, 1982 to 2025
upsert.description: The debt crisis brings a lost decade of falling income; by 1990 elected governments have replaced military rule almost everywhere, and governments privatize, open trade and end high inflation. A commodity boom driven by China's demand (2003 to 2014) roughly halves poverty in many countries and carries left-wing governments to power; its end brings recession, corruption scandals and protest. With about 8% of the world's people, the region comes to count about a third of its homicides; millions migrate north, and Venezuela's collapse drives out nearly eight million.
provenance: sources to check: Skidmore, Smith and Green (2018); UNODC, Global Study on Homicide (2019)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: The export age, 1880 to 1930
upsert.description: Railways and steamships tie the region to the industrial world: Argentina's wheat and beef, Brazil's coffee and rubber, Chile's nitrates and copper, Cuba's sugar, Central America's bananas, Mexico's silver and oil. Oligarchic republics and dictators such as Díaz keep order for exports; millions of Europeans settle in Argentina, Uruguay, southern Brazil and Cuba; the United States intervenes again and again in the Caribbean and Central America. The Mexican Revolution (1910) is the first of the century's great upheavals, and the collapse of export prices after 1929 ends the model.
provenance: sources to check: Bulmer-Thomas, The Economic History of Latin America since Independence (3rd ed. 2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: Independence and the new republics, 1808 to 1880
upsert.description: Napoleon's seizure of Spain (1808) sets off juntas and wars across Spanish America until 1826, while Brazil separates from Portugal as an empire (1822). About eighteen republics emerge; caudillos, liberals and conservatives fight over the Church, federalism and land, Mexico loses half its territory to the United States, and output per person stagnates in much of the region for half a century, by most estimates. Spanish America abolishes slavery between the 1820s and the 1850s; Brazil and Cuba keep it.
provenance: sources to check: Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America vol. 3 (1985); Bértola and Ocampo, The Economic Development of Latin America since Independence (2012)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: Populism, state-led industry and the Cold War, 1930 to 1982
upsert.description: The collapse of export prices and a wave of coups in 1930 open half a century of state-led development: tariffs, state oil and steel firms and development banks build industry behind protection, and output per person roughly doubles between 1950 and 1980. Vargas, Perón and Cárdenas bring workers into politics; cities swell as people leave the countryside; fertility begins to fall in the 1960s. After the Cuban revolution (1959) the Cold War arrives: guerrillas, US-backed coups and military rule in most of the region. Borrowing in the 1970s ends in Mexico's default of August 1982.
provenance: sources to check: Bértola and Ocampo (2012); Skidmore, Smith and Green, Modern Latin America (9th ed. 2018)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean

upsert.boundary: The Archaic in Northern America, 8000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: With the big game gone and the climate warming, people forage region by region: deer, nuts and shellfish in the eastern woodlands, bison on the plains, salmon and sea mammals on the north-west coast, seeds and small game in the desert west. Native copper is hammered into tools around Lake Superior from about 4000 BCE; foragers raise mounds at Watson Brake (about 3500 BCE) and the earthworks of Poverty Point (about 1700 to 1100 BCE); the eastern woodlands domesticate squash, sunflower, marsh elder and goosefoot by about 1800 BCE, and maize from Mexico reaches the Southwest about 2100 BCE. Paleo-Inuit hunters cross the Arctic to Greenland from about 2500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Sassaman, The Eastern Archaic, Historicized (2010); Smith 2006, PNAS 103 (eastern domestication); Raghavan et al. 2014, Science 345 (Paleo-Eskimo genomes)

upsert.boundary: Colonies and Native nations, 1607 to 1763
upsert.description: English colonies grow along the Atlantic coast from Jamestown (1607) and Massachusetts Bay (1630) to Georgia (1733); New France spreads along the St Lawrence and the Mississippi, New Netherland lasts until 1664, and Spain holds Florida and New Mexico. Native nations, cut by epidemics, trade furs and fight for position: the Haudenosaunee in the Beaver Wars, the Wampanoag and their allies in King Philip's War, the Pueblos in their revolt of 1680; horses carried north from New Mexico remake the Plains. Slavery becomes hereditary and racial in the southern colonies. The Seven Years' War ends with Britain taking Canada and Florida (1763).
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, American Colonies (2001); Richter, Facing East from Indian Country (2001)

upsert.boundary: Civil war, industry and immigration, 1861 to 1941
upsert.description: The Civil War ends slavery; Reconstruction gives freed people rights that Jim Crow takes back after 1877. Railways, homesteads and the army's wars open the West, as the Plains nations are confined to reservations and Canada, confederated in 1867, settles its prairies. The United States becomes the largest industrial economy by about 1890, with steel, oil, electricity and mass production, and takes in about 25 million immigrants before the quota acts of 1921 and 1924; Black Southerners begin the Great Migration north. The crash of 1929 and the Depression bring the New Deal.
provenance: sources to check: White, The Republic for Which It Stands (2017); Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016)

upsert.boundary: Mississippian towns, Pueblos and the Thule, 800 to 1607
upsert.description: Maize becomes the staple of the eastern woodlands after about 900, and Mississippian chiefdoms build platform-mound towns from the Gulf to the Great Lakes, Cahokia the largest; Chaco Canyon and later Mesa Verde rise and are abandoned in the Southwest; the Thule, ancestors of the Inuit, cross the Arctic, and the Norse reach Greenland and Newfoundland. After about 1350 Cahokia and much of the central Mississippi valley empty, and the Haudenosaunee confederacy forms. From 1497 Europeans fish the Grand Banks and probe the coasts; Spanish expeditions cross the South-east and the Southwest (1539 to 1543), and epidemics move ahead of colonists in ways still debated, before English and French colonies take root in 1607 and 1608.
provenance: sources to check: Pauketat, Cahokia (2009); Kehoe, America Before the European Invasions (2002); Fagan, Ancient North America (2005)

upsert.boundary: Paleo-Indian Northern America, about 16,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: People come south of the ice sheets, first along the Pacific coast and later, once it could support life about 13,000 years ago, through the corridor between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice: the Paisley Caves in Oregon hold human coprolites about 14,300 years old. Clovis hunters (13,050 to 12,750 years ago) and then Folsom bison hunters spread across the continent as mammoths, mastodons, horses and camels die out. Whether people came far earlier, as the White Sands footprints (23,000 to 21,000 years ago) would show if their dates hold, is debated; this era begins with the arrivals no one disputes.
provenance: sources to check: Meltzer, First Peoples in a New World (2nd ed. 2021); Jenkins et al. 2012, Science 337 (Paisley Caves); Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature 537 (ice-free corridor)

upsert.boundary: World power, 1941 to 2025
upsert.description: Pearl Harbor brings the United States into the Second World War, from which it emerges with about half the world's manufacturing output and nuclear weapons. Through the Cold War it leads an alliance system and the world economy; the GI Bill, highways and suburbs make a mass middle class, the civil rights movement ends legal segregation, and the 1965 immigration act opens the country to Latin America and Asia. The microprocessor, the personal computer and the commercial internet come largely from its universities and firms. Canada builds a welfare state and a bilingual federation that survives Quebec's referendums. Since about 2000 the region has faced the 2008 crash, opioid deaths, sharper political division and China's rise.
provenance: sources to check: Patterson, Grand Expectations (1996); Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016)

upsert.boundary: Revolution, republic and expansion, 1763 to 1861
upsert.description: Britain's attempt to tax and govern the colonies after 1763 leads to their revolution and independence (1775 to 1783) and a federal constitution (1787). The United States doubles with Louisiana (1803), forces the eastern Native nations west (1830s), takes Texas and half of Mexico (1836 to 1848) and fills with immigrants; cotton and the domestic slave trade spread slavery across the Deep South, while canals, steamboats and railways bind the North and West. Loyalists settle Upper Canada, the War of 1812 leaves Canada British, and the Canadas win responsible government (1848). The quarrel over slavery in the new territories ends in secession.
provenance: sources to check: Wood, Empire of Liberty (2009); Howe, What Hath God Wrought (2007); Taylor, American Revolutions (2016)

upsert.boundary: Woodland peoples and the south-western farmers, 1000 BCE to 800 CE
upsert.description: Pottery, burial mounds and the eastern crops spread through the woodlands; Adena and Hopewell peoples of the Ohio valley build earthworks and trade copper, obsidian and shell across half the continent; the bow and arrow replaces the spear-thrower between about 400 and 700 CE. In the Southwest, maize farmers dig the first canals, the Hohokam irrigate the Salt and Gila valleys, and Ancestral Puebloans live in pit-house villages. On the north-west coast, fishing peoples in plank-house villages are ranked by birth; in the Arctic the Dorset succeed the first Paleo-Inuit.
provenance: sources to check: Milner, The Moundbuilders (2004); Fagan, Ancient North America (4th ed. 2005)

upsert.boundary: Spanish and Portuguese South America, 1533 to 1808
upsert.description: The Viceroyalty of Peru rules Spanish South America from Lima; Viceroy Toledo resettles Andean villagers into towns and organizes the mita that sends them to Potosí's mines. Portuguese Brazil grows from sugar coasts worked by enslaved Africans to the gold and diamond fields of Minas Gerais; bandeirantes raid inland for captives and gold, and the Jesuits gather the Guaraní into missions. The Mapuche hold the south. Indigenous risings culminate in Túpac Amaru's and Túpac Katari's (1780 to 1783).
provenance: sources to check: Bethell (ed.), Colonial Latin America (1984); Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society (1985)

upsert.boundary: Democracy, booms and crises, 1990 to 2025
upsert.description: Elected governments rule almost everywhere, though Fujimori's Peru (1992 to 2000) and Maduro's Venezuela slide into authoritarian rule; Brazil's Real plan ends hyperinflation (1994) and Argentina's currency board collapses (2001). China's demand for soy, iron ore, copper and oil drives a boom from 2003 to 2014, poverty roughly halves and the left governs most of the continent; Colombia's FARC signs peace (2016). The Amazon forest is cut fastest in the 1990s and early 2000s, more slowly under enforcement from 2004, then faster again; Venezuela's collapse drives out nearly eight million people.
provenance: sources to check: Skidmore, Smith and Green (2018); INPE PRODES deforestation series

upsert.boundary: The Early Horizon: Chavín, 900 to 200 BCE
upsert.description: Chavín de Huántar's cult and art style spread along the Andes from the northern highlands, the first horizon to unite much of Peru in religion though not, as far as is known, in rule; Paracas weavers flourish on the south coast.

upsert.boundary: Regional kingdoms: Moche, Nazca and Lima, 200 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: After Chavín the Andes divide among regional societies: the Moche of the north coast, with lords buried in gold at Sipán; the Nazca of the south coast, who draw lines on the desert and tap groundwater; Lima, Recuay and Pukara. In Amazonia, settled villagers make dark earths and earthworks, as in the Upano valley's towns.
provenance: sources to check: Moseley (2001); Quilter, The Ancient Central Andes (2nd ed. 2022)

upsert.boundary: The Late Horizon: the Inca, 1438 to 1533
upsert.description: From about 1438 Pachacuti and his successors conquer the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile, about ten million people, ruled through roads, storehouses, labour turns and resettlement. On the Atlantic coast Cabral claims Brazil for Portugal (1500) and traders cut brazilwood with Tupi labour. An epidemic, perhaps smallpox, kills the emperor Huayna Capac about 1528, and the war of succession between his sons is ending when Pizarro arrives.
provenance: sources to check: D'Altroy, The Incas (2nd ed. 2014)

upsert.boundary: The Initial Period: temples and canals, 1800 to 900 BCE
upsert.description: Pottery and canal irrigation spread through the Andes; coastal valleys build huge U-shaped temple complexes such as Sechín Alto, Cardal and Garagay, among the largest monuments of the Americas in their time, while highland centres such as Kotosh keep older fire rites. Andean smiths hammer the first gold foil (Waywaka, about 1500 BCE).
provenance: sources to check: Burger, Chavín and the Origins of Andean Civilization (1992); Moseley (2001)

upsert.boundary: Chimú, the highland kingdoms and Amazonian towns, 1000 to 1438
upsert.description: Chimú rules the north coast from Chan Chan; Aymara kingdoms divide the altiplano and the Chincha trade by sea; the Muisca of the Colombian highlands form confederations; in Amazonia, towns of the Casarabe culture in the Llanos de Moxos and of the Upper Xingu are linked by causeways and ditches. In the valley of Cusco the Inca are one small chiefdom among many.
provenance: sources to check: Moseley (2001); Prümers et al. 2022, Nature 606 (Casarabe); Heckenberger et al. 2008, Science 321 (Upper Xingu)

upsert.boundary: The Middle Horizon: Wari and Tiwanaku, 600 to 1000
upsert.description: Wari, from near Ayacucho, builds the first Andean empire, with administrative centres, roads and knotted-cord records; Tiwanaku, by Lake Titicaca, farms raised fields and spreads its religion south. Both fall apart by about 1000, perhaps in drought.
provenance: sources to check: Isbell and Silverman (eds.), Andean Archaeology III (2008); Quilter (2022)

upsert.boundary: Paleo-Indian South America, about 16,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: People reach the far south fast: Monte Verde in Chile is occupied by about 14,500 years ago, and fishtail points mark hunters of horses and ground sloths on the pampas and in Patagonia (Fell's Cave) by about 13,000 years ago. Others live by the Amazon's rivers and in the Brazilian highlands at Lagoa Santa. Claims of far older sites, such as Pedra Furada in Brazil, are disputed.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE (Monte Verde); Meltzer (2021)

upsert.boundary: The Archaic and Preceramic: domestication and the first monuments, 8000 to 1800 BCE
upsert.description: South Americans domesticate crops in several places: squash and manioc in the forest islands of south-western Amazonia from about 8300 BCE, potatoes and quinoa in the Andes and llamas and alpacas on the high grasslands, peanuts, peppers and cotton. The Chinchorro of the Atacama coast mummify their dead from about 5000 BCE; people on the lower Amazon make some of the hemisphere's first pottery about 5000 BCE; shell-mound builders line the Brazilian coast. In the valleys north of Lima, Caral and the Norte Chico build pyramids and plazas from about 3000 BCE without pottery.
provenance: sources to check: Lombardo et al. 2020, Nature 581; Moseley, The Incas and Their Ancestors (rev. ed. 2001); Roosevelt et al. 1991, Science 254 (Taperinha)

upsert.boundary: Independence, caudillos and export republics, 1808 to 1930
upsert.description: The Portuguese court flees to Rio (1808), and Brazil becomes independent as an empire (1822); Bolívar and San Martín free Spanish South America by 1826. Caudillos and civil wars follow; wars between the new states (the Paraguayan war, 1864 to 1870; the War of the Pacific, 1879 to 1884) redraw borders. Guano, nitrates, rubber, coffee, wheat and beef link the continent to world markets; Argentina and Chile conquer the Indigenous south, millions of Europeans settle in Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, and Brazil abolishes slavery, the last in the Americas (1888).
provenance: sources to check: Bethell (ed.), Cambridge History of Latin America vols. 3 to 5 (1985 to 1986); Bulmer-Thomas (2014)

upsert.boundary: Populism, development and dictatorship, 1930 to 1990
upsert.description: Coups in Argentina and Brazil in 1930 open the age of Vargas and later Perón; governments build industry behind tariffs and draw workers into politics. Colombia's Violencia (1948 to 1958) kills about 200,000; Bolivia's revolution (1952) brings land reform and the vote for Indigenous people. From 1964 to 1976 the military take power in Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Uruguay, Chile and Argentina, killing and disappearing tens of thousands; the debt crisis of the 1980s helps end their rule by 1990, as the Shining Path's war tears Peru apart.
provenance: sources to check: Skidmore, Smith and Green (2018)

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 1: each of the Americas' subregions gets its own eras, in the periodization its own historians use, from the first arrivals to 2025. Northern America: Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Woodland, Mississippian, colonial, the republic's expansion, industry, world power. The Caribbean: Archaic, Saladoid, Ostionoid and Taíno, the Spanish Caribbean, the sugar islands, emancipation, the American century, independence. Central America: Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Preclassic, Classic, Postclassic, New Spain, the republics, revolution, crisis. South America: Paleo-Indian, the Preceramic, the Initial Period, the Early Horizon, the Early Intermediate, the Middle Horizon, the Late Intermediate, the Inca, colonial rule, the republics, state-led development, democracy. Latin America and the Caribbean as a whole from 1492, when its parts begin a shared colonial and national history. The hemisphere's own eras, drawn on Mesoamerica's sequence, stay as the hemisphere's frame.

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 2: every existing Event of the Americas is re-filed in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f). An Event of one subregion or intermediate region moves from the hemisphere's era into that region's own era; one across Latin America into Latin America's era; one that crosses its region's era boundary into the region's lifecycle, as the events pass did for the hemisphere. The old contains relation is replaced, not doubled, so each Event has one frame; Events that are also parts of a longer Event (the Spanish conquest, the Atlantic revolutions, the peopling, the Columbian exchange) keep those links. The peopling, the megafauna's extinction, the Americas' isolation, their rise in share, the Mexican-American War and NAFTA, which span Northern and Latin America, stay in the hemisphere's frame. The New Laws, filed in Latin America's era, are placed in Latin America as well. No Event, interval or description changes.

upsert.boundary: Maize spreads through the Americas, about 4700 BCE to 1200 CE
upsert.description: From its domestication in south-western Mexico, maize travels as seed from farmer to farmer: it reaches South America, still only partly domesticated, by about 4500 BCE, the American Southwest by about 2100 BCE and the eastern woodlands by about 200 CE, changing as it goes into hundreds of local varieties. It becomes a staple slowly, as cobs grow larger: the Maya, the Andes and the Southwest depend on it within a few thousand years, the eastern woodlands only between about 900 and 1200. The crop spread farther than any people did.
provenance: sources to check: Kistler et al. 2018, Science 362; Staller, Tykot and Benz (eds.), Histories of Maize (2006)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern, Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The Beaver Wars and the Great Peace of Montreal, 1640 to 1701
upsert.description: Armed with Dutch guns and seeking beaver pelts and captives to replace their epidemic dead, the Haudenosaunee destroy or scatter the Wendat (1649), the Neutral, the Erie and others and fight New France for half a century, until the Great Peace of Montreal (1701) binds them, the French and some forty nations to peace.
provenance: sources to check: Richter, The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Lakes and the St Lawrence)

upsert.boundary: The bow and arrow spreads across the eastern woodlands and plains, about 400 to 700
upsert.description: Small arrow points replace the heavier darts of the spear-thrower across the eastern woodlands and the plains within a few centuries; hunters kill game at greater range, and the same weapon makes raiding deadlier, which some link to the palisaded and crowded villages that follow. The bow had reached the Arctic thousands of years earlier.
provenance: inferred: the spread as recalled; its link to rising violence is exploring
sources to check: Blitz 1988, American Antiquity 53; Milner 1999, Journal of Archaeological Research 7
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (eastern woodlands and plains)

upsert.boundary: Cabot, Cartier and the Grand Banks fishery, 1497 to 1542
upsert.description: John Cabot reaches Newfoundland for England (1497); within a decade Breton, Basque, Portuguese and English fishermen come every summer for the cod of the Grand Banks, and Basque whalers later work the Strait of Belle Isle. Jacques Cartier sails up the St Lawrence to Stadacona and Hochelaga (1534 to 1542) and takes the Iroquoian leader Donnacona to France; his attempt at a colony fails.
provenance: sources to check: Trudel, Histoire de la Nouvelle-France vol. 1 (1963); Kurlansky, Cod (1997)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Newfoundland and the St Lawrence); Europe

upsert.boundary: The Comanche ascendancy on the southern plains, about 1750 to 1850
upsert.description: Mounted Comanche bands, at peace with Spanish New Mexico after 1786, dominate the southern plains for a century, trading horses and captives, raiding deep into northern Mexico and holding Spanish, Mexican and Texan settlers at bay, until smallpox, cholera, drought and the thinning of the bison weaken them. Whether this was an empire, as Hämäläinen argues, or a powerful set of allied bands is debated.
provenance: inferred: the Comanche ascendancy as recalled; whether to call it an empire is debated
sources to check: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008); DeLay, War of a Thousand Deserts (2008)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the southern plains) and Central America (northern Mexico)

upsert.boundary: The Crow Creek massacre, about 1325
upsert.description: At a fortified farming village on the Missouri in South Dakota, nearly 500 men, women and children are killed and mutilated and lie in the village's own ditch; their skeletons show earlier hunger. Dated only to within a few decades of 1325, it is the clearest evidence of how deadly war among the plains villages could be in a time of drought and crowding.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date is known only to within decades
sources to check: Willey, Prehistoric Warfare on the Great Plains (1990)

upsert.boundary: The eastern woodlands domesticate their own crops, about 3000 to 1800 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers along the rivers of the Mississippi basin, tending the weedy plants of their camps, domesticate a local squash, sunflower, marsh elder and goosefoot (chenopod): one of the world's dozen or so independent centres of plant domestication, without maize, which arrives much later. The seeds add to nuts, fish and game; for two thousand years farming here supplements foraging rather than replacing it.
provenance: sources to check: Smith 2006, PNAS 103; Smith and Yarnell 2009, PNAS 106
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Mississippi basin)

upsert.boundary: De Soto and Coronado: the Spanish expeditions of 1539 to 1543
upsert.description: Hernando de Soto's army of about 600 marches from Florida through the Mississippian chiefdoms to the Mississippi, seizing food and porters and fighting at Mabila (1540); Francisco Vázquez de Coronado leads another from Mexico through the Pueblos to the plains of Kansas. When the French come down the Mississippi 140 years later, most of the towns de Soto saw are gone. Whether epidemics spreading ahead of colonists caused most of that loss, or the slave raids and wars of the later 1600s did, is debated.
provenance: inferred: the expeditions as recalled; how far epidemics ran ahead of colonists is debated
sources to check: Hudson, Knights of Spain, Warriors of the Sun (1997); Kelton, Epidemics and Enslavement (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the South-east and the Southwest)

upsert.boundary: Folsom bison hunters, about 12,800 to 11,900 years ago
upsert.description: On the Great Plains and in the Rockies, hunters with finely fluted Folsom points kill herds of an extinct, larger bison; at the Folsom site in New Mexico in 1927 a point found between bison ribs proved that people had lived in the Americas in the Ice Age. As mammoths disappear, bison become the plains hunters' staple, as they remain until the 1880s.
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Plains)

upsert.boundary: The Great Awakening, about 1730 to 1755
upsert.description: Revivals led by Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield and itinerant preachers sweep the colonies, splitting churches between 'new lights' and 'old lights', bringing enslaved Africans into evangelical Christianity and spreading a religion that is personal, emotional and wary of established authority.
provenance: sources to check: Kidd, The Great Awakening (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the British colonies)

upsert.boundary: Hohokam canals in the Salt and Gila valleys, about 450 to 1450
upsert.description: In the Sonoran Desert around modern Phoenix, the Hohokam dig hundreds of kilometres of canals, the largest irrigation system in pre-Columbian North America, grow maize, beans, squash and cotton, build ball courts like Mesoamerica's and trade shell from the Gulf of California; their towns are largely abandoned by about 1450, after floods and droughts.
provenance: sources to check: Fish and Fish (eds.), The Hohokam Millennium (2007)

upsert.boundary: Horses reach the Plains peoples, about 1680 to 1750
upsert.description: Horses taken in the Pueblo Revolt and traded and raided north from New Mexico reach the northern plains by about 1730. Comanche, Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow, Blackfoot and others become mounted bison hunters and warriors: farmers and foragers move onto the grasslands, wealth in horses divides rich from poor, and new powers rise. Guns arrive from the east at the same time, and epidemics follow both.
provenance: sources to check: Hämäläinen 2003, Journal of American History 90; Ewers, The Horse in Blackfoot Indian Culture (1955)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Plains)

upsert.boundary: The ice-free corridor opens, about 13,800 to 12,600 years ago
upsert.description: As the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets pull apart east of the Rockies, a corridor of meltwater lakes and bare ground opens from Alaska to the plains; on one reading of its plant and animal DNA it could support people along its whole length only from about 12,600 years ago, on another bison used it by 13,000. Either way it opened after people were at Monte Verde and the Paisley Caves, which is why most now think the first people came south along the Pacific coast, though the coastal sites lie drowned under the risen sea.
provenance: exploring: when the corridor could support people, and so which route came first, is debated
sources to check: Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature 537; Heintzman et al. 2016, PNAS 113

upsert.boundary: King Philip's War, 1675 to 1676
upsert.description: Metacom (Philip) of the Wampanoag leads Native nations of southern New England against colonies pressing on their land; perhaps a tenth of the colonists' men of military age and a far larger share of the region's Native people die, and many of the survivors are sold into slavery in the Caribbean, in the deadliest war per head in colonial North America. Native independence in southern New England ends.
provenance: sources to check: Lepore, The Name of War (1998)

upsert.boundary: Maize becomes the staple of the eastern woodlands, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: Maize, grown in small amounts in the east since about 200 CE, becomes the main food of the Mississippi valley and the South-east within a few centuries, as a hardier northern flint variety spreads and carbon isotopes in skeletons show diets turning to it; beans come later. The surplus feeds the Mississippian towns, and their people grow shorter and their teeth decay.
provenance: sources to check: Smith 1989, Science 246; Emerson et al. 2020, American Antiquity 85
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Mississippi valley and the South-east)

upsert.boundary: Maize farming reaches the Southwest, about 2100 to 1200 BCE
upsert.description: Maize is grown at Las Capas and other sites in the Tucson basin by about 2100 BCE, with irrigation canals by about 1200 BCE, the oldest in North America. Whether it came north with migrating farmers, perhaps speakers of Uto-Aztecan languages, or was taken up by local foragers is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how maize came north, with migrants or by adoption, is debated
sources to check: Mabry (ed.), Las Capas (2008); Merrill et al. 2009, PNAS 106

upsert.boundary: Mesa Verde and the abandonment of the Four Corners, about 1190 to 1290
upsert.description: Ancestral Puebloans build the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde and gather into larger, defensible villages; then, through the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299 and amid violence, tens of thousands leave the Four Corners within a generation for the Rio Grande, Zuni and Hopi, where their descendants live today.
provenance: sources to check: Kohler et al. 2014, PNAS 111
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Four Corners)

upsert.boundary: Epidemics among the north-eastern nations, 1616 to 1640
upsert.description: An epidemic of 1616 to 1619, perhaps leptospirosis, perhaps another disease, kills most of the coastal peoples of southern New England before the Pilgrims land in their empty fields (1620); smallpox follows in 1633 to 1634, and between 1634 and 1640 the Wendat (Huron) lose about half of their perhaps 20,000 people to measles, smallpox and influenza. The losses reshape the fur trade and the wars that follow.
provenance: inferred: the deaths as recalled; the disease of 1616 to 1619 is debated
sources to check: Marr and Cathey 2010, Emerging Infectious Diseases 16; Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (New England and the Great Lakes)

upsert.boundary: Ranked fishing societies of the north-west coast, about 1800 BCE to 1774
upsert.description: From the Columbia River to south-east Alaska, peoples who live on salmon, shellfish, sea mammals and cedar settle in plank-house villages and come to rank people as nobles, commoners and slaves, raise carved poles and give away wealth at potlatch feasts: unequal, complex societies of foragers, which accounts tying rank to farming did not expect. Spanish and British ships arrive in 1774 and 1778, and smallpox in the 1770s.
provenance: sources to check: Ames and Maschner, Peoples of the Northwest Coast (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Pacific north-west)

upsert.boundary: Old Copper: native copper worked around Lake Superior, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers of the upper Great Lakes dig pure native copper from veins and glacial drift and cold-hammer and anneal it into spear points, knives, awls and fishhooks, among the earliest metalworking anywhere; recent dates would push its start back to about 7500 BCE, which is disputed. They never smelt ore, and copper later becomes a material of ornament and exchange, reaching the Hopewell across half a continent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are disputed
sources to check: Pompeani et al. 2021, Quaternary International; Martin, Wonderful Power (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the upper Great Lakes)

upsert.boundary: People at the Paisley Caves, about 14,300 years ago
upsert.description: In caves above a vanished lake in Oregon, dried human faeces dated about 14,300 years ago carry Native American mitochondrial DNA, and stemmed points lie in layers as old as Clovis: people lived in the Great Basin before the Clovis hunters spread. Questions about contamination of the samples have been raised and answered; most now accept the dates.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; contamination of the samples has been argued and answered
sources to check: Gilbert et al. 2008, Science 320; Jenkins et al. 2012, Science 337

upsert.boundary: The first Arctic peoples cross to Greenland, about 2500 BCE
upsert.description: Hunters of the Arctic Small Tool tradition, with tiny chipped blades, bows and skin tents, move from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland within a few centuries (Saqqaq, Independence I). A 4,000-year-old Saqqaq genome shows they came from Siberia in a migration separate from that of other Native Americans; their Dorset successors hold the high Arctic until the Thule arrive.
provenance: sources to check: Rasmussen et al. 2010, Nature 463; Raghavan et al. 2014, Science 345
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Arctic and Greenland)

upsert.boundary: Poverty Point, about 1700 to 1100 BCE
upsert.description: On a bluff in north-eastern Louisiana, people who fish, hunt and gather raise six concentric earthen ridges over a kilometre across and mounds up to 22 metres high, one of them heaped up in a few months, and bring copper, galena, soapstone and flint from as far as 1,500 kilometres away: monumental building and long-distance exchange without farming or, as far as is known, a state.
provenance: sources to check: Ortmann and Kidder 2013, Geoarchaeology 28; Gibson, The Ancient Mounds of Poverty Point (2001)

upsert.boundary: Slavery becomes hereditary and racial in English America, 1619 to 1705
upsert.description: About twenty Africans are sold at Point Comfort, Virginia, in 1619; for decades bound Africans and English servants work the tobacco fields side by side. Then the law hardens: Virginia makes a child's status follow its mother's (1662), and after Bacon's Rebellion (1676), in which servants and slaves rose together, planters turn to enslaved Africans as servants grow scarce and dear; the slave codes of 1705 bind slavery to race. Carolina, founded on the Barbados model (1670), is a slave society from the start.
provenance: sources to check: Morgan, American Slavery, American Freedom (1975); Berlin, Many Thousands Gone (1998)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Virginia and the Carolinas)

upsert.boundary: Spanish Florida and New Mexico, 1565 to 1607
upsert.description: Spain founds St Augustine (1565), the oldest town of European origin in the United States, to guard the treasure fleets' route, and builds missions among the Timucua and Guale; in 1598 Juan de Oñate leads settlers up the Rio Grande to New Mexico and destroys Acoma Pueblo (1599), beginning the colony that Santa Fe (1610) will govern.
provenance: sources to check: Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (1992)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Florida and New Mexico)

upsert.boundary: The Vacant Quarter: the central Mississippi valley empties, about 1350 to 1450
upsert.description: Cahokia and the towns around the meeting of the Mississippi and the Ohio are abandoned, and a large region is left almost empty for centuries. Droughts and floods recorded in lake sediments and tree rings, war (palisades, burned towns) and the failure of the chiefdoms' politics are all proposed; the evidence in hand fits each, and their weight is debated. The people moved south and west, and Mississippian chiefdoms continue elsewhere into the sixteenth century.
provenance: exploring: the abandonment is inferred; its causes are debated
sources to check: Cobb and Butler 2002, American Antiquity 67; Munoz et al. 2015, PNAS 112
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the central Mississippi valley)

upsert.boundary: Latin American migration to the United States, from 1965
upsert.description: The 1965 immigration act ends national-origin quotas, and the end of the Bracero programme (1964) pushes Mexican labour migration outside the law; Mexicans, then Cubans, Dominicans, Central Americans, Colombians and Venezuelans move north, and the Hispanic share of the United States rises from about 4% (1960) to about 19% (2020), some 62 million people. Remittances become a mainstay of Mexico's and Central America's economies, while enforcement and the politics of the border harden from the 1990s.
provenance: sources to check: Massey, Durand and Malone, Beyond Smoke and Mirrors (2002); Pew Research Center, Hispanic population estimates

upsert.boundary: The Monroe Doctrine, December 1823
upsert.description: President Monroe declares the Americas closed to new European colonization and warns that the United States will treat European intervention in the new republics as hostile, while staying out of Europe's affairs. Britain's navy, not American power, enforces it at first; Roosevelt's corollary (1904) turns it into a claim to police the Caribbean and Central America.
provenance: sources to check: Sexton, The Monroe Doctrine (2011)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America and Latin America

upsert.boundary: The Apollo programme and the Moon landings, 1961 to 1972
upsert.description: Answering Sputnik and Gagarin, Kennedy commits the United States to a Moon landing (May 1961); at its peak taking about 4% of the federal budget and some 400,000 workers, NASA lands twelve men on the Moon in six missions from Apollo 11 (July 1969) to Apollo 17 (December 1972). Its lasting effects are argued: the race spurred integrated circuits and computing, and the photographs of the whole Earth became emblems of the environmental movement.
provenance: sources to check: Logsdon, John F. Kennedy and the Race to the Moon (2010)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: Rebellion and responsible government in Canada, 1837 to 1848
upsert.description: Failed rebellions in Lower and Upper Canada (1837 to 1838) lead to Lord Durham's report, the union of the Canadas (1841) and, in 1848, responsible government: the colony's ministers answer to its elected assembly rather than to the governor, a model of self-rule within the empire that the Australian colonies and New Zealand follow.
provenance: sources to check: Careless, The Union of the Canadas (1967)

upsert.boundary: Canadian Confederation, 1867 to 1871
upsert.description: The British North America Act unites Canada (Ontario and Quebec), Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as a self-governing dominion (1 July 1867); it buys Rupert's Land from the Hudson's Bay Company (1869 to 1870), adds Manitoba after the Red River resistance, and reaches the Pacific when British Columbia joins on the promise of a railway (1871).
provenance: sources to check: Morton, The Critical Years (1964)

upsert.boundary: Cotton and the second slavery in the United States, 1793 to 1860
upsert.description: After the cotton gin (1793) short-staple cotton spreads across the Deep South to Texas; about a million enslaved people are sold or marched west in the domestic slave trade, their families broken at auction. The enslaved population grows, mostly by births, from 0.7 million in 1790 to 3.95 million in 1860, and raw cotton becomes the largest American export and the main fibre of Britain's mills. How the planters raised output per worker, by the whip as Baptist argues or by better cotton seed as Olmstead and Rhode answer, is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the source of the rise in output per worker is debated
sources to check: Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Olmstead and Rhode 2018, Explorations in Economic History 67; Berlin, Generations of Captivity (2003)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the US South)

upsert.boundary: The crash and the Great Depression in the United States, 1929 to 1933
upsert.description: After the stock market crash of October 1929, banks fail in waves (about 9,000 by 1933), the money supply shrinks by about a third, prices fall and output falls by about a quarter; a quarter of workers are unemployed by 1933. The gold standard and the collapse of American lending and imports carry the slump around the world. Why it was so deep is argued: the monetary contraction and bank failures, the gold standard, debt and falling demand each have their advocates.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weights of its causes are debated
sources to check: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (1963); Eichengreen, Golden Fetters (1992); Bernanke 1983, American Economic Review 73
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Erie Canal, 1817 to 1825
upsert.description: New York State digs a 584-kilometre canal from the Hudson to Lake Erie; freight costs between Buffalo and New York City fall by about nine tenths, the Great Lakes' farms are tied to the Atlantic, New York becomes the country's leading port and city, and a boom of canals, then railways, follows.
provenance: sources to check: Sheriff, The Artificial River (1996); Howe, What Hath God Wrought (2007)

upsert.boundary: The great immigration, 1880 to 1924
upsert.description: About 25 million immigrants arrive in the United States, most from southern and eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Jews from the Russian empire), others from Scandinavia, Germany, Ireland, Mexico and, until the exclusion act of 1882, China; by 1910 about one American in seven was born abroad. Canada takes another three million, many of them to the prairies. They work the mines, mills and building sites of the industrial cities.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Great Migration, 1916 to 1970
upsert.description: About six million Black Southerners leave the cotton South, its sharecropping and its lynchings for the cities of the North and West, first for wartime factory jobs; Chicago, Detroit, New York and Los Angeles gain large Black communities, and the politics, music and civil rights movement of the century are made there as much as in the South.
provenance: sources to check: Wilkerson, The Warmth of Other Suns (2010); Gregory, The Southern Diaspora (2005)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Homestead Act and the settlement of the Plains, 1862 to 1934
upsert.description: The United States offers 160 acres of public land to any settler who farms it for five years; about 1.6 million claims succeed, covering about a tenth of the country's land, much of it taken from Plains nations by treaty and war. Railways, barbed wire and windmills turn the grasslands to wheat and cattle, until the Dust Bowl.
provenance: sources to check: Edwards, Friefeld and Wingo, Homesteading the Plains (2017)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Plains)

upsert.boundary: The United States restricts immigration, 1921 to 1924
upsert.description: Quota acts limit arrivals by national origin to a small share of each group's numbers in the census of 1890, cutting immigration from southern and eastern Europe by about nine tenths and barring Asians altogether; Mexicans and Canadians stay outside the quotas. Mass immigration to the United States ends for forty years.
provenance: sources to check: Ngai, Impossible Subjects (2004)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Boeing 707 begins scheduled jet service, October 1958
upsert.description: Pan Am's first scheduled Boeing 707 flight from New York to Paris (26 October 1958), three weeks after the British Comet 4 had flown the Atlantic and two years after the Soviet Tu-104 began jet service, opens the jet age of mass travel: at about 900 km/h, nearly twice the speed of the piston airliners, the 707 and the Douglas DC-8 cut the Atlantic crossing to under eight hours and, with lower costs per seat, make flying ordinary within two decades.
provenance: sources to check: Heppenheimer, Turbulent Skies (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (New York); Europe

upsert.boundary: The moving assembly line and the mass-produced car, 1913 to 1929
upsert.description: Ford's moving assembly line at Highland Park (1913) cuts the time to build a Model T from about twelve hours to about ninety minutes and its price by about two thirds; by 1929 Americans own about 23 million cars, most of the world's, and the mass production of cars, radios and appliances, sold on credit, spreads through the economy and abroad.
provenance: sources to check: Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production (1984)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Red River and North-West resistances, 1869 to 1885
upsert.description: When Canada takes over Rupert's Land without consulting its people, the Métis of Red River under Louis Riel form a provisional government (1869 to 1870) and win the province of Manitoba; as settlers, surveyors and the railway come west and the bison vanish, Métis and some Cree rise again in 1885, are defeated, and Riel is hanged. The numbered treaties (1871 to 1921) confine the prairie nations to reserves.
provenance: sources to check: Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Canadian prairies)

upsert.boundary: From the integrated circuit to the smartphone: American computing, 1958 to 2007
upsert.description: The integrated circuit (Kilby and Noyce, 1958 to 1959), the microprocessor (Intel's 4004, 1971), the personal computer (Apple II 1977, IBM PC 1981), the ARPANET's protocols and the commercial web, search (Google, 1998) and the iPhone (2007) come largely from American universities, defence budgets and the firms of Silicon Valley and Seattle; the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years, and computing becomes the general-purpose technology of the age.
provenance: sources to check: Ceruzzi, A History of Modern Computing (2nd ed. 2003); Isaacson, The Innovators (2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The opioid epidemic in the United States, from 1996
upsert.description: After OxyContin's launch (1996) and aggressive marketing, prescribed opioids, then heroin (from about 2010) and fentanyl (from about 2013) kill over 800,000 Americans by 2023, more than 100,000 a year at the peak (2021 and 2022); with suicides and alcohol, these deaths of despair among working-age adults hold US life expectancy down from 2014 to 2017 while it rises in other rich countries. Deaths begin to fall in 2024.
provenance: sources to check: Case and Deaton, Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism (2020); CDC WONDER mortality data
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: Quebec's Quiet Revolution and the sovereignty referendums, 1960 to 1995
upsert.description: Quebec's governments take education and health from the Catholic Church, nationalize hydroelectricity and make French the language of work; a sovereigntist party wins power (1976) and loses referendums on independence in 1980 (60% against) and 1995 (50.6% against). Canada becomes officially bilingual (1969) and brings home its constitution with a Charter of Rights (1982) without Quebec's assent.
provenance: sources to check: Behiels, Prelude to Quebec's Quiet Revolution (1985); McRoberts, Misconceiving Canada (1997)

upsert.boundary: Native self-determination, 1969 to 1999
upsert.description: From the occupation of Alcatraz (1969) and Wounded Knee (1973), Native activists press for treaty rights; the United States ends its policy of terminating tribes and passes the Indian Self-Determination Act (1975), and tribal governments gain control of schools, health care and, after 1988, gaming; Canada's constitution recognizes Aboriginal and treaty rights (1982), and Nunavut, governed by its Inuit majority, is created in 1999.
provenance: sources to check: Wilkinson, Blood Struggle (2005)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States and Canada)

upsert.boundary: Boarding and residential schools for Native children, 1879 to 1996
upsert.description: The United States, from the Carlisle school (1879), and Canada, through church-run residential schools made compulsory in 1920, take Native children from their families to strip them of their languages and religions; about 150,000 children pass through Canada's schools, the last of which closes in 1996, and thousands die in them. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) calls the system cultural genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, Final Report (2015); Adams, Education for Extinction (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States and Canada)

upsert.boundary: The United States becomes the largest industrial economy, 1870 to 1913
upsert.description: Steel from Carnegie's mills, oil from Rockefeller's refineries, electricity from Edison's and Westinghouse's systems, the corporation, the research laboratory and mass distribution make the United States the world's largest manufacturer by about 1890 and the maker of about a third of the world's manufactures by 1913, with the highest output per worker. A continental market, cheap land, abundant coal, iron and oil, immigrant labour and secure property all played a part; how much each mattered is argued.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weights of its causes are debated
sources to check: Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016); Wright 1990, American Economic Review 80; Bairoch 1982, Journal of European Economic History 11
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Seneca Falls convention, July 1848
upsert.description: About 300 women and men meet in upstate New York; Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments, modelled on the Declaration of Independence, demands women's equality, including, by a narrow vote, the right to vote: the start of an organized women's rights movement in the United States, which wins the federal vote in 1920.
provenance: sources to check: Wellman, The Road to Seneca Falls (2004)

upsert.boundary: The GI Bill, the highways and the suburbs, 1944 to 1970
upsert.description: Cheap federally insured mortgages, the GI Bill's loans and college places, the Interstate highways (from 1956) and the baby boom turn the United States into a nation of homeowners and suburbs: home ownership rises from about 44% (1940) to 63% (1970). Redlining and restrictive covenants keep most Black families out, widening the gap in wealth between Black and white households.
provenance: sources to check: Jackson, Crabgrass Frontier (1985); Rothstein, The Color of Law (2017)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: Texas breaks from Mexico, 1835 to 1836
upsert.description: American settlers in Mexican Texas, many of them slaveholders, and some Tejanos revolt against Santa Anna's centralist government; after the Alamo and Goliad, Texan forces capture Santa Anna at San Jacinto (April 1836). The Republic of Texas, recognized by the United States but not by Mexico, is annexed in 1845, the immediate cause of the Mexican-American War.
provenance: sources to check: Howe, What Hath God Wrought (2007)

upsert.boundary: The United States at war, 1941 to 1945
upsert.description: After Pearl Harbor the United States puts 16 million people into uniform and nearly doubles its output; it builds most of the Allies' aircraft, ships and trucks, fights across the Pacific and in Europe, loses about 405,000 dead, and makes and uses the atomic bomb. It also interns about 120,000 Japanese Americans. It ends the war as the strongest power on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, Freedom from Fear (1999); Overy, Why the Allies Won (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The War of 1812, 1812 to 1815
upsert.description: The United States declares war on Britain over impressment, trade and the western frontier, invades Canada and fails; British forces burn Washington (1814). The peace restores the old borders, Upper Canada's settlers and Loyalists stay British, and Tecumseh's confederacy of Native nations, allied with Britain, is defeated and Tecumseh killed (1813), ending Native resistance to settlement in the Old Northwest.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, The Civil War of 1812 (2010)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Lakes, Chesapeake and Gulf coast)

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 3, Northern America from 1763 to 2025: the Events inside its last three eras, from the War of 1812 and the cotton South to Canada's confederation and the Métis resistances, the second industrial revolution, mass immigration and its end, the Great Migration, the Depression, the boarding and residential schools, the war, the suburbs, the jet airliner, Apollo, American computing, Quebec, Native self-determination and the opioid epidemic; with two Events of the whole hemisphere, the Monroe Doctrine and Latin American migration north. The jet airliner names the fastest regular passenger speed, which it moves; its values follow in a later revision.

Cuba's example, training and arms help the Sandinistas and the Salvadoran guerrillas; fear of another Cuba shapes the American response.
The constitution of 1917, which puts land and subsoil under the nation, is the law Cárdenas applies.

Land taken from villages, a closed political system and Díaz's re-election in 1910 set off the revolt.
The droughts strike kingdoms already crowded and at war; how much of the collapse they explain is debated.

An Event of Central America's history that crosses the boundary of two of its eras.
