Mexico's transition, part of the spread of democracy since 1945.
Forced labour, tribute, hunger and the resettlement of villages leave people less able to survive the epidemic, whatever its disease.

upsert.boundary: United Fruit and the banana republics, 1899 to 1954
upsert.description: The United Fruit Company (1899) and its rivals take vast concessions of land, railways and ports in Guatemala, Honduras, Costa Rica and elsewhere, grow bananas for the American market and work closely with governments and dictators such as Ubico; US Marines occupy Nicaragua (1912 to 1933) and fight Sandino. When Guatemala's elected government expropriates the company's unused land, a CIA-backed coup overthrows it (1954).
provenance: sources to check: Bucheli, Bananas and Business (2005); Gleijeses, Shattered Hope (1991)

upsert.boundary: Cárdenas: land reform and the oil expropriation, 1934 to 1940
upsert.description: President Lázaro Cárdenas gives about 18 million hectares to peasant communities as ejidos, more than all his predecessors together, organizes workers and peasants within the ruling party, and nationalizes the foreign oil companies (March 1938) to found Pemex; the party of the Revolution becomes the corporate state that rules Mexico until 2000.
provenance: sources to check: Knight 1994, Journal of Latin American Studies 26; Meyer, Sherman and Deeds, The Course of Mexican History (11th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: The Caste War of Yucatán, 1847 to 1901
upsert.description: Maya peasants of eastern Yucatán, squeezed by sugar estates and taxes, rise against the creole elite and nearly take Mérida (1848); driven back, rebels guided by the Speaking Cross hold an independent territory in the eastern forests for half a century, until Mexican troops take their shrine town in 1901. Perhaps a third to a half of the peninsula's people die or flee.
provenance: sources to check: Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán (rev. ed. 2001); Rugeley, Yucatán's Maya Peasantry (1996)

upsert.boundary: The cocoliztli epidemic of 1545 to 1548
upsert.description: A haemorrhagic fever the Nahua called cocoliztli sweeps New Spain, killing perhaps 5 to 15 million on the highest estimates, or far fewer on critics' lower counts of the population before it: the deadliest epidemic of the conquest, worse than the smallpox of 1520. What it was is debated: an Old World disease, such as the Salmonella Paratyphi C found in victims' teeth at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, or a native fever spread by rodents in a great drought, as Acuña-Soto argues. On either account forced labour, hunger and the herding of people into new towns made it deadlier.
provenance: inferred: the epidemic as recalled; its toll and its disease are debated
sources to check: Acuña-Soto et al. 2002, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8; Vågene et al. 2018, Nature Ecology & Evolution 2; Borah and Cook (1963)

upsert.boundary: The cocoliztli epidemic of 1576 to 1580
upsert.description: A second great cocoliztli kills perhaps 2 million, about half of the Indigenous people left in central Mexico; with the earlier epidemics it leaves central Mexico's Indigenous population at a tenth or less of its size in 1519 by about 1600, on the usual figures. Its disease is debated as that of 1545 is.
provenance: inferred: the epidemic as recalled; its toll and its disease are debated
sources to check: Acuña-Soto et al. 2002, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8; Borah and Cook (1963)

upsert.boundary: Costa Rica's civil war and the abolition of its army, 1948 to 1949
upsert.description: After a disputed election, José Figueres wins a six-week civil war (1948); his junta abolishes the army and nationalizes the banks, and the constitution of 1949 confirms women's vote and full citizenship for Black Costa Ricans. Spending on schools and clinics rather than soldiers, Costa Rica stays a democracy through the region's coups and wars.
provenance: sources to check: Lehoucq and Molina, Stuffing the Ballot Box (2002)

upsert.boundary: Mexico's drug war, from December 2006
upsert.description: President Calderón sends the army against the cartels; they splinter and fight each other and the state, and homicides rise from about 8,900 (2007) to over 27,000 (2011) and about 36,000 a year (2018 to 2020), the highest in Mexico's modern record, with more than 100,000 people disappeared. American demand for drugs and American guns carried south feed the war, and the cartels move into extortion, fuel theft and the smuggling of migrants.
provenance: sources to check: INEGI homicide statistics; Grillo, El Narco (2011)

upsert.boundary: The Federal Republic of Central America, 1823 to 1841
upsert.description: After independence and a brief union with Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica form a federal republic; civil wars between liberals and conservatives break it apart, and by 1841 the five are separate republics, while Chiapas stays with Mexico.
provenance: sources to check: Woodward, Central America: A Nation Divided (3rd ed. 1999)

upsert.boundary: El Fin del Mundo: Clovis hunters in Sonora, about 13,400 years ago
upsert.description: At a spring in the Sonoran desert, hunters with Clovis points kill and butcher gomphotheres, elephant relatives that lived on in Mexico after they had vanished farther north. Among the oldest securely dated Clovis sites, it puts Clovis people in Mexico as early as anywhere in the north.
provenance: sources to check: Sanchez et al. 2014, PNAS 111

upsert.boundary: Mexico's wheat programme begins the Green Revolution, 1943 to 1963
upsert.description: Mexico's government and the Rockefeller Foundation set up a programme to breed better crops; Norman Borlaug's team crosses wheats for resistance to rust and, from the 1950s, for short, stiff stems that carry heavy grain with fertilizer and water. Mexico's wheat yields roughly triple, and the semi-dwarf wheats sent to India and Pakistan in the 1960s begin the Green Revolution; the programme becomes CIMMYT (1966).
provenance: sources to check: Perkins, Geopolitics and the Green Revolution (1997)

upsert.boundary: The coup in Guatemala, June 1954
upsert.description: A small rebel force, organized, armed and given aircraft by the CIA, and the army's refusal to defend him, overthrow Jacobo Árbenz, whose land reform had redistributed about a sixth of the country's farmland, including United Fruit's unused acres. The reform is reversed, and the military governments that follow fight a civil war (1960 to 1996) in which about 200,000 die, most of them Maya civilians.
provenance: sources to check: Gleijeses (1991); Comisión para el Esclarecimiento Histórico, Guatemala: Memoria del Silencio (1999)

upsert.boundary: The Manila galleons, 1565 to 1815
upsert.description: Once Urdaneta finds the eastward return across the North Pacific (1565), one or two Spanish galleons a year sail between Acapulco and Manila for 250 years, carrying American silver west and Chinese silk and porcelain east: the first regular trade route across the Pacific, which binds the economies of the Americas, Asia and Europe together.
provenance: sources to check: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez 1995, Journal of World History 6
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Acapulco); Asia: South-eastern Asia (Manila)

upsert.boundary: Street gangs and violence in the northern isthmus, from 1992
upsert.description: Gangs formed among Salvadoran refugees in Los Angeles, MS-13 and Barrio 18, are carried home by deportations after the peace accords; with the drug trade's transit routes they push homicide rates in El Salvador and Honduras above 80 per 100,000 in the 2010s, the highest of any countries at peace, and drive families north. El Salvador's state of exception from 2022 jails over 80,000 people and cuts its homicide rate to among the region's lowest, at the cost of due process.
provenance: sources to check: UNODC, Global Study on Homicide (2019); International Crisis Group reports on El Salvador (2022 to 2024)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala)

upsert.boundary: Mayapán, about 1220 to 1441
upsert.description: After Chichén Itzá's decline, the walled city of Mayapán rules much of the northern Yucatán through a council of lords who live in the city, with perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people; it is sacked in a revolt about 1441, in a time of drought and famine, and the peninsula divides into sixteen or so rival states, the ones the Spanish meet.
provenance: sources to check: Masson and Peraza Lope, Kukulcan's Realm (2014)

upsert.boundary: Mexico's democratic alternation, 2000
upsert.description: After reforms that made the Federal Electoral Institute independent (1996), the opposition wins the lower house (1997), and Vicente Fox of the National Action Party wins the presidency (July 2000), ending 71 years of rule by the party of the Revolution; power passes peacefully on 1 December.
provenance: sources to check: Magaloni, Voting for Autocracy (2006)

upsert.boundary: Mokaya villages and the first ball court, about 1900 to 1400 BCE
upsert.description: On the Pacific coast of Chiapas, Mokaya villagers make Barra pottery, some of the oldest in Mesoamerica, build a large house for a leading family at Paso de la Amada and, about 1650 BCE, the oldest known ball court: the rubber-ball game that spreads across Mesoamerica, with its rites and wagers, for three thousand years.
provenance: sources to check: Hill, Blake and Clark 1998, Nature 392

upsert.boundary: The Porfiriato, 1876 to 1911
upsert.description: Porfirio Díaz rules Mexico for most of 35 years; railways grow from about 600 to 19,000 kilometres, foreign capital flows into mines and oil, and exports multiply, while laws on vacant land let haciendas and companies take village lands, so that by 1910 most rural families own none. The Revolution begins against his re-election.
provenance: sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution vol. 1 (1986); Katz (ed.), Riot, Rebellion and Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: La Reforma and the French intervention, 1855 to 1867
upsert.description: Mexico's liberals end the Church's and the army's special courts, force the sale of the corporate lands of the Church and of villages (the Lerdo law, 1856) and write the constitution of 1857; conservatives fight the War of the Reform (1857 to 1861) and then back the French-installed emperor Maximilian, until Benito Juárez's republic defeats him and has him shot (1867).

upsert.boundary: The Tarascan state, about 1350 to 1530
upsert.description: From Tzintzuntzan by Lake Pátzcuaro, the Purépecha kings build a state in western Mexico that works copper and bronze and defeats an Aztec invasion (1478), the one neighbour the Triple Alliance never conquered; its last king submits to the Spanish in 1522 and is executed in 1530.
provenance: sources to check: Pollard, Taríacuri's Legacy (1993)

upsert.boundary: Droughts of the Terminal Classic, about 800 to 1000
upsert.description: Lake sediments and cave stalagmites in the Yucatán and Belize record a series of multi-year droughts between about 800 and 1000, among the driest spells of the past two thousand years there, with rainfall cut by perhaps a third to a half at their worst. Their timing matches the failure of the southern lowland kingdoms; how much they caused it, beside war and the strain of dense populations on cleared land, is debated.
provenance: inferred: the droughts from lake and cave records as recalled; their weight in the collapse is debated
sources to check: Hodell, Curtis and Brenner 1995, Nature 375; Kennett et al. 2012, Science 338; Evans et al. 2018, Science 361
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (the Maya lowlands)

upsert.boundary: The wars of Tikal and Calakmul, about 537 to 736
upsert.description: The Classic Maya's two great powers fight for two centuries through networks of allied and vassal kingdoms: Calakmul's Snake dynasty and its ally Caracol defeat Tikal (562), whose monuments fall silent for over a century; Tikal recovers under Jasaw Chan K'awiil and defeats Calakmul (695). The inscriptions that record these wars, read only since the 1980s, turned the Maya from peaceful astronomer-priests into the warring kingdoms they were.
provenance: sources to check: Martin and Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2nd ed. 2008)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Guatemala and Campeche)

upsert.boundary: Mesoamerican writing and the calendars, about 650 to 36 BCE
upsert.description: Glyphs appear on Olmec and Zapotec monuments by about 600 BCE (the dating of the earliest is disputed), with the 260-day ritual calendar; by the first century BCE the Long Count, a count of days from a fixed date in 3114 BCE written by place value, is carved at Chiapa de Corzo (36 BCE). Writing was invented here independently of the Old World, one of perhaps four inventions anywhere; the Maya script that grows from it is a full system of word signs and syllables, and the Maya later write a sign for zero.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are disputed
sources to check: Houston (ed.), The First Writing (2004); Saturno, Stuart and Beltrán 2006, Science 311
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Oaxaca, the Gulf coast and Chiapas)

upsert.boundary: The silver frontier: Zacatecas and the Chichimeca war, 1546 to 1600
upsert.description: Silver strikes at Zacatecas (1546) and Guanajuato draw Spaniards, Indigenous workers and enslaved Africans north into the lands of the nomadic peoples the Spanish called Chichimecas, who fight a forty-year war of raids on the silver roads (1550 to 1590), ended by gifts of food and goods and by settling Tlaxcalan colonists among them. New Spain's silver soon rivals Potosí's.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico (1971); Powell, Soldiers, Indians and Silver (1952)

upsert.boundary: The Zapatista rising in Chiapas, January 1994
upsert.description: On the day NAFTA takes effect, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation, mostly Maya peasants, seizes towns in Chiapas; after twelve days of fighting a ceasefire holds, and the Zapatistas, reaching supporters abroad through the new internet, govern autonomous communities in the highlands for decades: a challenge to the ruling party in the year its candidate was murdered and the peso collapsed.
provenance: sources to check: Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion (1998)

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 3, Central America: the Events inside Mexico's and the isthmus's own eras, from the Clovis hunters of Sonora, the first ball court and the invention of writing, through the Classic wars, the Terminal Classic droughts, Mayapán and the Tarascan state, the cocoliztli epidemics, the silver frontier and the Manila galleons, to the federation, the Caste War, La Reforma, the Porfiriato, the banana companies, Cárdenas, the wheat programme that began the Green Revolution, Costa Rica's abolition of its army, the 1954 coup, the Zapatistas, the alternation of 2000, the drug war and the gangs of the northern isthmus. The two cocoliztli epidemics name the Americas' share of humanity, which they move; their values follow in a later revision. Where the cause of an epidemic or a collapse is debated, the debate is stated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b), and disease is not credited alone (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd, its failure mode 'germs absolve').

upsert.boundary: Banwari Trace, Trinidad, about 6000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: A shell midden of foragers who came from the South American mainland, then all but joined to Trinidad, holds the oldest human burial in the Caribbean; the people fish, gather shellfish and hunt in the forest.
provenance: sources to check: Boomert, Trinidad, Tobago and the Lower Orinoco Interaction Sphere (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Baptist War and emancipation in the British Caribbean, 1831 to 1838
upsert.description: In the Baptist War of Christmas 1831, perhaps 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica strike and rise under Samuel Sharpe; its brutal suppression helps push Parliament to abolish slavery (1833, in force 1834). About 670,000 people in the British Caribbean are freed after an 'apprenticeship' of unpaid labour that ends in 1838; the owners, not the enslaved, receive £20 million in compensation, about two fifths of the government's yearly spending.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The Problem of Freedom (1992); Draper, The Price of Emancipation (2010)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The British Caribbean's independence, 1962 to 1983
upsert.description: After the West Indies Federation breaks up (1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent (1962), then Barbados and, on the mainland, Guyana (1966), the Bahamas (1973), Grenada (1974) and the smaller islands, the last St Kitts and Nevis (1983); most remain parliamentary democracies on the Westminster model. Anguilla, the Cayman Islands and others stay British.
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The Code Noir, March 1685
upsert.description: Louis XIV's edict governs slavery in France's islands: it requires baptism, forbids work on Sundays and the separation of families by sale, and defines the enslaved as movable property whom masters may chain and whip and the state may mutilate or kill for flight or for striking a master. Its protections are rarely enforced; its definition of people as property is.
provenance: sources to check: Sala-Molins, Le Code noir ou le calvaire de Canaan (1987)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the French islands)

upsert.boundary: Slavery ends in Cuba, 1880 to 1886
upsert.description: A law of 1880 turns Cuba's remaining enslaved people into 'apprentices' (the patronato) bound to their masters; many buy or win their freedom early, and the system ends in October 1886, two years before Brazil's abolition. Puerto Rico had abolished slavery in 1873.
provenance: sources to check: Scott, Slave Emancipation in Cuba (1985)

upsert.boundary: The Duvaliers in Haiti, 1957 to 1986
upsert.description: François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier, elected in 1957, rules through terror and his militia, the Tontons Macoutes, declares himself president for life (1964) and passes power to his son Jean-Claude (1971), who is driven out by protest in 1986; tens of thousands are killed and hundreds of thousands, many of the educated, leave.
provenance: sources to check: Abbott, Haiti: The Duvaliers and Their Legacy (1988)

upsert.boundary: Africans and sugar on Hispaniola, 1501 to 1530
upsert.description: The first enslaved Africans are taken to Hispaniola from Spain (1501), and as the Taíno die the Crown licenses shipments direct from Africa (1518); the island's first sugar mills grind by about 1516, and by the 1530s some thirty mills worked by enslaved Africans make Santo Domingo the first plantation colony in the Americas. The first slave revolt in the Americas breaks out there in 1521.
provenance: sources to check: Stevens-Arroyo 1993, Comparative Studies in Society and History 35; Higman, A Concise History of the Caribbean (2011)

upsert.boundary: The first people reach Cuba and Hispaniola, about 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers cross open sea to the Greater Antilles, the first settlement in the Americas of islands out of sight of the mainland; their flaked-stone tools resemble those of Belize and Yucatán, which suggests a crossing from Central America, but a route from South America is also argued, and the evidence fits both. Ground sloths and other island animals disappear in the millennia after people arrive.
provenance: inferred: the arrival as recalled; its source is debated
sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Steadman et al. 2005, PNAS 102
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Cuba and Hispaniola)

upsert.boundary: The Haiti earthquake, January 2010
upsert.description: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes near Port-au-Prince; estimates of the dead range from under 100,000 to over 300,000, the figures disputed, and much of the capital, the presidential palace included, collapses. A cholera epidemic brought by UN peacekeepers follows and kills about 10,000.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is disputed
sources to check: USGS event summary; Piarroux et al. 2011, Emerging Infectious Diseases 17

upsert.boundary: Haiti's independence debt, 1825 to 1947
upsert.description: With warships off Port-au-Prince, France demands 150 million francs, later cut to 90 million, as compensation for former slaveholders and the price of recognizing Haiti; Haiti borrows from French banks to pay, and services the debt and its refinancing for over a century, the last payments made in 1947. How much it held back Haiti's development is argued; one estimate puts the growth lost at 21 to 115 billion dollars today.
provenance: inferred: the debt as recalled; the estimate of its cost is exploring
sources to check: Gaffield (ed.), The Haitian Declaration of Independence (2016); The New York Times, 'The Ransom' (May 2022)

upsert.boundary: Havana and the treasure fleets, 1561 to 1640
upsert.description: From 1561 Spain's silver ships sail in convoys that gather at Havana each year before crossing to Seville; the harbour is ringed with forts and the city grows on provisioning, shipbuilding and repairs. French, English and Dutch privateers raid the coasts, Drake sacks Santo Domingo (1586), and Piet Heyn captures a whole silver fleet off Cuba (1628).
provenance: sources to check: de la Fuente, Havana and the Atlantic in the Sixteenth Century (2008)

upsert.boundary: Cuba's War of Independence, 1895 to 1898
upsert.description: José Martí, killed in its first weeks, Máximo Gómez and Antonio Maceo lead a war that burns the sugar estates; Spain's general Weyler herds rural Cubans into reconcentration camps, where perhaps 100,000 to 170,000 die of hunger and disease. The United States intervenes in 1898 and takes the war and the peace into its own hands.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the camp deaths are disputed
sources to check: Ferrer (1999); Pérez, The War of 1898 (1998)

upsert.boundary: England takes Jamaica, May 1655
upsert.description: Cromwell's Western Design fails to take Santo Domingo but seizes lightly held Jamaica; the Spanish free their slaves, who take to the mountains as the first maroons, and Port Royal becomes a base for buccaneers before sugar makes Jamaica Britain's richest colony.
provenance: sources to check: Burnard, Jamaica in the Age of Revolution (2020); Higman (2011)

upsert.boundary: The Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, about 1200 to 1797
upsert.description: The people Europeans called Island Caribs hold the Lesser Antilles; whether they were late migrants from the mainland or descendants of the islands' earlier farmers is debated. They resist Spanish slave raids and fight the English and French for two centuries; on St Vincent they mix with escaped Africans as the Garifuna, whom Britain deports to the coast of Honduras in 1797 after the Second Carib War. A Kalinago territory survives on Dominica.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; their origin is debated
sources to check: Hulme, Colonial Encounters (1986); Keegan and Hofman (2017)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Lesser Antilles)

upsert.boundary: The labour rebellions of the British Caribbean, 1934 to 1939
upsert.description: Strikes and riots spread among sugar, oil and dock workers from St Kitts and Trinidad (1937) to Jamaica (1938), where dozens are killed; from them come the trade unions and parties, Bustamante's and Manley's in Jamaica, Butler's in Trinidad, that win universal adult suffrage (Jamaica, 1944) and lead the islands to independence.
provenance: sources to check: Bolland, On the March (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: English, French and Dutch footholds in the Lesser Antilles, 1624 to 1640
upsert.description: England and France share St Kitts (1624) and massacre its Kalinago (1626); England settles Barbados (1627), Nevis and Antigua, France Martinique and Guadeloupe (1635), and the Dutch Curaçao (1634). Settled first for tobacco and cotton by indentured Europeans, these islands are where the sugar revolution begins.
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, Sugar and Slaves (1972)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Lesser Antilles)

upsert.boundary: The First Maroon War and the treaties of 1739
upsert.description: Maroons of Jamaica's mountains, led by Cudjoe in the west and Nanny and Quao in the east, fight the colony's troops for a decade, until Britain signs treaties recognizing their freedom and land in return for sending back future runaways and fighting rebels: a free Black people inside a slave colony, like the quilombos of Brazil and the maroon nations of Suriname.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell, The Maroons of Jamaica 1655-1796 (1988)

upsert.boundary: The Cuban missile crisis, October 1962
upsert.description: American spy planes find Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba; for thirteen days the United States blockades the island and the superpowers come closer to nuclear war than at any other time, until Khrushchev withdraws the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba and the quiet removal of US missiles from Turkey.
provenance: sources to check: Fursenko and Naftali, One Hell of a Gamble (1997); Dobbs, One Minute to Midnight (2008)

upsert.boundary: Saladoid farmers sail from the Orinoco to Puerto Rico, about 500 to 300 BCE
upsert.description: Canoe-borne farmers from the lower Orinoco settle the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico within a few centuries, skipping islands as they go; ancient DNA shows them to be a population from South America that largely replaces or absorbs the Archaic islanders of the east, though in places the two live side by side for centuries.
provenance: sources to check: Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590; Keegan and Hofman (2017)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico)

upsert.boundary: Cuba's Special Period, 1991 to 2000
upsert.description: When Soviet aid and trade end, Cuba's economy shrinks by about a third between 1990 and 1993; food and fuel run short, Cubans lose weight, and an epidemic of optic neuropathy follows malnutrition. The government legalizes the dollar and opens to tourism and foreign investment; tens of thousands flee by raft in 1994.
provenance: sources to check: Pérez (2015); Franco et al. 2013, BMJ 346

upsert.boundary: Taíno chiefdoms, about 1200 to 1492
upsert.description: In Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and eastern Cuba, chiefs (caciques) rule districts of villages from towns with stone-lined ball courts and plazas, lead the cohoba rite in which they speak with the zemís, and organize mounded fields of cassava; five paramount chiefdoms divide Hispaniola when Columbus arrives. Taíno words for hurricane, canoe, hammock, tobacco and barbecue pass into European languages.
provenance: sources to check: Rouse, The Tainos (1992); Oliver, Caciques and Cemí Idols (2009)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Greater Antilles)

upsert.boundary: Cuba's Ten Years' War, 1868 to 1878
upsert.description: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes frees his slaves and declares Cuba's independence (October 1868); a decade of war in the east, with Antonio Maceo among its generals, ends in the Pact of Zanjón without independence, but with the end of slavery set in motion.
provenance: sources to check: Ferrer, Insurgent Cuba (1999)

upsert.boundary: Trujillo's dictatorship in the Dominican Republic, 1930 to 1961
upsert.description: Rafael Trujillo, commander of the guard the Americans trained, rules the Dominican Republic as his estate for 31 years; in the Parsley Massacre of October 1937 his army kills perhaps 12,000 to 20,000 Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian descent along the border. He is assassinated in 1961.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the massacre's toll is disputed
sources to check: Turits, Foundations of Despotism (2003)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Dominican Republic)

upsert.boundary: US occupations of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, 1915 to 1934
upsert.description: US Marines land in Haiti (1915) after its president is killed, and in the Dominican Republic (1916); they take over customs and finances, build roads with forced labour, crush the Caco rebels in Haiti and train the national guards from which Trujillo rises. The Dominican occupation ends in 1924, the Haitian in 1934.
provenance: sources to check: Renda, Taking Haiti (2001); Calder, The Impact of Intervention (1984)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Haiti and the Dominican Republic)

upsert.boundary: The Windrush generation, 1948 to 1962
upsert.description: The Empire Windrush lands about 500 Caribbean migrants at Tilbury in June 1948; by 1962, when Britain's Commonwealth Immigrants Act restricts entry, about a quarter of a million West Indians have come to work in its hospitals, transport and factories. Thousands of their descendants find their right to stay questioned in the scandal of 2018.
provenance: sources to check: Phillips and Phillips, Windrush (1998)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean; Europe: Northern Europe (Britain)

upsert.boundary: The clearing of the Amazon, from 1970
upsert.description: The Trans-Amazonian Highway (from 1970) and subsidized settlement open the forest to ranchers, farmers, loggers and miners; by the 2020s about a fifth of Brazil's Amazon forest is gone, most of it to cattle pasture and later soy. Clearing peaks at about 27,000 square kilometres a year (2004), falls by about four fifths under enforcement by 2012, then rises again; parts of the south-east Amazon now give off more carbon than they absorb.
provenance: sources to check: INPE PRODES deforestation series; Gatti et al. 2021, Nature 595

upsert.boundary: Early pottery on the lower Amazon, about 5500 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: At Taperinha, a shell mound near Santarém, people who gather shellfish and fish make sand- and shell-tempered pottery about 7,000 years old, among the oldest in the Americas and older than any in Mesoamerica or the Andes; pottery appears later on the coasts of Colombia (San Jacinto) and Ecuador (Valdivia, about 3800 BCE).
provenance: sources to check: Roosevelt et al. 1991, Science 254
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (the lower Amazon)

upsert.boundary: Towns and earthworks of Amazonia, about 500 BCE to 1600 CE
upsert.description: Laser surveys from the air and excavation show that the Amazon was not an empty forest: the Upano valley of Ecuador holds towns of platforms and straight roads (about 500 BCE to 600 CE); Marajó island has mound villages and fine painted pottery (about 400 to 1400); the Casarabe towns of the Llanos de Moxos are linked by causeways and canals (about 500 to 1400); the Upper Xingu holds walled settlements joined by roads (about 1250 to 1650); and fertile dark earths mark long settlement along the rivers. How many people lived in Amazonia in 1492 is debated, from about 2 to perhaps 8 million or more: the forest's silence was evidence of emptiness only as far as earlier searches could have found what lay under it.
provenance: inferred: the sites as recalled; the population is debated
sources to check: Rostain et al. 2024, Science 383; Prümers et al. 2022, Nature 606; Heckenberger et al. 2008, Science 321; Denevan 1992, Annals of the Association of American Geographers 82

upsert.boundary: Argentina's export boom and mass immigration, 1880 to 1914
upsert.description: Railways built with British capital open the pampas, taken from their Indigenous peoples in the Conquest of the Desert (1878 to 1885), to wheat and to cattle shipped as chilled beef; about four million immigrants arrive, mostly Italians and Spaniards, and by 1914 a third of the people of Argentina are foreign-born. Growth puts Argentina among the ten or so richest countries per person by 1913 on Maddison's figures, a ranking some economists think overstated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the ranking is debated
sources to check: Della Paolera and Taylor (eds.), A New Economic History of Argentina (2003); Maddison Project Database

upsert.boundary: The bandeirantes, about 1600 to 1720
upsert.description: Armed expeditions of São Paulo's mixed Portuguese and Indigenous settlers range deep into the interior, enslaving tens of thousands of Indigenous people, Guaraní from the Jesuit missions among them, and searching for gold; they push Brazil's frontier far west of the Tordesillas line and find the gold of Minas Gerais in the 1690s.
provenance: sources to check: Monteiro, Negros da terra (1994)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Brazil and Paraguay)

upsert.boundary: The Bolivian revolution, 1952 to 1953
upsert.description: Miners and townspeople of the National Revolutionary Movement defeat the army in April 1952; the new government gives the vote to all adults, most of them Indigenous and unable to read, nationalizes the great tin mines and, as peasants seize the haciendas, decrees a land reform (1953).
provenance: sources to check: Klein, A Concise History of Bolivia (2nd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: Cabral claims Brazil for Portugal, April 1500
upsert.description: A Portuguese fleet bound for India under Pedro Álvares Cabral swings wide into the Atlantic, reaches the coast of Bahia and claims the land, which falls on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line; for thirty years traders cut brazilwood for its red dye with the labour of the coastal Tupi, until settlement and sugar begin in the 1530s.
provenance: sources to check: Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society (1985)

upsert.boundary: The Chaco War, 1932 to 1935
upsert.description: Bolivia and Paraguay fight over the dry Chaco, thought to hold oil; perhaps 90,000 to 100,000 soldiers die, many of thirst and disease, and Paraguay keeps most of the territory. Defeat discredits Bolivia's old order and sets it on the road to the revolution of 1952.
provenance: sources to check: Farcau, The Chaco War (1996)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Bolivia and Paraguay)

upsert.boundary: Chávez's Bolivarian revolution, 1999 to 2013
upsert.description: Hugo Chávez, a former officer who had led a failed coup (1992), wins the presidency (1998), rewrites the constitution, survives a coup (2002) and an oil strike, and spends the oil boom on social programmes, price controls and expropriations while concentrating power; poverty falls while oil prices are high, and the state oil company's output declines.
provenance: sources to check: Corrales and Penfold, Dragon in the Tropics (2nd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The coup in Chile, 11 September 1973
upsert.description: With American encouragement and the economy in crisis, the armed forces bomb the presidential palace, and Salvador Allende, the elected socialist president, dies inside. General Pinochet rules for seventeen years: over 3,000 people are killed or disappeared and tens of thousands tortured, while his 'Chicago boys' privatize and open the economy. A plebiscite he loses in 1988 leads to elections and democracy in 1990.
provenance: sources to check: Rettig Commission report (1991); Kornbluh, The Pinochet File (2003)

upsert.boundary: Chinchorro mummies, about 5050 to 1720 BCE
upsert.description: Fishing people of the Atacama coast take apart their dead, rebuild them with sticks, reeds and clay, paint them black or red and give them masks: the oldest deliberate mummification known, two thousand years before Egypt's, made for children and adults alike, ordinary people rather than rulers.
provenance: sources to check: Arriaza, Beyond Death (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (northern Chile and southern Peru)

upsert.boundary: Coffee makes São Paulo, 1850 to 1930
upsert.description: Coffee spreads from the Paraíba valley onto the red soils of São Paulo, and Brazil grows most of the world's coffee, at first with enslaved labour and, after the slave trade's end (1850) and abolition (1888), with about two million subsidized immigrants from Italy, Portugal, Spain and Japan. Coffee money builds São Paulo's railways and first factories, and the collapse of its price in 1929 helps bring Vargas to power.
provenance: sources to check: Holloway, Immigrants on the Land (1980); Dean, The Industrialization of São Paulo (1969)

upsert.boundary: Colombia's armed conflict, 1964 to 2016
upsert.description: Communist guerrillas (the FARC from 1964, and the ELN), right-wing paramilitaries, drug cartels and the state fight for half a century, and cocaine money sustains them all from the 1980s. About 450,000 people are killed and some 8 million displaced, the largest internal displacement in the hemisphere, until the FARC signs a peace accord (2016) that a referendum narrowly rejects and congress then approves.
provenance: sources to check: Comisión de la Verdad (Colombia), Informe final (2022)

upsert.boundary: Argentina's Dirty War, 1976 to 1983
upsert.description: Argentina's junta kidnaps, tortures and kills suspected leftists and many others in secret camps; the truth commission documented about 9,000 disappearances and human rights groups count up to 30,000, a number that is disputed. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo march for their children from 1977, and defeat in the Falklands War (1982) brings the junta down.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is disputed
sources to check: CONADEP, Nunca Más (1984)

upsert.boundary: Dutch Brazil, 1630 to 1654
upsert.description: The Dutch West India Company takes Recife and Pernambuco, the world's richest sugar coast, and seizes Portuguese slaving posts in Angola to supply it; under Johan Maurits it brings painters and naturalists. Luso-Brazilian planters drive the Dutch out by 1654, and Dutch and Sephardic Jewish planters and merchants carry the sugar mill, its credit and its slaving methods to Barbados and the Caribbean.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how much the Dutch carried sugar to the Caribbean is debated
sources to check: Boxer, The Dutch in Brazil (1957); Schwartz (1985)

upsert.boundary: Peru's guano age, 1840 to 1880
upsert.description: Bird droppings piled on the Chincha islands become the richest fertilizer of Europe and North America; Peru's state earns most of its revenue from them for forty years, dug by about 100,000 Chinese indentured labourers in brutal conditions, and borrows against them until the deposits run out and the state defaults (1876). The Atacama's nitrates follow, and with them war.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Between Silver and Guano (1989); Cushman, Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World (2013)

upsert.boundary: Epidemic and civil war in the Inca empire, about 1527 to 1532
upsert.description: An epidemic, perhaps smallpox carried ahead of the Spanish, kills the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir about 1527; his sons Huascar, in Cusco, and Atahualpa, with the northern army at Quito, fight a war of succession that Atahualpa's generals win in 1532, killing much of Huascar's lineage, just as Pizarro lands. Whether the disease was smallpox, and so how early it arrived, is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the disease is debated
sources to check: D'Altroy, The Incas (2nd ed. 2014); Cook, Born to Die (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Jesuit missions of Paraguay, 1609 to 1768
upsert.description: Jesuits gather Guaraní into some thirty mission towns along the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, with up to about 140,000 people at their height, where Guaraní is written and spoken, fields and workshops are run in common, and armed militias defend them against slave raiders. Spain and Portugal's exchange of territory brings the Guaraní war (1754 to 1756), and the Jesuits' expulsion (1767 to 1768) ends the missions.
provenance: sources to check: Ganson, The Guaraní under Spanish Rule in the Río de la Plata (2003)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil)

upsert.boundary: La Violencia in Colombia, 1948 to 1958
upsert.description: The murder of the Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán (April 1948) sets off riots in Bogotá and a decade of killing between Liberals and Conservatives in the countryside that claims about 200,000 lives; it ends in a power-sharing pact, the National Front, that shuts others out, and its peasant self-defence groups are the seed of the FARC (1964).
provenance: sources to check: Palacios, Between Legitimacy and Violence (2006)

upsert.boundary: The Falklands War, April to June 1982
upsert.description: Argentina's junta seizes the British-held Falkland Islands (Malvinas); Britain sends a task force and retakes them in ten weeks, with about 650 Argentine and 255 British dead. Defeat brings the junta's fall and Argentina's return to democracy in 1983.
provenance: sources to check: Freedman, The Official History of the Falklands Campaign (2005)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (the Falkland Islands and Argentina)

upsert.boundary: Squash and manioc in the forest islands of south-western Amazonia, about 8300 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: In the Llanos de Moxos of Bolivia, people build up thousands of forest islands in the seasonally flooded savanna and grow squash by about 8300 BCE and manioc by about 6800 BCE, among the earliest cultivation in the Americas. Amazonia is one of the world's centres of plant domestication, the home of manioc, peanuts, peach palm and cacao, grown in the upper Amazon of Ecuador by about 3300 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lombardo et al. 2020, Nature 581; Zarrillo et al. 2018, Nature Ecology & Evolution 2

upsert.boundary: The Mapuche hold the south, 1550 to 1883
upsert.description: The Mapuche, who had checked the Inca at the Maule river, kill the conquistador Valdivia (1553) and in the rising of 1598 destroy the Spanish towns south of the Biobío; for nearly three centuries the river is a frontier, crossed by trade and by treaties made at parliaments with the Spanish Crown. Only between the 1860s and the 1880s do Chile's 'Pacification of Araucanía' and Argentina's 'Conquest of the Desert' conquer the Mapuche and the peoples of the pampas and Patagonia.
provenance: sources to check: Bengoa, Historia del pueblo mapuche (1985)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Chile and Argentina)

upsert.boundary: Andean metalworking begins, about 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Smiths of the southern Peruvian highlands hammer gold into thin foil (Waywaka, about 1500 BCE); later Andean smiths smelt copper, alloy it with arsenic and then tin into bronze, and gild and silver copper by chemical means. In the Andes metal serves rank and ritual far more than work.
provenance: sources to check: Aldenderfer et al. 2008, PNAS 105; Lechtman 1984, Technology and Culture 25

upsert.boundary: The Muisca of the Colombian highlands, about 600 to 1537
upsert.description: In the high valleys around Bogotá, the Muisca, perhaps half a million to two million maize and potato farmers, live under two rival paramount chiefs, the zipa and the zaque, mine salt and emeralds and cast gold into votive figures; the rite of a chief covered in gold dust at Lake Guatavita becomes the legend of El Dorado. Jiménez de Quesada's expedition conquers them in 1537.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; their numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Langebaek, Los muiscas (2019)

upsert.boundary: Palmares, about 1605 to 1695
upsert.description: In the hills of Alagoas, people who escaped Pernambuco's sugar estates build a federation of quilombo villages, perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 strong at its height, that defeats Dutch and Portuguese expeditions for most of a century; it falls to a bandeirante army in 1694, and its leader Zumbi is killed in 1695. The day of his death, 20 November, is Black Consciousness Day in Brazil.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Anderson 1996, Journal of Latin American Studies 28

upsert.boundary: The Portuguese court in Rio and Brazil's independence, 1808 to 1822
upsert.description: Fleeing Napoleon's invasion under British escort, Portugal's prince regent and thousands of courtiers reach Rio (March 1808), open Brazil's ports to friendly nations and make it a kingdom equal to Portugal (1815); when the king returns to Lisbon, his son Pedro declares Brazil independent (September 1822) and becomes its emperor, keeping the country united, monarchical and slaveholding.
provenance: sources to check: Wilcken, Empire Adrift (2004); Barman, Brazil: The Forging of a Nation (1988)

upsert.boundary: The Amazon rubber boom, 1879 to 1912
upsert.description: Demand for tyres and insulation makes wild Amazonian rubber one of the world's most valuable commodities; Manaus builds an opera house, Brazil takes Acre from Bolivia, and tappers, many of them indebted migrants from the drought-stricken north-east, spread up every river. In the Putumayo the Peruvian Amazon Company's agents enslave and kill tens of thousands of Indigenous people. Plantations in Malaya and Ceylon, grown from seeds taken from Brazil in 1876, undercut it after 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Weinstein, The Amazon Rubber Boom (1983); Goodman, The Devil and Mr Casement (2009)

upsert.boundary: The sambaquis: shell mounds of the Brazilian coast, about 6000 BCE to 1000 CE
upsert.description: Along the lagoons and bays of southern Brazil, fishing peoples heap shells, earth and the bones of their dead into mounds, some over 30 metres high, raised and used as cemeteries for thousands of years; like Poverty Point and the north-west coast, they are monuments and settled lives made by people who did not farm.
provenance: sources to check: Gaspar et al. 2008, in Silverman and Isbell (eds.), Handbook of South American Archaeology
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (the Brazilian coast)

upsert.boundary: U-shaped temples of the Peruvian coast, about 1800 to 900 BCE
upsert.description: In the valleys of the central and north coast, people who farm irrigated fields and fish build huge U-shaped platform complexes facing the mountains and their rivers; Sechín Alto in the Casma valley, about 300 by 250 metres at its base, is among the largest buildings anywhere in its time.
provenance: sources to check: Burger, Chavín and the Origins of Andean Civilization (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Shining Path's war in Peru, 1980 to 2000
upsert.description: A Maoist party led by Abimael Guzmán begins a war in the Ayacucho highlands (May 1980) that kills about 69,000 people, most of them Quechua-speaking peasants, killed by the Shining Path and by the army and police in comparable numbers; Guzmán's capture (1992) breaks it, under Fujimori's authoritarian rule.
provenance: sources to check: Comisión de la Verdad y Reconciliación, Informe final (2003)

upsert.boundary: Viceroy Toledo's reforms, 1569 to 1581
upsert.description: Francisco de Toledo tours the viceroyalty, resettles about 1.5 million Andean people into some 800 Spanish-style towns, fixes their tribute, organizes the mita that sends a seventh of the men of sixteen highland provinces to Potosí each year, brings in mercury amalgamation that multiplies the silver output, and executes the last Inca of Vilcabamba, Túpac Amaru (1572).
provenance: sources to check: Stern, Peru's Indian Peoples and the Challenge of Spanish Conquest (1982); Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (the Viceroyalty of Peru)

upsert.boundary: The War of the Pacific, 1879 to 1884
upsert.description: Chile, allied with British-owned nitrate companies, fights Bolivia and Peru over the nitrate deserts of the Atacama; it wins at sea, occupies Lima (1881) and takes Bolivia's coast and Peru's southern provinces, leaving Bolivia landlocked and Chile rich on nitrate exports for forty years, until synthetic nitrogen ends the boom.
provenance: sources to check: Sater, Andean Tragedy (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Chile, Bolivia and Peru)

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 3, South America: the Events inside the continent's own eras, from the Chinchorro mummies, the forest islands where squash and manioc were first grown, the first pottery and the shell mounds, through the Initial Period's temples and the first metalworking, the towns of Amazonia, the Muisca and the Mapuche, Cabral and the Inca civil war, Toledo's reforms, Palmares, Dutch Brazil, the bandeirantes and the Jesuit missions, to the Portuguese court in Rio, the guano and nitrate wars, the rubber and coffee booms, Argentina's boom, the Chaco War, La Violencia, Bolivia's revolution, the coups and dirty wars, the Falklands, the Shining Path, Colombia's conflict, Chávez and the clearing of the Amazon. Where earlier accounts read the forest's silence as emptiness, the debate over Amazonia's people is stated (AbsenceEvidence#10a3).

upsert.boundary: Cocaine, the drug trade and the war on drugs, from 1971
upsert.description: Nixon declares a war on drugs (1971); as American demand for cocaine grows, coca from Peru, Bolivia and Colombia is refined in Colombia and smuggled through the Caribbean and, from the 1990s, Mexico; the Medellín and Cali cartels and then Mexico's cartels grow rich and armed. Eradication, extradition and Plan Colombia (2000) shift the trade rather than end it, and fentanyl joins it after 2013. The trade fuels the region's wars and its homicide rates.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Andean Cocaine (2008); UNODC, World Drug Report
upsert.region: The Americas: South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Northern America

upsert.boundary: Spanish America abolishes slavery, 1821 to 1854
upsert.description: The new republics first free the children of the enslaved (free-womb laws) and the slaves who fought for independence, then abolish slavery outright: Chile (1823), Central America (1824), Mexico (1829), Uruguay (1842), Colombia (1851), Argentina (1853), Venezuela and Peru (1854). Owners are usually compensated; the freed are not.
provenance: sources to check: Andrews, Afro-Latin America 1800-2000 (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Bourbon and Pombaline reforms, 1759 to 1808
upsert.description: Spain's Charles III and Portugal's Pombal tighten imperial rule: new viceroyalties (New Granada, Río de la Plata), intendants, monopolies on tobacco and spirits, higher sales taxes, standing militias, the expulsion of the Jesuits (1759 from Portugal's lands, 1767 from Spain's) and Spaniards preferred over American-born creoles for office. Revenue rises sharply; so do revolts, Túpac Amaru's and the Comuneros' among them, and the creoles' sense of being colonials.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, Bourbon Spain (1989); Brading, The First America (1991)

upsert.boundary: The society of castas, about 1550 to 1800
upsert.description: Spanish America ranks people by descent and status: Spaniards born in Spain or in America, Indians bound to tribute and labour drafts in their own 'republic' of towns, and the growing numbers of mestizos, mulattos and free and enslaved Africans between and below them, named in a vocabulary of castas that painters of the 1700s illustrate in series. The categories are fluid in daily life and can sometimes be bought out of, but they decide taxes, offices and marriage.
provenance: sources to check: Katzew, Casta Painting (2004); Martínez, Genealogical Fictions (2008)

upsert.boundary: Caudillos and civil wars, 1826 to 1870
upsert.description: After independence, strongmen with their own armies, from Rosas in Buenos Aires to Santa Anna in Mexico and Páez in Venezuela, rule or contest most of Spanish America, and liberals and conservatives fight over the Church, federalism and the lands of Indigenous communities. Output per person stagnates or falls in much of the region for half a century after 1820 by most estimates; whether the wars and disorder of independence or the institutions inherited from colonial rule did more to cause it is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the cause of the stagnation is debated
sources to check: Lynch, Caudillos in Spanish America (1992); Coatsworth 2008, Journal of Latin American Studies 40

upsert.boundary: The commodity boom and the left turn, 2003 to 2014
upsert.description: China's demand lifts the prices of soy, iron ore, copper and oil; South America grows fast, governments of the left, from Lula and Chávez to Morales and Correa, expand cash transfers such as Brazil's Bolsa Família, and extreme poverty and inequality fall in most countries, inequality for the first time in decades. When prices fall after 2014, recession, the Car Wash corruption scandal and protest follow.
provenance: sources to check: Lustig, López-Calva and Ortiz-Juarez 2013, World Development 44

upsert.boundary: The return to democracy, 1979 to 1990
upsert.description: Military rulers hand back power, discredited by repression, economic failure and, in Argentina, defeat in war: Ecuador (1979), Peru (1980), Bolivia (1982), Argentina (1983), Uruguay and Brazil (1985), Guatemala (1986), Paraguay (1989) and Chile (1990); Brazil's constitution of 1988 gives the vote to every adult, the illiterate included. With the Philippines and South Korea, these are the core of the third wave of democracy in the 1980s.
provenance: sources to check: Huntington, The Third Wave (1991); Mainwaring and Pérez-Liñán, Democracies and Dictatorships in Latin America (2013)

upsert.boundary: Export-led growth, 1880 to 1929
upsert.description: Steamships, railways and foreign capital make Latin America a supplier of food and raw materials: exports grow about 4% a year, output per person grows faster than in most of the world, and cities, ports and railways are built for export. But each country depends on one or two commodities and on foreign lenders, and the gains go mostly to landowners, mine owners and merchants. The collapse of commodity prices after 1929 ends the era.
provenance: sources to check: Bulmer-Thomas, The Economic History of Latin America since Independence (3rd ed. 2014)

upsert.boundary: Latin America's fertility transition, 1965 to 2005
upsert.description: Children per woman fall from about six in the early 1960s to about 2.4 by 2005, with the move to cities, schooling for girls, family-planning programmes and the pill, and television's picture of small families; Brazil's fall, with no state programme at all, is among the fastest anywhere. The Americas' share of humanity, which had risen for 150 years, stops rising by 1965 and falls after 1980.
provenance: sources to check: UN Population Division, World Population Prospects; Potter, Schmertmann and Cavenaghi 2002, Population Studies 56

upsert.boundary: Latin America's homicide epidemic, from about 1980
upsert.description: Homicide rates climb across much of the region from the 1980s, with the drug trade, urban gangs, guns, weak police and courts, and inequality: Colombia's reaches about 80 per 100,000 (1991); El Salvador's, Honduras's, Venezuela's and Jamaica's pass 50 in the 2000s and 2010s; Brazil records about 60,000 killings a year (2017). With about 8% of the world's people, Latin America and the Caribbean come to count about a third of its homicides, enough to halt the fall of the world's rate in the early 1990s.
provenance: sources to check: UNODC, Global Study on Homicide (2019); Igarapé Institute homicide monitor

upsert.boundary: Indentured labour from India and China, 1838 to 1917
upsert.description: After emancipation, planters bring workers bound by contracts of five years or more: about 240,000 Indians to British Guiana, about 145,000 to Trinidad, others to Suriname, Jamaica and the French islands; about 125,000 Chinese to Cuba (1847 to 1874) and about 100,000 to Peru's guano islands and plantations. Their descendants are the largest group in Guyana and Trinidad today.
provenance: sources to check: Northrup, Indentured Labor in the Age of Imperialism (1995); Hu-DeHart 1993, Slavery and Abolition 14
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean and South America; Asia: Southern and Eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: Import-substituting industrialization, 1930 to 1982
upsert.description: Cut off from export markets by the Depression and the war, governments build industry behind tariffs and quotas, found state oil, steel and power companies (Pemex, Petrobras, YPF) and development banks, guided after 1948 by the UN's Economic Commission for Latin America and Raúl Prebisch. Output per person roughly doubles from 1950 to 1980, as Brazil and Mexico become industrial economies, but industry stays protected and uncompetitive and, in the 1970s, runs on borrowed money.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its record is debated
sources to check: Bértola and Ocampo, The Economic Development of Latin America since Independence (2012)

upsert.boundary: Liberation theology and the Church of the poor, 1968 to 1990
upsert.description: At Medellín (1968) Latin America's bishops commit the Church to a 'preferential option for the poor'; priests and lay people organize tens of thousands of base communities, and Gutiérrez, Boff and others write theologies of liberation. Many are murdered by military regimes and death squads, Archbishop Romero of San Salvador among them (1980), and Rome reins the movement in during the 1980s.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Emergence of Liberation Theology (1991)

upsert.boundary: The rise of Pentecostal and evangelical churches, from about 1970
upsert.description: Pentecostal and evangelical churches, small before 1960, grow among the urban poor and in the countryside to about a fifth of Latin Americans by the 2010s, near half in Guatemala and Honduras and about a third in Brazil: the largest religious change in the region since the conversions of the 1500s, as the Catholic share falls from about nine tenths to about three fifths. Their pastors become a force in politics.
provenance: sources to check: Pew Research Center, Religion in Latin America (2014)

upsert.boundary: The Treaty of Tordesillas, June 1494
upsert.description: With the pope's blessing, Castile and Portugal divide the lands outside Christendom at a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: the Americas west of it to Castile; Africa, the route to India and, as it turns out, the bulge of Brazil to Portugal. Other European powers never accept it, but it sets the boundary between Spanish and Portuguese America.
provenance: sources to check: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America; Europe: Southern Europe (Iberia)

upsert.boundary: Latin America moves to the cities, 1940 to 1990
upsert.description: As deaths fall and the countryside fills, tens of millions move to the cities: Latin America goes from about a third urban to about 70%, the most urban developing region, and Mexico City and São Paulo grow past 15 million to become among the largest cities on Earth. Much of the new city is built by its own residents, in favelas, villas miseria and colonias populares.
provenance: sources to check: UN Population Division, World Urbanization Prospects

upsert.boundary: US interventions in the Caribbean and Central America, 1898 to 1934
upsert.description: After 1898 the United States makes the Caribbean basin its sphere: the Platt Amendment gives it the right to intervene in Cuba, it backs Panama's secession (1903) to build the canal, Roosevelt's corollary (1904) claims a police power over the hemisphere, and Marines occupy Nicaragua, Haiti and the Dominican Republic and land in Mexico and Honduras, often to collect debts or protect companies. The Good Neighbor policy (1933) ends the occupations.
provenance: sources to check: Schoultz, Beneath the United States (1998)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean and Central America

upsert.boundary: Market reforms, 1985 to 2002
upsert.description: After the debt crisis, governments privatize state firms, cut tariffs, free capital flows and fight inflation, often as conditions of IMF and World Bank loans; hyperinflations end (Bolivia 1985, Argentina 1991, Brazil 1994), and trade and foreign investment grow. But growth is modest, inequality stays among the world's highest, and crises recur, from Mexico's peso crisis (1994) to Argentina's collapse (2001 to 2002). Whether the reforms failed or were not given time is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; their verdict is debated
sources to check: Williamson (ed.), Latin American Adjustment (1990); Ocampo, in Serra and Stiglitz (eds.), The Washington Consensus Reconsidered (2008)

changes.value: The Americas pass, step 3, Latin America and the Caribbean as a whole: the Events that span two or three of its intermediate regions, from Tordesillas, the society of castas and the Bourbon reforms, through Spanish America's abolitions, the caudillos, indentured labour from Asia, export-led growth and the US interventions, to import substitution, the move to the cities, the fertility transition, liberation theology, the Pentecostal rise, the homicide epidemic, the return to democracy, the market reforms and the commodity boom; with the drug trade, which spans the whole hemisphere. The fertility transition names the Americas' share of humanity, the homicide epidemic the world's homicide rate, and the return to democracy the share living in democracies, because each explains a turn already in those series.

upsert.boundary: Tlaxcala and the Indigenous allies of the conquest, 1519 to 1521
upsert.description: After fighting Cortés's company in September 1519, Tlaxcala, long encircled and besieged by the Triple Alliance, allies with the Spanish; with defectors from Texcoco and other subject towns, tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors, porters and boat-builders do most of the fighting and the labour of the siege of Tenochtitlan. Spanish chronicles played the alliance down; Indigenous records such as the Lienzo de Tlaxcala, and the privileges Tlaxcala won from the Crown, set it out.
provenance: sources to check: Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003); Matthew and Oudijk (eds.), Indian Conquistadors (2007)

upsert.boundary: Leclerc's expedition and yellow fever in Saint-Domingue, 1802 to 1803
upsert.description: Napoleon sends about 30,000 soldiers under his brother-in-law Leclerc to retake Saint-Domingue and, as in Guadeloupe, restore slavery; Toussaint Louverture is seized and shipped to France, where he dies (1803). Yellow fever, carried by mosquitoes among troops who had never met it, kills most of the expedition, Leclerc among them, while Dessalines's army fights on and wins at Vertières (November 1803).
provenance: sources to check: McNeill, Mosquito Empires (2010); Dubois, Avengers of the New World (2004)

The Americas pass, step 6: values only where a new Event of the Americas moves a measure. The two cocoliztli epidemics give the Americas' share of humanity its shape between 1533 and 1600, which the series drew as straight lines: higher before each epidemic, a step down across it. The Boeing 707 lifts the fastest regular passenger speed to the jet airliner's 900 km/h. Three existing turns are recorded again unchanged with a note naming the new Event that explains them: the share's fall after 1980 (Latin America's fertility transition), the world homicide rate's pause in the early 1990s (Latin America's homicide epidemic) and the democracy share's rise from 1980 to 1985 (the return to democracy). Stretches the new Events pass over without moving a measure get no interpolated values here; they are left for the last pass of the night.
