provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (4th ed. 2016); Belich, Making Peoples (1996)

upsert.boundary: Federation, dominions and the world wars, 1901 to 1945
upsert.description: Australia federates (1901) behind the White Australia policy and New Zealand becomes a dominion (1907); both build arbitration courts, pensions and Labour governments; they lose about 60,000 and 18,000 dead in the First World War and are shaken by the Depression, and Japan's advance in 1942 turns them from Britain toward the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre (2016); King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

upsert.boundary: The first Australians, about 65,000 or 50,000 to 30,000 years ago
upsert.description: People cross from Wallacea to Sahul's northern shores and spread across the continent: the coasts, the rivers of the south-east, the arid interior and, by about 40,000 years ago, Tasmania, joined to the mainland while the sea was low. They grind the edges of stone axes, bury their dead with ochre at Lake Mungo, and within some thousands of years of their arrival the giant marsupials, birds and reptiles are gone. When the first people came is debated: luminescence dates at Madjedbebe put them there by 65,000 years ago, while most secure sites are about 50,000 years old.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the start of the era is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547 (Madjedbebe); O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Hiscock, Archaeology of Ancient Australia (2008)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Australia, with Tasmania)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum's deserts and refuges, about 30,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the last glacial deepens, Australia's interior dries, dunes spread and lakes such as Mungo empty; people withdraw from much of the arid interior to refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall. Tasmania's hunters live on wallaby at the southern edge of the inhabited world. From about 18,000 years ago the climate eases and the seas rise.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far people left the deserts is debated
sources to check: Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013); Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61

upsert.boundary: Holocene Australia, about 12,000 years ago to 1280
upsert.description: The rising sea cuts off Tasmania and then New Guinea and drowns the coastal plains. In a warmer and, from about 5,000 years ago, more variable climate, Aboriginal societies change: small backed tools spread, seed-grinding and eel-trapping grow, the Pama-Nyungan languages spread across most of the continent, and about 3,500 years ago the dingo arrives from island South-east Asia. Aotearoa New Zealand, the subregion's other land, has no people yet.
provenance: sources to check: Mulvaney and Kamminga, Prehistory of Australia (1999); Hiscock (2008)

upsert.boundary: Migration, Asia and the first peoples' rights, 1945 to 2025
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish' millions of migrants arrive, first from Britain and Europe and, after White Australia ends (1973), from Asia; trade turns from Britain to Japan and China; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people win citizenship rights, land rights and native title, and Maori a tribunal for Treaty claims and a revival of their language; both countries grow rich on minerals, farm exports and services.

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal Australia and Maori Aotearoa, about 1280 to 1788
upsert.description: East Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa, the last large land on Earth to be peopled; within two centuries the moa are gone, and Maori live from gardens of kumara, fern root and the sea, building fortified pa and forming iwi and hapu. Across the Tasman, hundreds of Aboriginal nations keep their country by law, ceremony and fire; Makassan fishermen visit the north coast from about 1720, and Dutch and English ships chart the west and south from 1606.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014); Mulvaney and Kamminga (1999)

upsert.boundary: Traders, labour recruiters, missions and colonies, 1840 to 1942
upsert.description: Sandalwood and beche-de-mer traders, missionaries and labour recruiters come; France takes New Caledonia (1853) for convicts and nickel, Britain takes Fiji (1874) and brings Indian indentured labourers, and New Guinea is divided among the Dutch, Germans and British (1884); measles kills a quarter or more of Fijians in 1875. Gold draws prospectors inland, and in the 1930s patrols find about a million people in the New Guinea highlands unknown to the outside world.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al., The Cambridge History of the Pacific Islanders (1997)

upsert.boundary: Big men, chiefs and exchange, about 500 BCE to 1840
upsert.description: After Lapita, people with Papuan ancestry reshape the population of Vanuatu and other islands while their languages stay Austronesian; Melanesian societies form around big men who win followings by giving, and around hereditary chiefs in Fiji and New Caledonia; rings of exchange such as the kula of the Massim and the hiri of the Papuan coast carry shell valuables, pots and sago; and some three centuries ago the sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands, where people and pig herds multiply.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the highland changes after the sweet potato are debated
sources to check: Spriggs (1997); Posth et al. 2018, Nature Ecology and Evolution 2; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Pleistocene New Guinea and the Bismarcks, about 65,000 or 50,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: The first people of Sahul reach New Guinea, then joined to Australia, and by about 49,000 years ago are in its highlands, harvesting pandanus nuts and yams and thinning forest with waisted axes; voyagers cross to New Ireland and New Britain by about 40,000 years ago and to Buka in the northern Solomons by about 30,000, and later carry obsidian and animals between the islands. Beyond the main Solomons no one yet lives.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first arrival's date is debated as for Sahul
sources to check: Summerhayes et al. 2010, Science 330; Spriggs, The Island Melanesians (1997)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago, the northern Solomons)

upsert.boundary: The first gardens, about 10,000 to 1350 BCE
upsert.description: As the climate warms, New Guineans at Kuk and elsewhere in the highlands tend taro, bananas, yams and sugarcane, then dig drains and build mounded gardens, one of the world's few independent beginnings of farming; the rising sea separates New Guinea from Australia.
provenance: sources to check: Denham et al. 2003, Science 301; Golson et al., Ten Thousand Years of Cultivation at Kuk Swamp (2017)

upsert.boundary: Independent Melanesia, 1980 to 2025
upsert.description: Papua New Guinea's people grow from about three million to ten million or more, speaking over 800 languages; the war over the Panguna mine on Bougainville (1988 to 1998) ends in autonomy and a vote for independence (2019); Fiji passes through four coups (1987 to 2006), Solomon Islands through ethnic conflict and an Australian-led intervention (2003 to 2017), and New Caledonia through three referendums on independence (2018 to 2021) and the riots of 2024.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Papua New Guinea's population is uncertain
sources to check: Denoon, A Trial Separation (2005); UN World Population Prospects

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers in island Melanesia, about 1350 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking potters with pigs, chickens, dogs and outrigger canoes appear in the Bismarck Archipelago about 1350 BCE and within three centuries settle the empty islands beyond the Solomons: Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji; their earliest cemetery, at Teouma on Efate, holds people of East Asian ancestry. The dentate-stamped pottery fades after about 500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Bedford et al. 2006, Antiquity 80
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Bismarcks, Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji)

upsert.boundary: War, new movements and independence, 1942 to 1980
upsert.description: Japan's invasion turns the north coast of New Guinea, the Kokoda track and Guadalcanal into battlefields (1942 to 1945), with tens of thousands of Melanesians as carriers and scouts; afterwards movements such as John Frum's on Tanna and Paliau's on Manus seek the wealth and dignity the war revealed; Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), Solomon Islands (1978) and Vanuatu (1980) become independent, while New Caledonia stays French.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al. (1997)

upsert.boundary: Free association and rising seas, 1986 to 2025
upsert.description: Under Compacts of Free Association (1986, Palau 1994, renewed 2023) the United States funds and defends the Marshall Islands, the Federated States and Palau, whose citizens may live and work in the United States, where a large share of them now live; Kiribati and the Marshall Islands face rising seas, and Nauru's phosphate runs out.
provenance: sources to check: Hezel, Making Sense of Micronesia (2013)

upsert.boundary: German, Japanese and British rule, 1899 to 1945
upsert.description: Germany mines phosphate and plants copra; Japan takes Germany's islands in 1914 and governs them as the League of Nations' South Seas Mandate, bringing Japanese, Okinawan and Korean settlers who outnumber the islanders by 1940; Britain rules the Gilberts and mines Banaba, and Australia administers Nauru; from 1941 the islands are battlefields of the Pacific war, from Tarawa to Saipan and Tinian.
provenance: sources to check: Peattie, Nan'yo (1988); Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995)

upsert.boundary: Latte houses, Nan Madol and island chiefdoms, about 1000 to 1668
upsert.description: In the Marianas, Chamorro houses stand on stone pillars, the latte, and rice is grown, the only rice in Oceania before contact; on Pohnpei the Saudeleur build Nan Madol and on Kosrae chiefs build Leluh; Yap's chiefs bind the outer islands in the sawei exchange and quarry stone money on Palau; Carolinian navigators keep the star compass. Magellan reaches Guam in 1521 and the Manila galleons call there from 1565.
provenance: sources to check: Rainbird, The Archaeology of Micronesia (2004)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Marianas and the Carolines, about 1500 BCE to 1000 CE
upsert.description: Seafarers from the Philippines make the longest open-sea crossing of their time to settle the Marianas about 3,500 years ago; about 2,000 years ago, as the falling sea leaves coral atolls habitable, voyagers from island Melanesia settle the Carolines, the Marshalls and Kiribati, speaking the Nuclear Micronesian languages.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first settlement's date and origin are debated
sources to check: Carson et al. 2013, Journal of Island and Coastal Archaeology 8; Pugach et al. 2021, PNAS 118; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Spanish Guam, whalers and missions, 1668 to 1899
upsert.description: Jesuits found a mission on Guam (1668); the Spanish-Chamorro wars and epidemics reduce the Chamorro by nine-tenths and Spain resettles the survivors; in the 1800s whalers, traders and Protestant missionaries from Hawai'i and New England reach the Carolines and Marshalls, and smallpox strikes Pohnpei (1854); Germany claims the Marshalls (1885), and after the war of 1898 Spain cedes Guam to the United States and sells the rest to Germany (1899).
provenance: sources to check: Hezel, The First Taint of Civilization (1983); Rogers, Destiny's Landfall (1995)

upsert.boundary: The Trust Territory and the nuclear tests, 1945 to 1986
upsert.description: The United States governs most of Micronesia as a UN strategic trust (from 1947) and tests 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak (1946 to 1958); Nauru (1968) and Kiribati (1979) become independent, and the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau negotiate free association, while Guam and the Northern Marianas stay American.

upsert.boundary: The first Polynesians: Tonga and Samoa, about 900 BCE to 900 CE
upsert.description: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga about 880 BCE and Samoa soon after; there, and on Futuna and 'Uvea, their descendants become the first Polynesians, with the Proto-Polynesian language, chiefs, tapu and mana, and stop making pottery. For nearly two thousand years, the 'long pause', no one settles the islands to the east; its length and its reasons are debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the pause and its reasons are debated
sources to check: Kirch and Green, Hawaiki, Ancestral Polynesia (2001); Burley et al. 2012, PLOS ONE 7

upsert.boundary: Chiefdoms and island states, about 1200 to 1767
upsert.description: On every high island chiefs build marae and ahu; the Tu'i Tonga's maritime chiefdom reaches Samoa, 'Uvea and Fiji; Hawai'i's paramount chiefs rule irrigated taro lands and fishponds through land divisions and kapu; Rapa Nui's clans raise the moai; voyaging between distant archipelagos grows rarer. Europeans pass by: Mendana in the Marquesas (1595), Le Maire and Schouten (1616), Roggeveen at Rapa Nui (1722).
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings (2010)

upsert.boundary: Colonial rule and resistance, 1900 to 1962
upsert.description: Samoa is divided between Germany and the United States (1899) and New Zealand takes the German part (1914); influenza kills a fifth of Western Samoans in 1918, and the Mau movement demands self-rule; Tonga remains a protected kingdom; Pearl Harbor (1941) brings the Pacific war; Hawai'i becomes an American state (1959).
provenance: sources to check: Meleisea, Lagaga (1987); Campbell (1989)

upsert.boundary: Contact, missions, island kingdoms and annexation, 1767 to 1900
upsert.description: Wallis (1767), Bougainville and Cook bring Tahiti into Europe's imagination; diseases cut island peoples by half or more; Protestant missions convert Tahiti, Tonga, Samoa and Hawai'i; chiefs with muskets build kingdoms (Kamehameha's Hawai'i, Pomare's Tahiti, Tupou's Tonga); France annexes Tahiti, Peruvian slavers take a third of Rapa Nui's people (1862), and Hawai'i's monarchy is overthrown (1893) and annexed by the United States (1898).
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al. (1997); Campbell, A History of the Pacific Islands (1989)

upsert.boundary: Island nations, territories and the diaspora, 1962 to 2025
upsert.description: Samoa (1962), Tonga (1970) and Tuvalu (1978) become independent, and the Cook Islands and Niue self-governing in free association with New Zealand; France tests nuclear weapons at Moruroa until 1996; more Cook Islanders and Niueans, and very many Samoans and Tongans, come to live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States; the voyaging canoe Hokule'a revives navigation without instruments; the atolls face rising seas.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell (1989); Denoon et al. (1997)

upsert.boundary: The great voyages east, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: Voyagers in double-hulled canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, settle the Society and Cook Islands, then the Marquesas, Hawai'i and Rapa Nui, carrying taro, breadfruit, pigs, dogs, chickens and the Pacific rat. The dating is debated: a short chronology puts the Society Islands about 1025 and the remotest islands about 1200, a longer one centuries earlier.
provenance: exploring: the chronology of East Polynesian settlement is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Kirch (2017)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (East Polynesia, with Hawai'i and Rapa Nui)

upsert.boundary: Archaic humans of Sunda and Wallacea, to about 70,000 years ago
upsert.description: At low sea level Java, Sumatra and Borneo join the mainland as Sundaland, while Wallacea's islands stay parted by deep water. Homo erectus lives on Java until about 110,000 years ago; small-bodied humans, Homo floresiensis on Flores and Homo luzonensis on Luzon, live on islands only a sea crossing could reach; Denisovans leave their genes in the ancestors of today's Filipinos and Papuans.
provenance: sources to check: Rizal et al. 2020, Nature 577; Sutikna et al. 2016, Nature 532; Detroit et al. 2019, Nature 568; Larena et al. 2021, Current Biology 31

upsert.boundary: Bronze drums, iron and the first trade with India and China, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: Dong Son chiefs on the Red River cast great bronze drums that travel as far as eastern Indonesia; iron spreads; Sa Huynh jar burials hold ornaments of Taiwanese jade; Indian beads and pottery reach the Thai-Malay peninsula; Han China conquers the Red River delta (111 BCE).
provenance: sources to check: Higham (2014); Bellina 2014, in Asian Perspectives

upsert.boundary: The classical kingdoms: Angkor, Pagan, Dai Viet and Java, 802 to 1350
upsert.description: Jayavarman II founds Angkor (802); the Sailendras build Borobudur; Pagan unites the Irrawaddy (1044) and turns to Theravada Buddhism; Vietnam wins independence from China (938) and builds a Confucian state; Dai Viet and Champa repel the Mongols (1258 to 1288); Tai peoples move south and found Sukhothai (1238); Majapahit rises in Java (1293). These charter states set the frames of the mainland's later nations.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; 'charter era' is Lieberman's term
sources to check: Lieberman, Strange Parallels, vol. 1 (2003)

upsert.boundary: Colonial conquest and export economies, 1824 to 1941
upsert.description: Britain conquers Burma in three wars (1824 to 1885) and the Malay states; the Dutch subdue Java (1830) and Aceh (1904); France takes Indochina (1858 to 1907); the United States takes the Philippines (1898 to 1902); Siam alone stays independent. Rice frontiers open in the great deltas, Malaya produces most of the world's rubber and tin, Java's people quadruple, Chinese and Indian migrants come by the million, and nationalist movements form from 1908.
provenance: sources to check: Tarling (ed.), The Cambridge History of Southeast Asia, vol. 2 (1992); Owen (ed.), The Emergence of Modern Southeast Asia (2005)

upsert.boundary: Ayutthaya, Malacca and the age of commerce, 1350 to 1700
upsert.description: Ayutthaya (1351) and Lan Xang (1353) rise as Angkor declines; Malacca (about 1400) becomes the great entrepot of Asian trade and turns Muslim, and Islam spreads through the islands; Vietnam expels the Ming (1428) and pushes south; the Portuguese take Malacca (1511), Spain Manila (1571) and the Dutch Batavia (1619); Toungoo Burma conquers the western mainland; pepper, cloves and nutmeg sell across the world until the Dutch monopolies and wars of the 1600s close the age of commerce.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; 'the age of commerce' is Reid's term and its end is debated
sources to check: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce 1450-1680 (1988, 1993)

upsert.boundary: Consolidated kingdoms and the companies, 1700 to 1824
upsert.description: On the mainland three states absorb their neighbours: Konbaung Burma (from 1752), which sacks Ayutthaya (1767); the Chakri kingdom of Siam, with its capital at Bangkok (1782); and the Nguyen Vietnam that the Tay Son wars leave behind (1802). In the islands the Dutch company rules Java's coasts and trade until it is dissolved (1799); Britain takes Penang (1786) and founds Singapore (1819); Tambora's eruption (1815) cools the world.
provenance: sources to check: Lieberman (2003); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Early states and Indic kingship, about 100 to 802
upsert.description: Port states and river kingdoms grow on the trade between India and China: Funan on the Mekong delta, Champa on the Vietnamese coast, the Pyu cities of the Irrawaddy, the Mon towns of Dvaravati, Chenla in Cambodia and, from 671, Srivijaya on the Strait; their rulers take up Sanskrit, Hindu gods and Buddhism, while northern Vietnam stays under Chinese rule.
provenance: sources to check: Tarling (ed.), The Cambridge History of Southeast Asia, vol. 1 (1992); Coedes, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia (1968)

upsert.boundary: Farmers and seafarers from the north, about 2500 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Rice and millet farmers from southern China, probably speaking Austroasiatic languages, move into the river valleys of the mainland, and Austronesian speakers from Taiwan sail to the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and beyond; ancient genomes show both mixing with the foragers already there. Bronze-working begins on the mainland about 1100 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lipson et al. 2018, Science 361; McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Bellwood (2017)

upsert.boundary: Peace, growth and ASEAN, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: Once the Cambodian war ends (1989 to 1991) the region becomes one of the world's fastest-growing: Vietnam's reforms (1986), export factories in Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, and Singapore's rise among the richest countries; extreme poverty falls from about half of the people to a few per cent; the Philippines (1986) and Indonesia (1998) end their dictatorships while Myanmar's army rules, opens and seizes power again (2021); oil palm and logging clear much of Borneo and Sumatra; ASEAN grows to eleven members.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, World Development Indicators; Owen (2005)

upsert.boundary: Holocene foragers and the drowning of Sundaland, about 10,000 to 2500 BCE
upsert.description: The rising sea floods the Sunda shelf, making Borneo, Sumatra and Java islands and opening the Java Sea and the Strait of Malacca; Hoabinhian foragers live in the hills and rock shelters of the mainland, and island peoples on forest, sago and the sea.
provenance: sources to check: Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014); Bellwood, First Islanders (2017)

upsert.boundary: Modern humans on Sunda and Wallacea, about 70,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: Homo sapiens arrives, perhaps by 70,000 years ago (Lida Ajer, Tam Pa Ling) and certainly by 45,000 (Niah Cave); foragers live in rainforest and on coasts, cross Wallacea's straits to Sahul, paint the oldest known figurative art in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo and fish the deep sea off Timor. At the glacial maximum Sundaland's land area is about twice today's.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are debated
sources to check: Westaway et al. 2017, Nature 548; Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.boundary: Japanese occupation, revolutions and wars, 1941 to 1979
upsert.description: Japan conquers the whole region (1941 to 1942), and famine and forced labour kill millions; after its surrender Vietnam and Indonesia declare independence and fight France and the Netherlands; the Philippines (1946), Burma (1948), Malaya (1957) and the rest become independent; the Indochina wars draw in the United States; Indonesia's army and its allies kill half a million or more in 1965 to 1966; the Khmer Rouge rule Cambodia until Vietnam invades (January 1979).

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 1: each subregion gets its own eras, in the periodization its own historians use, from the first arrivals to 2025. Australia and New Zealand: the first Australians, the glacial maximum, Holocene Australia, Aboriginal Australia and Maori Aotearoa, the colonies, federation and the dominions, and the postwar nations. Melanesia: Pleistocene New Guinea and the Bismarcks, the first gardens, Lapita, big men and exchange, colonies, war and independence, and independent Melanesia. Micronesia: settlement, the latte and Nan Madol, Spanish Guam, German and Japanese rule, the Trust Territory, and free association. Polynesia: the first Polynesians and the long pause, the voyages east, chiefdoms and island states, contact and annexation, colonial rule, and the island nations. South-eastern Asia: archaic humans, modern humans on Sunda, Holocene foragers, farmers from the north, bronze and iron, early states, the charter kingdoms, the age of commerce, consolidation, colonial conquest, occupation and wars, and growth since 1979. Oceania's and Asia's eras stay as the regions' frames. With them, placements the region text already states but the bindings lacked: Tasman's and Mendana's landfalls in the European arrival, Melanesia and Micronesia in the depopulation, Hawai'i in Northern America and Rapa Nui in South America by 2026 borders beside Polynesia (Labelsqueeze#5363: the model's Polynesia boundary includes both, UN M49 counts them in the Americas), the sweet-potato contact in South America, Cook's voyages in Northern America, Australia in the nuclear tests and the Pacific war, Micronesia in the island independences, and South-eastern Asia in Asia's fall in births.

upsert.boundary: Cave paintings in Sulawesi and Borneo, about 51,000 to 40,000 years ago
upsert.description: A painted wild pig with three human-like figures at Leang Karampuang in Sulawesi, dated by uranium in the mineral crusts over it to at least 51,200 years ago, and painted pigs, buffalo and hand stencils in other limestone caves of Sulawesi and Borneo from about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago are the oldest figurative art known, older than Europe's Chauvet; the Leang Karampuang panel may show a scene, the oldest known telling of a story in pictures.

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 2: every existing Event of Oceania and South-eastern Asia is re-filed in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f). An Event of one subregion moves from the region's era or lifecycle into that subregion's own era; one that crosses its subregion's era boundary into the subregion's lifecycle (Angkor, Srivijaya and Islam's spread in South-eastern Asia; the rock art, the frontier wars, settler growth and the stolen generations in Australia and New Zealand; Hawai'i's chiefdoms in Polynesia). The old contains relation is replaced, not doubled. Events across subregions keep the region's frame (the arrival in Sahul, Lapita, the Polynesian settlement, Cook, the depopulation, the Pacific war, the island independences, the Portuguese and the Dutch company in Asia, the tigers). One correction: the cave art of Sulawesi is now dated from at least 51,200 years ago, the age published in 2024 for the panel at Leang Karampuang; the Event said 45,000.

The diggers' demands, after the Eureka Stockade (1854), help bring Victoria the ballot and wider suffrage.
With the moa gone, gardens and stores worth defending become the base of life, and wars over land and mana follow.

upsert.description: Opposition to the French tests at Moruroa grows into the nuclear-free movement.
Victory lets the colonial government confiscate land and impose the court.
The first Australians bring or soon invent the technique of grinding an axe's edge.
The spread south from the first landfalls reaches Tasmania within ten thousand years or so.
The flooding of Bass Strait cuts Tasmania off.
The inquiry into the removals and the apology for them are at the heart of reconciliation.
The treaty's promises, read in te reo, become the ground of the claims.
A warmer, drier climate lengthens the fire season and makes extreme fire weather more likely.

upsert.boundary: The alliance with the United States, from 1951
upsert.description: Having seen Britain fail to hold Singapore (1942), Australia and New Zealand sign the ANZUS treaty with the United States (1951); Australia fights beside it in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq and joins AUKUS (2021) to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, while New Zealand's ban on nuclear ships (1984 to 1987) ends its part in the alliance's defence commitments.

upsert.boundary: Trade turns from Britain to Asia, from 1957
upsert.description: The Australia-Japan commerce agreement (1957) and Britain's entry into the European Community (1973), which ends New Zealand's assured market, turn both economies toward Asia; Japan, then China, become the chief buyers of Australian iron ore, coal and gas, and the China boom of 2003 to 2013 lifts Australia's terms of trade to their highest in over a century.
provenance: sources to check: Reserve Bank of Australia, terms of trade series

upsert.boundary: The Black Summer fires, 2019 to 2020
upsert.description: After Australia's hottest and driest year on record, bushfires burn some 24 million hectares in the south-east, kill 33 people directly, destroy over 3,000 homes and kill or displace perhaps three billion animals; a royal commission links their scale to a warming climate.
provenance: sources to check: Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements (2020); Van Oldenborgh et al. 2021, Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences 21
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-eastern Australia)

upsert.boundary: Tasmania's Black War, 1824 to 1832
upsert.description: As settlers' sheep spread over the island's grasslands, Palawa bands fight back; martial law (1828), bounties and the 'Black Line' of 1830 follow, and by 1832 George Augustus Robinson has led most of the survivors, a few hundred from several thousand, to Wybalenna on Flinders Island, where most die. Their descendants live on: the belief that Tasmania's Aboriginal people died out with Truganini (1876) is false.
provenance: sources to check: Ryan, Tasmanian Aborigines (2012); Clements, The Black War (2014)

upsert.boundary: Gunditjmara eel aquaculture at Budj Bim, from about 6,600 years ago
upsert.description: In the young lava fields of south-western Victoria, the Gunditjmara cut channels and weirs to trap and hold short-finned eels and build stone houses beside them, a system some 6,600 years old in its earliest parts and still worked when settlers came; it has been a World Heritage site since 2019. Whether such practices amount to agriculture, as some recent books argue, or to skilled management of wild resources, as their critics answer, is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the age of the oldest channels and the 'agriculture' debate are open
sources to check: McNiven et al. 2012, Journal of Archaeological Science 39; Pascoe, Dark Emu (2014); Sutton and Walshe, Farmers or Hunter-Gatherers? (2021)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-western Victoria)

upsert.boundary: Convict transportation to Australia, 1788 to 1868
upsert.description: Britain transports about 162,000 convicts, one in six of them women, to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land and, last, Western Australia (to 1868); assigned to settlers and public works, most stay when freed, and their labour builds the colonies' roads, farms and towns.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987); Nicholas (ed.), Convict Workers (1988)

upsert.boundary: The dingo arrives, about 3,500 to 3,200 years ago
upsert.description: Dogs brought by seafarers from island South-east Asia spread across the mainland within a few centuries and become the dingo; the thylacine and the Tasmanian devil vanish from the mainland soon after, surviving only in Tasmania, which the dingo never reached. Whether the dingo, people or a drier climate caused those losses is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the cause of the mainland extinctions is debated
sources to check: Balme et al. 2018, Scientific Reports 8; Brown 2006, The Holocene 16
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (mainland Australia)

upsert.boundary: Dutch ships chart New Holland and reach Aotearoa, 1606 to 1644
upsert.description: Willem Janszoon's Duyfken lands on Cape York (1606), the first recorded European landfall in Australia, and clashes with Wik people; Dutch ships bound for Java chart the west coast; Abel Tasman sights Tasmania (1642) and anchors in Golden Bay, where Ngati Tumatakokiri kill four of his men, and charts New Zealand's west coast.
provenance: sources to check: Sigmond and Zuiderbaan, Dutch Discoveries of Australia (1979); Salmond, Two Worlds (1991)

upsert.boundary: Continental exchange routes, about 2000 BCE to the 1850s
upsert.description: Goods pass hand to hand along routes linked to the songlines: pearl and baler shell from the Kimberley and Cape York to the south coast, greenstone axes from the Mount William quarry, red ochre from Wilgie Mia and Pukardu, and pituri, a stimulant, from the Mulligan River; most routes are known from the last few thousand years, and some quarries are far older.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the routes' ages are mostly unknown
sources to check: McBryde 1984, World Archaeology 16; Mulvaney 1976, 'The chain of connection'

upsert.boundary: The Federation Drought, 1895 to 1903
upsert.description: The longest and worst drought since European settlement halves Australia's sheep from about 106 million to 54 million and its cattle by some 40%, ruins wheat crops and pastoral companies, and turns inland soils to dust; it speeds the turn to dry-farmed wheat and irrigation.
provenance: sources to check: Garden, Droughts, Floods and Cyclones (2009)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (eastern Australia)

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal fire on the land, from the first arrivals
upsert.description: People burn country in small, frequent fires to drive game, open paths and renew plants, making a mosaic of vegetation that Europeans later mistook for parkland; charcoal records show fire regimes changing after people arrived, though whether burning began with them or followed the loss of the megafauna is debated (at Lynch's Crater the giant browsers' dung spores decline before charcoal rises). Suppressed after 1788 across much of the continent, cultural burning is being revived.
provenance: exploring: when and how far people changed fire regimes is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Jones 1969, Australian Natural History 16 ('Fire-stick farming'); Rule et al. 2012, Science 335; Bowman 1998, New Phytologist 140; Gammage, The Biggest Estate on Earth (2011)

upsert.boundary: Australia and New Zealand in the First World War, 1914 to 1918
upsert.description: From populations under five million and one million, Australia sends about 330,000 and New Zealand about 100,000 soldiers overseas, all volunteers in Australia, where two referendums reject conscription; some 60,000 and 18,000 die, at Gallipoli and above all on the Western Front.
provenance: sources to check: Beaumont, Broken Nation (2013)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand; Europe (Western Europe); Asia (Western Asia)

upsert.boundary: The oldest ground-edge axes, about 49,000 to 35,000 years ago
upsert.description: In the Kimberley and Arnhem Land people grind the edges of stone axes: a fragment from Carpenter's Gap, about 44,000 to 49,000 years old, and axes from Nawarla Gabarnmang, about 35,000, are the oldest ground-edge axes known anywhere, tens of thousands of years before the technique appears in Europe or western Asia. Claims of still older fragments at Madjedbebe are debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the oldest dates are debated
sources to check: Hiscock et al. 2016, Australian Archaeology 82; Geneste et al. 2012, Cambridge Archaeological Journal 22
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (northern Australia)

upsert.boundary: Port Arthur and the gun buyback, 1996
upsert.description: After a gunman kills 35 people at Port Arthur, Tasmania (April 1996), the National Firearms Agreement bans rapid-fire rifles and shotguns and buys back about 650,000 guns; mass shootings largely cease, though how much of the later fall in gun deaths the law caused is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the law's effect on gun deaths is debated
sources to check: Chapman et al. 2016, JAMA 316; Leigh and Neill 2010, American Law and Economics Review 12

upsert.boundary: The Kingitanga, the Maori King movement, from 1858
upsert.description: Waikato and other iwi raise Potatau Te Wherowhero as Maori King (1858) to hold land against sale and unite tribes under one mana; the colonial government's invasion of the Waikato (1863 to 1864) and the confiscations follow; the movement endures, with a monarch to this day.
provenance: sources to check: Belich, The New Zealand Wars (1986); King (2003)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the continent cools and dries, dunes advance and inland lakes fail; people leave much of the arid interior for refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the broad coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall by half or more before they reoccupy the deserts as the climate eases. How far the deserts were abandoned and how far numbers fell are debated: radiocarbon dates used as a proxy for population are read both ways.
provenance: exploring: the size of the fall is debated
sources to check: Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61; Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Waitangi Tribunal and the Maori renaissance, from 1975
upsert.description: The land march of 1975 and the occupation of Bastion Point (1977 to 1978) come with the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), empowered from 1985 to hear claims back to 1840; Crown settlements from the 1990s return land and money to iwi such as Tainui and Ngai Tahu, and kohanga reo (1982) and Maori-language schools revive te reo, an official language since 1987.
provenance: sources to check: Walker, Ka Whawhai Tonu Matou (1990); Orange, The Treaty of Waitangi (2nd ed. 2011)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Floating currencies and open markets, 1983 to 1996
upsert.description: Australia floats its dollar (1983) and cuts tariffs; New Zealand's Labour government (1984) removes farm subsidies, sells state firms and makes its central bank the first with a formal inflation target (1989); both economies are remade, and Australia then goes 29 years without a recession (1991 to 2020).
provenance: sources to check: Kelly, The End of Certainty (1992); Easton, The Commercialisation of New Zealand (1997)

upsert.boundary: New tools, new places and more people, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Across mainland Australia small backed blades and points spread, seed-grinding grows, sites multiply and people settle harsher country, as rainfall becomes less reliable with the strengthening of El Nino. Whether this was an 'intensification' driven by society and population growth or a response to a more variable climate is a long debate.
provenance: sources to check: Lourandos, Continent of Hunter-Gatherers (1997); Hiscock (2008); Williams et al. 2015, Quaternary Science Reviews 123
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (mainland Australia)

upsert.boundary: Moriori on Rekohu, about 1500 to 1835
upsert.description: Polynesians from mainland Aotearoa settle the Chatham Islands (Rekohu) and become Moriori; under Nunuku's law they renounce killing in war. In 1835 Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama, displaced by the Musket Wars, arrive on a European ship, kill some 300 Moriori and enslave the rest. The old belief that Moriori were a people of another race who came before Maori is false.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date of settlement is uncertain
sources to check: King, Moriori: A People Rediscovered (rev. ed. 2000)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (the Chatham Islands)

upsert.boundary: The Musket Wars in Aotearoa, about 1807 to 1842
upsert.description: Iwi who obtain muskets from traders, above all Ngapuhi under Hongi Hika after his visit to England in 1820, raid their rivals the length of the North Island; perhaps 20,000 die and tens of thousands are enslaved or driven from their lands before the guns spread to every side; the displacements shape the land claims the Crown later meets.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated
sources to check: Crosby, The Musket Wars (1999); Ballara, Taua (2003)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The Native Land Court turns Maori land into saleable titles, 1865 to 1900
upsert.description: Created to convert customary title into individual titles that can be sold, the court, with the confiscations after the wars, leaves Maori by the 1890s with perhaps a sixth of New Zealand's land, while Maori numbers fall to about 42,000 by 1896.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the land share is approximate
sources to check: Ward, An Unsettled History (1999); Belich (1996)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Nuclear-free New Zealand, 1984 to 1987
upsert.description: The Lange government bars nuclear-armed or nuclear-powered ships (1984); French agents sink Greenpeace's Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour (July 1985), killing a photographer; the 1987 act makes New Zealand nuclear-free, and the United States suspends its ANZUS obligations to New Zealand.
provenance: sources to check: Clements, Back from the Brink (1988)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Maori build fortified pa, about 1450 to 1769
upsert.description: As the moa and seals are exhausted and kumara gardens and fern root become the base of life, Maori build thousands of pa, hilltop and headland strongholds with terraces, ditches and palisades, defending gardens, stores and mana in wars between hapu and iwi; some 6,000 or more pa sites are known.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris (2014); Schmidt 1996, Journal of World Prehistory 10
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Pama-Nyungan languages spread across most of Australia, about 4000 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: One language family, Pama-Nyungan, spreads from the Gulf country across seven-eighths of the continent, displacing or absorbing others everywhere but the north; a phylogenetic study dates its origin about 6,000 years ago. Whether it spread with migrating people or by people changing language, with little movement, is debated: Aboriginal genomes show deep regional continuity.
provenance: exploring: its date and manner of spread are debated
sources to check: Bouckaert et al. 2018, Nature Ecology and Evolution 2; Malaspinas et al. 2016, Nature 538

upsert.boundary: Reconciliation, the apology and the Voice, 1991 to 2023
upsert.description: A royal commission into Aboriginal deaths in custody (1991), the Bringing Them Home report on the stolen generations (1997) and the national apology (February 2008) lead to the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017), which asks for an Indigenous Voice to Parliament; Australians reject it in the referendum of October 2023, by 60 to 40 per cent.
provenance: sources to check: Australian Electoral Commission, 2023 referendum results

upsert.boundary: The Dunedin carries frozen meat to London, 1882
upsert.description: The first successful shipment of refrigerated mutton from New Zealand reaches London after 98 days at sea; frozen meat, then butter and cheese, make New Zealand Britain's farm across the world, the basis of its prosperity until Britain joins the European Community.
provenance: sources to check: Belich, Paradise Reforged (2001)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Self-government and the secret ballot, 1855 to 1858
upsert.description: As New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania gain responsible government, Victoria and South Australia adopt the government-printed secret ballot (1856), soon known worldwide as the 'Australian ballot', and South Australia elects its assembly by manhood suffrage; Britain adopts the secret ballot in 1872 and American states from 1888.
provenance: sources to check: Brett, From Secret Ballot to Democracy Sausage (2019)

upsert.boundary: Smallpox at Sydney, 1789
upsert.description: Fifteen months after the First Fleet, smallpox breaks out among the Eora and their neighbours around Port Jackson (April 1789), killing perhaps half of them or more, while almost no colonists fall ill; it spreads inland along the rivers. Whether it came from variolous matter carried by the fleet's surgeons or with Makassan visitors in the north is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the source of the virus is debated
sources to check: Campbell, Invisible Invaders (2002); Warren 2014, Journal of Australian Colonial History 16
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Sydney and New South Wales)

upsert.boundary: The 'social laboratory': arbitration, pensions and labour parties, about 1890 to 1910
upsert.description: After the great strikes of 1890 to 1894, the colonies and then the Commonwealth build compulsory arbitration courts (New Zealand 1894), old-age pensions (New Zealand 1898, Australia 1908) and, in the Harvester judgment (1907), a legal basic wage for a family; Australia has the world's first national Labor government (1904), and observers from Europe and America come to study the 'social laboratory'.
provenance: sources to check: Castles, The Working Class and Welfare (1985); Macintyre (2016)

upsert.boundary: People reach Tasmania, about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago
upsert.description: Walking across the land bridge the low sea has exposed in Bass Strait, people reach Tasmania by about 40,000 years ago (Parmerpar Meethaner, Warreen Cave), the southernmost humans on Earth; through the glacial maximum they hunt red-necked wallaby in the cold grasslands of the south-west valleys.
provenance: sources to check: Cosgrove 1999, Journal of World Prehistory 13; Allen and O'Connell 2014, Australian Archaeology 79

upsert.boundary: Tasmania alone, about 12,000 years ago to 1803
upsert.description: When Bass Strait floods, Tasmanians, perhaps 3,000 to 10,000 people, are cut off from all other humans for some 12,000 years, the longest isolation of any people known. Their toolkit is simpler than the mainland's: about 3,500 years ago bone points vanish and scaled fish leave the diet. Whether this shows skills lost in a small, isolated population, as Henrich argued, or choices suited to the place, as his critics argue, is debated; British settlement at Risdon Cove (1803) ends the isolation.
provenance: exploring: the meaning of the losses is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Jones 1977, in Sunda and Sahul; Henrich 2004, American Antiquity 69; Read 2006, American Antiquity 71; Taylor 2008

upsert.boundary: The White Australia policy, 1901 to 1973
upsert.description: The Immigration Restriction Act (December 1901) bars non-Europeans through a dictation test in any European language, and the Pacific Island Labourers Act deports most Melanesian workers; New Zealand adopts similar rules. The policy is relaxed from 1966 and ended by the Whitlam government in 1973.
provenance: sources to check: Tavan, The Long, Slow Death of White Australia (2005)

upsert.boundary: The squatters' wool frontier, about 1820 to 1860
upsert.description: Merino sheep and the men who 'squat' on Crown land spread across the grasslands of New South Wales, Port Phillip and the Western District; wool becomes the colonies' chief export and by the 1840s Australia is the largest supplier of Britain's mills, while the frontier of dispossession and massacre moves with the flocks.
provenance: sources to check: Roberts, The Squatting Age in Australia (1935); Butlin, Investment in Australian Economic Development (1964)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-eastern Australia)

changes.value: The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, Australia and New Zealand: the Events inside its own eras, longest first, from the first ground-edge axes, the peopling of Tasmania, fire on the land and the glacial refuges, through Tasmania's isolation, the mid-Holocene changes, the spread of Pama-Nyungan, the dingo, Budj Bim's eel channels and the continental exchange routes, Maori pa and Moriori on Rekohu, to the convicts, smallpox at Sydney, the Black War, the wool frontier, the Musket Wars, the secret ballot, the Kingitanga and the Native Land Court, frozen meat, the 'social laboratory', the Federation Drought, White Australia, the First World War, the alliance with the United States, the turn to Asian trade, the Maori renaissance, the market reforms, nuclear-free New Zealand, the gun buyback, reconciliation and the Voice, and the Black Summer fires. Aboriginal and Maori history known from archaeology, genetics and oral tradition stands beside colonial history (SurvivorCorrect#3780); debated claims are stated as debates (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). Two Events are claimed as instances of mechanism concepts: the 1789 smallpox (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd) and, as a debated hypothesis, Tasmania's isolation (CumulativeCulture#4f93).

upsert.boundary: The Bougainville war and its settlement, from 1988
upsert.description: Sabotage of the Panguna mine (1988) becomes a war between the Bougainville Revolutionary Army and Papua New Guinea's forces, with a blockade of the island; perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 die before the ceasefire of 1998; the peace agreement (2001) brings autonomy, and in the referendum of 2019, 97.7% vote for independence, which awaits ratification.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Regan (2010); Bougainville Referendum Commission (2019)

upsert.boundary: Cargo movements and new churches, from 1919
upsert.description: From the 'Vailala madness' of 1919 to John Frum on Tanna (from about 1940) and the Paliau movement on Manus (1946), Melanesian movements seek the wealth and equality that colonial rule and the war's vast stores displayed, through ritual, prophecy and remade village life. The label 'cargo cult' is criticized as reducing religious and political movements to a misunderstanding of goods.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the label and the interpretation are debated
sources to check: Worsley, The Trumpet Shall Sound (1957); Lindstrom, Cargo Cult (1993)

upsert.boundary: Fiji's chiefdoms and the rise of Bau, about 1500 to 1874
upsert.description: Fijian chiefdoms (matanitu) compete in war from fortified villages; in the 1800s the small island of Bau, armed by beachcombers' muskets, dominates the east under Ratu Seru Cakobau, who proclaims a kingdom of Fiji (1871) and then, in debt and facing rivals and Tongan power, cedes Fiji to Britain (October 1874).
provenance: sources to check: Derrick, A History of Fiji (1946); Lal, Broken Waves (1992)

upsert.boundary: Fiji's coups, 1987 to 2014
upsert.description: Lieutenant-Colonel Rabuka's two coups (1987) overthrow a government backed by Indo-Fijians; a civilian coup (2000) and Commodore Bainimarama's coup (2006) follow before elections in 2014; tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrate, and their share of the population falls from about half to about a third.
provenance: sources to check: Lal, Islands of Turmoil (2006)

upsert.boundary: Measles kills a quarter of Fijians, 1875
upsert.description: Cakobau's party, back from Sydney with the disease, lands without quarantine; within months measles kills about 40,000 Fijians, between a quarter and a third of them, adults as well as children, and the sick go untended as whole villages fall ill at once.
provenance: sources to check: Cliff and Haggett, The Spread of Measles in Fiji and the Pacific (1985)

upsert.boundary: Indian indentured labour in Fiji, 1879 to 1916
upsert.description: To work the sugar plantations without disturbing Fijian villages, the colonial government brings 60,965 Indians under five-year contracts (girmit); most stay, and by 1946 Indo-Fijians outnumber indigenous Fijians, while most land stays in Fijian hands: the root of the political conflicts after independence.

upsert.boundary: First contact in the New Guinea highlands, 1930 to 1939
upsert.description: Gold prospectors, among them Michael and Dan Leahy with the patrol officer Jim Taylor (1933), walk into the Wahgi and other highland valleys and find about a million people, gardeners in dense populations whom no outsider had known of; the Leahys' film records the meeting, and government patrols, missions and coffee follow.
provenance: sources to check: Connolly and Anderson, First Contact (1987)

upsert.boundary: The hiri voyages of the Papuan coast, about 1500 to the 1960s
upsert.description: Each year Motu potters near today's Port Moresby sail great multi-hulled lakatoi west to the Gulf of Papua with thousands of clay pots, returning with tons of sago; the voyages, perhaps five centuries old, end in the mid-twentieth century and are now remembered in a festival.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its start is uncertain
sources to check: Dutton (ed.), The Hiri in History (1982)

upsert.boundary: Highlanders of the Ivane valley, about 49,000 to 44,000 years ago
upsert.description: At some 2,000 metres in New Guinea's Owen Stanley Range, people camp seasonally, harvest pandanus nuts and yams and use waisted stone axes, probably to thin the forest: the earliest known human presence in a tropical highland anywhere.
provenance: sources to check: Summerhayes et al. 2010, Science 330

upsert.boundary: New Caledonia's struggle over independence, 1984 to 2024
upsert.description: The Kanak independence movement's boycott and the violence of 1984 to 1988, ending at the Ouvea cave, lead to the Matignon (1988) and Noumea (1998) accords; three referendums (2018, 2020, 2021) vote to stay French, the last boycotted by most Kanak, and a plan to widen the electorate sets off the riots of May 2024.
provenance: sources to check: Chappell, The Kanak Awakening (2013)

upsert.boundary: The kula ring of the Massim, from about 1000
upsert.description: Across the islands off New Guinea's eastern tip, partners carry shell necklaces clockwise and armshells anticlockwise around a ring of islands, a ceremonial exchange that builds renown and alliances alongside ordinary trade; Malinowski's account (1922) made it a founding case for the study of gift and exchange. Archaeology suggests the ring took its classic form within the last thousand years or so; when exactly is uncertain.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its age is uncertain
sources to check: Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922); Irwin, in Leach and Leach (eds.), The Kula (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Massim, Papua New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Bismarcks and the Solomons, about 40,000 to 29,000 years ago
upsert.description: Crossing straits mostly within sight of land, people reach New Ireland and New Britain by about 40,000 years ago (Buang Merabak, Matenkupkum) and Buka in the northern Solomons by about 29,000 (Kilu), the eastern edge of the inhabited world for the next 25,000 years.
provenance: sources to check: Leavesley et al. 2002, Australian Archaeology 54; Spriggs (1997)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Bismarck Archipelago and northern Solomons)

upsert.boundary: France takes New Caledonia: convicts and nickel, 1853 to 1897
upsert.description: France annexes New Caledonia (1853) and from 1864 sends some 22,000 convicts, Communards among them; nickel, found in 1864, makes it one of the world's great producers; the Kanak are confined to reserves on a small part of the main island. The rising of 1878, led by Atai, kills some 200 settlers and perhaps 1,000 or more Kanak.
provenance: sources to check: Aldrich, The French Presence in the South Pacific (1990); Connell, New Caledonia or Kanaky? (1987)

upsert.boundary: New Guinea divided, 1884
upsert.description: Germany raises its flag over north-eastern New Guinea and the Bismarcks and Britain proclaims a protectorate over the south-east (November 1884); the Dutch have claimed the west since 1828. The lines drawn then, through peoples who knew nothing of them, become the border between Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.
provenance: sources to check: Firth, New Guinea under the Germans (1982)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (New Guinea); Asia: South-eastern Asia (western New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: Obsidian and animals carried across the Bismarck Sea, from about 20,000 years ago
upsert.description: Obsidian from Talasea on New Britain is carried to New Ireland, and people release cuscus, and later bandicoots and wallabies, on islands that had none, stocking them with game: among the oldest known long-distance transfers of stone and the earliest deliberate introductions of animals.
provenance: sources to check: Summerhayes and Allen 1993; White 2004, in Smith and Hesse (eds.)

upsert.boundary: The Panguna mine on Bougainville, 1972 to 1989
upsert.description: One of the world's largest open-pit copper and gold mines provides nearly half of Papua New Guinea's exports while its tailings poison the Jaba river; landowners' anger over the damage and the sharing of its wealth closes it in 1989.
provenance: sources to check: Regan, Light Intervention (2010)

upsert.boundary: Papuan migrants transform the islands' ancestry, about 500 to 300 BCE
upsert.description: Ancient genomes from Vanuatu show that within a few centuries after Lapita nearly all the islanders' ancestry was replaced by people with Papuan ancestry from the Bismarck Archipelago, yet their languages stayed Austronesian: a rare case of languages surviving the near-replacement of the people who spoke them. How it happened is unknown.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the timing and manner are uncertain
sources to check: Posth et al. 2018, Nature Ecology and Evolution 2; Lipson et al. 2018, Nature Communications 9

upsert.boundary: Papua New Guinea becomes independent, 16 September 1975
upsert.description: Australia's territories of Papua and New Guinea become one independent state under Michael Somare, with more than 800 languages; it has kept elected parliamentary government ever since, through frequent changes of government.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon, A Trial Separation (2005)

upsert.boundary: Solomon Islands' tensions and the regional mission, 1998 to 2017
upsert.description: Fighting between militias from Guadalcanal and Malaita, a coup in 2000 and the collapse of the state lead to the Australian-led Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (2003 to 2017).
provenance: sources to check: Moore, Happy Isles in Crisis (2004)

upsert.boundary: The sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands, about 1600 to 1750
upsert.description: A South American crop, carried by Spanish and Portuguese ships to the Moluccas in the 1500s, spreads by exchange into the highlands, where it grows higher up and on poorer soils than taro and feeds pigs; people, pig herds and the great exchange ceremonies such as the Melpa moka and the Enga tee grow. Whether this was a sudden 'Ipomoean revolution' or the speeding-up of a long intensification already under way is debated.
provenance: exploring: the size and speed of the change are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Watson 1965, Ethnology 4; Golson, in May and Nelson (eds.) (1982); Bayliss-Smith, Golson and Hughes, in Golson et al. (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Lapita cemetery at Teouma, about 1000 to 850 BCE
upsert.description: On Efate in Vanuatu the first settlers bury their dead, some without their skulls, with decorated Lapita pots; their ancient DNA shows East Asian ancestry with almost none from Papuans, overturning the view that the Lapita people had mixed with Near Oceanians before moving on.
provenance: sources to check: Bedford, Spriggs and Regenvanu 2006, Antiquity 80; Skoglund et al. 2016, Nature 538

upsert.boundary: People settle the Carolines, Marshalls and Kiribati, about 200 BCE to 200 CE
upsert.description: As the mid-Holocene high sea falls, coral atolls become habitable; voyagers from the south-east Solomons and Vanuatu settle them and spread west through the Carolines, speaking the Nuclear Micronesian languages and growing giant swamp taro and breadfruit in pits dug down to the freshwater lens.
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (the Carolines, Marshalls and Kiribati)

upsert.boundary: Castle Bravo, 1 March 1954
upsert.description: The largest American nuclear test, 15 megatons at Bikini, two and a half times what was expected, rains fallout on Rongelap and Utirik and on the Japanese fishing boat Lucky Dragon No. 5; the islanders' sickness and the crew's set off the worldwide campaign that leads to the partial test-ban treaty (1963).
provenance: sources to check: Hewlett and Holl, Atoms for Peace and War (1989)

upsert.boundary: The Compacts of Free Association, from 1986
upsert.description: The United States funds and defends the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands (1986) and Palau (1994), whose citizens may live and work in the United States without visas; perhaps a third of them have moved there, to Guam, Hawai'i and the mainland; the compacts are renewed in 2023 and 2024.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the share living abroad is approximate

upsert.boundary: The latte period in the Marianas, about 1000 to 1668
upsert.description: Chamorro villages build houses on rows of stone pillars capped with stone hemispheres, the latte, some over five metres tall, and grow rice in wet fields, the only rice in Oceania before contact.
provenance: sources to check: Rainbird (2004); Laguana et al. 2012

upsert.boundary: Seafarers from the Philippines settle the Marianas, about 1500 to 1300 BCE
upsert.description: Bringing red-slipped pottery like that of the northern Philippines, voyagers cross more than 2,000 kilometres of open ocean to Saipan, Tinian and Guam, the longest sea crossing of its time; ancient genomes link the first Chamorro ancestors to the Philippines. The date (1500 or about 1100 BCE) and the exact origin are debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; date and origin debated
sources to check: Carson et al. 2013; Hung et al. 2011, Antiquity 85; Pugach et al. 2021, PNAS 118

upsert.boundary: Phosphate mining on Nauru and Banaba, 1900 to the 2000s
upsert.description: British, German and later British, Australian and New Zealand companies strip-mine phosphate for the farms of Australia and New Zealand; the Banabans are moved to Rabi in Fiji (1945); independent Nauru (1968) briefly has one of the world's highest incomes, but by the 2000s four-fifths of the island is mined out and its trust funds are lost.
provenance: sources to check: Williams and Macdonald, The Phosphateers (1985); McDaniel and Gowdy, Paradise for Sale (2000)

upsert.boundary: Smallpox on Pohnpei, 1854
upsert.description: Brought by a whaling ship, smallpox kills perhaps half of Pohnpei's people within months; the missionaries from Hawai'i who arrived in 1852 gain converts among the survivors.

upsert.boundary: Japan's South Seas Mandate, 1914 to 1944
upsert.description: Japan seizes Germany's islands (October 1914) and rules them under a League of Nations mandate (1920); sugar plantations on Saipan and Tinian draw Japanese, Okinawan and Korean settlers, some 80,000 by 1940, outnumbering the islanders; the islands are fortified and become battlefields from 1943.

upsert.boundary: The Spanish-Chamorro wars, 1668 to 1698
upsert.description: Jesuit missionaries under Sanvitores arrive on Guam (1668); resistance after his killing (1672) turns into decades of war, and soldiers resettle the Chamorro into mission villages; war, smallpox and influenza cut them from perhaps 40,000 or more to about 5,000 by 1710. Their number before contact is debated (from about 20,000 to 100,000).
provenance: sources to check: Rogers (1995); Hezel 1982, Journal of Pacific History 17

upsert.boundary: The Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, 1947 to 1994
upsert.description: The United Nations entrusts Micronesia to the United States as its only strategic trust, letting it build bases and test weapons; its districts become the Northern Mariana Islands (a United States commonwealth, from 1978), the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands (1986) and Palau (1994).

upsert.boundary: Yap's stone money and island empire, from about 1400
upsert.description: Yapese voyagers quarry great limestone discs, rai, on Palau, 400 kilometres away, and ship them home, where ownership passes by agreement without the stones moving, a case economists cite for money as a shared ledger of credit; Yap's chiefs also receive tribute from the outer Caroline atolls in the sawei exchange. Most large stones were quarried in the 1800s with an Irish-American trader's ships; when quarrying began is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its beginning is debated
sources to check: Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Friedman 1991, Hoover Institution Working Paper; Fitzpatrick 2003

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, Melanesia and Micronesia: the Events inside their own eras, longest first. Melanesia: the Ivane highlanders, the first voyagers to the Bismarcks and Solomons, obsidian and animals carried across the Bismarck Sea, the Lapita cemetery at Teouma and the later Papuan turnover of the islands' ancestry, the kula and hiri exchanges, Fiji's chiefdoms, the sweet potato in the highlands, New Caledonia's convicts and nickel, measles in Fiji, the girmit, the partition of New Guinea, first contact in the highlands, the cargo movements, Papua New Guinea's independence, Panguna and Bougainville, Fiji's coups, New Caledonia's referendums and Solomon Islands' tensions. Micronesia: the crossing to the Marianas, the settlement of the atolls, the latte, Yap's stone money, the Spanish-Chamorro wars, smallpox on Pohnpei, phosphate on Nauru and Banaba, Japan's mandate, Castle Bravo, the Trust Territory and the Compacts. Western New Guinea, in Indonesia, is placed in South-eastern Asia too (Labelsqueeze#5363). Instances of mechanisms: measles in Fiji and smallpox on Pohnpei (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), the Spanish-Chamorro wars as a debated one (the card's failure mode 'germs absolve'), and the sweet potato in the highlands as a hypothesis (DensityRatchet#2ace).

upsert.boundary: Oceania becomes Christian, 1797 to about 1900
upsert.description: London Missionary Society missionaries land on Tahiti from the Duff (1797); after Pomare II's victory at Fei Pi (1815) Tahiti turns Christian, followed by Hawai'i (from 1820), Tonga and Samoa (1820s and 1830s), Fiji (1850s) and, largely through Pacific Islander teachers, much of Melanesia; Marsden preaches in New Zealand from 1814. Missions bring writing in the islanders' own languages; today about nine in ten Pacific Islanders are Christian.
provenance: sources to check: Garrett, To Live Among the Stars (1982)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia, Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: The Pacific Islands Forum and regional order, from 1971
upsert.description: Newly independent island states with Australia and New Zealand found the South Pacific Forum (1971), which makes the region a nuclear-free zone (Treaty of Rarotonga, 1985) and a voice on fisheries and climate; from the 2000s China and Taiwan compete for recognition, Solomon Islands and Kiribati switch to Beijing (2019) and sign security and policing agreements, and Australia answers with aid and treaties such as the Falepili Union with Tuvalu (2023).
provenance: sources to check: Fry, Framing the Islands (2019)

upsert.boundary: Whalers, sealers and traders across the Pacific, about 1790 to 1860
upsert.description: Sealers and whalers from Britain, the United States and France work the southern and central Pacific, using the Bay of Islands, Honolulu and Lahaina as their ports; beachcombers, muskets, alcohol and venereal disease spread with them, and traders buy sandalwood, beche-de-mer and pork for the China and colonial markets.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell (1989); Shineberg, They Came for Sandalwood (1967)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Micronesia, Melanesia, Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Ancestral Polynesian society takes shape, about 500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: In Tonga and Samoa the descendants of Lapita develop Proto-Polynesian, the language from which every Polynesian tongue descends, with its words for chief (ariki), sacred restriction (tapu) and power (mana); they give up making pottery and live on taro, yams, breadfruit and the reef.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; reconstructed from comparative linguistics and archaeology
sources to check: Kirch and Green (2001)

upsert.boundary: The Polynesian diaspora, from 1962
upsert.description: Samoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders and Niueans migrate to New Zealand, Australia and the United States for work; by the 2000s more Cook Islanders and Niueans live in New Zealand than at home, and remittances are among the largest shares of national income in the world for Tonga and Samoa.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, remittance data; Lee and Francis (eds.), Migration and Transnationalism (2009)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: The overthrow and annexation of Hawai'i, 1893 to 1898
upsert.description: American planters and businessmen, backed by marines from a United States warship, depose Queen Lili'uokalani (January 1893) when she seeks a new constitution; their republic (1894) is annexed by the United States in 1898 despite petitions against it signed by most Native Hawaiians; in 1993 Congress apologizes.
provenance: sources to check: Silva, Aloha Betrayed (2004)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Hawai'i's sugar plantations and their workers, 1850 to 1946
upsert.description: Planters bring some 400,000 contract workers from China, Japan, Portugal, Korea and the Philippines; by 1900 Japanese are the largest group in the islands and Native Hawaiians, about 40,000, a minority; the reciprocity treaty with the United States (1875), renewed in 1887 in return for Pearl Harbor, gives Hawaiian sugar free entry.
provenance: sources to check: Takaki, Pau Hana (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Hokule'a sails to Tahiti, 1976
upsert.description: A double-hulled voyaging canoe built by the Polynesian Voyaging Society sails from Hawai'i to Tahiti, navigated without instruments by Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia; the voyage answers the claim that Polynesia was settled by accidental drift and starts a revival of voyaging and of Hawaiian language and culture.
provenance: sources to check: Finney, Hokule'a: The Way to Tahiti (1979); Sharp, Ancient Voyagers in the Pacific (1956); Lewis, We, the Navigators (1972)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i, Tahiti), Micronesia (Satawal); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: The Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption, 15 January 2022
upsert.description: An undersea volcano in Tonga explodes with the largest blast in the atmosphere recorded since Krakatoa, sending pressure waves around the world, tsunamis across the Pacific and some 150 million tonnes of water vapour into the stratosphere; Tonga is cut off for weeks when its undersea cable breaks.
provenance: sources to check: Millan et al. 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49; Matoza et al. 2022, Science 377

upsert.boundary: Hawai'i abolishes the kapu, November 1819
upsert.description: Months after Kamehameha's death, his son Liholiho and the widow queen Ka'ahumanu eat together in public, breaking the kapu that forbade men and women to eat together, and order the temples destroyed, ending the old religion before the first missionaries land (1820).
provenance: sources to check: Kame'eleihiwa, Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: The Great Mahele, 1848 to 1850
upsert.description: Hawai'i's King Kamehameha III divides the kingdom's land among the crown, the government and the chiefs; the Kuleana Act lets commoners claim the plots they farm, which come to under 1% of the land, and foreigners may buy land (1850); American planters buy large estates for sugar.
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: The Mau of Samoa, 1926 to 1936
upsert.description: A non-violent movement of Samoan chiefs and part-Samoan merchants refuses cooperation with New Zealand's rule; on Black Saturday (28 December 1929) police fire on a procession in Apia, killing the high chief Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III and ten others. Western Samoa becomes the first Pacific island colony to win independence, in 1962.
provenance: sources to check: Field, Mau (1984); Meleisea (1987)

upsert.boundary: French nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa, 1966 to 1996
upsert.description: France explodes 193 weapons on two atolls of French Polynesia, 46 of them in the atmosphere until 1974; the test centre transforms Tahiti's economy, and the resumption of tests in 1995 sets off riots in Papeete and protests across the Pacific before France signs the test-ban treaty (1996). A 2021 study finds that fallout reached most of the territory's people.
provenance: sources to check: Philippe and Statius, Toxique (2021); Danielsson and Danielsson, Poisoned Reign (1986)

upsert.boundary: The attack on Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941
upsert.description: Japanese carrier aircraft strike the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on O'ahu, sinking or damaging eight battleships and killing some 2,400 Americans; the United States enters the Second World War.
provenance: sources to check: Prange, At Dawn We Slept (1981)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Influenza in Samoa, November 1918
upsert.description: New Zealand's administration lets the steamer Talune land passengers with influenza at Apia; about 8,500 die, a fifth of Western Samoa's people, while American Samoa, under strict quarantine, has no deaths: one of the clearest tests of quarantine in the pandemic.
provenance: sources to check: Tomkins 1992, Social History of Medicine 5; Shanks et al. 2012

upsert.boundary: Peruvian slave raids, 1862 to 1863
upsert.description: Ships from Callao kidnap or lure some 3,500 Polynesians and Micronesians from Rapa Nui, Tuvalu, Tokelau, the Cook Islands, Niue and Kiribati to work in Peru; most die of disease within a year, and the few returned bring smallpox to Rapa Nui, whose people fall to 111 by 1877, taking much of its knowledge with them, perhaps including the reading of the rongorongo script.
provenance: sources to check: Maude, Slavers in Paradise (1981)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Micronesia (Kiribati); the Americas: South America (Peru, and Rapa Nui by 2026 borders)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Society Islands, about 1025 to 1120
upsert.description: After the long pause, canoes from Samoa reach the Society Islands; radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains put the first settlement about 1025 to 1120, and Ra'iatea, with the marae of Taputapuatea, becomes a centre from which voyagers go on to the remoter islands. upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa, about 880 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Potters from Fiji settle Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE, a date fixed by uranium in their coral tools, and soon Samoa, where the Mulifanua site now lies under the lagoon: the first people of what becomes Polynesia.
provenance: sources to check: Burley et al. 2012, PLOS ONE 7; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: George Tupou I unites Tonga and gives it a constitution, 1845 to 1875
upsert.description: Taufa'ahau, a Methodist convert, defeats his rivals and becomes King George Tupou I (1845), frees commoners from chiefly service, gives every man a right to land and grants a constitution (1875); Tonga is the only Pacific kingdom never formally colonized, though a British protected state from 1900 to 1970.

upsert.boundary: Westerly winds open the way east, about 1140 to 1260
upsert.description: Reconstructions of past climate suggest that in these decades El Nino-like conditions brought more frequent westerly winds across the central Pacific, which would have made eastward voyages to Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa easier and may explain why East Polynesia was settled then and not during the long pause; the hypothesis is debated, with better canoes and the pressures of chiefly society as its rivals.
provenance: exploring: a hypothesis about the timing of the settlement
