upsert.boundary: The people of Bikini leave their atoll for the tests, March 1946
upsert.description: The navy moves the 167 people of Bikini to Rongerik, where food runs short, so that Operation Crossroads can test atomic bombs on warships in their lagoon; moved again to Kwajalein and then Kili (1948), some return in the 1970s only to be evacuated again in 1978, when they are found to have taken up radioactive caesium. Bikini remains uninhabited.
provenance: sources to check: Kiste, The Bikinians (1974); Niedenthal, For the Good of Mankind (2001)

upsert.boundary: The central Pacific campaign, November 1943 to August 1945
upsert.description: American forces cross Micronesia island by island: Tarawa (November 1943), Kwajalein and Enewetak (February 1944), the carrier raid that wrecks the fleet anchorage at Truk, then Saipan, Guam and Tinian (June to August 1944), where about 30,000 Japanese soldiers and thousands of Japanese, Okinawan, Korean and Chamorro civilians die, hundreds of them by suicide at Saipan's northern cliffs, and Peleliu (September to November 1944). From the Marianas, B-29s burn Japan's cities, and from Tinian the Enola Gay carries the atomic bomb to Hiroshima.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; civilian deaths on Saipan are uncertain
sources to check: Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985); Peattie, Nan'yo (1988); Poyer, Falgout and Carucci, The Typhoon of War (2001)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (Kiribati, the Marshalls, the Carolines, the Marianas, Palau)

upsert.boundary: German Micronesia, 1885 to 1914
upsert.description: Germany annexes the Marshall Islands (1885), where its firms dominate the copra trade, loses a quarrel with Spain over the Carolines that the Pope settles in Spain's favour (1885), and after Spain's defeat by the United States buys the Carolines and Northern Marianas (1899); officials order copra planting and road labour, and on Pohnpei the Sokehs rise against them (1910 to 1911), after which the leaders are shot and their people exiled to Palau.
provenance: sources to check: Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995); Firth, New Guinea under the Germans (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (the Marshalls, the Carolines, the Northern Marianas)

upsert.boundary: Guam and the Northern Marianas under the United States, from 1950
upsert.description: The Organic Act (1950) makes Guam's Chamorros United States citizens under a civilian government while the armed forces hold about a third of the island; the Northern Marianas choose commonwealth status (approved 1975, in force 1986); Japanese tourism, and garment factories that bring tens of thousands of Asian workers to Saipan (1980s to 2009), remake both economies, and Chamorro activists press for decolonization and against the build-up of bases.
provenance: sources to check: Rogers, Destiny's Landfall (1995); Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands)

upsert.boundary: The Gilbert and Ellice Islands part and become Kiribati and Tuvalu, 1975 to 1979
upsert.description: The Polynesian Ellice Islanders vote to separate from the Micronesian Gilbertese (1974) and become Tuvalu, independent on 1 October 1978; the Gilberts, with Banaba and the Line and Phoenix Islands, become Kiribati on 12 July 1979, a state of 33 atolls and islands spread over more than three million square kilometres of ocean.
provenance: sources to check: Macdonald, Cinderellas of the Empire (1982)

upsert.boundary: Kwajalein's missile range and Ebeye, from 1959
upsert.description: The United States makes Kwajalein lagoon the target of its intercontinental missile tests and a missile-defence range; the Marshallese who work there live on Ebeye, an islet of about 36 hectares with some 10,000 to 15,000 people, among the most crowded places in the Pacific, and landowners' sail-ins (1982) win higher lease payments.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Ebeye's population approximate
sources to check: Hanlon, Remaking Micronesia (1998); Johnson, Collision Course at Kwajalein (1984)

upsert.boundary: Leluh, the walled town of Kosrae's paramount chiefs, about 1250 to 1850
upsert.description: On an islet off Kosrae, rulers who unite the island build a town of basalt and coral walls, canals and royal tombs for perhaps 1,500 people, the capital of one of Micronesia's most stratified chiefdoms, until the diseases of whaling ships and the missions of the 1800s cut Kosrae's people from several thousand to about 300 (1880).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the town's size and the date of unification are approximate
sources to check: Cordy, The Lelu Stone Ruins (1993); Rainbird, The Archaeology of Micronesia (2004)

upsert.boundary: Nauru becomes independent, 31 January 1968
upsert.description: Led by Hammer DeRoburt, Nauruans refuse resettlement on an Australian island, leave Australian trusteeship as the world's smallest republic and buy the phosphate industry from the British Phosphate Commissioners (1970); their suit against Australia over the mined-out land is settled in 1993.
provenance: sources to check: Viviani, Nauru: Phosphate and Political Progress (1970); Weeramantry, Nauru: Environmental Damage under International Trusteeship (1992)

upsert.boundary: Carolinian navigators keep the art of wayfinding, documented from the 1600s to today
upsert.description: On the low islands of the central Carolines, navigators trained within their kin groups hold a star compass of rising and setting stars, read swells and birds, and track a voyage by moving an imagined reference island along the horizon (etak); they sail to Yap in the sawei exchange and, in the early 1800s, resettle Saipan, which the Spanish had emptied. When instrument-free navigation had died out in most of Polynesia, Mau Piailug of Satawal taught it to Hawaiians and guided Hokule'a to Tahiti (1976).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the tradition is far older than its first European description
sources to check: Gladwin, East Is a Big Bird (1970); Lewis, We, the Navigators (1972); Hezel, The First Taint of Civilization (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (the central Carolines, Yap, Saipan)

upsert.boundary: Palau's nuclear-free constitution and the long road to its compact, 1979 to 1994
upsert.description: Palau adopts the first constitution to ban nuclear weapons and materials from a country's territory (1979); because the compact offered by the United States required their transit, it fails seven referendums amid violence, including the assassination of the first president, Haruo Remeliik (1985), until the required majority is lowered and the compact passes (1993). Palau becomes independent in free association on 1 October 1994.
provenance: sources to check: Leibowitz, Embattled Island (1996); Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers from Island South-east Asia settle Palau, about 1100 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Speakers of a Western Malayo-Polynesian language, close to those of the Philippines and eastern Indonesia, settle the high limestone and volcanic islands of Palau, the westernmost of Micronesia; charcoal and pollen in lake cores suggest people burning the forest a thousand years or more earlier, which is debated. Yap's first settlement and the place of its language are debated too.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date of first settlement is debated (the earliest firm archaeology about 3,000 years ago; burning in pollen cores from about 4,500 years ago)
sources to check: Clark, Anderson and Wright 2006, Journal of Island and Coastal Archaeology 1; Rainbird, The Archaeology of Micronesia (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Pacific islands close their borders against COVID-19, 2020 to 2022
upsert.description: Most island states shut their borders in March 2020 and keep the virus out for one to two years, Tonga, Samoa and Kiribati into 2022; tourism stops and Fiji's economy shrinks by about a sixth in 2020, while Australia's and New Zealand's elimination strategies keep their deaths among the world's lowest until vaccines arrive.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; output figures approximate
sources to check: Asian Development Bank, Pacific Economic Monitor (2021); IMF Article IV reports for Fiji

upsert.boundary: The nuclear-free Pacific movement, 1975 to 1996
upsert.description: Churches, unions, island leaders and activists from Fiji, Vanuatu, Palau, Tahiti, Aotearoa and Australia join the Nuclear-Free and Independent Pacific movement (first conference in Suva, 1975) against French testing, the dumping of nuclear waste and the transit of nuclear weapons; Palau writes a ban into its constitution (1979), the Forum adopts the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone at Rarotonga (1985), French agents sink the Rainbow Warrior (1985), and riots in Papeete against the last series of tests precede France's end of testing (1996).
provenance: sources to check: Firth, Nuclear Playground (1987); Maclellan, Grappling with the Bomb (2017)

upsert.boundary: The island states claim the ocean: exclusive economic zones and tuna, 1977 to 2025
upsert.description: As states declare 200-nautical-mile zones (from 1977) and the Law of the Sea Convention (1982, in force 1994) confirms them, small island states gain rights over seas many thousand times their land; Kiribati's zone is about 3.4 million square kilometres. Through the Forum Fisheries Agency (1979) and the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (1982), whose vessel day scheme (from 2007) makes distant-water fleets bid for fishing days, licence revenue from the world's largest tuna fishery rises several-fold, to over half a billion dollars a year.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; revenue figures approximate
sources to check: Aqorau, Fishing for Success (2019); Forum Fisheries Agency economic and development indicators

upsert.boundary: The Festival of Pacific Arts, from 1972
upsert.description: Every four years from Suva (1972), dancers, singers, carvers, weavers, navigators and canoe builders from some two dozen Pacific countries and territories meet to show and revive arts that missions and colonial rule had discouraged, a meeting place for the region's new national and Pacific identities.
provenance: sources to check: the Pacific Community's records of the festival

upsert.boundary: French agents sink the Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, 10 July 1985
upsert.description: Agents of France's foreign intelligence service bomb Greenpeace's flagship in Auckland harbour before it can lead a flotilla to Moruroa, killing the photographer Fernando Pereira; New Zealand treats the attack as state terrorism, and it hardens the country's nuclear-free stand and its break with the alliance with the United States.
provenance: sources to check: King, Death of the Rainbow Warrior (1986)

upsert.boundary: Rugby across Oceania, from the 1870s
upsert.description: Brought by British settlers, soldiers and schools, rugby becomes New Zealand's national game, whose All Blacks tour Britain in 1905 and win three World Cups, rugby league becomes the game of eastern Australia's working towns, and rugby the national game of Fiji, Samoa and Tonga; island-born players fill professional teams in New Zealand, Australia, Europe and Japan, and Fiji's sevens team wins the islands' first Olympic gold (2016).
provenance: sources to check: Ryan (ed.), Tackling Rugby Myths (2005); Besnier, Brownell and Carter, The Anthropology of Sport (2018)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia, Polynesia)

upsert.boundary: France takes Tahiti: the protectorate and the Franco-Tahitian war, 1842 to 1847
upsert.description: After Queen Pomare IV expels two French Catholic priests, Admiral Dupetit-Thouars forces a protectorate on Tahiti (1842); Tahitians fight French troops from 1844 to 1847, while Britain, despite its Protestant missionaries' pleas, does not intervene, and the islands stay French.
provenance: sources to check: Newbury, Tahiti Nui (1980)

upsert.boundary: The Cook Islands and Niue choose free association with New Zealand, 1965 and 1974
upsert.description: The Cook Islands (August 1965) and Niue (October 1974) become self-governing in free association with New Zealand, which keeps responsibility for their defence and whose citizenship the islanders keep; free to move, most Cook Islanders and Niueans come to live in New Zealand.
provenance: sources to check: Crocombe (ed.), Cook Islands Politics (1979)

upsert.boundary: Hawai'i becomes the fiftieth state, August 1959
upsert.description: After a plebiscite in which over nine in ten voters approve, Hawai'i is admitted as a state on 21 August 1959; jet airliners reach Honolulu the same year, and tourism overtakes sugar and pineapple. The ballot offered no choice of independence, which sovereignty activists later contest.
provenance: sources to check: Bell, Last Among Equals (1984)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: The Hawaiian renaissance and sovereignty movement, from 1970
upsert.description: Native Hawaiians revive voyaging, hula and the Hawaiian language, banned as a medium of schooling since 1896: immersion preschools (Punana Leo, from 1984) bring back a language that only a few hundred children still spoke; protests end the navy's bombing of Kaho'olawe (1990), the United States apologizes for the overthrow of the kingdom (1993), and the stand against a telescope on Mauna Kea (2019) draws thousands.
provenance: sources to check: Trask, From a Native Daughter (1993); Wilson and Kamana 2001, in Hinton and Hale (eds.), The Green Book of Language Revitalization
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: The Marquesas lose nine-tenths of their people, 1790s to 1920
upsert.description: With whalers, traders and the French (1842) come venereal disease, tuberculosis, smallpox (1863), opium, alcohol and wars fought with muskets; the islanders fall from perhaps 50,000 or more at contact to about 2,000 by the 1920s, the steepest fall of any Polynesian people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the population at contact is debated, from about 35,000 to over 100,000
sources to check: Dening, Islands and Beaches (1980); Rallu, Les populations océaniennes aux XIXe et XXe siècles (1990)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians settle the outlier islands of Melanesia and Micronesia, about 1000 to 1500
upsert.description: Voyagers from Tuvalu, Samoa and the islands nearby sail back westward, against the general direction of settlement, to small islands on the edges of Melanesia and Micronesia, among them Tikopia, Anuta, Rennell and Bellona, Ontong Java, Sikaiana, Nukuoro and Kapingamarangi, where Polynesian languages are still spoken among Melanesian and Micronesian neighbours.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates vary by island
sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Feinberg and Scaglion (eds.), Polynesian Outliers (2012)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (Solomon Islands, Vanuatu), Micronesia (Federated States of Micronesia)

upsert.boundary: The Pomare kingdom of Tahiti, 1788 to 1880
upsert.description: Pomare I, a chief of Tahiti's north-west, uses the muskets and men of visiting ships and of the Bounty's mutineers to rise over his rivals; his son Pomare II, driven to Mo'orea, returns with the missionaries' backing, wins at Fei Pi (1815) and rules a Christian kingdom with a written law code (1819); under Queen Pomare IV France imposes a protectorate (1842), and Pomare V cedes the kingdom to France (1880).
provenance: sources to check: Newbury, Tahiti Nui (1980); Gunson 1969, Journal of Pacific History 4
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Tahiti and the Society Islands)

upsert.boundary: Chile annexes Rapa Nui, which is run as a sheep ranch, 1888 to 1966
upsert.description: Policarpo Toro signs an agreement with Rapa Nui's chiefs (September 1888) that the islanders understood as a protectorate; Chile leases the island to a sheep company, which confines the surviving Rapanui, about a hundred in the 1880s, to the village of Hanga Roa behind a wall until 1966, when the Easter Island Law makes them Chilean citizens under civilian government.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the meaning of the 1888 agreement is disputed
sources to check: Fischer, Island at the End of the World (2005); Delsing, Articulating Rapa Nui (2015)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Rapa Nui); the Americas: South America by 2026 borders (Chile)

upsert.boundary: Samoa becomes the first independent Pacific island state, 1 January 1962
upsert.description: After a constitutional convention and a United Nations plebiscite, Western Samoa leaves New Zealand's trusteeship with a parliament elected by the matai, the holders of family titles, and two paramount chiefs as joint heads of state; every adult gains the vote only in 1990.
provenance: sources to check: Davidson, Samoa mo Samoa (1967); Meleisea, The Making of Modern Samoa (1987)

upsert.boundary: Samoa's civil wars and partition, 1886 to 1899
upsert.description: Rival claimants to Samoa's paramount titles, Malietoa, Tupua Tamasese and Mata'afa, fight a series of wars, each backed by German, British or American consuls and warships; a cyclone wrecks the three powers' squadrons at Apia (March 1889), and the Tripartite Convention (December 1899) divides the islands, the west to Germany and the east to the United States as American Samoa.
provenance: sources to check: Gilson, Samoa 1830 to 1900 (1970); Meleisea, The Making of Modern Samoa (1987)

upsert.boundary: Tonga's democracy movement, 1992 to 2010
upsert.description: Commoners' representatives led by 'Akilisi Pohiva campaign against a parliament dominated by the king's appointees and the nobles; after riots burn much of central Nuku'alofa (November 2006), a new constitution lets the people elect 17 of 26 seats (2010), and Pohiva becomes the first commoner prime minister chosen by parliament (2014).
provenance: sources to check: Campbell, Island Kingdom (2nd ed. 2001)

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3 completed for Micronesia, Polynesia and Oceania as a whole. Micronesia: the settlement of Palau, Carolinian wayfinding, Leluh on Kosrae, German rule and the Sokehs rising, the central Pacific campaign, Bikini's people, Nauru's independence, Kiribati and Tuvalu, Palau's nuclear-free constitution, Kwajalein and Ebeye, and Guam and the Northern Marianas under the United States. Polynesia: the outliers, the Pomare kingdom and the French protectorate, the Marquesas' depopulation, Samoa's civil wars and partition, Rapa Nui under Chile, Hawai'i's statehood and renaissance, Samoa's independence, free association with New Zealand and Tonga's democracy movement. Oceania as a whole: the ocean claims and tuna, the nuclear-free Pacific movement and the Rainbow Warrior, the Festival of Pacific Arts, rugby, and the border closures against COVID-19. Each is placed in its subregion's innermost frame (Nestmap#8b8f), realizes one to three dimensions with the principal first, and names where its claims are to be checked. The Marquesas' collapse is claimed as an instance of VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd and Twinflow#9474, with the card's warning against crediting germs alone.

upsert.boundary: Austronesian seafarers reach the Philippines and the islands south, about 2200 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: From Taiwan, voyagers bring red-slipped pottery to the Cagayan valley of Luzon (Nagsabaran) and spread into Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas and Java; their languages replace earlier ones almost everywhere in the islands, while genomes show they mixed with the people already there; rice, important in Taiwan, drops out of many island economies.

sources to check: Bellwood, First Islanders (2017); Hung et al. 2011, Antiquity 85
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas)

upsert.boundary: Ngo Quyen defeats the Southern Han at the Bach Dang River, 938
upsert.description: Ngo Quyen plants iron-tipped stakes in the riverbed, lures the Southern Han fleet in at high tide and destroys it as the tide falls; he declares himself king (939), and the Vietnamese state remains independent of China, apart from the Ming occupation of 1407 to 1427.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

upsert.boundary: Borobudur and Prambanan, about 780 to 856
upsert.description: On the Kedu plain of central Java, the Sailendra kings build Borobudur, a stepped mountain of stone with 2,672 carved relief panels and 504 Buddhas, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth; a rival line builds the Shaiva temples of Prambanan (856). Volcanic ash and the court's move to east Java leave both to the forest.
provenance: sources to check: Miksic, Borobudur: Golden Tales of the Buddhas (1990)

upsert.boundary: Bronze working spreads on the mainland, from about 1100 BCE
upsert.description: Copper is mined at Phu Lon and Khao Wong Prachan and cast with tin into axes, bangles and bells at Ban Chiang, Ban Non Wat and Non Nok Tha; richer burials show rank growing. Ban Chiang's bronze was once dated to 3600 BCE; the dates are now much later, and a gap remains between the shorter and longer chronologies.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the chronology is debated
sources to check: Higham et al. 2015, Journal of World Prehistory 28; White and Hamilton 2014, in Roberts and Thornton (eds.), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective

upsert.boundary: Champa, the Cham kingdoms of the Vietnamese coast, about 192 to 1832
upsert.description: From the kingdom of Linyi (192), Cham-speaking Austronesian rulers of the central coast build brick temples to Shiva at My Son, trade and raid by sea, sack Angkor (1177) and fight Dai Viet for centuries; Le Thanh Tong takes their capital Vijaya (1471), and the last Cham principality is absorbed by Vietnam in 1832.
provenance: sources to check: Hardy, Cucarzi and Zolese (eds.), Champa and the Archaeology of My Son (2009); Kiernan, Viet Nam (2017)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (central and southern Vietnam)

upsert.boundary: Chenla and the first Khmer kingdoms, about 550 to 802
upsert.description: Khmer rulers inland of Funan build the temple city of Sambor Prei Kuk and leave the oldest dated inscription in Khmer (611); Chinese sources say Chenla split into a 'land' and a 'water' kingdom in the 700s, before Jayavarman II unites them.
provenance: sources to check: Vickery, Society, Economics and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia (1998)

upsert.boundary: A thousand years of Chinese rule in northern Vietnam, 111 BCE to 938 CE
upsert.description: The Han conquer Nam Viet and the Red River delta (111 BCE); the Trung sisters' rising (40 to 43) is crushed, Ly Bi's kingdom of Van Xuan (544 to 602) is brief, and under the Tang the delta is the Protectorate of Annam; Chinese writing, Confucian learning and Buddhism take hold among its elites while the Viet language endures, until Ngo Quyen's victory at Bach Dang (938).
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, The Birth of Vietnam (1983); Kiernan, Viet Nam (2017)

upsert.boundary: Dong Son and its bronze drums, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: Chiefs of the Red River delta, remembered in later Vietnamese tradition as the kings of Van Lang and Au Lac, cast great bronze drums decorated with boats, feathered warriors and houses on stilts; the drums travel as gifts of prestige to Thailand, Malaysia and eastern Indonesia.
provenance: sources to check: Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014); Kim 2015, The Origins of Ancient Vietnam

upsert.boundary: Dvaravati, the Mon Buddhist towns of central Thailand, about 550 to 1050
upsert.description: Moated towns of the Chao Phraya valley, Nakhon Pathom and U Thong among them, worship at Buddhist stupas and write in Mon and Pali; their Theravada carries on into the Tai kingdoms that later rule the valley.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; whether Dvaravati was one kingdom is debated
sources to check: Higham, The Civilization of Angkor (2001); Murphy 2016, Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 47

upsert.boundary: Modern humans reach Sunda, about 70,000 to 45,000 years ago
upsert.description: Teeth from Lida Ajer in Sumatra, dated to 73,000 to 63,000 years ago, and remains from Tam Pa Ling in Laos suggest Homo sapiens arrived before the main dispersal out of Africa, while the Niah Cave skull in Borneo (about 40,000 years ago) is the oldest firm modern skull; living people's genomes, which all share the Neanderthal admixture of about 47,000 years ago, fit a later arrival, so the early dates and the genomes are still being reconciled.
provenance: exploring: an early arrival is debated against the genomic timing
sources to check: Westaway et al. 2017, Nature 548; Demeter et al. 2015, Journal of Human Evolution 84; Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.boundary: Homo floresiensis on Flores, to about 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: On Flores, beyond the deep strait that kept Wallacea apart from the mainland even at the lowest sea levels, a hominin about a metre tall with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's lives from at least 700,000 years ago, as the fossils and tools of Mata Menge show, until about 50,000 years ago at Liang Bua. Whether it descends from a Homo erectus that shrank on the island or from an earlier, smaller hominin is debated, as is whether the arrival of modern humans ended it.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its ancestry and the cause of its end are debated
sources to check: Sutikna et al. 2016, Nature 532; van den Bergh et al. 2016, Nature 534

upsert.boundary: Funan, the port kingdom of the Mekong delta, about 100 to 550
upsert.description: Known from Chinese envoys of the 200s and from the excavated port of Oc Eo, where Roman coins, Indian seals and Chinese mirrors lie together, Funan's kings dig canals across the delta, trade between India and China, and take Indian titles; its trade fades as ships begin to sail straight through the Strait of Malacca.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far Funan was one state is debated
sources to check: Manguin 2009, in Hauser-Schäublin and Ingvar (eds.); Stark 2006; Vickery 2003, Bulletin de l'EFEO 90

upsert.boundary: Hoabinhian foragers of the mainland, about 22,000 to 4,000 years ago
upsert.description: Foragers who flake river pebbles on one side live in the rock shelters and hills of Vietnam, Laos, Thailand and Malaysia; ancient genomes show they are related to today's Semang of the Malay peninsula and to the Onge of the Andamans, and that their descendants mixed with the farmers who came from the north.
provenance: sources to check: McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014)

upsert.boundary: Indic kingship, Sanskrit and Brahmi scripts take hold, about 300 to 700
upsert.description: Rulers from Borneo to the Mekong take Sanskrit names, worship Shiva and Vishnu or patronize Buddhism, and leave the region's oldest inscriptions, on the sacrificial pillars of Kutai in Borneo (about 400) and the rock edicts of Tarumanagara in Java (about 450). Older accounts saw Indian colonists founding 'Indianized states'; most historians now see local rulers choosing what served them from Indian ideas, which they reshaped.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the nature of 'Indianization' is debated
sources to check: Coedès, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia (1968); Wolters, History, Culture and Region in Southeast Asian Perspectives (1999)

upsert.boundary: Port towns of the Thai-Malay isthmus trade with India and China, about 400 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: At Khao Sam Kaeo and Ban Don Ta Phet, Indian craftsmen make glass and stone beads, carnelian lions travel with Buddhist symbols, and Han bronze mirrors arrive from the north: the first ports of the trade between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
provenance: sources to check: Bérardé et al. 2017, in Bellina (ed.), Khao Sam Kaeo; Glover 1989

upsert.boundary: Deep-sea fishing at Jerimalai in Timor, about 42,000 years ago
upsert.description: Bones of tuna and other open-sea fish from 42,000 years ago, and a shell fish-hook from about 23,000 to 16,000 years ago, show island foragers fishing the deep sea, the oldest evidence of open-ocean fishing.
provenance: sources to check: O'Connor, Ono and Clarkson 2011, Science 334

upsert.boundary: Sundaland at the glacial maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: With the sea about 120 metres lower, Java, Sumatra and Borneo form one land with the mainland, about twice today's area; drier climate may open a corridor of savanna through its centre that separates the rainforests of the west and the east, which is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the savanna corridor is debated
sources to check: Bird, Taylor and Hunt 2005, Quaternary Science Reviews 24; Wurster et al. 2010, PNAS 107

upsert.boundary: Homo luzonensis on Luzon, known from about 67,000 to 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: Teeth and bones from Callao Cave, with curved finger and toe bones suited to climbing, show another small hominin on an island only a sea crossing could reach; butchered rhinoceros bones at Kalinga show hominins on Luzon some 700,000 years ago.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the fossils give minimum ages
sources to check: Détroit et al. 2019, Nature 568; Ingicco et al. 2018, Nature 557

upsert.boundary: The Ly and Tran dynasties build Dai Viet, 1009 to 1400
upsert.description: The Ly move the capital to Thang Long, today's Hanoi (1010), found the Temple of Literature (1070) and hold the first civil examinations (1075); the Tran dike the Red River and, under Tran Hung Dao, defeat Mongol invasions three times (1258, 1285, 1288); a script for Vietnamese, chu nom, comes into use beside Chinese.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013); Whitmore, in Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

upsert.boundary: Rice and millet farmers settle mainland South-east Asia, about 2500 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Villages with rice, millet, pigs and pottery appear at Man Bac in Vietnam and Khok Phanom Di and Ban Non Wat in Thailand; ancient genomes show farmers of East Asian ancestry arriving and mixing with Hoabinhian foragers, and Austroasiatic languages, among them Vietnamese and Khmer, probably spread with them. How much the farmers moved and how much the foragers adopted farming is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the balance of migration and adoption is debated
sources to check: McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Lipson et al. 2018, Science 361; Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014)

upsert.boundary: Majapahit, about 1293 to 1527
upsert.description: From the Brantas valley of east Java, Majapahit's kings and the minister Gajah Mada extend their claims over much of the archipelago; the court poem Nagarakretagama (1365) lists nearly a hundred tributaries, a list that exaggerates their rule. Hindu and Buddhist, it declines as Muslim port states rise along Java's north coast, and Demak takes its capital in the 1520s; Indonesian nationalists later claim it as their forerunner.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the reach of its rule is debated
sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008); Pigeaud, Java in the 14th Century (1960 to 1963)

upsert.boundary: The Mongols attack Dai Viet, Champa, Pagan and Java, 1257 to 1293
upsert.description: After taking Dali (1253), Mongol armies invade Dai Viet three times and are beaten, the last time at Bach Dang (1288); they occupy Champa's coast (1283 to 1285), break Pagan's power (1287), and send a fleet against Java (1293) that Raden Wijaya uses to defeat his rival before driving it out, founding Majapahit.
provenance: sources to check: Lo, China as a Sea Power 1127 to 1368 (2012); Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

upsert.boundary: The last Homo erectus at Ngandong in Java, about 117,000 to 108,000 years ago
upsert.description: A dozen skulls in a terrace of the Solo River belong to the last known population of Homo erectus, which had lived on Java for over a million years; they die out as open woodland gives way to rainforest.
provenance: sources to check: Rizal et al. 2020, Nature 577

upsert.boundary: Rainforest foragers at Niah Cave in Borneo, about 50,000 to 30,000 years ago
upsert.description: Foragers at the Great Cave of Niah burn forest edges to promote useful plants, leach poisonous tubers and nuts to make them edible, and hunt pigs and monkeys: among the oldest evidence of people living in tropical rainforest rather than at its edges.
provenance: sources to check: Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.boundary: Pagan unites the Irrawaddy valley, 1044 to 1287
upsert.description: Anawrahta unites the Irrawaddy basin and, by tradition after conquering the Mon of Thaton, makes Theravada Buddhism the court's religion; his successors build over ten thousand temples and monasteries on the plain of Bagan, about two thousand of which still stand, and the Burmese language is first written; the kingdom breaks up after Mongol attacks (1287).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Thaton conquest story is doubted
sources to check: Aung-Thwin, Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma (1985); Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Pyu cities of the Irrawaddy, about 200 BCE to 870 CE
upsert.description: Walled brick cities, Sri Ksetra, Beikthano and Halin, with Buddhist stupas, burial urns and a script of their own, rule the dry zone of Burma until raids from Nanzhao (832) end them; Pagan rises in their world.
provenance: sources to check: Stargardt, The Ancient Pyu of Burma (1990); Moore, Early Landscapes of Myanmar (2007)

upsert.boundary: Sa Huynh jar burials and the jade trade of the South China Sea, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: On the central Vietnamese coast, people bury their dead in great jars with ear ornaments of a style found around the South China Sea; the nephrite of many comes from Taiwan, worked in the Philippines and Vietnam and traded as far as Thailand and Borneo, one of the oldest maritime trades of jade.
provenance: sources to check: Hung et al. 2007, PNAS 104
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines, Borneo, Thailand)

upsert.boundary: The sea drowns Sundaland, about 12,000 to 6,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the ice sheets melt, the sea rises by some sixty metres over the Sunda shelf, in surges that flood a hundred kilometres of coast in a lifetime; Borneo, Sumatra and Java become islands, the Java Sea and the Strait of Malacca open, and the land area is halved; around 4000 BCE the sea stands a metre or two above today's.
provenance: sources to check: Hanebuth, Stattegger and Grootes 2000, Science 288; Sathiamurthy and Voris 2006

upsert.boundary: Tai peoples move south and found Sukhothai and Lan Na, about 1000 to 1300
upsert.description: Tai-speaking rice farmers from Guangxi and Yunnan spread into the upland valleys of Laos, the Shan hills and northern Thailand, take over Mon and Khmer towns and found Sukhothai (about 1238) and Lan Na at Chiang Mai (1296); an inscription credited to Sukhothai's king Ram Khamhaeng (1292), whose authenticity is debated, becomes the founding text of Thai history.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the inscription's date is debated
sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Ayutthaya (2017); Wyatt, Thailand (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Theravada Buddhism becomes the mainland's religion, about 1050 to 1450
upsert.description: Monks ordained in Sri Lanka's reformed Theravada lineage spread from Pagan to Sukhothai, Lan Na, Cambodia and Laos; village monasteries teach boys to read and write, and by the 1400s Theravada has displaced the Mahayana and Hindu cults of the courts, even at Angkor.
provenance: sources to check: Swearer, The Buddhist World of Southeast Asia (2nd ed. 2010)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia)

upsert.boundary: The Trung sisters' rising, 40 to 43
upsert.description: Trung Trac and Trung Nhi lead the Lac lords of the Red River delta against the Han governor and rule as queens until the general Ma Yuan crushes them (43); they become heroines of Vietnamese resistance to China.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, The Birth of Vietnam (1983)

upsert.boundary: Seafarers cross Wallacea toward Sahul, about 65,000 to 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: From Sunda's edge, groups cross the straits of Wallacea, by a northern route through Sulawesi and the Moluccas to New Guinea or a southern one through Timor to Australia, with gaps of at least 70 kilometres; to found the people of Sahul they must have crossed on purpose, on rafts or canoes, in groups of men, women and children.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the route and the date of the first crossing are debated
sources to check: Kealy, Louys and O'Connor 2018, Journal of Human Evolution 125; Bird et al. 2019, Scientific Reports 9
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Wallacea: Sulawesi, the Moluccas, Timor)

inferred: the range of Homo sapiens extends
inferred: life on an isolated island
inferred: ancestry carried into later peoples

exploring: the genomes show farmers' ancestry spreading and mixing with foragers, which fits the first invariant; whether the farmers advanced as a front of short moves, as the second and third require, or by jumps along rivers and coasts, is not known. The card's failure mode 'empty land assumed' applies: the Hoabinhians were there, and their ancestry survives in the farmers' descendants.

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, South-eastern Asia to 1350: the Events inside its first seven eras, longest first. Archaic humans (Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis, the last Homo erectus at Ngandong); modern humans' arrival, the crossings of Wallacea, the rainforest foragers of Niah, deep-sea fishing at Jerimalai, Sundaland at the glacial maximum and the Hoabinhian foragers; the drowning of Sundaland; the rice farmers of the mainland, the Austronesians' arrival in the Philippines and the first bronze; Dong Son, Sa Huynh's jade trade, the isthmus ports and a thousand years of Chinese rule in northern Vietnam with the Trung sisters' rising; Funan, Champa, the Pyu cities, Dvaravati, Chenla, Indic kingship and Borobudur; Bach Dang (938), the Ly and Tran, Pagan, the Mongol attacks, the Tai migrations, Theravada Buddhism and Majapahit. Foragers and peoples known from archaeology and genetics stand beside the states of the inscriptions (SurvivorCorrect#3780). Each Event sits in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f); where a point is debated (the date of modern humans' arrival, the farmers' spread, 'Indianization') the description states the debate (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The farmers' spread is claimed, as a hypothesis, as an instance of WaveOfAdvance#4cec.

upsert.boundary: Aceh's age of power, about 1520 to 1641
upsert.description: Aceh's sultans take the pepper trade of north Sumatra, ally with the Ottomans, who send gunners, and besiege Portuguese Malacca; under Iskandar Muda (1607 to 1636) Aceh is the strongest Muslim power in the islands and a centre of Malay Islamic learning and writing.
provenance: sources to check: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce vol. 2 (1993); Lombard, Le sultanat d'Atjéh au temps d'Iskandar Muda (1967)

upsert.boundary: The Aceh War, 1873 to 1904
upsert.description: The Netherlands invades the sultanate of Aceh to secure north Sumatra; Acehnese guerrillas led by ulama fight for three decades in the Dutch East Indies' longest and costliest war, which kills perhaps 60,000 to 100,000 Acehnese and some 37,000 colonial soldiers and labourers, most of them of disease.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the tolls are estimates
sources to check: Reid, The Contest for North Sumatra (1969); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: American rule in the Philippines, 1901 to 1946
upsert.description: The United States rules through Filipino elites: American teachers found a public school system taught in English, an elected assembly meets from 1907, and the Tydings-McDuffie Act (1934) sets up a Commonwealth under Manuel Quezon with independence promised for 1946; landlords keep their estates and the economy is tied to the American market.
provenance: sources to check: Abinales and Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Britain conquers Burma in three wars, 1824 to 1885
upsert.description: The first war (1824 to 1826), the costliest in British Indian history, takes Arakan and Tenasserim; the second (1852) takes Lower Burma and its delta; the third (1885) takes Mandalay and exiles King Thibaw, and Burma is ruled as a province of British India until 1937.
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The Making of Modern Burma (2001)

upsert.boundary: Ayutthaya, 1351 to 1767
upsert.description: Founded on an island in the Chao Phraya, Ayutthaya absorbs Sukhothai, sacks Angkor (1431) and trades rice, deerskins and forest goods with China, Japan, India, Persia and Europe; with Japanese, Persian, Portuguese and Dutch quarters and perhaps 200,000 people, it is one of Asia's great ports until Burmese armies destroy it in 1767.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the city's population is approximate
sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Ayutthaya (2017)

upsert.boundary: Burmese armies sack Ayutthaya, April 1767
upsert.description: After a fourteen-month siege the Konbaung armies take and burn the city, carry off tens of thousands of captives, the royal family among them, and end the four-century kingdom.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Ayutthaya (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch East India Company conquers Banda, 1621
upsert.description: To monopolize nutmeg, Jan Pieterszoon Coen's forces kill, enslave or drive out most of the roughly 15,000 Bandanese; the islands are divided into plantations worked by enslaved people for Dutch planters, the perkeniers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the population before the conquest is approximate
sources to check: Loth 1995, Modern Asian Studies 29; Hanna, Indonesian Banda (1978)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Banda islands, Indonesia)

upsert.boundary: British Malaya: tin, rubber and migrant workers, 1874 to 1941
upsert.description: The Pangkor treaty (1874) puts British residents beside the Malay sultans; Chinese miners make Malaya the world's largest producer of tin, and from about 1900 Tamil workers from India tap rubber on estates that make it the largest producer of rubber too; by 1931 Malays are fewer than half of the peninsula's people, the plural society that independent Malaysia inherits.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Drabble, An Economic History of Malaysia (2000)

upsert.boundary: Taksin and the Chakri kings rebuild Siam, 1767 to 1851
upsert.description: Taksin drives out the Burmese and reigns at Thonburi (1767 to 1782); Rama I founds Bangkok and the Chakri dynasty (1782), and his successors make Siam the mainland's strongest kingdom, overlord of Laos and Cambodia and the northern Malay states.
provenance: sources to check: Wyatt, Thailand: A Short History (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: The Cultivation System in Java, 1830 to 1870
upsert.description: Villages must grow coffee, sugar, indigo and other export crops on part of their land or give labour to the government, which pays them little and sells the crops in Amsterdam; the surplus sent home pays for about a third of the Dutch state's revenue in the 1850s, while rice land is squeezed and famines strike Cirebon (1844) and Demak and Grobogan (1849 to 1850).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how much it impoverished Java is debated
sources to check: Elson, Village Java under the Cultivation System (1994); Fasseur, The Politics of Colonial Exploitation (1992)

upsert.boundary: France conquers Indochina, 1858 to 1907
upsert.description: A Franco-Spanish fleet attacks Da Nang (1858); France takes Cochinchina (1862 to 1867), makes Cambodia a protectorate (1863), takes Tonkin and Annam in wars with Vietnam and China (1883 to 1885), forms the Indochinese Union (1887), takes Laos from Siam (1893) and western Cambodia's provinces (1907).
provenance: sources to check: Brocheux and Hémery, Indochina: An Ambiguous Colonization (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Java War, 1825 to 1830
upsert.description: Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta, claiming a mission to purify Java under Islam, leads a war against the Dutch and the courts that serve them; some 200,000 Javanese die, mostly of famine and disease, and 15,000 colonial soldiers, until Diponegoro is seized at a parley and exiled. The war's cost leads the Dutch to the Cultivation System.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Javanese toll is an estimate
sources to check: Carey, The Power of Prophecy (2007)

upsert.boundary: Konbaung Burma, 1752 to 1885
upsert.description: Alaungpaya reunites Burma from the dry zone (1752); his successors sack Ayutthaya (1767), defeat four Qing invasions, conquer Arakan (1785), Manipur and Assam (1817 to 1819), where their frontier meets British India, and lose three wars to Britain, the last ending the monarchy (1885).
provenance: sources to check: Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003); Thant Myint-U, The River of Lost Footsteps (2006)

upsert.boundary: Krakatoa erupts, August 1883
upsert.description: The volcano in the Sunda Strait explodes with a sound heard 4,800 kilometres away; its tsunamis kill about 36,000 people on the coasts of Java and Sumatra, telegraph cables carry the news round the world within hours, and the haze it leaves colours sunsets worldwide and cools the world for a few years.
provenance: sources to check: Simkin and Fiske, Krakatau 1883 (1983)

upsert.boundary: Lan Xang, the kingdom of a million elephants, 1353 to 1707
upsert.description: Fa Ngum unites the Lao principalities of the middle Mekong with Khmer backing (1353); its kings patronize Theravada Buddhism and move the capital to Vientiane (1560); after a long peace under Sourigna Vongsa the kingdom splits into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak (1707).
provenance: sources to check: Stuart-Fox, The Lao Kingdom of Lan Xang (1998)

upsert.boundary: Makassar's open port and its fall, about 1600 to 1669
upsert.description: Gowa and Tallo, Muslim from 1605, keep an open port for Portuguese, English, Danish and Malay merchants against the Dutch company's monopoly; the company, allied with Arung Palakka of Bone, conquers it (Treaty of Bongaya, 1667; fall of Somba Opu, 1669), and Bugis and Makassarese sailors and soldiers scatter across the archipelago.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya, The Heritage of Arung Palakka (1981); Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce vol. 2 (1993)

upsert.boundary: The Malacca sultanate, about 1400 to 1511
upsert.description: Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, founds Malacca where the monsoons of the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea meet, wins Ming protection during Zheng He's visits and turns Muslim; its harbour masters serve merchants from Gujarat, Tamil country, Java, China and the Ryukyus, Malay becomes the language of trade across the islands, and Tomé Pires writes that whoever is lord of Malacca has his hand on the throat of Venice.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Cortesão (ed.), The Suma Oriental of Tomé Pires (1944)

upsert.boundary: The Portuguese take Malacca, August 1511
upsert.description: Afonso de Albuquerque storms the city; the sultan's court flees to found Johor, and Muslim merchants shift their trade to Aceh, Johor, Banten and Brunei, so the Portuguese hold the port but never the trade they came for.
provenance: sources to check: Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia 1500 to 1700 (2nd ed. 2012)

upsert.boundary: The Ming occupy Vietnam, and Le Loi drives them out, 1407 to 1428
upsert.description: The Yongle emperor's armies take Dai Viet (1407) and rule it as a Chinese province, carrying off books and craftsmen; Le Loi's ten-year war from the hills of Thanh Hoa ends with the Ming withdrawal (1427) and the Le dynasty (1428), which builds a Confucian state on the Ming model.
provenance: sources to check: Whitmore, Vietnam, Ho Quy Ly and the Ming (1985); Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

upsert.boundary: Vietnam's march south, 1471 to 1757
upsert.description: Le Thanh Tong takes Champa's capital Vijaya (1471); from the 1600s the Nguyen lords of the south, at war with the Trinh of the north, settle Cham lands and then the Khmer lands of the Mekong delta, Prey Nokor becoming Saigon (1698), until by 1757 the delta is theirs, doubling the land of the Vietnamese.
provenance: sources to check: Li Tana, Nguyen Cochinchina (1998); Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (central and southern Vietnam, Cambodia)

upsert.boundary: The Chinese diaspora in South-east Asia, the Nanyang, from about 1400
upsert.description: Chinese traders settle in Malacca, Ayutthaya, Manila and Batavia; Spanish Manila's Chinese are massacred in 1603 and 1639 and Batavia's in 1740; in the 1800s and early 1900s millions come to work in tin mines and on plantations, and Chinese merchants come to dominate the region's commerce; violence against them recurs, in Indonesia in 1965 and 1998 among other times, and about 30 million people of Chinese descent live in the region today.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the present number depends on how descent is counted
sources to check: Wang Gungwu, The Chinese Overseas (2000); Kuhn, Chinese among Others (2008)

upsert.boundary: Nationalist movements form, 1908 to 1941
upsert.description: Budi Utomo (1908) and Sarekat Islam (1912), with some two million members by 1919, open Indonesian nationalism, and the Youth Pledge (1928) proclaims one nation and one language, Indonesian; Ho Chi Minh founds the Indochinese Communist Party (1930), the Nghe-Tinh soviets rise and are crushed (1930 to 1931), and in Burma the Thakins and the Saya San rebellion (1930 to 1932) challenge British rule.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Kahin, Nationalism and Revolution in Indonesia (1952); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Britain takes Penang and founds Singapore, 1786 to 1819
upsert.description: The East India Company takes Penang from the sultan of Kedah (1786) and Raffles founds Singapore as a free port (1819); the Anglo-Dutch treaty of 1824 divides the Malay world along the Strait of Malacca, the north to Britain and the south to the Netherlands, a line that still divides Malaysia from Indonesia.
provenance: sources to check: Turnbull, A History of Modern Singapore (3rd ed. 2009)

upsert.boundary: The Philippine-American War, 1899 to 1902
upsert.description: When the United States annexes the islands it bought from Spain, Aguinaldo's republic fights; about 20,000 Filipino soldiers and 4,200 Americans are killed, and perhaps 200,000 or more civilians die of violence, famine and cholera, while fighting in the Muslim south goes on to 1913. The civilian toll is debated, with estimates up to several times higher.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the civilian toll is debated
sources to check: Linn, The Philippine War 1899 to 1902 (2000); Gates 1984, Pacific Historical Review 53

upsert.boundary: The Philippine Revolution, 1896 to 1898
upsert.description: The Katipunan, a secret society led by Andres Bonifacio, rises against Spain (August 1896); Spain executes the reformist writer Jose Rizal (December 1896); Emilio Aguinaldo, who has Bonifacio executed, leads the revolution and declares the Philippines independent (12 June 1898), the first republic in Asia to fight a colonial power.
provenance: sources to check: Agoncillo, The Revolt of the Masses (1956); Ileto, Pasyon and Revolution (1979)

upsert.boundary: The Qing invade Burma four times, 1765 to 1769
upsert.description: The Qianlong emperor sends four armies into Burma to settle the Shan borderlands; disease and Burmese resistance destroy them, and the war ends in a truce that leaves both sides claiming victory; it also draws Burmese armies away from Siam just as Taksin rebuilds it.
provenance: sources to check: Dai Yingcong 2004, Modern Asian Studies 38

upsert.boundary: Rice frontiers of the great deltas, about 1850 to 1930
upsert.description: Settlers clear the swamps of the Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya and Mekong deltas for export rice: Lower Burma's rice land grows from about one million acres to about ten, and the three deltas feed India, China and Europe; peasants borrow from Chettiar and Chinese lenders, and when rice prices collapse in the Depression (1930) many lose their land.
provenance: sources to check: Adas, The Burma Delta (1974); Brocheux, The Mekong Delta (1995)

upsert.boundary: Siam's revolution of 1932
upsert.description: The People's Party, officers and officials educated in Europe, ends absolute monarchy in a bloodless coup (24 June 1932); military men soon dominate, and under Phibun the country is renamed Thailand (1939).
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed. 2014)

upsert.boundary: Siam keeps its independence: Mongkut's and Chulalongkorn's reforms, 1851 to 1910
upsert.description: Mongkut opens Siam to trade with the Bowring Treaty (1855); Chulalongkorn abolishes slavery and corvée step by step (1874 to 1905), builds ministries, railways and schools and brings the provinces under Bangkok, while ceding Laos, western Cambodia and the northern Malay states to France and Britain (1893 to 1909), leaving Siam a buffer between their empires and the only state in the region never colonized.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed. 2014); Wyatt, Thailand: A Short History (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: The spice islands and the world: cloves, nutmeg and pepper, about 1400 to 1650
upsert.description: Cloves from Ternate and Tidore, nutmeg and mace from the six small Banda islands, and pepper from Sumatra and west Java sell in China, India, the Middle East and Europe; their ports grow rich, Ternate's sultan Baabullah expels the Portuguese (1575), and the search for them draws the Portuguese, Spanish, English and Dutch into Asia, in what Anthony Reid calls the region's age of commerce.
provenance: sources to check: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce (1988 and 1993); Andaya, The World of Maluku (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Moluccas, Banda, Sumatra, Java)

upsert.boundary: Tambora erupts, April 1815
upsert.description: The largest eruption in recorded history blows away the top of the mountain on Sumbawa; perhaps 10,000 die at once and about 70,000 or more in the famine that follows on Sumbawa and Lombok, and the sulphate it sends into the stratosphere cools the world: 1816 is the 'year without a summer' in Europe and North America, with famine in Yunnan.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is uncertain
sources to check: Oppenheimer 2003, Progress in Physical Geography 27; Stothers 1984, Science 224

upsert.boundary: The Tay Son rebellion and the Nguyen unification of Vietnam, 1771 to 1802
upsert.description: Three brothers from Tay Son rise against the Nguyen lords, then overthrow the Trinh and the Le, defeat a Siamese army (1785) and a Qing army at Dong Da (1789); the surviving Nguyen prince, Nguyen Anh, with Siamese help and a few French volunteers, wins the long war and rules all Vietnam from Hue as the Gia Long emperor (1802).
provenance: sources to check: Dutton, The Tay Son Uprising (2006)

upsert.boundary: Toungoo Burma conquers the western mainland, 1531 to 1599
upsert.description: Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung, with Portuguese gunners and the wealth of the Mon ports, build the largest empire in the region's history, taking Lan Na, Ayutthaya (1564 and 1569) and Lan Xang; it collapses in the 1590s and is rebuilt on a smaller scale from Ava.
provenance: sources to check: Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

exploring: villagers tied to irrigated rice land that their kin had built could not leave without losing their livelihood (first invariant), and a colonial state working through Javanese regents took a share of their land and labour (second); but in the famine districts many did flee, so the third invariant held only in part. The card's caution applies: it is used here to recognize the arrangement, not to justify it.

changes.value: The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, South-eastern Asia from 1350 to 1941, inside the age of commerce, the consolidated kingdoms and the colonial era: Ayutthaya, Lan Xang, Malacca and its fall, the Ming occupation of Vietnam and Le Loi, Vietnam's march south, the spice islands, Toungoo Burma, the conquest of Banda, Makassar, Aceh and the Chinese diaspora; Konbaung Burma, the sack of Ayutthaya, the Qing invasions, Taksin and the Chakri, the Tay Son, Penang and Singapore, Tambora; the Anglo-Burmese wars, the Java War and the Cultivation System, French Indochina, Siam's reforms, the Aceh War, British Malaya, the rice frontiers of the deltas, Krakatoa, the Philippine Revolution and the Philippine-American War, American rule in the Philippines, the nationalist movements and Siam's revolution of 1932. The Cultivation System is claimed, as a hypothesis, as an instance of ExitCage#eef7, with the card's caution. Three relation ids written in r84 named a kind ('enables', 'contains') that their kind 'other' does not have; they are replaced by ids that say 'other', with the same content (Coursecandor#639e).

upsert.boundary: The August Revolution and Vietnam's declaration of independence, August to September 1945
upsert.description: In the gap between Japan's surrender and the Allies' arrival, the Viet Minh seize Hanoi (19 August 1945), the emperor Bao Dai abdicates, and on 2 September Ho Chi Minh declares the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Ba Dinh Square. Chinese troops take Japan's surrender in the north and British troops in the south, where they help the French return to Saigon.
provenance: sources to check: Marr, Vietnam 1945: The Quest for Power (1995); Logevall, Embers of War (2012)

upsert.boundary: The Asian–African Conference at Bandung, April 1955
upsert.description: Sukarno hosts the leaders of 29 Asian and African states, Nehru, Zhou Enlai and Nasser among them, who condemn colonialism 'in all its manifestations' and adopt ten principles of peaceful coexistence. The conference becomes the founding moment of the Third World as a political idea and leads to the Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961).
provenance: sources to check: Lee (ed.), Making a World after Empire: The Bandung Moment (2010)

upsert.boundary: Burma becomes independent, 4 January 1948
upsert.description: Aung San, who turned the Burma National Army from Japan's side to the Allies' in 1945, agrees independence with Attlee (January 1947) and the Panglong agreement with Shan, Kachin and Chin leaders (February 1947), but is assassinated with most of his cabinet in July 1947. Burma leaves the empire as a republic outside the Commonwealth under U Nu.
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The River of Lost Footsteps (2006); Charney, A History of Modern Burma (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Burma–Siam railway, 1942 to 1943
upsert.description: To supply its army in Burma, Japan builds a 415-kilometre railway from Ban Pong in Thailand to Thanbyuzayat in Burma with about 60,000 Allied prisoners of war and perhaps 200,000 or more Asian labourers, Tamils, Malays, Burmese, Javanese and Chinese. About 12,000 of the prisoners and perhaps 70,000 to 90,000 or more of the Asian labourers die of overwork, cholera, starvation and beatings.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Asian labourers' numbers and deaths are uncertain
sources to check: Kratoska (ed.), The Thailand–Burma Railway 1942–1946 (2006)

upsert.boundary: Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva conference, March to July 1954
upsert.description: Viet Minh divisions under Vo Nguyen Giap, with artillery hauled over the hills, besiege and take the French fortress of Dien Bien Phu (13 March to 7 May 1954). At Geneva (21 July) France agrees to leave; Vietnam is divided at the 17th parallel pending elections that are never held, and Laos and Cambodia are confirmed independent.
provenance: sources to check: Logevall, Embers of War (2012)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia); Europe (Western Europe: France, Switzerland)

upsert.boundary: Singapore falls to Japan, 15 February 1942
upsert.description: After a ten-week campaign down the Malay peninsula, General Percival surrenders Singapore and some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops to Yamashita's smaller army, the largest surrender in British military history. In the Sook Ching purge that follows, the Japanese kill tens of thousands of Singapore's Chinese men, by estimates from about 25,000 to 50,000.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Sook Ching toll is debated
sources to check: Farrell, The Defence and Fall of Singapore 1940–1942 (2005); Kratoska (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Huk rebellion in central Luzon, 1946 to 1954
upsert.description: The Hukbalahap, the communist-led peasant army that fought the Japanese, take up arms again when their elected congressmen are unseated and landlords return to central Luzon's rice estates. At its height (1950) it threatens Manila, until Ramon Magsaysay's mix of American-backed counterinsurgency, amnesty and land resettlement breaks it; its leader Luis Taruc surrenders in May 1954.
provenance: sources to check: Kerkvliet, The Huk Rebellion (1977)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines: central Luzon)

upsert.boundary: Japan conquers and occupies South-east Asia, December 1941 to August 1945
upsert.description: Japanese forces land in Thailand and Malaya on 8 December 1941 and within five months take Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, Burma and the Philippines; Thailand allies with Japan and French Indochina is occupied under Vichy's administration. The occupiers requisition rice, conscript labour, back nationalist leaders such as Sukarno and Ba Maw and arm and drill young men (PETA in Java, the Burma Independence Army). Famine in northern Vietnam and Java, forced labour and the fighting kill perhaps three to five million people across the region; the totals are poorly documented and debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the regional death toll is uncertain
sources to check: Kratoska, The Japanese Occupation of Malaya 1941–1945 (1998); Owen (ed.), The Emergence of Modern Southeast Asia (2005); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Forced labour and hunger in occupied Java, 1943 to 1945
upsert.description: The occupation government conscripts millions of Javanese as romusha, labourers for railways, airfields and fortifications in Java and across the region, some 270,000 of them sent beyond Java, of whom few return; it requisitions rice at fixed prices, and hunger spreads through 1944 and 1945. Estimates of the deaths from hunger and forced labour run from several hundred thousand to over two million; the figures are poorly documented and contested.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; numbers mobilized and dead are contested
sources to check: Sato, War, Nationalism and Peasants: Java under the Japanese Occupation (1994); Ricklefs (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Malayan Emergency, 1948 to 1960
upsert.description: After guerrillas kill three planters (June 1948) the British declare an emergency against the Malayan Communist Party's army, mostly ethnic Chinese. Under the Briggs Plan about 500,000 rural Chinese squatters are moved into fenced 'New Villages'; with food control, promised independence and Templer's campaign, the insurgency is pushed back to the Thai border by the late 1950s. About 11,000 people die, some 6,700 of them guerrillas.
provenance: sources to check: Stubbs, Hearts and Minds in Guerrilla Warfare (1989); Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Malaya becomes independent, 31 August 1957
upsert.description: The Federation of Malaya becomes independent under Tunku Abdul Rahman's Alliance of Malay, Chinese and Indian parties, on a bargain that keeps the Malay rulers and a special position for Malays and gives citizenship to most Chinese and Indians; British and Commonwealth troops stay to finish the Emergency.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's civil wars, from 1948
upsert.description: Within months of independence the Communist Party of Burma (March 1948) and the Karen National Union (January 1949) rise against the government, later joined by Kachin, Shan, Mon and other armies of the borderlands. The army, the Tatmadaw, makes itself the guardian of the union; the fighting waxes and wanes through ceasefires from 1989 and the opium and methamphetamine economies of the borderlands, and is counted the longest-running civil war in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Burma: Insurgency and the Politics of Ethnicity (1999); Callahan, Making Enemies (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Philippines becomes independent, 4 July 1946
upsert.description: The United States grants independence on the date the Tydings–McDuffie Act set, to a republic under Manuel Roxas. The Bell Trade Act ties its economy to the American market and gives Americans equal rights to its resources, and the agreements of 1947 keep American bases at Clark and Subic.
provenance: sources to check: Abinales and Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: The return to the Philippines: Leyte Gulf and the battle of Manila, October 1944 to August 1945
upsert.description: American forces land on Leyte (20 October 1944), and the battle of Leyte Gulf, the largest naval battle in history, destroys most of what remains of Japan's fleet. In the month-long battle for Manila (February to March 1945) about 100,000 civilians die, killed by Japanese troops or in the American shelling, and the city is left among the most destroyed of the war; fighting goes on in Luzon until Japan surrenders.
provenance: sources to check: Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985); Connaughton, Pimlott and Anderson, The Battle for Manila (1995)

upsert.boundary: Famine in northern Vietnam, 1944 to 1945
upsert.description: Japanese and French requisitions of rice, the forced planting of jute and other industrial crops, the Allied bombing of the railway and shipping from the south, and a poor harvest bring famine to Tonkin and northern Annam. About a million people die, by commonly cited estimates of 400,000 to two million. The Viet Minh's seizures of granaries win it the villages of the north.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated
sources to check: Gunn, Rice Wars in Colonial Vietnam (2014); Marr, Vietnam 1945 (1995)

changes.value: The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, South-eastern Asia from 1941 to about 1960, inside the era of occupation, revolutions and wars: Japan's conquest and occupation with the fall of Singapore, the Burma railway, forced labour and hunger in Java, the famine in northern Vietnam and the return to the Philippines; the August Revolution, the independence of the Philippines, Burma and Malaya, the Huk rebellion, Myanmar's civil wars, the Malayan Emergency, Dien Bien Phu and Geneva, and Bandung. Each sits in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f): the occupation's parts inside it and inside Japan's war, the battles of the Indochina wars inside them, the independences inside decolonization, and Myanmar's civil wars, which cross the era's end, in the region's lifecycle. Tolls that are debated are given as ranges with the debate stated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). Each realizes one to three dimensions, the principal first, and names where its recalled claims are to be checked.
