upsert.boundary: The American war in Vietnam, 1965 to 1973
upsert.description: After the Gulf of Tonkin resolution (August 1964) the United States begins bombing the North (March 1965) and lands combat troops, about 540,000 by 1969. Search-and-destroy, defoliants such as Agent Orange, free-fire zones and the Viet Cong's and North's war of attrition kill perhaps a million or more Vietnamese soldiers and civilians in these years and about 58,000 Americans, until the Paris Peace Accords (January 1973) take American forces out. The total Vietnamese toll of the wars is debated, from under two to over three million.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Vietnamese deaths are debated
sources to check: Herring, America's Longest War (5th ed. 2013); Hirschman, Preston and Loi, 'Vietnamese casualties during the American war', Population and Development Review 21 (1995)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam); Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: ASEAN is founded at Bangkok, 8 August 1967
upsert.description: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand sign the Bangkok Declaration, setting up the Association of Southeast Asian Nations a year after the confrontation ended. Anticommunist and wary of China and of each other, its members agree to consult rather than bind and not to interfere in each other's affairs, the 'ASEAN way'.
provenance: sources to check: Acharya, Constructing a Security Community in Southeast Asia (3rd ed. 2014)

upsert.boundary: Re-education camps and the boat people, 1975 to 1996
upsert.description: After the fall of Saigon the victors send hundreds of thousands of former officials and officers to re-education camps, and from 1978, as Vietnam turns on its ethnic Chinese and on private trade, people flee by sea. About 800,000 reach Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Hong Kong and the Philippines, and many die at sea of storms and pirates, estimates running from tens of thousands to 200,000 or more. Most are resettled in the United States, Canada, Australia and France under the Geneva agreements of 1979 and the Comprehensive Plan of Action (1989), which ends in 1996.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths at sea are unknown and debated
sources to check: Robinson, Terms of Refuge (1998); UNHCR, The State of the World's Refugees 2000
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam and the countries of first asylum), Eastern Asia (Hong Kong)

upsert.boundary: Cambodia's civil war and the American bombing, 1970 to 1975
upsert.description: Lon Nol deposes Prince Sihanouk (March 1970), and American and South Vietnamese troops strike North Vietnamese bases across the border. Sihanouk allies with the Khmer Rouge, whose army grows from a few thousand to tens of thousands, while American bombers drop hundreds of thousands of tonnes of bombs on the countryside until August 1973, killing perhaps 50,000 to 150,000, a debated range. About 250,000 to 300,000 or more die in the war in all, and refugees swell Phnom Penh to two million before it falls (17 April 1975).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; bombing tonnage and deaths are debated
sources to check: Kiernan, How Pol Pot Came to Power (2nd ed. 2004); Chandler, A History of Cambodia (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Indonesia invades and occupies East Timor, 1975 to 1999
upsert.description: Nine days after Fretilin declares East Timor independent of Portugal, Indonesia invades (7 December 1975), with American and Australian acquiescence, and annexes it (1976). In the war, the forced resettlement and the famine of 1977 to 1979, between about 100,000 and 180,000 Timorese die by the truth commission's estimates, a fifth or more of the people, about 18,600 of them killed outright. The Santa Cruz massacre (1991) brings the occupation to the world's notice.
provenance: sources to check: CAVR, Chega! (2005); Kiernan, 'The demography of genocide in Southeast Asia', Critical Asian Studies 35 (2003)

upsert.boundary: Saigon falls and Vietnam is reunified, March to April 1975
upsert.description: North Vietnam's spring offensive breaks the South's army in seven weeks; as the last Americans leave by helicopter from the embassy roof, tanks enter the presidential palace (30 April 1975), and the country is formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976. Phnom Penh had fallen to the Khmer Rouge on 17 April, and the Pathet Lao take Laos by December.
provenance: sources to check: Herring (2013); Veith, Black April (2012)

upsert.boundary: Miracle rice: the green revolution in South-east Asia, 1966 to 1990
upsert.description: The International Rice Research Institute at Los Baños in the Philippines, founded by the Ford and Rockefeller foundations (1960), releases IR8 (November 1966), a short-stemmed rice that doubles yields with fertilizer and irrigation; with its successors it spreads across Asia, and Indonesia, the world's largest rice importer in the 1970s, becomes self-sufficient by 1984. Farmers without irrigation or credit gain less, and pests and pesticide use grow.
provenance: sources to check: Hazell, The Asian Green Revolution (IFPRI, 2009); IRRI histories
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines, Indonesia, and across rice-growing Asia)

upsert.boundary: Sukarno's Guided Democracy, 1957 to 1966
upsert.description: Regional rebellions (1957 to 1958) and martial law end Indonesia's parliamentary democracy; Sukarno restores the 1945 constitution (1959) and rules by balancing the army against the growing Communist Party (PKI), seizes Dutch firms (1957) and West New Guinea (1962), confronts Malaysia, and lets inflation run past 600% a year by 1965. It ends in the crisis of 1965 and Suharto's order of 11 March 1966.
provenance: sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia (4th ed. 2008); Feith, The Decline of Constitutional Democracy in Indonesia (1962)

upsert.boundary: The killings in Indonesia, October 1965 to 1966
upsert.description: After the 30 September Movement kills six generals in Jakarta (1 October 1965), the army under Suharto blames the Communist Party and, with Muslim and nationalist militias and civilians it arms, kills about half a million alleged communists, by estimates from about 400,000 to a million or more, chiefly in Java and Bali; hundreds of thousands are imprisoned, many for a decade or more, as on Buru. The PKI, the largest communist party outside the communist states, is destroyed. American and British officials knew of and aided the campaign; who planned the 30 September Movement is still debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated
sources to check: Robinson, The Killing Season (2018); Cribb (ed.), The Indonesian Killings 1965–1966 (1990); Roosa, Pretext for Mass Murder (2006)

upsert.boundary: The secret war and the bombing of Laos, 1964 to 1973
upsert.description: As North Vietnam runs the Ho Chi Minh Trail through eastern Laos, the United States flies some 580,000 bombing missions and drops about two million tonnes of bombs on the country, more per person than on any other, while the CIA arms a Hmong army under Vang Pao against the Pathet Lao. Unexploded cluster bombs still kill and maim. The Pathet Lao take power in December 1975, and tens of thousands of Hmong flee to Thailand.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; tonnage figures vary by source
sources to check: Kurlantzick, A Great Place to Have a War (2017); Stuart-Fox, A History of Laos (1997)

upsert.boundary: Malaysia is formed, Indonesia confronts it, and Singapore leaves, 1963 to 1966
upsert.description: Malaya joins Singapore, Sarawak and Sabah as Malaysia (16 September 1963); Sukarno answers with Konfrontasi, raids across the Borneo border and landings on the peninsula, fought off by Malaysian and Commonwealth forces. Singapore, with its Chinese majority and Lee Kuan Yew's party at odds with the federation's Malay leaders, is expelled and becomes independent (9 August 1965), and the confrontation ends after Sukarno loses power (August 1966).
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Easter, Britain and the Confrontation with Indonesia (2004)

upsert.boundary: Marcos's martial law and dictatorship, 1972 to 1986
upsert.description: Ferdinand Marcos, barred from a third term, declares martial law (September 1972), closes Congress and the press and rules by decree; tens of thousands are detained, thousands tortured and some 3,000 killed, and the Marcos family and its cronies take over monopolies and borrow abroad. When Benigno Aquino returns from exile and is shot at Manila's airport (August 1983), the debt crisis and outrage turn business, the Church and young officers against the regime.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; counts of victims follow Amnesty International's estimates as usually cited
sources to check: McCoy, Closer than Brothers (1999); Abinales and Amoroso (2017)

upsert.boundary: The great cities: Jakarta, Manila and Bangkok, 1950 to 2025
upsert.description: As deaths fall and the countryside fills, migrants crowd the capitals: greater Jakarta grows from under two million people to about 30 million or more, greater Manila to over 25 million, and Bangkok's region to some 15 million, many in informal settlements on flood-prone land; the region's urban share rises from about 15% to about half. Jakarta sinks as its groundwater is pumped, and Indonesia begins building a new capital, Nusantara, in Borneo (2022).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; metropolitan totals depend on where the boundary is drawn
sources to check: UN, World Urbanization Prospects (2018); Demographia World Urban Areas
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand)

upsert.boundary: The Moro conflict in Mindanao, 1972 to 2019
upsert.description: Muslim Moros, outnumbered on their own island by Christian settlers since the American era, rise under Nur Misuari's Moro National Liberation Front (1972). After the Tripoli agreement (1976) and an autonomous region (1989 and 1996) the Moro Islamic Liberation Front fights on, until the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (2014) and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, ratified in January 2019. Perhaps 100,000 to 150,000 people die and millions are displaced over the decades.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: McKenna, Muslim Rulers and Rebels (1998); Abinales and Amoroso (2017)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines: Mindanao and Sulu)

upsert.boundary: Ne Win's military rule and the Burmese Way to Socialism, 1962 to 1988
upsert.description: General Ne Win seizes power (2 March 1962), nationalizes trade and industry, drives out much of the Indian community, closes the country to foreigners and rules through the army's Burma Socialist Programme Party. Once Asia's largest rice exporter, Burma becomes one of the poorest countries, and applies for least-developed status in 1987.
provenance: sources to check: Charney, A History of Modern Burma (2009); Taylor, The State in Myanmar (2009)

upsert.boundary: Suharto's New Order, 1966 to 1998
upsert.description: Taking power from Sukarno by stages (the order of 11 March 1966, president from 1967), Suharto rules through the army and Golkar. Western-trained technocrats tame inflation, and oil money from 1973 pays for schools, clinics, roads and rice self-sufficiency (1984); the share of Indonesians in poverty falls steeply. Dissent is suppressed, East Timor is occupied, and the Suharto family's businesses grow. The Asian crisis brings him down in May 1998.
provenance: sources to check: Elson, Suharto: A Political Biography (2001); Ricklefs (2008)

upsert.boundary: Filipino workers overseas, from 1974
upsert.description: The Labor Code of 1974 makes labour export a national policy, at first to the Gulf's construction boom. By the 2010s about two million Filipinos work abroad under contract at any time, as domestic workers in Hong Kong and the Gulf, as nurses and as about a quarter of the world's merchant seafarers, and their remittances, about a tenth of national income, sustain households across the islands.
provenance: sources to check: Rodriguez, Migrants for Export (2010); Philippine Statistics Authority, Survey on Overseas Filipinos
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines), Western Asia (the Gulf), Eastern Asia (Hong Kong)

upsert.boundary: Singapore's rise, 1965 to 2025
upsert.description: Expelled from Malaysia with no hinterland, water or army, Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party government courts foreign manufacturers, builds public flats that house over 80% of the people by the 1980s, a compulsory savings fund and English-medium schools, and governs as a dominant-party state with tight limits on dissent. By the 2010s Singapore's income per head is among the highest in the world, its port among the busiest, and it is the region's financial centre.
provenance: sources to check: Huff, The Economic Growth of Singapore (1994); Lee Kuan Yew, From Third World to First (2000), as a participant's account

upsert.boundary: The South China Sea disputes, from 1974
upsert.description: China takes the western Paracels from South Vietnam (January 1974), sinks Vietnamese ships at Johnson South Reef in the Spratlys (1988) and builds on Mischief Reef (1995); from 2013 it dredges seven reefs into artificial islands with runways and missile batteries. A tribunal under the Law of the Sea rules for the Philippines (July 2016) that China's 'nine-dash line' has no legal basis; China rejects the award, its coast guard and maritime militia press Vietnamese, Philippine and Malaysian fishermen and ships, and the United States sails through to assert free navigation.
provenance: exploring: read against SecurityDilemma#a61b, it is an instance only in part: each claimant reads the others' bases and patrols as threats and answers with its own, but China's island-building also aims at a territorial claim, not only at security, and an aggression answered by defence is not an instance
sources to check: Hayton, The South China Sea (2014); the award of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, Philippines v. China (12 July 2016)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei), Eastern Asia (China, Taiwan)

upsert.boundary: The Tet Offensive, January to March 1968
upsert.description: On the lunar new year (30 to 31 January 1968) the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese attack more than a hundred towns and cities across the South, the American embassy in Saigon among them. They are thrown back with heavy losses, and at Hue, held for nearly a month, they kill some 2,800 or more civilians, but the shock turns American opinion against the war: Johnson stops escalating and says he will not run again (31 March 1968). The My Lai massacre of 16 March comes to light the next year.
provenance: sources to check: Willbanks, The Tet Offensive: A Concise History (2007)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam); Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: Thailand's student uprising and the massacre at Thammasat, 1973 to 1976
upsert.description: Mass protests led by students force out the military rulers Thanom and Praphas (14 October 1973) and open three years of elected government and labour and peasant movements. On 6 October 1976 police and right-wing militias storm Thammasat University, killing at least 46 by the official count and probably many more, and the army takes power again; thousands of students join the communist insurgency in the hills.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed. 2014)

changes.value: The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, South-eastern Asia from about 1957 to 1979, and the long developments that begin in the era of wars and run past 1979. Inside the era: Guided Democracy, Malaysia and the confrontation, the bombing of Laos, the American war and the Tet Offensive, the killings in Indonesia of 1965 to 1966, ASEAN's founding, Cambodia's civil war, Thailand's uprising and massacre, and the fall of Saigon. In the region's lifecycle, because they cross 1979: Ne Win's rule, Suharto's New Order, the green revolution's rice, Marcos's martial law, the Moro conflict, Filipino workers abroad, the occupation of East Timor, the boat people, the South China Sea, Singapore's rise and the great cities. Each sits in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f); the Indochina wars contain their battles and the green revolution its South-east Asian part. The killings of 1965 to 1966 name the war and safety measures they move, for values in a later revision. Debated tolls are given as ranges (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b); the South China Sea is read against SecurityDilemma#a61b and found an instance only in part.

upsert.boundary: Burma's 1988 uprising and the stolen election of 1990
upsert.description: Ne Win's demonetization (1987) and police killings of students (March 1988) bring a general strike and mass protests that peak on 8 August 1988; the army crushes them in September, killing perhaps 3,000, and a new junta, the SLORC, takes power. Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy wins about four-fifths of the seats in the election of May 1990, but the junta refuses to hand over power and keeps her under house arrest.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Lintner, Outrage: Burma's Struggle for Democracy (1989); Charney (2009)

upsert.boundary: Peace in Aceh, August 2005
upsert.description: Eight months after the tsunami killed some 170,000 people in Aceh, the Indonesian government and the Free Aceh Movement, at war since 1976, sign a memorandum at Helsinki (15 August 2005): the movement disarms and drops independence, Aceh gets self-government with its own parties and a share of its oil and gas revenues, and the peace holds.
provenance: sources to check: Aspinall, Islam and Nation: Separatist Rebellion in Aceh (2009)

upsert.boundary: ASEAN's free trade area and enlargement, 1992 to 2025
upsert.description: The ASEAN Free Trade Area (January 1992) begins cutting tariffs among members; after Brunei (1984), Vietnam (1995), Laos and Myanmar (1997) and Cambodia (1999) join, uniting the region's ten states, and Timor-Leste joins as the eleventh in October 2025. The economic community (2015) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership with China, Japan, Korea, Australia and New Zealand (signed 2020) widen the market, while the ASEAN way leaves Myanmar's coup and the South China Sea unresolved.
provenance: sources to check: ASEAN Secretariat, ASEAN Integration Report; Acharya (2014)

upsert.boundary: China's war on Vietnam, February to March 1979
upsert.description: To punish Vietnam for invading Cambodia and allying with the Soviet Union, Deng Xiaoping sends some 200,000 troops into northern Vietnam (17 February 1979); after a month of fighting that kills tens of thousands on both sides and razes Lang Son and other border towns, China withdraws, claiming its lesson taught. Border clashes go on through the 1980s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are disputed by both sides
sources to check: Zhang Xiaoming, Deng Xiaoping's Long War (2015)

upsert.boundary: Doi Moi: Vietnam's reform and opening, from 1986
upsert.description: Facing hunger, inflation of several hundred per cent and the loss of Soviet aid, the Communist Party's Sixth Congress (December 1986) adopts 'renovation': farm households get their land and harvests (1988), prices are freed, and private firms and foreign investment are allowed. Vietnam turns from importing rice to being one of the largest exporters (from 1989), joins ASEAN (1995) and the WTO (2007), and by the 2020s assembles a large share of the world's phones and electronics; extreme poverty falls from about half of the people to a few per cent. Laos's New Economic Mechanism (1986) follows the same path.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, Vietnam 2035 (2016); Beresford, 'Doi Moi in review', Journal of Contemporary Asia 38 (2008)

upsert.boundary: Duterte's war on drugs, 2016 to 2022
upsert.description: President Rodrigo Duterte, elected on a promise to kill drug dealers, unleashes the police and vigilantes on the urban poor: over 6,000 suspects are killed in police operations by the government's own count, and rights groups estimate 12,000 to 30,000 deaths in all. The International Criminal Court opens an investigation, and Duterte is arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; totals are disputed
sources to check: Human Rights Watch, 'License to Kill' (2017); ICC, Situation in the Philippines

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's coup and the civil war that follows, from 2021
upsert.description: The army arrests Aung San Suu Kyi and seizes power (1 February 2021), calling the 2020 election fraudulent; it shoots down mass protests, and a resistance of people's defence forces allied with the ethnic armies grows into a nationwide war in which, after Operation 1027 (October 2023), the regime loses much of its border territory. About three million or more are displaced, the economy and public services collapse, and the army plans a staged election from December 2025.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; displacement figures change quickly
sources to check: UNHCR operational data on Myanmar; International Crisis Group reports

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's opening, 2010 to 2021
upsert.description: Under the army's 2008 constitution, which reserves a quarter of parliament's seats for the military, a nominally civilian government under Thein Sein frees Aung San Suu Kyi (November 2010) and other political prisoners, lifts censorship and opens the economy; mobile phones reach most people within a few years. Her party wins the elections of 2015 and 2020, and she defends the army over the Rohingya at The Hague (2019).
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The Hidden History of Burma (2019)

upsert.boundary: Oil palm and the clearing of Borneo and Sumatra, 1980 to 2025
upsert.description: Logging, pulpwood and oil palm plantations clear much of the lowland rainforest of Borneo and Sumatra: Indonesia and Malaysia come to grow about 85% of the world's palm oil, and Borneo's forest shrinks by about a third between 1973 and 2010. Fires set to clear land, on drained peat in the El Niño years of 1997 and 2015, send haze across the region and large pulses of carbon into the air; orangutans and other forest animals decline steeply.
provenance: sources to check: Gaveau et al., 'Four decades of forest persistence, clearance and logging on Borneo', PLOS ONE 9 (2014); FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment

upsert.boundary: People Power topples Marcos, February 1986
upsert.description: After a snap election (7 February 1986) that Marcos claims against the count of the citizens' watchdog, Defence Minister Enrile and General Ramos break with him; Cardinal Sin calls Manila out to protect them, and hundreds of thousands fill Epifanio de los Santos Avenue between the soldiers. After four days Marcos flies to Hawai'i and Corazon Aquino becomes president; the example is invoked from Seoul to Eastern Europe.
provenance: sources to check: Thompson, The Anti-Marcos Struggle (1995); Abinales and Amoroso (2017)

upsert.boundary: Mount Pinatubo erupts, June 1991
upsert.description: After two months of warnings that let some 60,000 people be evacuated, Pinatubo on Luzon produces the second-largest eruption of the twentieth century (15 June 1991) as a typhoon passes; about 850 people die, mostly when roofs collapse under wet ash and in later mudflows, and the United States gives up Clark Air Base. The 15 to 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide it puts into the stratosphere cool the Earth by about half a degree at the peak and by a few tenths of a degree over 1992.
provenance: sources to check: Newhall and Punongbayan (eds), Fire and Mud (1996); Hansen et al., 'Potential climate impact of Mount Pinatubo eruption', Geophysical Research Letters 19 (1992)

upsert.boundary: Reformasi: Suharto falls and Indonesia becomes a democracy, 1998 to 2004
upsert.description: With the rupiah collapsed and riots in Jakarta in which over a thousand die and Chinese Indonesians are targeted, students occupy parliament and Suharto resigns (21 May 1998). His successor Habibie frees the press and parties; Indonesia holds its first free election since 1955 (June 1999), lets East Timor vote, and devolves power to the districts, and in 2004 Indonesians elect their president directly for the first time.
provenance: sources to check: Aspinall, Opposing Suharto (2005); Ricklefs (2008)

upsert.boundary: The expulsion of the Rohingya, 2016 to 2017
upsert.description: After attacks by a small Rohingya armed group on border posts (October 2016 and August 2017), Myanmar's army and local mobs burn hundreds of Rohingya villages in northern Rakhine, killing thousands, at least 6,700 in the first month by one survey, and raping women. About 740,000 Rohingya, whom Myanmar had denied citizenship since 1982, flee to Bangladesh, where some 900,000 or more live in camps around Cox's Bazar; the Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar is before the International Court of Justice.
provenance: sources to check: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar, report (2018); Médecins Sans Frontières mortality surveys (2017)

upsert.boundary: Thailand's coups and colour-coded conflict, 2006 to 2023
upsert.description: The army overthrows Thaksin Shinawatra, whose parties win every election on rural votes (September 2006); his 'red shirt' supporters and the royalist 'yellow shirts' take turns occupying Bangkok, about 90 die when the army clears the red-shirt protest (2010), and a second coup (May 2014) brings General Prayut, who rules under a constitution written to keep the army's power until 2023.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit (2014)

upsert.boundary: Vietnam occupies Cambodia: the third Indochina war, 1979 to 1991
upsert.description: After Khmer Rouge raids on its border provinces, Vietnam invades (25 December 1978), takes Phnom Penh (7 January 1979) and installs a government of Khmer Rouge defectors under Heng Samrin and later Hun Sen. China, Thailand, ASEAN and the West back a coalition of the Khmer Rouge and two non-communist factions fighting from the Thai border, which keeps Cambodia's seat at the UN. Vietnam withdraws in 1989, and the Paris Peace Agreements (23 October 1991) end the war.
provenance: sources to check: Chandler, A History of Cambodia (4th ed. 2008); Westad and Quinn-Judge (eds), The Third Indochina War (2006)

upsert.boundary: East Timor votes for independence and becomes Timor-Leste, 1999 to 2002
upsert.description: In the UN-run referendum of 30 August 1999, 78.5% vote for independence; militias organized by the Indonesian army kill some 1,400 people and burn most of the territory's buildings, until an Australian-led force lands in September. After a UN administration, Timor-Leste becomes independent on 20 May 2002.
provenance: sources to check: CAVR, Chega! (2005); Martin, Self-Determination in East Timor (2001)

upsert.boundary: The UN in Cambodia, 1991 to 1993
upsert.description: Under the Paris agreements the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia, about 22,000 soldiers, police and civilians, the largest UN mission yet, brings home some 360,000 refugees from Thailand and holds an election (May 1993) in which nine-tenths of registered voters take part. Hun Sen's party loses but forces a shared government, which he ends by force in 1997; the Khmer Rouge boycott, fight on and fall apart after Pol Pot's death (1998).
provenance: sources to check: Doyle, UN Peacekeeping in Cambodia (1995); Chandler (2008)

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, step 3, South-eastern Asia from 1979 to 2025, inside the era of peace, growth and ASEAN: Vietnam's occupation of Cambodia and China's war on Vietnam, People Power, Doi Moi, Burma's 1988 uprising, the UN in Cambodia, ASEAN's free trade area and enlargement, oil palm and the clearing of Borneo and Sumatra, Pinatubo, Reformasi, East Timor's independence, peace in Aceh, Thailand's coups, Myanmar's opening, the Rohingya's expulsion and Myanmar's coup and war, and Duterte's drug war. Each sits in the innermost frame whose place and time hold it (Nestmap#8b8f): China's war inside the third Indochina war, oil palm inside the clearing of tropical forest, People Power and Reformasi inside the spread of democracy, the coup inside Myanmar's long civil war. People Power and Reformasi name the democracy share and Pinatubo the Earth's temperature, for values in a later revision. Debated tolls are given as ranges (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Oceania's top_10 is already full with ten Events and none of the new ones displaces them; its top_100 takes those with the longest or widest consequence for the region's later people, judged by consequence rather than fame (HindsightBlock#5d8d). Levels for South-eastern Asia's eras and Events of this pass, on everyone's scale, Asia's (the region's own), the principal realized dimension's and, for the American war and Tet, the Americas' and, for Geneva, Europe's. The reference class first (BaseRateInclude#1e63): everyone's top_100 already holds 122 Events and Asia's top_100 111, both past the hundred their names allow, so no Event of the pass stands at everyone's top_100 and only six at Asia's: Indic kingship and a thousand years of Chinese rule in Vietnam, which set the region's two political traditions; the spice trade, which drew Europe east; Japan's occupation, which ended colonial rule; the killings of 1965 in the world's fourth most populous country; and the green revolution's rice. The rest are top_1000 or noted, by consequence for later lives rather than fame (HindsightBlock#5d8d). Eras are frames: noted for everyone, top_1000 for Asia.

upsert.reason: Second within Asia to China's reform and growth, which stands at Asia's top_10.
Some 650 million people leave mass poverty within two generations, a part of the world's escape from poverty, which stands higher.

upsert.description: South-eastern Asia's part of the world's escape from extreme poverty.
The change that names the era of growth.

upsert.boundary: South-eastern Asia escapes mass poverty, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: Once the wars end, the region's economies grow among the world's fastest: output per person roughly quadruples in Indonesia and Thailand and grows about sixfold in Vietnam from 1990, Singapore becomes one of the richest places on Earth, and the share of the region's people below the World Bank's extreme-poverty line falls from about half in the early 1980s to a few per cent by the 2020s. The Asian crisis of 1997 to 1998 interrupts it, and the Philippines, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia lag.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; growth multiples and poverty shares are approximate
sources to check: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform; Maddison Project Database 2023; World Bank, The East Asian Miracle (1993)
inferred: output and work move from fields to factories

value: inferred: recalled history, every claim to be checked against the sources the Event names

changes.value: Before weighing causes: South-eastern Asia's escape from mass poverty after 1979 is a turning point the era's description states but no Event carries, so its causes had nothing to stand on. It becomes an Event of its own inside the era of growth and inside the world's escape from extreme poverty, placed in the region, realizing wealth (principal) and provisioning, with its levels on everyone's scale, Asia's and wealth's. The era stays the frame; a frame cannot be caused by its own parts, so the causes link to the new Event instead (Nestmap#8b8f).

provenance: sketch: Without Lapita's crossing to Remote Oceania there are no Polynesians; like the society it is a condition, not the timing.
upsert.reason: Without Lapita's crossing to Remote Oceania there are no Polynesians; like the society it is a condition, not the timing.

provenance: sketch: The gold rushes tripled Australia's people in the 1850s and peopled Otago; assisted emigration would have come anyway, more slowly.
upsert.reason: The gold rushes tripled Australia's people in the 1850s and peopled Otago; assisted emigration would have come anyway, more slowly.

provenance: sketch: Seventy years of civil war made the army a state within the state, with its own economy and the belief that it alone holds the union together; Indonesia's army, its separatist wars mostly over, had less to keep.
upsert.reason: Seventy years of civil war made the army a state within the state, with its own economy and the belief that it alone holds the union together; Indonesia's army, its separatist wars mostly over, had less to keep.

provenance: sketch: Vietnam's reform brings the region's third most populous country into the boom; the ASEAN members would have grown without it.
upsert.reason: Vietnam's reform brings the region's third most populous country into the boom; the ASEAN members would have grown without it.

provenance: sketch: Frontier killings, tens of thousands in Australia by recent counts, account for part of the loss, most in Queensland and Tasmania, and block recovery.
upsert.reason: Frontier killings, tens of thousands in Australia by recent counts, account for part of the loss, most in Queensland and Tasmania, and block recovery.

provenance: sketch: Sukarno's balancing of the army against the PKI, the party's unilateral land seizures against Muslim and landowning villagers in Java and Bali, and inflation past 600% had divided the countryside into armed camps; without them the army's purge would have found fewer willing killers.
upsert.reason: Sukarno's balancing of the army against the PKI, the party's unilateral land seizures against Muslim and landowning villagers in Java and Bali, and inflation past 600% had divided the countryside into armed camps; without them the army's purge would have found fewer willing killers.

provenance: sketch: The coup came in 1893, but annexation waited until the war with Spain made Hawai'i a base on the way to Manila; without the war the planters' republic might have stood alone for years.
upsert.reason: The coup came in 1893, but annexation waited until the war with Spain made Hawai'i a base on the way to Manila; without the war the planters' republic might have stood alone for years.

provenance: sketch: Sugar made a class of American planters who owned most of the kingdom's wealth, wanted lasting free entry to the American market, and armed the militia that backed the coup.
upsert.reason: Sugar made a class of American planters who owned most of the kingdom's wealth, wanted lasting free entry to the American market, and armed the militia that backed the coup.

provenance: sketch: In Australia the losses follow the colony: smallpox at Sydney in 1789 and the frontier's advance; without it Aboriginal losses come from disease alone, by ships and the Macassans.
upsert.reason: In Australia the losses follow the colony: smallpox at Sydney in 1789 and the frontier's advance; without it Aboriginal losses come from disease alone, by ships and the Macassans.

provenance: sketch: Without the movement built since 1908, its leaders and parties and the idea of one Indonesian nation and language, there would have been no republic to proclaim and defend.
upsert.reason: Without the movement built since 1908, its leaders and parties and the idea of one Indonesian nation and language, there would have been no republic to proclaim and defend.

provenance: sketch: Peace among the members after the confrontation lets governments spend on growth rather than on war with one another.
upsert.reason: Peace among the members after the confrontation lets governments spend on growth rather than on war with one another.

provenance: sketch: Without the occupation, the Dutch administration and army would have stood intact in 1945, with the nationalist leaders in prison or exile and no Indonesian army.
upsert.reason: Without the occupation, the Dutch administration and army would have stood intact in 1945, with the nationalist leaders in prison or exile and no Indonesian army.

provenance: sketch: Ships' crews brought the first epidemics and venereal disease to the islands decades before any colony; without them the diseases come later, with the colonists.
upsert.reason: Ships' crews brought the first epidemics and venereal disease to the islands decades before any colony; without them the diseases come later, with the colonists.

provenance: sketch: Cheap rice fed the growing cities and freed labour and foreign exchange for industry.
upsert.reason: Cheap rice fed the growing cities and freed labour and foreign exchange for industry.

provenance: sketch: Falling births give a generation in which workers outnumber dependants, the dividend of the lag between falling deaths and births (DemographicTransition#6e31); without it growth per person is slower.
upsert.reason: Falling births give a generation in which workers outnumber dependants, the dividend of the lag between falling deaths and births (DemographicTransition#6e31); without it growth per person is slower.

provenance: sketch: Wool gave the colonies their export and their credit in London, which paid for assisted passages.
upsert.reason: Wool gave the colonies their export and their credit in London, which paid for assisted passages.

provenance: sketch: Without the voyaging society of Tonga and Samoa there is no one to sail east; present through the pause, it makes the voyages possible, not timely.
upsert.reason: Without the voyaging society of Tonga and Samoa there is no one to sail east; present through the pause, it makes the voyages possible, not timely.

provenance: sketch: The tigers showed the export-led path and, after the yen and the won rose from 1985, moved their factories and capital south to Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.
upsert.reason: The tigers showed the export-led path and, after the yen and the won rose from 1985, moved their factories and capital south to Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

provenance: sketch: The Cold War made the PKI a global enemy: American and British officials supplied lists, money and propaganda and stayed silent; without that frame the army would have had less license, though the killing was organized in Indonesia.
upsert.reason: The Cold War made the PKI a global enemy: American and British officials supplied lists, money and propaganda and stayed silent; without that frame the army would have had less license, though the killing was organized in Indonesia.

provenance: sketch: Before 1970 the Khmer Rouge were a few thousand guerrillas in the hills; Lon Nol's coup gave them Sihanouk's name, the war their recruits and the bombing a grievance.
upsert.reason: Before 1970 the Khmer Rouge were a few thousand guerrillas in the hills; Lon Nol's coup gave them Sihanouk's name, the war their recruits and the bombing a grievance.

provenance: sketch: The Mahele made land saleable and foreigners bought much of it; in Tonga land could not be sold.
upsert.reason: The Mahele made land saleable and foreigners bought much of it; in Tonga land could not be sold.

provenance: sketch: France's advance took Laos and western Cambodia and, in the Paknam crisis of 1893, nearly Siam itself; without it Siam would more likely have kept all its lands and its independence.
upsert.reason: France's advance took Laos and western Cambodia and, in the Paknam crisis of 1893, nearly Siam itself; without it Siam would more likely have kept all its lands and its independence.

provenance: sketch: Native Hawaiians fell from perhaps 300,000 or more at contact to about 40,000 by 1890, outnumbered in their own kingdom by immigrant workers and foreigners.
upsert.reason: Native Hawaiians fell from perhaps 300,000 or more at contact to about 40,000 by 1890, outnumbered in their own kingdom by immigrant workers and foreigners.

provenance: sketch: Without the Chakri kings' rebuilt, centralized kingdom after 1767, a weaker and divided Siam would have offered the openings that Burma's wars and Vietnam's divisions offered Britain and France.
upsert.reason: Without the Chakri kings' rebuilt, centralized kingdom after 1767, a weaker and divided Siam would have offered the openings that Burma's wars and Vietnam's divisions offered Britain and France.

provenance: sketch: Twenty-six years of military rule built the army's businesses, its officer caste and its contempt for civilian politics.
upsert.reason: Twenty-six years of military rule built the army's businesses, its officer caste and its contempt for civilian politics.

provenance: sketch: If westerlies did open the way east in these decades, they explain the timing; the band is wide because the hypothesis rests on few climate records.
upsert.reason: If westerlies did open the way east in these decades, they explain the timing; the band is wide because the hypothesis rests on few climate records.

provenance: sketch: North Vietnam's army destroyed much of Lon Nol's army in 1970 to 1972 and armed and trained the Khmer Rouge until they could fight alone; without the wider war Cambodia would not have become a battlefield.
upsert.reason: North Vietnam's army destroyed much of Lon Nol's army in 1970 to 1972 and armed and trained the Khmer Rouge until they could fight alone; without the wider war Cambodia would not have become a battlefield.

provenance: sketch: The collapse of the first peoples by disease and violence opened the south-east's grasslands and much of Aotearoa to settlement; where Maori held their land, as in the North Island until the 1860s, settlement came slower.
upsert.reason: The collapse of the first peoples by disease and violence opened the south-east's grasslands and much of Aotearoa to settlement; where Maori held their land, as in the North Island until the 1860s, settlement came slower.

provenance: sketch: The rice export boom of the Chao Phraya delta after 1855 gave Britain the trade it wanted without rule, and the crown the revenue to pay for its new ministries, army and railways.
upsert.reason: The rice export boom of the Chao Phraya delta after 1855 gave Britain the trade it wanted without rule, and the crown the revenue to pay for its new ministries, army and railways.

provenance: sketch: Without the convict colony of 1788, British settlement would probably still have come, later and smaller; a French or other claim is the rival possibility.
upsert.reason: Without the convict colony of 1788, British settlement would probably still have come, later and smaller; a French or other claim is the rival possibility.

provenance: sketch: After the republic crushed the communist rising at Madiun (1948), the United States, wanting an anticommunist Indonesia, threatened Marshall aid to make the Dutch transfer sovereignty; without that pressure they could have held the cities for years more.
upsert.reason: After the republic crushed the communist rising at Madiun (1948), the United States, wanting an anticommunist Indonesia, threatened Marshall aid to make the Dutch transfer sovereignty; without that pressure they could have held the cities for years more.

provenance: sketch: Nearly all the growth comes from British and Irish emigrants and their children; without mass emigration the colonies grow from convicts and natural increase alone.
upsert.reason: Nearly all the growth comes from British and Irish emigrants and their children; without mass emigration the colonies grow from convicts and natural increase alone.

The Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass, values only where an Event of the pass moves a measure. Three eruptions in the Earth's temperature: Tambora (1815), Krakatoa (1883) and Pinatubo (1991), each a dip and recovery the decade readings smoothed over. changes.value: Opens the five parts of the carve carve.concept.humanity.asia, the shares of all living people in Asia's M49 subregions, which sum to Asia's share (h.region-asia) at every date given. Each subregion's share is Asia's share times a within-Asia split recalled from Maddison's and McEvedy and Jones's country series (1500 to 1945), the UN World Population Prospects (1950 to 2025) and, before 1500, sketched from the census of Han China, the archaeology of the first farmers and cities and the dispersal's dates. The splits are recalled and share one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca); India's ancient numbers are the widest debate (from about 35 to 75 million in 1 CE). Also fills Asia's own three missing values at the finest level of the schedule, interpolated so the five regional shares still sum to 100.

points.note: Homo sapiens reaches the steppe and its oases after the coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago; Neanderthals and Denisovans were there before.
The cold, dry glacial maximum thins the steppe's people.
Farming reaches the foot of the Kopet Dag at Jeitun, about 6000 BCE.
The oasis towns of the Bactria-Margiana complex, and herders spreading over the steppe with horses and wagons.
Samanid Bukhara and Samarkand, among the richest oases of the Islamic world.
The Mongol destruction of Khwarazm's and Transoxiana's cities (1219 to 1221); some oases never regain their numbers.
The Black Death passes through the steppe on its way west.
Flat across the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, which killed about one and a half to two million, some two fifths of the Kazakhs, and drove many into China.
The Virgin Lands campaign brings settlers to Kazakhstan, and high fertility in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the Soviet Union's end, Russians and Germans leave Kazakhstan by the million and births fall: the share dips.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Central Asia's part of it: the oases of Sogdiana, Bactria's north and Khwarazm, and the Kazakh steppe.

points.note: Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

Between -44000 and -37000, set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's, Europe's and Oceania's interpolated values.
Farming in south-west Asia and China multiplies Asia's numbers first.

Recalled from Barnosky (2008) and Bar-On, Phillips and Milo (2018) for wild mammals, and from Krausmann and colleagues (2009) and the UNEP International Resource Panel for material extraction since 1900; before 1900 both are sketches from what was built, mined and hunted. points.note: Stone for tools and ochre for colour: a few kilograms per person a year.
Natufian and early Neolithic stone houses, mortars and querns.
Villages of mud brick and lime plaster, as at Çatalhöyük and Jericho; lime is burned from stone. Earth for building is the first large draw on the stores.
Cities of mud brick, copper and then bronze smelted from ores.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant.
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the mines of Spain: lead in Greenland's ice reaches a peak in the first century CE not matched again until the Middle Ages (as recalled from the ice-core studies).
Western Roman building and mining collapse; the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China burns coal for iron, and Europe builds in stone.
Potosí's silver and Britain's first coal boom, small against the stone and earth of building.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Krausmann and colleagues: about 7 Gt of materials taken in 1900, about a quarter of it coal, ores and building minerals; the rest is harvested biomass, not counted here.
Mines and cities wrecked in Europe and Asia: extraction per person dips in the last year of the war.
The great acceleration: oil, cement and steel for reconstruction and for growth, faster than people.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries build less and use energy better.
China's building boom: it poured more cement in 2011 to 2013 than the United States in the whole twentieth century, and coal and iron ore follow.
The UNEP International Resource Panel counts about 100 Gt taken in 2020, three quarters of it non-metallic minerals, fossil fuels and metal ores.

upsert.reason: From 1900 Krausmann and colleagues' material flows (about 7 Gt of materials in 1900, a quarter of it minerals and fuels) and the UNEP International Resource Panel's (about 100 Gt in 2020, three quarters minerals and fuels), as recalled; before 1900 sketched from building, mining and toolmaking.

points.note: The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

upsert.reason: Pleistocene level from the reconstructions of megafaunal biomass (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On and colleagues 2018 put it near 0.02 Gt C), the present from Bar-On and colleagues and Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), as recalled; the path between is sketched from the dated extinctions and the nineteenth-century slaughters.

points.note: Homo sapiens reaches the steppe and its oases after the coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago; Neanderthals and Denisovans were there before.

Homo sapiens spreads onto the steppe and into the oases of Central Asia after the southern coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, meeting the Neanderthals and Denisovans already there; the share triples from a tiny base.
The cold, dry glacial maximum thins the steppe's people.
Farming reaches the foot of the Kopet Dag at Jeitun, about 6000 BCE.
The oasis towns of the Bactria-Margiana complex, and herders spreading over the steppe with horses and wagons.
Samanid Bukhara and Samarkand, among the richest oases of the Islamic world.
The Mongol destruction of Khwarazm's and Transoxiana's cities (1219 to 1221); some oases never regain their numbers.
The Black Death passes through the steppe on its way west.
Flat across the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, which killed about one and a half to two million, some two fifths of the Kazakhs, and drove many into China.
The Virgin Lands campaign brings settlers to Kazakhstan, and high fertility in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the Soviet Union's end, Russians and Germans leave Kazakhstan by the million and births fall: the share dips.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Central Asia's part of it: the oases of Sogdiana, Bactria's north and Khwarazm, and the Kazakh steppe.

points.note: Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

Range: Every human society from 320,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures of the living population.

changes.value: Opens the parts of the carves carve.concept.humanity.americas and carve.concept.humanity.americas.latin-america. Each share is the Americas' share (h.region-americas) times a within-hemisphere split, so Northern America and Latin America and the Caribbean sum to the Americas, and the Caribbean, Central and South America to Latin America and the Caribbean, at every date given. The splits are recalled: from 1950 the UN World Population Prospects; 1800 to 1945 national series (the United States census, Mexico's, Brazil's) as summarized by Maddison; 1492 to 1800 the contact-population debate (Denevan's hemispheric synthesis of about 54 million, with Borah and Cook's high and Sanders's low counts for central Mexico, Ubelaker's and Thornton's for the north); before 1492, sketched from the archaeology of the first Americans, the farming centres and the Classic and Postclassic states. One foundation underlies all of them (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: The first islanders: Banwari Trace on Trinidad, then Cuba and Hispaniola by about 4000 BCE.
Saladoid farmers and potters move up the island chain from the Orinoco.
The Taíno and their neighbours, perhaps two and a half million on the middle estimates; Hispaniola alone has been put anywhere from a few hundred thousand to eight million.
War, forced labour and earlier disease have killed most of the Greater Antilles' Taíno before smallpox arrives in December 1518; Hispaniola's census of 1514 finds about 26,000 left.
The low point: the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, a few Spanish towns and the first enslaved Africans, perhaps a third of a million.
Barbados's sugar boom of the 1640s begins the sugar islands' growth on enslaved Africans.
Saint-Domingue alone holds half a million enslaved people, the most valuable colony in the world.
The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) costs perhaps 150,000 to 350,000 lives.
The Caribbean's peak share: from here emigration to North America and Europe and early-falling births hold its growth below the world's.
Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz by about 8000 BCE; teosinte becomes maize over the next millennia.
The Olmec centres of the Gulf coast.
Teotihuacan, perhaps 100,000 people, and the Classic Maya cities near their height.
The Classic Maya collapse (ev.am.maya-collapse): the southern lowland cities empty between about 800 and 950, as droughts strike and wars multiply; the share dips while the Andes' rises.
About 21 million, on a middle reading: central Mexico alone has been put at 25 million by Borah and Cook and at 6 to 12 million by their critics, the sharpest of the contact-population debates.
Smallpox in 1520 and the siege of Tenochtitlan (ev.smallpox-americas): perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), perhaps the deadliest single epidemic in Mexico's history; whether it was an introduced Salmonella or a native haemorrhagic fever is debated.
The second cocoliztli (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576) kills perhaps two million.
Perhaps one in ten of central Mexico's people of 1519 remain; New Spain's whole population is about three million, Spaniards, Africans and mixed included.
Flat through the Mexican Revolution (ev.am.mexican-revolution): perhaps one to two million die or flee in 1910 to 1920, and Mexico's people barely grow.
Monte Verde, about 14,500 years ago.
The largest share of the hemisphere's foragers: the Andes, the Amazon and the pampas, with squash, gourds and later potatoes and manioc taken into cultivation.
Caral and the monumental sites of the Peruvian coast.
Moche and Nasca on the coast, Tiwanaku by Lake Titicaca.
Wari and Tiwanaku, and the earthwork towns of Amazonia and the Llanos de Mojos; Amazonia's numbers are among the most debated (AbsenceEvidence#10a3).
About 22 million on a middle reading: the Inca realm perhaps 10 to 14 million, Amazonia and the rest of the continent the remainder, with estimates for Amazonia from 1 to 10 million.
Smallpox reaches the Andes ahead of the Spaniards, about 1525 to 1528, and kills the Inca Huayna Capac; the civil war that follows is fought among the survivors (ev.am.inca-fall).
The nadir: the Andes' people perhaps a sixth of 1520's, Brazil's coastal peoples largely gone, and about a million Europeans and Africans.
The Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870) kills perhaps half of Paraguay's people, invisible at this scale beside Brazil's and Argentina's growth.
Mass immigration from Italy and Spain to Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil.
South America's peak share; Brazil's fertility falls below replacement in the early 2000s (ev.lac.fertility-transition).
Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few thousand years of entering the hemisphere.
About 45 million, nine in ten of the hemisphere's people, on a middle reading of a debate that runs from under 10 to over 100 million for the Americas as a whole.
The nadir: perhaps ten million, Indigenous, African, European and mixed.
Northern America has passed it, about 1875: for the first time since the first Americans, most of the hemisphere's people live north of Mexico.
Back ahead of Northern America about 1955: deaths fall fast while births stay near six per woman.
The peak share: from here births below the world's average and emigration north bring it down.
Zero on the usual account; the White Sands footprints in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would make it a small positive share. Their dating is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
People south of the ice in the far north-west and the Pacific coast (Paisley Caves, Cooper's Ferry) and in the east (Page-Ladson), soon after the ice-free corridor and the coast open.
The Clovis hunters spread across the continent within a few centuries.
Archaic foragers; from here the farming centres of Mesoamerica and the Andes grow faster, and Northern America's part of the hemisphere falls for six thousand years.
Maize farming spreads through the eastern woodlands and the Mississippian towns begin.
Cahokia empties and the Great Drought (1276 to 1299) drives the Ancestral Puebloans from the Four Corners.

Perhaps 4 to 5 million north of Mexico on middle estimates; the range runs from about 2 million (Ubelaker) to 18 million (Dobyns), with Thornton's 7 million between, a debate this value does not settle.
The Native nations' losses begin in earnest after de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the first coastal epidemics; the settlers are not yet a thousand.
The epidemics among the north-eastern nations of 1616 to 1640 and the Huron losses of the 1630s (ev.nam.northeast-epidemics) (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The low point: about a million Native people and a quarter of a million colonists and enslaved Africans.
The British colonies double every 25 years or so, the fastest growth then known, as Franklin and Malthus both noted.
Immigration is cut by the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, and the share rises more slowly.
Northern America's peak share, with the baby boom; from here births fall below the world's and the share declines.
Immigration keeps the decline slow: about one in seven of its people was born abroad.

Hunters return to Britain and the Baltic as the ice retreats (the Creswellian and Hamburgian).
Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 6500 BCE.
Foragers still, while farmers fill the Balkans and the Danube valley: the north's share of Europe falls until farming arrives about 4000 BCE.
Roman Britain at its fullest, perhaps two to three million.
England near its medieval peak, perhaps four and a half to five million before the famine of 1315 and the plague.

Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.

Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, about 230,000 years ago.
The dispersal out of Africa probably leaves from Eastern Africa, across the Bab el-Mandeb or the Sinai.
Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands; Bantu-speaking farmers reach the Great Lakes.
Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili coast's towns at their height.

The low point: about 26 million, a share less than half of 1750's.

Blombos Cave's engraved ochre and shell beads, Still Bay and Howiesons Poort.
Foragers only, while farmers elsewhere multiply: the San's share of humanity shrinks for ten thousand years.
Khoe herders with sheep have arrived; Bantu-speaking farmers follow within a few centuries.
Mapungubwe on the Limpopo, about 1220 to 1290, the first kingdom of the region.
Smallpox from the Cape (1713) devastates the Khoe; the Dutch colony grows slowly.
The wars and migrations of the Mfecane (about 1815 to 1840) on the highveld; their scale is debated.

The peak share: AIDS cuts life expectancy in South Africa and Botswana by a decade or more in the 2000s, and births fall faster than elsewhere in Africa.
Pearl millet domesticated in the Sahel about 2500 BCE; yams and oil palm in the forest margins.
The Nok culture's iron and terracottas on the Jos plateau.
The empire of Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade; Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes.
The Mali empire at its height, Ife's and Benin's cities in the forest.

The Bights of Benin and Biafra and the Gold Coast lose tens of thousands a year to the Atlantic trade: on Manning's estimates Western Africa's numbers stand still from about 1700 to 1850, while the rest of the world's grow.
The Nigerian civil war (1967 to 1970): perhaps one to two million Biafrans die, most of hunger.
Nigeria, about 230 million, is half of the region; Niger's births are the world's highest, near seven per woman.

Homo sapiens lives only in Africa; how it was spread across the continent is debated: an eastern or southern cradle, or a pan-African web of populations linked by migration, with Jebel Irhoud in the north among the oldest.

The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara: Northern Africa's share rises to perhaps a sixth (the Aterian).
The low point: about 14 million south of the Sahara against about 9 million in Egypt, the Maghreb and Nubia, on recalled reconstructions.
Bantu-speaking farmers with iron have reached the far south-east, and Sub-Saharan Africa grows faster than the Mediterranean world in decline.
Untouched or barely touched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Eurasia's and Egypt's people fall; whether plague reached south of the Sahara is debated.
