Opens the parts of carve.concept.humanity.wants.alive (adult survival) and carve.concept.causes-of-death (infection, birth, hunger, injury, chronic disease, beside the existing violent deaths, h.safety). The six cause rates are set to sum to a crude death rate consistent with the model's life expectancy and growth: about 3,300 per 100,000 a year for foragers (one over a life expectancy of 30), 3,600 to 4,000 for agrarian societies, 3,200 in 1900, 1,950 in 1950 (UN) and about 760 now. The split before 1950 is sketched from ethnographic causes of death among foragers (Gurven and Kaplan), the historical demography of plague and famine, and the first and second epidemiological transitions (Omran, Armelagos); from 1990 the Global Burden of Disease's groups, as recalled. Birth counts maternal deaths and all deaths of newborns in their first four weeks, so infection excludes newborns' infections; hunger counts famines' excess deaths whatever their proximate disease, so infection excludes those. Adult survival is set against the model's life expectancy and child mortality. Also fills Oceania's subregions at the remaining deep schedule dates (zero before people arrive) and smooths Micronesia's early values.

points.note: Ethnographic foragers reaching fifteen live on about 37 to 43 years (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled); the model's life expectancy of 30 with child mortality of 45% would imply about 45, so one of those two existing values, most likely the forager child mortality, is too high: ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to a third of children before five.
Farmers' adults live shorter lives than foragers': crowd diseases from livestock and crowding, worse teeth and bones in the skeletons (Armelagos's first epidemiological transition).

points.note: All people are mobile foragers, moving camp with the seasons.
Some glacial-age winter settlements on the Russian plain were reoccupied for months, but their people still moved.
Turns down: the Natufians of the Levant settle in stone houses about 12,500 BCE, harvesting wild cereals before they farm; the Jomon of Japan settle about the same time.

Rome extends citizenship to Italy after the Social War (89 BCE): about a million adult men may vote, if they come to Rome.
Falls: under Augustus the Roman assemblies lose their elections to the Senate and the emperor (by 14 CE).
Iceland's Althing and Venice's popular assembly.
The Italian communes' councils, the Swiss cantons and the county electors of England's Commons.
England's forty-shilling freeholders (1430).
The nobles of Poland-Lithuania, perhaps a tenth of its people, vote in their dietines and elect the king.
Rises: some five to six million Frenchmen vote for the Estates-General, and the new American states widen their franchises.
Napoleon's plebiscites are open to all Frenchmen: votes without a choice of rulers, counted here because the measure is the formal right.
Falls: the restored French monarchy limits the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers.
France adopts manhood suffrage in 1848; most white American men vote.
Britain's Second Reform Act (1867) and the German Reich's manhood suffrage (1871).
New Zealand (1893) and South Australia (1894) give women the vote.
Rises most: women vote in Britain (1918), Germany (1919), the United States (1920) and Soviet Russia, where the franchise excludes only the 'former people'.
The Soviet constitution of 1936 grants universal suffrage in single-candidate elections.
Women vote in France (1944), Italy and Japan (1946).
India's constitution of 1950 gives all adults the vote.
China's first national elections under the constitution of 1954, with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses; formal right, not a choice of rulers.
Switzerland gives women the federal vote in 1971, nearly the last democracy to do so.
Myanmar's coup and the Taliban's return end national elections for some ninety million people.

points.note: Perhaps a third of foragers' energy. Debated: Cordain's survey of the ethnographic atlas puts most foragers above half, Marlowe and others find warm-climate foragers nearer a quarter to a third; glacial-age hunters of the cold steppe ate more meat. The band carries both.
Falls as farming spreads: farmers' diets narrow to grain, with meat and milk about a tenth of energy; early farmers' skeletons are shorter and their teeth worse (h.health).
Turns up: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour dear, and Europeans and Near Easterners eat more meat than before or for centuries after (Abel's age of meat).
Falls again as Europe's population recovers and grain displaces meat.

Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.

Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.

points.note: Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

points.note: News moves at the pace of a walker or runner passing it on; fire and smoke signals carry only a few agreed meanings.
Royal messengers of Egypt and Sumer carry written orders by boat and on foot.
Couriers with horses and chariots carry the letters of the Amarna age between Egypt, Babylon and the Hittites.
The Achaemenid relay riders carry the king's messages from Sardis to Susa, some 2,700 km, in about a week, as Herodotus tells it.
Augustus's cursus publicus and the Han relay posts.
The Tang relay posts and the Abbasid barid.
The Mongol yam: urgent riders change horses at stations and cover 300 to 400 km a day.
The Taxis postal relays in Europe from about 1490; the Ming courier stations.

Jumps: Chappe's semaphore line from Paris to Lille (1794) passes a message 230 km in minutes to an hour; lines spread across France, Britain and Sweden. Words now outrun riders for the first time on a regular service.
Jumps again: the electric telegraph (Cooke and Wheatstone 1837, Morse 1844) carries messages across a continent in minutes, slowed by relaying and copying.
The transatlantic cable (1866): London to New York in minutes instead of ten days.
A cable network girdles the world; news reaches the antipodes in hours.
Radio telegraphy and radio telephony connect continents without relays.
Communications satellites (1962) and direct long-distance dialling.
Fibre-optic cables carry signals near the speed of light in glass.
At the limit: light in fibre travels about 200,000 km a second. From here what changes is who can send and receive, read in being online (h.internet) and mass media (h.media).

upsert.reason: From the recorded speeds of relay posts (Herodotus on the Persian riders, the Mongol yam, European posts), the semaphore and telegraph lines, and the latency of cable, radio and fibre networks, as recalled; orders of magnitude after 1850.

points.note: No farming, no fuel beyond campfires and landscape burning, whose carbon the cycle takes back: no human addition that lasts.
Begins: Ruddiman dates the start of a human addition to forest clearing about 6000 BCE; most carbon-cycle modellers find too little cleared carbon to matter before 1000 BCE or later.
Dips: forest returns on fields abandoned after the Black Death.

Falls: the Americas' abandoned fields regrow forest after the Great Dying and draw carbon down, Lewis and Maslin's 1610 'Orbis spike'; how much of the dip is human and how much the Little Ice Age's colder ocean is confounded.
On the eve of industry: a few ppm by most accounts, about 35 by Ruddiman's; the midpoint is taken.
Rises: clearing in North America and Russia and Britain's coal.
The 1940s plateau: depression and war slow emissions, and the ocean takes up more.
Accelerates: oil and coal after 1950, the 'great acceleration'.
China's coal boom makes the 2000s the fastest decade of growth.
About 160 ppm of the air's 427 is people's: two thirds of the cumulative emissions from fossil fuel, a third from clearing land, about 45% of them still airborne.
Before farming all of the air's carbon dioxide is the carbon cycle's own: it swings between about 180 ppm at glacial maxima and 280 in interglacials, as the Antarctic ice cores show.
Termination II under way: the ocean releases carbon as the ice melts.

From here the Holocene's rise from about 260 to 280 ppm is read as mostly natural (ocean carbonate compensation, peat and reef growth) with a small human share: a midpoint between most carbon-cycle modellers, who find it natural, and Ruddiman, who reads it as human and has the natural level falling toward 245 ppm. The band holds both.
The Little Ice Age's colder oceans take up carbon too, so part of the 1610 dip may be natural; the attribution is confounded.
Held at its late-Holocene level from here: the natural level is a counterfactual nobody observes, taken as constant while the human addition grows.

upsert.boundary: The Bourbon and Pombaline reforms, 1759 to 1808
upsert.description: Spain's Charles III and Portugal's Pombal tighten imperial rule: a new viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata (1776), beside New Granada's, which Philip V had founded in 1717 and restored in 1739; intendants, monopolies on tobacco and spirits, higher sales taxes, standing militias, the expulsion of the Jesuits (1759 from Portugal's lands, 1767 from Spain's) and Spaniards preferred over American-born creoles for office. Revenue rises sharply; so do revolts, Tupac Amaru's and the Comuneros' among them, and the creoles' sense of being colonials.

upsert.boundary: Westerly winds open the way east, about 1140 to 1260
upsert.description: Reconstructions of past climate suggest that in these decades El Nino-like conditions brought more frequent westerly winds across the central Pacific, which would have made eastward voyages to Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa easier. The hypothesis is debated. This account's own Event for the settlement of the Society Islands (about 1025 to 1120) comes before the window, so if both datings hold the winds could have timed the later voyages to the margins of East Polynesia but not the end of the long pause. Its rivals for that are better double-hulled canoes and sails, falling seas that exposed atolls as stepping stones, the pressures of chiefly society and population in West Polynesia, and prolonged drought in West Polynesia, which Sear and colleagues (2020) set beside a human arrival on Atiu in the Cook Islands about 900, earlier than the archaeology shows.
provenance: exploring: a hypothesis about the timing of the settlement, with its rivals stated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Goodwin, Browning and Anderson 2014, PNAS 111; Anderson et al. 2006, Journal of Pacific History 41; Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Sear et al. 2020, PNAS 117

corrected 2026-10-15: the text offered the winds as the reason East Polynesia was settled 'then and not during the long pause', which the model's own Society Islands dates (ev.pol.society-islands) contradict; the drought rival was missing. Check: the radiocarbon ranges of the Society Islands' earliest sites against the wind window

upsert.boundary: Colombia's armed conflict, 1964 to 2016
upsert.description: Communist guerrillas (the FARC from 1964, and the ELN), right-wing paramilitaries, drug cartels and the state fight for half a century, and cocaine money sustains them all from the 1980s. The dead are counted two ways: about 260,000 documented by the National Centre for Historical Memory from 1958 to 2018, and about 450,000 estimated by the Truth Commission for 1985 to 2018, with its range reaching higher. Some 8 million are displaced, the largest internal displacement in the hemisphere, until the FARC signs a peace accord (2016) that a referendum narrowly rejects and congress then approves.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Comision de la Verdad (Colombia), Informe final (2022); Centro Nacional de Memoria Historica, Basta ya (2013) and its later counts

corrected 2026-10-15: the text gave the Truth Commission's estimate of about 450,000 as the toll; the documented count is about 260,000, and the two differ by method (documented cases against a statistical estimate of the undocumented). Check: both reports

upsert.boundary: Squash and manioc in the forest islands of south-western Amazonia, about 8400 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: In the Llanos de Moxos of Bolivia, people build up thousands of forest islands in the seasonally flooded savanna and grow manioc by about 8400 BCE and squash by about 8300 BCE, among the earliest cultivation in the Americas; maize, carried from Mexico, follows by about 4900 BCE. Amazonia is one of the world's centres of plant domestication, the home of manioc, peanuts, peach palm and cacao, grown in the upper Amazon of Ecuador by about 3300 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lombardo et al. 2020, Nature 581; Zarrillo et al. 2018, Nature Ecology & Evolution 2

corrected 2026-10-15: the text put manioc at 'about 6800 BCE'; Lombardo and colleagues date manioc phytoliths to about 10,350 years before present (about 8400 BCE), squash to 10,250 and maize to 6,850 (about 4900 BCE), so 6800 looks like maize's date read as manioc's; the interval now opens at 8400 BCE. Check: the dates in Lombardo et al. 2020

upsert.boundary: Tambora erupts, April 1815

changes.value: The review pass, step 3: the Americas' scale had eleven Events at its top level and about 110 at its second, past the ten and the hundred or so their names allow (BaseRateInclude#1e63: the reference class is the whole span for those who follow the Americas' history). Columbus's landfall comes down to the second level, since the Columbian exchange, which begins with it, stands at the top and carries its consequences, the same rule the Americas pass used for the independences beneath the Atlantic revolutions. Nine Events come down from the second level to the third, each either carried by a parent Event at a level as high or higher, or with few consequences for later lives beside its fame or its place in the evidence. Every other judgment of the three regional passes is left as it stood.

The review pass, step 4: values corrected where parts contradicted their whole or each other, or a figure was off what is known, each with what was wrong and a check in its note (Coursecandor#639e). (1) Hunger counted the famines of the Ming-Qing and Thirty Years wars and of the Second World War that war's toll (h.war) already counts, as the usual tolls of those wars do; the six causes of death counted those deaths twice. (2) Forager and early farmer child mortality (45 to 47%) did not fit life expectancy and adult survival; the three are tied, and child mortality is the one the ethnography says is too high. (3) Oceania's share before 1850 keeps its value but its band is widened to carry the debate over pre-contact numbers. (4) Pinatubo's dip was a little small.

upsert.lens: To follow the forests that change apart, which one share hides: the boreal forests that come and go with the ice and that people barely touched until the twentieth century; the temperate forests that farmers cleared first, in Europe, China and eastern North America, which turned back up in western Europe and eastern North America between about 1830 and 1930 but, for the temperate domain as a whole, only about mid-century, with the low dated in this account to about 1950 to 1976 as planting in China and elsewhere came to outweigh clearing; the subtropical forests of the Mediterranean, southern China and northern India cleared early; and the tropical forests, the largest, cleared mostly since 1950. Range: The Earth's land at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, through glacial cycles and the spread of farming; measured as shares of land.

changes.value: The review pass, step 5: three carves of the tree pass corrected where their own words were not true of the account. (1) The causes-of-death carve claimed each death is counted once by its underlying cause, but war's toll (h.war) has always counted the famine and epidemic deaths of the great wars, as their usual tolls do; the carve now states the rule the values follow, and its hunger, infection and violence parts say where war's famines and epidemics go. (2) The war carve routed war's famine and disease deaths to hunger and infection and left the choice to a later pass; the choice is made here, with the alternative stated. (3) The forest carve said temperate forest has grown back since about 1930, where its own values put the world's low about 1950 to 1976; its lens now states the regional and world turns and the debate. Original verdict lines are kept and a correction line added (Coursecandor#639e, Revisance#73f1).

Review pass, coverage: values for life expectancy, child mortality, adult survival and the five causes of death at the Events of humanity's lifecycle that fell between two of their values (the regional passes filed new Events under humanity's eras: the Haitian and Latin American revolutions, Saint-Domingue's yellow fever, the Pacific war, the Japanese occupation of South-east Asia and others). Where no Event moves the measure the value is interpolated from its neighbours, with their band and tag; where one does, its note says why. Bands are kept as wide as the neighbours' (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

points.note: Ethnographic foragers reaching fifteen live on about 37 to 43 years (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled); the model's life expectancy of 30 with child mortality of 45% would imply about 45, so one of those two existing values, most likely the forager child mortality, is too high: ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to a third of children before five.
Held from the deep forager reading: remaining years at 15 for mobile foragers, from the ethnographic range of recent foragers (about 37 to 43) widened for the deep past; no evidence turns it here.
Farmers' adults live shorter lives than foragers': crowd diseases from livestock and crowding, worse teeth and bones in the skeletons (Armelagos's first epidemiological transition).
Roman tombstones and Egyptian census returns give adults of fifteen some 30 to 35 more years: crowded cities and malaria kill adults as well as children.
The Justinianic plague kills adults as freely as children.
The Black Death at its height kills people of every age in the year it passes (ev.black-death).

Smallpox reaches the Caribbean (1518) and Mexico (1520) and kills adults as well as children, but in about a tenth of humanity: a fall of several years there moves the world's figure by under half a year, inside the band.
The Taiping war and the American Civil War kill young men above all.
On the eve of the First World War: the fall to 1918 is the war's and the influenza's, so the series holds until here and drops after.
The 1918 influenza kills young adults above all, with the war's dead: adult survival falls by a sixth in a year while child mortality barely moves.
The war's deadliest years and the famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
War deaths and the war's famines last into 1945 (Vietnam, Java, the Dutch hunger winter, the battles for Germany, Okinawa and Manila), so adult survival is still near the 1944 low.
The war ends in August and September 1945: young men stop dying in battle and the occupied lands' famines end, so adult survival jumps.
On the postwar rise; the lower value at 1960 is the Great Leap famine's dip, not the trend.
The Great Leap Forward famine holds adult survival down in 1959 to 1961.
Recovering from the Great Leap famine of 1959 to 1961.
Slowed by AIDS in eastern and southern Africa and by the mortality crisis of Russian and Ukrainian men after 1991.
COVID-19's first year: excess deaths in 2020 are under a third of the pandemic's toll, so adult survival falls about halfway to the 2021 trough.
COVID-19 kills adults, the old above all (ev.covid).
About 33 births a year per 1,000 people, of whom perhaps one in twelve dies in the first month, and about one mother in a hundred births.
Held: deaths of mothers and newborns around birth, scaled from natural fertility of about six births per woman and recent forager neonatal loss.
Farmers have more births, closer together, and so more deaths at birth per head.
Semmelweis shows in 1847 that childbed fever is carried by doctors' hands; antisepsis reaches maternity wards only after 1870.
Sulfa drugs cut deaths from puerperal fever in rich countries by half within a few years.
About five million newborns and half a million mothers die a year, as the UN's child-mortality group and maternal-mortality group count them.
About 2.3 million newborns and 260,000 mothers a year, more than half of each in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Few live long enough to die of them; the old who do are often recorded as dying of a last infection.
Held: degenerative deaths at older ages in the few who reach them; low because few live past 60, not because the old do not die of them.
As infections retreat in the industrial countries more people reach the ages of heart disease and cancer; cigarettes spread after 1880.

Heart disease and lung cancer peak in rich countries; their fall afterwards, with less smoking and treated blood pressure, is matched by the poor world's ageing, so the world rate per head holds near five hundred.
About 42 million deaths, three in four of all, by the Global Burden of Disease's count, as recalled.
Rising per head as the world ages, though each age's rate keeps falling.
Foragers go hungry in bad seasons but move to food; few die of starvation outright.
Held: hunger as a direct cause in foragers is seasonal and local, not famine of stored grain; a glacial maximum may push it up, which the band allows.
Farmers tied to fields and stores die when a harvest fails; famine becomes a recurring cause of death.
The 4.2 kiloyear drought: Egypt's Old Kingdom and Akkad fall amid famine (ev.event-4-2-ka, if dated so in the model).
The Han collapse and the Roman Empire's third-century crisis: wars and failed harvests together.
Lower than in the crises of the third century, before the volcanic winter of 536 and the plague.
The volcanic winter of 536 to 541, the coldest decade in two thousand years, and the plague's disruption of harvests bring dearth.
After Europe's great famine of 1315 to 1317, which killed perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people.
The plague empties fields and stops trade: dearth follows the dying.

The Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War begin; their famine and plague deaths are counted in war's toll (h.war, 180 a year to 1650), as the usual tallies of those wars count them, so hunger outside them holds at the century's level.

Corrected from 220, which counted the famines of the Ming-Qing transition and the Thirty Years War that war's toll (h.war) already counts. What remains is the Little Ice Age's own dearths. Check: at 1618 to 1650 the six causes of death no longer count those wars' famine deaths twice.
After Tambora's year without a summer (1816), Europe's last great subsistence crisis.
The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852, about a million dead.
A lull between the famines of the late 1870s and those of 1896 to 1902.
The Indian famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 and the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, perhaps 30 to 60 million dead in all, under El Niño droughts and colonial and imperial policy.
The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.
About two thirds of foragers' deaths are from illness, mostly respiratory and gut infections and parasites (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled).

Held: infection in small mobile bands without crowd diseases, mostly gut, respiratory and wound infections and parasites in children; the largest share of forager deaths, as in recent forager mortality studies.
Villages, stored grain, livestock and standing water bring crowd diseases and parasites: infections rise with farming, the first epidemiological transition (Armelagos).
Malaria in Italy's lowlands, gut infections in Rome's crowded city: about seven in ten deaths are infections.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), probably smallpox, which killed perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people.
The Justinianic plague (ev.justinian-plague), the first pandemic of Yersinia pestis.
The plague recurs until about 750 and then vanishes from the Mediterranean for six centuries; infection deaths fall back to their agrarian level.
The Black Death at its height (ev.black-death): the infection death rate more than doubles for the years it passes.
Plague returns every decade or two after 1348.
Smallpox reaches the Caribbean in 1518 and Mexico in 1520; the Americas' epidemics raise the world's infection deaths toward the 1550 value, though the Americas hold about a tenth of humanity.
Smallpox, measles and cocoliztli in the Americas (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd) add deaths, though the Americas are a tenth of humanity.
Jenner's vaccine (1796) begins the retreat of smallpox; plague has left Europe.
Cholera pandemics in the new industrial cities; sanitation's retreat of infection begins in Britain after the 1848 Public Health Act.
Germ theory, clean water and sewers cut infection deaths in Europe and North America; most of the world has not yet begun.
Before the influenza: the 1918 value is the pandemic's spike, not a trend, so the fall since 1900 continues to here; wartime typhus in Serbia and the east adds little at the world's scale.
The 1918 influenza kills perhaps 25 to 50 million in little more than a year, most in India and China (ev.flu-1918).
The influenza has passed by 1920 and the long fall of infection deaths resumes.
Sulfa drugs, from 1935, the first antibacterial medicines.
Penicillin, streptomycin and DDT spread after the war: infection deaths fall faster than at any time before.
About 1967 chronic disease passes infection as the world's leading cause of death.
Smallpox is declared eradicated (1980); the Expanded Programme on Immunization reaches most children by 1990.
HIV/AIDS climbs toward its peak of about two million deaths a year (2004).
COVID-19's first year: about four to five million excess deaths in 2020 on the WHO's estimate, under a third of the pandemic's toll, which peaks in 2021.
COVID-19: about 15 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 on the WHO's estimate, most of them in 2021 (ev.covid).
Hunting, falls, drowning, snakebite and burns: about one forager death in fifteen.
Held: accidents, falls, drowning, animal attack among mobile hunters; violence is counted in h.safety, not here.

Revised down from the agrarian level: the share of deaths from injury in early registration data (England, Sweden) is about one in twenty-five, lower than the forager and agrarian sketches assumed; the earlier values stay as they are with their wide bands.
Mines, railways and factories: industrial accidents peak in the late nineteenth century.
Road deaths peak in rich countries about 1970, then fall with seat belts and safer cars, while they rise in the poor world.
About 1.2 million road deaths, 700,000 suicides, and falls and drownings: the Global Burden of Disease's injuries without interpersonal violence and war, as recalled.
Early farming villages: denser settlement and zoonoses lowered life expectancy below foragers'.
The Antonine plague and the Han collapse.
Just after the first wave; during 1348–1350 period life expectancy in the stricken regions fell far lower.
Plague returned every decade or two after 1348; life expectancy below both 1300 and 1500.
Riley's world estimate for 1800 is about 28.5, as recalled.
Before the First World War and the 1918 influenza.
The influenza year, about five years below 1910.
The war widens to the Soviet Union and, in December, the Pacific.
The war at its deadliest and Bengal's famine (1943): period life expectancy keeps falling toward the 1944 low.
The war's deadliest stretch, with the Bengal and Henan famines of 1942-44: period life expectancy dips below 1940's.
War deaths and the famines of Bengal (1943), Henan (1942–43), Vietnam and the Netherlands (1944–45) hold life expectancy down until the war ends.
The war ends in August 1945; deaths fall at once.
Peace, sulfa drugs, penicillin and DDT: life expectancy rises fast after the war.
Revised from 50: the Great Chinese Famine pulls world life expectancy down in 1959–1961.
Recovered from the Chinese famine and rising fast with vaccines and antibiotics in the poor world.
The COVID-19 trough.

Corrected from 45: with life expectancy at 30 and adults of fifteen living on about 41 more years (h.alive.adult), the share dying before five must be about 42%, since life expectancy is roughly the survivors to fifteen times (15 plus their remaining years) plus the short lives of the rest; ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to two fifths of their children before five (Gurven and Kaplan, as recalled). Corrected from 45.1, as at the forager dates: farming begins and child mortality starts to rise with crowding and new diseases.

Corrected from 47: life expectancy of 27 with adults living on about 37 years fits about 44% dying before five.
Corrected from 46.5; from here the earlier values already fit life expectancy and adult survival within a point.

Review pass, coverage: values at the Events of humanity's lifecycle that fell between two values, for food and its parts and sixteen measures of the long-standing set. Interpolated from the neighbours where no Event moves the measure; the food parts are interpolated on their shared dates so they still sum to food. Where a neighbour's band was a ±10–20% placeholder that the evidence does not support (adult height, the share under a state above 100%), the band is narrowed to what is known and said so here. Two readings turn: Concorde's grounding from July 2000 to November 2001, and the Comet 1's jet service of 1952 to 1954, which an earlier note left for a finer reading.

points.note: Dugout canoes, no riding animals yet.
Sail on the Nile; the horse being domesticated on the steppe.
Stagecoaches on turnpikes.
Railways.
The DC-3 enters service.
Four-engined airliners such as the Constellation begin scheduled transatlantic service.

The de Havilland Comet 1, the first jet airliner, flies scheduled services from May 1952 at about 725 km/h, until its grounding on 8 April 1954 after two crashes; this is the finer reading the note at 1958.75 left open.
After the Comet's grounding the fastest regular speed falls back to the propeller airliners' (DC-7, Super Constellation, about 550 km/h): the first jet age is interrupted.
The Tupolev Tu-104 begins scheduled jet service in the Soviet Union in September 1956, at about 750 to 800 km/h.

Just before the Boeing 707: the fastest scheduled airliners are the Soviet Tu-104 (from 1956) and the British Comet 4 (from 4 October 1958), at about 750 to 800 km/h. The Comet 1's service of 1952 to 1954, at about 725 km/h, and its grounding after crashes lie between 1950 and here, left for a finer reading.

The Boeing 707 begins scheduled service from New York (26 October 1958, ev.nam.jet-age), cruising at about 900 km/h, near the speed jet airliners still fly; with the DC-8 it makes jet travel the norm.
Concorde's first scheduled flights.
Revised from 900: Concorde's scheduled service (1976–2003) at about Mach 2 is the fastest regular passenger speed.
Revised from 900: Concorde.
Revised from 900: Concorde, grounded July 2000 to November 2001 after the Paris crash, retired in October 2003.

Concorde is grounded from the Paris crash (25 July 2000) until 7 November 2001: for these sixteen months the fastest regular passenger speed is the subsonic jets' again, and it returns to Mach 2 until October 2003.
Concorde flies again after the 2000 crash, until October 2003 (ev.concorde).
Concorde's last scheduled flight.
After Concorde: subsonic jets only. The fastest regular speed fell, a rare reversal.
Before the war cuts births.
War and flu cut births.
The Depression lowers births in the industrial countries.
Wartime separations and famine lower births.
Wartime separations lower births for a few years.
The postwar baby boom in the rich world.
The world's fertility is near its postwar peak; the transition begins in East Asia and Latin America (ev.fertility-transition).
The fertility transition is under way in East Asia and Latin America (ev.fertility-transition).

points.note: Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Deserted villages and abandoned fields after the plague: below 1300 (4.5).
American fields begin to be abandoned as their farmers die.
Within SurplusBound#7fe3: about one in five working outside food-getting.

Perhaps a third of foragers' energy. Debated: Cordain's survey of the ethnographic atlas puts most foragers above half, Marlowe and others find warm-climate foragers nearer a quarter to a third; glacial-age hunters of the cold steppe ate more meat. The band carries both.
Falls as farming spreads: farmers' diets narrow to grain, with meat and milk about a tenth of energy; early farmers' skeletons are shorter and their teeth worse (h.health).
Turns up: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour dear, and Europeans and Near Easterners eat more meat than before or for centuries after (Abel's age of meat).
Falls again as Europe's population recovers and grain displaces meat.
Refrigerated ships bring Argentine, Australian and New Zealand meat to Europe from 1880, and dairying spreads.
Wartime shortages cut meat and fat first.
Rises with incomes from here: Popkin's nutrition transition, from the rich countries in the 1950s and 1960s to China after 1980.
About a sixth of all calories.
Fruit, nuts and honey: perhaps a quarter of foragers' energy; honey alone is about a sixth of the Hadza's.
Falls as farming narrows the diet to staples.
Olive oil, wine, fruit and vegetables in the Mediterranean; sesame and other oils in India and China.
Rises: Caribbean and Brazilian slave plantations make sugar cheap enough for Europe's working households (Mintz's Sweetness and Power).
Rises most from here: vegetable oils, sugar and fruit carry most of the world's gain in calories since 1960; palm and soybean oil above all after 1970.
About a third of all calories: oils about a tenth, sugar about a twelfth.
Foragers' tubers, wild seeds and staple nuts: perhaps two fifths of their energy, less in cold climates.
Wild grains ground at Ohalo II by the Sea of Galilee about 23,000 years ago: seeds were eaten long before they were sown.
Rises as farming spreads: grain, rice, millet and roots become three quarters of farmers' energy.
Maize, potatoes and cassava begin to spread from the Americas through Eurasia and Africa.
Flat per person from here: the Green Revolution's higher yields feed more people at the same staple ration, and the gain in calories goes to animal and other foods.
About half of all calories, most of them cereals.
More land per survivor after the plague; better diets than in 1300 (1950).
Before wartime shortages.
Wartime shortages.
Wartime shortages and the famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
Wartime shortages and famines.
The postwar food crisis of 1946–47 in Europe and Asia.
The green revolution's new wheats reach India and Pakistan (ev.green-revolution).
Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
Jericho, if a walled village counts as a town.
Çatalhöyük and a few large villages, if counted as towns.
Uruk growing; the Tripolye megasites.
Plague hit towns hardest.
Early Upper Palaeolithic people were tall.
Heights fell with the first farming diets and village disease.
The low point of the farming transition's heights.
After the Black Death, survivors ate better where land was plentiful; European skeletal heights rose.

Band narrowed from the ±20% placeholder at 1800 (131 to 197 cm): national height series for the early 1800s, from about 160 cm in parts of Asia to about 170 in North America, bound the world mean within a few centimetres.

Penultimate glacial; numbers in Africa possibly reduced.
Deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Last Interglacial: a green Sahara and Arabia open early ranges beyond Africa.
Around the Toba eruption; the genetic case for a bottleneck then is weak, so no dip is drawn.
The dispersal out of Africa under way.
Last Glacial Maximum: northern ranges abandoned.
The Americas entered about now.
Geometric growth from 4.4 million at -10000 to 18 million at -5000 gives about 12 million; set a little lower because farming populations grew fastest after -6000.
Rome and Han China near their peaks, about 65 and 56 million.
After the Antonine plague and as the Han collapsed.
Recovering from the Justinianic plague; Tang China after the An Lushan rebellion.
Song China past 100 million; Europe's high-medieval growth.
After the Black Death and the Ming–Yuan transition: below both 1300 (390 million) and 1500 (461 million). McEvedy and Jones's order of magnitude, as recalled.
Eurasia grows, but the Americas lose millions in the first smallpox epidemic: the world adds less than its trend.
Before the war: about 1.8 billion.
Growth near its all-time peak of about 2% a year: deaths have fallen, births not yet (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Cheap smartphones and mobile data bring most of Asia and much of Africa online (ev.internet).
Gravettian aggregation sites such as Dolní Věstonice.
Jericho's first settlement grows beside its spring.
Large PPNB villages such as Abu Hureyra or Jericho.
Çatalhöyük near its peak (7100–5700 BCE). Larger than the -5000 value (5): the largest settlements shrank before the Tripolye megasites and Uruk.
The Tripolye megasites and early Uruk.
Ur.
Babylon or Linzi.
Rome or Chang'an.
Rome, past its peak.
Daxing-Chang'an, rebuilt by the Sui, as the Tang take it (ev.as.tang).
Chang'an under the Tang; Baghdad just founded.

Hangzhou after the fall of Kaifeng.
Nanjing, the early Ming capital, in Chandler's estimate as recalled; Cairo and Vijayanagara next.
London overtakes Beijing.
Greater Tokyo.
Tokyo.
Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.

That estimate counts 46 billion births between 8000 BCE and 1 CE and 26 billion between 1 and 1200 by assuming 80 and 60 births per 1,000 a year; in a population that barely grows that means a life expectancy of about 12.5 and 17 years. This model's life expectancy is 25 to 30 in those periods, as palaeodemography and ancient censuses put it, which gives 35 to 40 births per 1,000 and about 22 billion by 1 CE. changes.value: Review pass, coverage: the carbon parts and the four forest domains, opened by the tree pass on a sparser grid than the measures they divide, gain values at the Events of humanity's lifecycle they passed over (their subject is humanity, so they answer to its Events): the first farmers, the first states, the Lapita and Micronesian voyages, the Axial age, the classical and postclassical turns, the age of revolutions and the twentieth century. No Event among these moves the carbon cycle's own level or the boreal forest by more than their bands; the values are interpolated, with their neighbours' bands.

points.note: No farming, no fuel beyond campfires and landscape burning, whose carbon the cycle takes back: no human addition that lasts.
Begins: Ruddiman dates the start of a human addition to forest clearing about 6000 BCE; most carbon-cycle modellers find too little cleared carbon to matter before 1000 BCE or later.
Dips: forest returns on fields abandoned after the Black Death.

Falls: the Americas' abandoned fields regrow forest after the Great Dying and draw carbon down, Lewis and Maslin's 1610 'Orbis spike'; how much of the dip is human and how much the Little Ice Age's colder ocean is confounded.
On the eve of industry: a few ppm by most accounts, about 35 by Ruddiman's; the midpoint is taken.
Rises: clearing in North America and Russia and Britain's coal.

About 160 ppm of the air's 427 is people's: two thirds of the cumulative emissions from fossil fuel, a third from clearing land, about 45% of them still airborne.
Before farming all of the air's carbon dioxide is the carbon cycle's own: it swings between about 180 ppm at glacial maxima and 280 in interglacials, as the Antarctic ice cores show.
The MIS 8 glacial: cold oceans and an expanded sea ice hold carbon, and the air's carbon dioxide is low.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: the ocean releases carbon and the level rises near interglacial values.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) sets in: the ocean takes carbon back.

Termination II: the warming Southern Ocean releases carbon as the Last Interglacial begins.
The Last Interglacial has ended; the ocean draws carbon down as the ice returns.
The last deglaciation: carbon dioxide rises from about 190 to 265 ppm in two steps, with the Southern Ocean venting deep carbon.

From here the Holocene's rise from about 260 to 280 ppm is read as mostly natural (ocean carbonate compensation, peat and reef growth) with a small human share: a midpoint between most carbon-cycle modellers, who find it natural, and Ruddiman, who reads it as human and has the natural level falling toward 245 ppm. The band holds both.
The Little Ice Age's colder oceans take up carbon too, so part of the 1610 dip may be natural; the attribution is confounded.
Held at its late-Holocene level from here: the natural level is a counterfactual nobody observes, taken as constant while the human addition grows.
The boreal forest moves most with the glacial cycles: it shrinks to refugia south of the ice at glacial maxima and reaches beyond today's treeline in the warmest interglacials.

changes.value: Review pass, coverage: the remaining parts opened by the tree pass gain values at the Events of humanity's lifecycle they passed over. The three sectors of output per person are set so they sum to output per person at every new date, including the interwar peak and the Depression's trough added to their whole this pass; industry falls most from 1929 to 1932 and food output holds. Notes give the reason wherever a value turns: the eve of each world war, the end of the Second, Concorde and the semaphore, India's Emergency, the revolutions of 1989, China's first elections under universal suffrage, and Napoleon's plebiscite franchise. The boreal forest's value at 8000 BCE gains the note the coverage report asked for.

points.note: Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
On the eve of the First World War world trade and shipping stand at their prewar peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from submarine sinkings and blockade.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
COVID-19's first year: world trade volume falls about a twentieth in 2020 and recovers in 2021.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

upsert.reason: Before 1850 sketched from loads and distances (a forager's camp moves, a farmer's surplus carried to market, Roman, Song and Dutch shipping); 1850 to 1950 from railway and shipping statistics as recalled; after 1970 from UNCTAD's seaborne tonne-miles and the International Transport Forum's land freight, as recalled.

points.note: News moves at the pace of a walker or runner passing it on; fire and smoke signals carry only a few agreed meanings.
Royal messengers of Egypt and Sumer carry written orders by boat and on foot.
Couriers with horses and chariots carry the letters of the Amarna age between Egypt, Babylon and the Hittites.
The Achaemenid relay riders carry the king's messages from Sardis to Susa, some 2,700 km, in about a week, as Herodotus tells it.
Augustus's cursus publicus and the Han relay posts.
The Tang relay posts and the Abbasid barid.
The Mongol yam: urgent riders change horses at stations and cover 300 to 400 km a day.
The Taxis postal relays in Europe from about 1490; the Ming courier stations.
Before Chappe's semaphore (1794): the jump to 1800 is its first line's, so the riders' speed holds until here.

Jumps: Chappe's semaphore line from Paris to Lille (1794) passes a message 230 km in minutes to an hour; lines spread across France, Britain and Sweden. Words now outrun riders for the first time on a regular service.
Jumps again: the electric telegraph (Cooke and Wheatstone 1837, Morse 1844) carries messages across a continent in minutes, slowed by relaying and copying.
The transatlantic cable (1866): London to New York in minutes instead of ten days.
A cable network girdles the world; news reaches the antipodes in hours.
Radio telegraphy and radio telephony connect continents without relays.
Communications satellites (1962) and direct long-distance dialling.
Fibre-optic cables carry signals near the speed of light in glass.

Reaches the limit: transoceanic fibre cables (from TAT-8 in 1988 to the round-the-world FLAG cable in 1997) replace satellite hops, whose round trip to geostationary orbit added about a quarter of a second, and messages cross the world at nearly the speed of light in glass.
At the limit: light in fibre travels about 200,000 km a second. From here what changes is who can send and receive, read in being online (h.internet) and mass media (h.media).

upsert.reason: From the recorded speeds of relay posts (Herodotus on the Persian riders, the Mongol yam, European posts), the semaphore and telegraph lines, and the latency of cable, radio and fibre networks, as recalled; orders of magnitude after 1850.

Glacial maximum: ice sheets cover most of the boreal forest's range in North America and Scandinavia, and steppe-tundra most of Siberia's; conifers survive south of the ice.
Rises most: the boreal forest follows the melting ice north.
The boreal forest follows the melting ice north: nearly all of the rise from the end of the Younger Dryas to the early Holocene's widest reach comes before here (the note at 7900 BCE).
The ice sheets are nearly gone and the early Holocene's summers are warmer than now: the boreal forest reaches its widest, beyond today's northern treeline.
The Neoglacial cooling pushes the northern treeline south from its mid-Holocene reach.
Logging and fire begin to cut into Scandinavia's, Russia's and Canada's boreal forests; most of it still stands.
About 27% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled; larger fires since 2000 in Siberia and Canada.
All people are mobile foragers, moving camp with the seasons.
Some glacial-age winter settlements on the Russian plain were reoccupied for months, but their people still moved.
Turns down: the Natufians of the Levant settle in stone houses about 12,500 BCE, harvesting wild cereals before they farm; the Jomon of Japan settle about the same time.
Farming villages in south-west Asia, China and New Guinea hold a growing share, because farmers live far denser than foragers.
Herders begin to move with their animals on the steppe and in the Sahara as it dries; pastoral nomadism will keep a share mobile after foraging shrinks.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe (the Scythians and their neighbours): herders now move on horseback over great ranges and threaten settled states.
The Mongols unite the steppe; about a third of the mobile are now herders rather than foragers.
The Qing destroy the Dzungar state (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: the last great nomad powers end, and settled states begin to fence and tax the herders.
Turns down faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh and other Central Asian nomads to settle, 1928 to 1934, and the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps.

Mobile herders in the Sahel, the Horn of Africa, Arabia, Iran, Central Asia, Mongolia and Tibet, and a few foraging bands; estimates of mobile pastoralists differ by a factor of two, since many herders now move only part of the household.

upsert.reason: Mobile foragers from the model's foraging share, taking about 7% of foragers as sedentary after 12,500 BCE; pastoral nomads sketched at 2 to 3% of humanity from mounted nomadism to 1500 (steppe, Arabia, Sahara, East Africa, Tibet), falling to about 1% by 1900 and about 0.3% now, as estimates of mobile pastoralists put them (some 30 to 40 million today, as recalled).

points.note: Foragers' spirits and ancestors rarely judge conduct between people: moralizing high gods are rare among foragers in the cross-cultural samples (Swanson's, and Peoples and Marlowe's). Debated: Purzycki and others find local gods that care about some conduct, which would raise this; the band allows it.
Early farmers' ancestor cults and shrines, as at Catalhoyuk, show no sign of gods that judge conduct.

The first states: Egypt's Maat and Mesopotamia's sun god as judge. Whether these count as moralizing gods is debated; the Seshat coding that placed them early was part of a study retracted in 2021 over its treatment of missing data.
Egypt's judgment of the dead spreads beyond the king in the Coffin Texts.
The Zhou claim Heaven's mandate (about 1046 BCE): Heaven judges rulers by their virtue.

Rises most between 800 and 500 BCE: karma taught as a law repaying conduct (the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira), Zoroaster's judging god, the Hebrew prophets, Confucius's Heaven. Whether this Axial Age is a break or a gradual growth is debated (Jaspers and Bellah against Mullins and others), as is why: Baumard and Boyer's affluence against the Big Gods case that such beliefs let large societies cooperate (Norenzayan).
Buddhist judgment of the dead enters Chinese folk religion; Christianity in the Mediterranean.
Enlightenment unbelief and deism are a few among the educated of Europe; the world share barely moves.
The peak: nearly all of humanity in traditions that teach judged conduct, before state atheism.
Turns down: the Soviet state teaches unbelief from 1917.
China's new state teaches unbelief from 1949.
The trough: China's Cultural Revolution closes temples and churches; Western Europe's young stop believing as well as attending.
Turns up: belief revives in the former Soviet lands and in China after the Cultural Revolution, and the Muslim and African Christian shares grow.
Unbelief grows in Europe, East Asia and the Americas while belief holds in Muslim and African populations (Pew and Gallup surveys, as recalled); the two nearly cancel.

upsert.reason: Sketched: before 1900 from the share of people in traditions coded as having moralizing high gods or broad supernatural punishment (Swanson; Peoples and Marlowe; Norenzayan's Big Gods; the Seshat moralizing-gods data and their critics, as recalled), counting part of the local and Chinese traditions; after 1900 lowered by the unaffiliated and by unbelief within traditions as surveys show.

points.note: No tradition open to every people exists before the Buddha; foragers' traditions are bound to their band and land.
The first states' traditions are bound to their city, king and land; Akhenaten's Aten cult (about 1350 BCE) does not seek converts abroad.
The Buddha's teaching begins in the Ganges plain, open to any who join the order whatever their birth: the first tradition of this kind.
Turns up: Ashoka's patronage and his missions to Sri Lanka, Gandhara and the Hellenistic kings carry the teaching beyond its first people.
Buddhism reaches China along the Silk Roads; Christians are still a few hundred thousand in the Roman Empire.
Turns up: the Roman Empire becomes Christian between Constantine's conversion (312) and Theodosius's decrees (380), and Buddhism spreads through China.
Islam enters the count after 610; most conquered peoples convert only slowly over the next three centuries.
Northern and Eastern Europe baptized from the 960s; conversion in Iran and the Near East passes the half.
The Black Death kills Christians and Muslims around the Mediterranean in greater shares than East Asian Buddhists; the sum barely moves.
The survivors in the Spanish Americas are baptized; the gain is small because so many of them die.
Turns up faster: Europe's and the Americas' Christian peoples grow faster than Asia's, and missions spread in Africa and Oceania.
Turns flat: Buddhists fall under state atheism after 1917 and 1949 while Christians grow in Africa and Muslims by births; the sum holds near 53 to 55 until 1970.
Rises again, mainly by the higher birth rates of Muslim and African Christian populations, not by conversion.
Christians about 31% and Muslims about 24.5% of humanity, Buddhists about 6% (Pew Research Center's Global Religious Futures estimates, as recalled).

upsert.reason: The sum of the model's Buddhist, Christian and Muslim shares at each date; its band carries theirs.

points.note: In bands the men who fight in raids and feuds also hunt and gather: almost no one is kept under arms, though most men may fight.
Chiefs begin to keep retinues of fighting men, but most fighting is still done by farmers and herders between seasons.
The first states keep guards and standing troops; Sargon of Akkad later boasts of 5,400 men who eat daily before him.
Chariot armies of Egypt, the Hittites and Shang China: specialists kept at great cost.
Assyria keeps the first great standing army.

The Warring States of China field conscript armies of hundreds of thousands; Rome mobilizes a large share of its citizens against Carthage; the Mauryan army is reported at hundreds of thousands. The share under arms in states peaks before unification.

Rome's legions and auxiliaries, about 300,000 to 400,000 of some 60 million, and Han China's standing and frontier forces of the same order: about one in two hundred people in the states, almost none beyond them.
Song China keeps more than a million soldiers, about one in a hundred of its people, the largest standing army of its age.
The Mongols make every adult man a soldier of the decimal army, a small people wholly under arms.
The military revolution: gunpowder and the bastion fort make European armies grow tenfold in two centuries; the Ottoman, Mughal and Ming armies are as large or larger.
Louis XIV's France keeps about 400,000 men, and the Qing banners and Green Standard about 800,000.
The Napoleonic peak: the levée en masse of 1793 and conscription put about six million under arms in Europe at once.
The Taiping and Qing armies of millions and the American Civil War's, about 1.5 million under arms at once in 1864.
On the eve of mobilization (August 1914): within weeks some twenty million men are called up, the jump to 1916.
The First World War: about 40 million under arms at the height, from conscript armies of a size no earlier war had seen.
Demobilized in the West; the Red Army of the Russian Civil War still about five million.
The invasion of the Soviet Union (June 1941): some 8 to 9 million under arms on the Eastern Front alone, and Japan's and the Allies' mobilization still rising.
The Second World War: about 70 million under arms at the height, the Soviet Union and the United States about 12 million each, Germany about 10, China, Japan and Britain about 5 to 6 each.
Japan surrenders in August and September 1945; demobilization has barely begun, so the fall to 1946 comes after.
Demobilization: tens of millions sent home within a year.
The Korean war and the Cold War's rearmament.
The World Bank counts about 29 million in armed forces, paramilitary included, at the Cold War's end.
Armies cut by about a quarter after the Cold War, in Russia above all.
About 27 to 28 million under arms; Russia's and Ukraine's wartime mobilization adds about a million, against a falling share elsewhere.
About four fifths of foragers' small output is food; the rest is tools, clothing and shelter, and services barely counted.
Farming feeds more people per hectare, not more per person: food-getting per person barely moves for five thousand years while its share of output begins to fall (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
After the Black Death the survivors farm the best land: food output per person rises with output per person.
Turns flat: from here food-getting per person grows far more slowly than output, so its share falls from about half to a third by 1900.
The new farmlands of the Americas, Russia and Australia feed Europe's cities by rail and steamship.
War cuts harvests in Europe and Russia.
Food output holds through the Depression while prices collapse: farmers keep producing, so the fall in output per person is industry's and services'.
The war's trough: occupied Europe, the Soviet Union and Asia harvest far less, and famine strikes Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
Food-getting falls below a tenth of world output. Value added grows more slowly than harvests, because fertilizer, fuel and machines bought from industry are counted there.
About 5% of world output (World Bank value added at market prices is about 4%, more at purchasing power).

upsert.reason: Sector shares of world output: about 80% food-getting for foragers (output counted as subsistence, mostly food), 55 to 65% in agrarian economies (Broadberry's and others' sectoral reconstructions for England, China and India, as recalled, averaged toward the more agrarian majority), about a third by 1900, a fifth by 1950, and from the World Bank's value-added shares after 1960, raised somewhat for purchasing power.

points.note: Stone tools, wooden spears, skins and shelters: about a sixth of foragers' output.
Pottery, weaving, houses and the first copper: farmers make more things than foragers.
Bronze, monumental building and specialist craftsmen in the first states.
The collapse of Roman manufacturing and trade in the West: pottery, coins and buildings become cruder and fewer.
Song China's iron output, perhaps over 100,000 tonnes a year by 1078 as Hartwell reconstructed it, is not matched until the eighteenth century.
Turns up: the industrial revolution's cotton mills, iron and steam spread from Britain.
Steel, chemicals and electricity: the second industrial revolution in Germany and the United States.
Making passes food-getting in world output about now.
World industrial production falls by about a third from 1929 to 1932, by the League of Nations' index as recalled: the Depression is above all industry's collapse.
Peak of war production: American and Soviet factories make arms on a scale never seen.
Demobilization: war production stops and factories convert.
Industry's share of world output near its peak, about 37%.
Turns flat: deindustrialization in the old industrial countries and the collapse of Soviet-bloc industry after 1989.
Turns up again: China becomes the world's workshop.
About 28% of world output.

upsert.reason: Industry's share of world output: about 15% for foragers' tools, clothing and shelters, 16 to 22% in agrarian economies, a third by 1950 and its peak about 37% in the 1960s, about 28% now (World Bank value added after 1960, as recalled).

points.note: Healing, teaching and ritual among foragers are done unpaid within the band; output counts little of them.
Turns up: temples, scribes, officials and long-distance traders of the first cities.
Services pass making in this sketch about now; whether agrarian services outweighed crafts is uncertain (England in 1381 had more industry than services), and the bands overlap.
Song China's commercial revolution: merchants, shippers, brokers and paper money.
Railways, shipping, banking and city trades grow with industry.
Services pass food-getting in world output about now.
Services reach half of world output.
About two thirds of world output.

upsert.reason: The remainder of output: about 5% for foragers, whose services are unpaid and barely counted; a fifth to a quarter in agrarian economies (trade, transport, housing, government, religion, servants); about a third by 1900, two fifths by 1950 and two thirds now.

points.note: Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.
The privatisation of Soviet-bloc property after 1991 creates new fortunes.
The World Inequality Report 2022 puts the richest tenth's share of world wealth at about 76%, as recalled.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1995 from the comparative wealth Ginis of foragers and farmers, Kohler and others' house-size Ginis, the agrarian estimates in Scheidel's Great Leveler and Piketty's series for Europe and the United States, all as recalled; from 1995 near the World Inequality Database's world top-tenth share.

points.note: Brush huts, windbreaks and caves; foragers live mostly in the open and sleep a family to a small shelter.
Glacial maximum: the mammoth-bone dwellings of the Russian plain, perhaps 20 to 30 m² for a household, show winter houses where there was no wood.
The Natufians' round stone houses, a few metres across, are the first permanent dwellings.
Rectangular mud-brick houses of the first farmers; at Catalhoyuk a main room of about 25 m² with storerooms for a household of five to eight.
Farmers' houses grow: the longhouses of Europe's first farmers, though part of them housed animals and stores.

Greek houses of the eighth century BCE have a median floor of about 45 m²; by the fourth century several times that (Morris's house-size series), a rise that was not general across the agrarian world.
Crowded insulae in Rome and the cities beside large peasant and villa houses; Han Chinese farmhouses of a few rooms.
After Rome's fall houses in the West are smaller and of timber; whether the world average fell is unknown.
Turns up: the Black Death leaves the same houses to fewer people.
After the plagues, peasants in western Europe and the Near East have more room and better houses, as wages are high.
Turns down: the industrial cities pack workers into cellars, courts and back-to-backs at a few square metres each.
Turns down: bombing and fighting destroy a fifth of Germany's dwellings, much of Japan's cities and of the western Soviet Union; tens of millions are homeless.
Turns up for good: mass housing in Europe, the Soviet Union and Japan, suburbs in North America.
China's housing reform of 1998 starts the largest building boom in history: urban floor space per person there rises from about 8 m² in 1978 to near 40 m² by 2020.

The world's buildings hold about 240 billion m² of floor, roughly three quarters of it dwellings (UN Environment's Global Status Reports for Buildings and Construction, as recalled): about 22 m² a person, from over 60 in the United States to under 10 in much of Africa and South Asia.

upsert.reason: Sketched from house floors in the archaeological record and household sizes before 1950, and from housing statistics and the global buildings floor-area estimates after; the band is wide because no one has summed dwelling space for the world before the late twentieth century.

points.note: No state, so no elections of rulers.

Rises: Greek democracies and oligarchies, the Roman Republic, Carthage's elected magistrates and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain, whose councils of clan heads chose their leaders; how competitive the last were is uncertain.
Roman Italy, with citizenship for all free Italians; the provinces are ruled, not represented.
Falls: the Republic gives way to the Principate.
Venice elects its doge.
The Italian communes elect their consuls.
Most Italian communes have fallen to lords (signori).
Rises: Poland-Lithuania's nobles elect their kings from 1573, and the Dutch Republic governs itself from 1581.
Britain's Parliament becomes supreme after 1688, its ministries resting on contested elections among a few percent of men.
The new United States.
Falls: Poland-Lithuania is partitioned (1795) and Napoleon takes power (1799).
France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.
Falls: Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 ends the Second Republic.
Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.
The Weimar Republic and the new republics of central Europe.
Mussolini's dictatorship and Poland's coup of 1926.
Falls: Hitler's dictatorship from 1933.
Germany occupies most of Europe's democracies.
Liberated western Europe is under provisional governments; its first postwar elections follow from October 1945 into 1946, the rise to 1946.
Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.
India's Emergency (June 1975) has not yet begun: the fall to 1976 comes with it.
Falls: India's Emergency suspends elections (1975 to 1977), with juntas in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; indices differ on India, hence the band.
India's election of March 1977 ends the Emergency and the Congress party loses power.
Before the revolutions of late 1989 the rise to 1990 has not yet come: most of it is Eastern Europe's free elections of 1990.
Rises: multiparty elections in Eastern Europe and Latin America's return to elected government.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (1999).
Falls slowly as elections lose their competitiveness in several large countries; whether some (India, Turkey) still count is debated, which the band carries.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the populations of republics, competitive oligarchies and parliamentary regimes at each date (as recalled), divided by the world's people.

points.note: No state, so no national elections: bands decide by consensus, which the parent's measure does not count.
The first states have assemblies of elders and citizens (Mesopotamian city assemblies, as Jacobsen argued), but no elections of rulers by a franchise that can be counted.
Citizens of Athens after 508 BCE and of other Greek democracies and the Roman Republic: a few hundred thousand men in a world of some sixty million adults.
Rome extends citizenship to Italy after the Social War (89 BCE): about a million adult men may vote, if they come to Rome.
Falls: under Augustus the Roman assemblies lose their elections to the Senate and the emperor (by 14 CE).
Iceland's Althing and Venice's popular assembly.
The Italian communes' councils, the Swiss cantons and the county electors of England's Commons.
England's forty-shilling freeholders (1430).
The nobles of Poland-Lithuania, perhaps a tenth of its people, vote in their dietines and elect the king.
Rises: some five to six million Frenchmen vote for the Estates-General, and the new American states widen their franchises.
Napoleon's plebiscites are open to all Frenchmen: votes without a choice of rulers, counted here because the measure is the formal right.
Under Napoleon's empire the plebiscite franchise holds until the Restoration of 1814 cuts the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers; the fall to 1820 comes then.
Falls: the restored French monarchy limits the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers.
France adopts manhood suffrage in 1848; most white American men vote.
Britain's Second Reform Act (1867) and the German Reich's manhood suffrage (1871).
New Zealand (1893) and South Australia (1894) give women the vote.
Before the war about a tenth of adults may vote; the great widening comes from 1917 to 1920, in Soviet Russia, Britain, Germany and the United States.
Rises most: women vote in Britain (1918), Germany (1919), the United States (1920) and Soviet Russia, where the franchise excludes only the 'former people'.
The Soviet constitution of 1936 grants universal suffrage in single-candidate elections.
Women vote in France (1944), Italy and Japan (1946).
India's constitution of 1950 gives all adults the vote.

China's first elections under its 1953 electoral law, held through 1953 and 1954 with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses, add about a quarter of the world's adults to the formal franchise: most of the rise to 1955.
China's first national elections under the constitution of 1954, with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses; formal right, not a choice of rulers.
Switzerland gives women the federal vote in 1971, nearly the last democracy to do so.
Myanmar's coup and the Taliban's return end national elections for some ninety million people.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the dates of franchise laws and the adult populations they covered (as recalled from the suffrage histories and V-Dem's suffrage indicator), divided by the world's adults.
