Review pass, coverage and two corrections in war's toll and its parts (averaged to the next date) and in violent deaths (homicide plus war). New dates mostly hold the rate before them, so every average is conserved. Where a period's average hid where its deaths fell, the period is split at the new date and the average kept: 490 to 90 BCE at 200 BCE, and 1950 to 1960 at 1954, when the Korean War is over. One correction: 1800 to 1820 was read at 10, below the French Revolutionary wars' 16, though the Napoleonic wars killed about 3.5 to 6.5 million, war's famine and disease included as this series counts them. It is raised to about 18 before 1808 and about 40 from 1808 to 1820, with the wars of Latin American independence; the band carries the spread of the toll's estimates (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The Earth's stores and the wild animals gain a value at the Last Glacial Maximum, whose Events begin 24,000 years ago.

points.note: Stone for tools and ochre for colour: a few kilograms per person a year.
Natufian and early Neolithic stone houses, mortars and querns.
Villages of mud brick and lime plaster, as at Çatalhöyük and Jericho; lime is burned from stone. Earth for building is the first large draw on the stores.
Cities of mud brick, copper and then bronze smelted from ores.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant.
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the mines of Spain: lead in Greenland's ice reaches a peak in the first century CE not matched again until the Middle Ages (as recalled from the ice-core studies).
Western Roman building and mining collapse; the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China burns coal for iron, and Europe builds in stone.
Potosí's silver and Britain's first coal boom, small against the stone and earth of building.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Krausmann and colleagues: about 7 Gt of materials taken in 1900, about a quarter of it coal, ores and building minerals; the rest is harvested biomass, not counted here.
Mines and cities wrecked in Europe and Asia: extraction per person dips in the last year of the war.
The great acceleration: oil, cement and steel for reconstruction and for growth, faster than people.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries build less and use energy better.
China's building boom: it poured more cement in 2011 to 2013 than the United States in the whole twentieth century, and coal and iron ore follow.
The UNEP International Resource Panel counts about 100 Gt taken in 2020, three quarters of it non-metallic minerals, fossil fuels and metal ores.

upsert.reason: From 1900 Krausmann and colleagues' material flows (about 7 Gt of materials in 1900, a quarter of it minerals and fuels) and the UNEP International Resource Panel's (about 100 Gt in 2020, three quarters minerals and fuels), as recalled; before 1900 sketched from building, mining and toolmaking.

points.note: The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

upsert.reason: Pleistocene level from the reconstructions of megafaunal biomass (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On and colleagues 2018 put it near 0.02 Gt C), the present from Bar-On and colleagues and Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), as recalled; the path between is sketched from the dated extinctions and the nineteenth-century slaughters.

Raids and ambushes between bands, the main form of forager war in Keeley's and Bowles's readings. Fry and Soderberg argue most forager killings are personal, not between groups, which would move part of the parent's deep values to homicide; the band carries that debate.
Wars of conquest between the first states and against their neighbours.
The Three Kingdoms counted as fighting between polities; that they were the fragments of one fallen empire makes this a matter of definition.
The Arab conquests.
The Mongol conquests' battles and sieges; their massacres of cities are counted as one-sided.
The Hundred Years War and Timur's campaigns from 1370.
The Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests and the conquest of Mexico and Peru.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China and the Thirty Years War. The parent's value appears to include these wars' famine and plague deaths, which belong to hunger and infection.
The Qing conquest of the south and the Swedish Deluge in Poland.
The Great Turkish War and the Nine Years War.
The Great Northern War and the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Seven Years War.
The French Revolutionary wars.
Corrected from 8 with the parent: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns and the Russo-Persian war.
The Napoleonic wars' deadliest years, the Russo-Turkish war and the War of 1812.
The Crimean war.
The Paraguayan, Franco-Prussian and Russo-Turkish wars and colonial conquests.
The Boer, Philippine-American and Russo-Japanese wars.
The Balkan wars.
The First World War.
The Polish-Soviet and Greco-Turkish wars.
Japan's war on China from 1937 and Italy's on Ethiopia.

Turns down for good: the Long Peace between great powers begins, and fighting between polities never again reaches a tenth of the world wars' rate. The Indochina war and the first Arab-Israeli war.
Revised from 10 with the parent: the Korean War, now averaged to 1954.2.
The Indo-Pakistani war of December 1971, with the Vietnam war.
The Ogaden war.

Turns up: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine from February 2022, the deadliest war between states since Iran and Iraq.

points.note: Massacres of whole camps; Nataruk by Lake Turkana, about 8000 BCE, is the earliest well-dated case.
Farmers' villages can be wiped out whole: the Neolithic massacres at Talheim and Schletz about 5000 BCE.
The first states kill and deport conquered peoples, as the Assyrian reliefs later boast.
The Mongols kill the people of cities that resist: Merv and Nishapur in 1221, Baghdad in 1258.
Timur's massacres from the 1370s.
Massacres in the conquest of the Americas; most of the Americas' dead died of disease, counted under infection.
Zhang Xianzhong's killings in Sichuan, the Qing massacres at Yangzhou, the sack of Magdeburg.
The Qing's destruction of the Dzungars, 1755 to 1758, perhaps half a million or more killed, averaged here over 1750 to 1780.
Massacres in the Dungan revolt and its suppression.
The Herero and Nama genocide, 1904 to 1908.
The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1916, with the Assyrian and Greek killings.
Pogroms in Ukraine and the Red and White terrors.
The Nanjing massacre and, if the parent counts it, part of the Soviet Great Terror of 1937 to 1938, about 680,000 shot; whether the parent's 25 includes the Terror is not recorded.
German and Soviet killings in occupied Poland.

The murder of Hungary's Jews at Auschwitz in 1944.

Partition's communal killings, 1947.

As the parent counts it. China's land reform and campaign against counter-revolutionaries, 1950 to 1953, killed perhaps one to two million or more, which would add 4 to 8 to the decade's average; whether the parent counts such campaigns is open.
The killings in Indonesia.

The killings in Bangladesh, March to December 1971.
Burundi's killings of Hutu in 1972.
The Khmer Rouge's executions, and East Timor.
Guatemala's highland massacres and Uganda.
Burundi 1993, Bosnia.

The Revolt of the Three Feudatories.
The Vendee, the Haitian revolution and the White Lotus rebellion.

The Dungan revolt and the Nian.
The Mexican revolution and China's revolution of 1911.
The Russian Civil War.
China's warlord and civil wars.
The Spanish and Chinese civil wars.
Civil wars inside the world war: Yugoslavia, Greece, and the communists and nationalists in China.
The Chinese civil war. From here fighting within polities carries most war deaths.
Algeria's war of independence and Colombia's Violencia.
The Vietnam war's civil side, the Congo crisis and Biafra.
Angola, Lebanon, Ethiopia.
Afghanistan.
Afghanistan, Central America, Ethiopia, Mozambique.
Bosnia, Somalia, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan, Tajikistan.
The Congo wars.
Syria, Iraq and Yemen.
Ethiopia's Tigray war, Myanmar and Sudan.

Averaged to 200 BCE (revised from 40 to 90 BCE): the Warring States at their deadliest, Alexander's conquests, the first two Punic wars and Qin's unification. With 200 BCE's 27 the 490 to 90 BCE average of 40 is conserved.
Averaged to 90 BCE: the Han–Xiongnu wars and Rome's conquests in Greece, Spain and Africa, lighter than the century before.
To 1 CE: Roman civil wars, Han–Xiongnu wars.

Revised from 30 (which averaged 200–500): now 200–280, the Three Kingdoms.

Averaged to the next date; the 500 rate held. The Arab conquests, the Tang founding wars and An Lushan fall here.
To 1000: Tang decline, Huang Chao, the Viking age.
Revised from 50: now 1140–1206, before the Mongols.
1206–1279: the Mongol conquests.

Average over 1400–1500: Timur's last campaigns, the Hundred Years War's end, Ming wars in Vietnam and the steppe, the Hussite wars. The 1300 value (30) now averages only 1300–1400, with the Red Turban rebellions and the Yuan collapse.
Averaged to the next date; the 1400 rate held.
Averaged to the next date; the 1400 rate held.
Averaged to the next date; the 1500 rate held.
Averaged to the next date. Held at 20 so the 1500 reading, now averaged over 1500 to 1520, is conserved: the Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests of Syria and Egypt and the conquest of Mexico.
Revised from 120: now 1600–1618, before the two great wars.
1618–1650: the Ming–Qing wars and the Thirty Years War.
Revised from 15: 1650–1670 holds the Qing conquest of the south and the Deluge in Poland.
To 1700: the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, the Great Turkish War.
Averaged to the next date; the 1683 rate held.
To 1750: Nader Shah, the Austrian Succession, the Dzungar wars.
Averaged to the next date; the 1750 rate held: the Seven Years War falls here.
Revised from 12: now averages 1780 to 1789, after the American war and before the French wars; with 1789's 16 the 1780-1800 average of 12 is conserved.
1789 to 1800: the French Revolutionary wars, the Haitian revolution and the White Lotus rebellion (ev.eu.french-revolution).

Corrected from 10, now averaged to 1808: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns (Austerlitz, Jena, Eylau, Friedland), the war in Saint-Domingue and the White Lotus rebellion's end, about 1.5 million dead with war's famine and disease. The earlier reading of 10 for 1800 to 1820 sat below the French Revolutionary wars' 16 though the Napoleonic wars were larger.

Averaged to 1820: the Napoleonic wars' deadliest years (the Peninsular War, Russia in 1812, Germany and France in 1813 and 1814) and the wars of Latin American independence. The Napoleonic wars' toll is put at 3.5 to 6.5 million soldiers and civilians, most of it from 1808 to 1815; about 5 million is taken here.
To 1850: the Latin American wars of independence, the Java war, the first Opium War.
Revised from 50: 1850–1859, the Taiping war's first years and the Crimean war.
Revised from 40: now 1859–1864, the Taiping war's deadliest years and the American Civil War.
Averaged to the next date; the 1859 rate held: the Taiping war and the American Civil War.
1864–1890: the Dungan revolt, the Paraguayan and Franco-Prussian wars.
Averaged to the next date: the 1864 rate held, so the 1864–1890 average is conserved.
Averaged to the next date; the 1865 rate held.
Revised from 65: now 1910–1914, the Balkan wars and the Mexican revolution.
Averaged to the next date; the 1914.6 rate held, the war's last year.
To 1920: the Russian Civil War and the wars of the empires' successor states.
Averaged to the next date; the 1920 rate held.

Averaged to the next date; the 1930 rate held, so the 1930–1939.7 average is conserved. The Spanish civil war and the Sino-Japanese war from 1937 fall here.
Revised from 500: now averages 1940 to mid-1941, before the invasion of the Soviet Union and the Pacific war. With the values at 1941.5, 1944 and 1945 the 1940-1945.7 average of 500 is conserved.
Mid-1941 to 1944: the war's deadliest years, from the invasion of the Soviet Union (ev.eu.eastern-front) and the Holocaust (ev.eu.holocaust) to the Pacific war (ev.oc.pacific-war).
Averaged to the next date; the 1941.5 rate held, so the 1941.5–1944 average is conserved.

Averaged to the next date: the 1940 rate held, so the 1940–1945.7 average is conserved.
To 1950: the Chinese Civil War and Partition.
Averaged to the next date; the 1945.7 rate held: the Chinese civil war and Partition.
Averaged to the next date; the 1945.7 rate held: the Chinese civil war and the first Arab–Israeli war.
Revised from 14, now averaged to 1954.2: the Korean War, about 2.5 to 3 million dead in three years, falls here. With 1954.2's 5.3 the 1950–1960 average of 14 is conserved.
Averaged to 1960: after Korea's armistice, the end of the French Indochina war, Algeria's war and Colombia's Violencia.
Averaged to the next date: the 1960 rate held, so the 1960–1970 average is conserved; Vietnam and the 1965 Indo-Pakistani war fall here.

The killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million killed, by estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, in some nine months, about 20 per 100,000 a year of the world's people on top of the Vietnam war's 6. The 1960s decade reading had left them out, so its average rises from 6 to about 7.5.
The killings end by mid-1966; the Vietnam war's rate, held from 1960, continues.
Averaged to the next date; the 1966.5 rate held: the Vietnam war, with the Tet offensive, and Biafra.
Now averages 1970 to March 1971: the Vietnam war and Cambodia's civil war.

Pakistan's army begins its crackdown in East Pakistan on 25 March 1971; to the surrender at Dhaka on 16 December, killings of Bengalis, above all Hindus, students and intellectuals, and the Indo-Pakistani war of December. The dead are debated: about 270,000 violent deaths by a survey-based estimate (Obermeyer and others, 2008), 300,000 to 500,000 in many scholarly accounts, 1.5 million in Rummel's, 3 million in Bangladesh's official figure. Taken here as about 500,000, some 18 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over nine months, with the Vietnam war's 3. The parent's 1970 reading had left it out.
After Bangladesh's independence: the Vietnam war, Burundi's killings of 1972 and the 1973 Arab-Israeli war carry the rate to 1975.

The Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh (ev.as.khmer-rouge): perhaps a million of their 1.5 to 2 million victims are executed or killed outright, about 6.5 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over 3.7 years; deaths from hunger and disease in the labour camps are not counted here. Angola, Lebanon, East Timor and Ethiopia add about 4.5.
Revised from 5, which held the 1970 rate: the Khmer Rouge's killings continue until January 1979.
Vietnam ends the Khmer Rouge regime (January 1979); China's war on Vietnam, Afghanistan's and Uganda's carry the rate to 1980.
To 1990: the end of the Iran–Iraq war, Afghanistan.
Now averages 1990 to April 1994: the Gulf war, the Bosnian and Somali wars, Afghanistan, Angola and Algeria.

The Rwandan genocide, 7 April to mid-July 1994. Estimates run from about 500,000 (Human Rights Watch) through 600,000 to 800,000 in most scholarly work to over a million in Rwanda's own count of victims; taken here as about 650,000 in a hundred days, some 43 per 100,000 a year of the world's people, with other wars at about 1.5. The parent's 1990 reading had left it out.
After the genocide: Chechnya, Bosnia to 1995, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan and Burundi carry the rate to 1996.
To 2000: the Congo wars, Eritrea–Ethiopia.
Averaged to the next date; the 2000 rate held: Afghanistan, Iraq and Congo.
To 2020: Syria, Iraq, Yemen.

changes.value: Review pass, coverage: Oceania's share and its four subregions' gain values at the Events placed in them that fell between two of their values (the First Fleet and Sydney's smallpox, the Pacific's annexations, the Fiji measles and the girmit, federation, the island independences of 1962 to 1980 and others). The shares are interpolated: none of these Events moves a share of humanity by more than its band, as the existing notes on the Spanish-Chamorro wars and the Marquesas already say. Three residuals of humanity's and the Earth's measures are closed too: the Earth at Pinatubo's cooling, the largest polity at the Han's founding, and leisure across the abolitions of the 1820s and 1830s.

points.note: MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c, a warm substage of the penultimate interglacial complex.
Penultimate glacial (MIS 6).
Deepest MIS 6.
Last Interglacial peak, warmer than pre-industrial.
MIS 5d.
MIS 5b.
Entering MIS 4.
Toba erupts (ev.toba). A volcanic winter of a few years is argued by some and doubted by others; the slide into the MIS 4 cold stage is orbital, not volcanic.
End of the MIS 4 cold stage.
MIS 3, near Heinrich event 4.
Last Glacial Maximum.
Deglaciation under way, before the Bølling warming.
About 14,000 years ago, the Bølling–Allerød warm interval of the deglaciation.
Start of the Younger Dryas: a pause in global warming, a deep cold in the north Atlantic.
Revised from -1.5: about 12,000 years ago, inside the Younger Dryas; global reconstructions of the deglaciation (Shakun and others, as recalled) reach Holocene levels only about 10,000 years ago.
The Holocene begins.
Early Holocene, near the 8.2 ka cold event.
The 4.2 ka event: drought more than global cooling.
Medieval warmth, regional more than global.
Entering the Little Ice Age.
Maunder Minimum, the coldest part of the Little Ice Age.
The Maunder minimum, deep in the Little Ice Age (ev.little-ice-age).
Just before Tambora: the 1810s are already cool after an unidentified eruption of 1809.
Tambora's sulphate (ev.sea.tambora) cools the Earth by about a quarter to half a degree for a year: 1816 is the year without a summer.
The sulphate washes out within two or three years and the temperature recovers toward the cool decade's level.
After Tambora (1815) and the cold 1810s.
Just before Krakatoa, on the line from 1870 to 1890.
Krakatoa's haze (ev.sea.krakatoa) cools the world by about two tenths of a degree in 1884.
Recovering after Krakatoa; the 1880s stay cool.
Aerosols and the Agung eruption of 1963 hold temperature flat (ev.aerosols).
Just before Pinatubo, on the line from 1990 to 1996.
Pinatubo's sulphate spreads through the stratosphere from June 1991; the cooling deepens into 1992.

Corrected from 0.42: Pinatubo's sulphate (ev.sea.pinatubo) cools the world by about 0.2 to 0.3 degrees in 1992's annual mean and up to half a degree at the monthly peak, as climate models predicted beforehand; the instrumental record runs about two tenths below the line from 1990 to 1996 in 1992 despite an El Nino. Check: the annual global means of 1990 to 1994.
The aerosol clears and warming resumes.
Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.
New Kingdom Egypt and the Shang each rule a few million as the Bronze Age collapse begins.
Before the Achaemenid empire: Assyria, Egypt and the Zhou each rule a few million.
Cyrus takes the Median kingdom (ev.as.achaemenid); Lydia and Babylon fall to him within twelve years.
Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace: the Achaemenid empire holds perhaps a fifth of humanity (ev.as.achaemenid).
The Achaemenid empire.
Qin unifies China (ev.as.qin) as the Maurya empire declines after Ashoka: each holds perhaps a sixth to a fifth of humanity.
Han China.
Rome, about 65 million of 245.
Rome, with the Han breaking up.
Rome's western half has fallen (ev.eu.rome-fall) and China is divided between north and south: no polity holds more than about a seventh of humanity.
Sui China, whose census of 609 counts about 46 million.
Tang China.
The Northern Song, perhaps 80 million of 295 million, before the Jin take the north (ev.as.song).
Southern Song after losing the north to the Jin.
The Southern Song, with the Jin close behind.
Yuan China after the fall of the Song.
Revised from 28: Yuan China holds about the same quarter of humanity as at 1279; the 28 was the coarse fill's value and rose with no cause.
Ming China, about 80 million of 350 million; the 1393 census count of 60 million is taken as an undercount.
Qing China at its population peak.
Qing China and the British Empire about equal.
Wartime hours (h.toil) cut leisure in the belligerents.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
The postwar migration programmes, 'populate or perish', hold the share steady while the world grows fastest.
About 33 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.
The Ivane valley in the highlands about 49,000 years ago, and the Bismarck islands by about 45,000 (ev.mel.ivane, ev.mel.near-oceania).
Gardens at Kuk Swamp: New Guinea's highlanders cultivate taro and bananas, one of the world's independent inventions of farming (ev.oc.new-guinea-farming).
Lapita potters in the Bismarck archipelago, about 1350 BCE (ev.oc.lapita).
The sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands from the Americas, and highland valleys grow dense (ev.mel.sweet-potato) (DensityRatchet#2ace).
Australia and New Zealand pass Melanesia, about 1868: for the first time since farming began, most of Oceania's people do not live in Melanesia.
Measles kills about a quarter of Fiji's people in 1875 (ev.mel.fiji-measles), and labour recruiting takes tens of thousands to Queensland and Fiji.
The highland valleys, with perhaps a million people, are first entered by outsiders in 1933 (ev.mel.highlands-contact).

Papua New Guinea's count is disputed: the UN's model gives about 10.5 million, while a 2021 study for the government suggested about 17, which would raise this share by half; the band reaches toward it.
Voyagers from the Philippines cross some 2,000 kilometres of open sea to the Marianas, about 1500 BCE, the longest sea crossing yet made (ev.mic.marianas).
Nan Madol on Pohnpei, the Saudeleur capital of basalt islets, at its height.
The Spanish-Chamorro wars and epidemics (1668 to 1695) cut the Marianas' people from perhaps 40,000 or more to under 5,000, too few to move the subregion's share by a thousandth.
Smallpox on Pohnpei (1854) kills perhaps half its people.
Japanese settlers in the South Seas Mandate outnumber the islanders by 1940; they are deported after 1945.
About 550,000 people; emigration to Guam, Hawai'i and the United States under the compacts of free association holds the share flat.
Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa, about 850 BCE (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita); then the long pause of nearly two thousand years.
The voyages east begin: the Society Islands and the Marquesas are settled about 1000 to 1100 (ev.oc.polynesia-settlement).
Wallis (1767) and Cook (1769) at Tahiti: contact brings venereal disease, tuberculosis and dysentery.
The Marquesas lose perhaps nine in ten of their people in the nineteenth century, and Tahiti's fall to about a fifth of Cook's estimate (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The Peruvian slave raids of 1862 to 1863 carry off about 3,600 islanders, a third of Rapa Nui's people among them, and the smallpox of the few returned kills more (ev.pol.slave-raids).
The low point, about a third of the pre-contact numbers.
The influenza of 1918 kills about a fifth of Western Samoa's people (ev.pol.samoa-influenza) (Twinflow#9474).
About 720,000 at home; more Samoans and Tongans now live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States than in their islands (ev.pol.diaspora).

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.
Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The band now carries both; moving the value needs Asia's and Europe's shares rebalanced with it.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney (ev.oc.first-fleet); smallpox and the frontier wars begin to cut Aboriginal numbers while settlers are still few. The usual pre-contact estimates would put Oceania at 0.25 to 0.35% here; the band carries them.
Before gold is found: about 2.5 million people in Oceania, some 0.47 million of them settlers in Australia and New Zealand and about 2 million islanders and first peoples.
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) nearly double Australia's settlers in four years.
Corrected from 0.2, which left the gold rushes out: settlers reach about 1.1 million against roughly 2 million first peoples and islanders.
Corrected from 0.2: Otago's rush (1861) adds New Zealand's settlers to Australia's.
Corrected from 0.2: about 1.6 million settlers.
Corrected from 0.22: about 1.9 million settlers, while the first peoples keep falling (ev.oc.depopulation).

Corrected from 0.3: about 3.8 million settlers after the 1880s boom and Western Australia's rush, on the way to the 0.4% of 1900. The few hundredths of a point come from Asia's and Europe's shares, within their bands, and are not rebalanced here.

changes.value: Review pass, coverage: the Americas' share and its five subregions' gain values at the Events bound to them that fell between two values, from Columbus's landfall and the conquest to the Monroe Doctrine, the Civil War, the export age, the revolutions and coups of the twentieth century and NAFTA. Each is read from the binding list of its place, so a share answers only to its own Events. The values are interpolated with their neighbours' bands; the turns they cross (the conquest epidemics, the cocoliztli, the nadir of about 1650, the migrations) are already explained by the series' existing notes. Where the Americas' series had no band the new values carry one.

points.note: The first islanders: Banwari Trace on Trinidad, then Cuba and Hispaniola by about 4000 BCE.
Saladoid farmers and potters move up the island chain from the Orinoco.
The Taíno and their neighbours, perhaps two and a half million on the middle estimates; Hispaniola alone has been put anywhere from a few hundred thousand to eight million.
War, forced labour and earlier disease have killed most of the Greater Antilles' Taíno before smallpox arrives in December 1518; Hispaniola's census of 1514 finds about 26,000 left.
The low point: the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, a few Spanish towns and the first enslaved Africans, perhaps a third of a million.
Barbados's sugar boom of the 1640s begins the sugar islands' growth on enslaved Africans.
Saint-Domingue alone holds half a million enslaved people, the most valuable colony in the world.
The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) costs perhaps 150,000 to 350,000 lives.
The Caribbean's peak share: from here emigration to North America and Europe and early-falling births hold its growth below the world's.
Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz by about 8000 BCE; teosinte becomes maize over the next millennia.
The Olmec centres of the Gulf coast.
Teotihuacan, perhaps 100,000 people, and the Classic Maya cities near their height.
The Classic Maya collapse (ev.am.maya-collapse): the southern lowland cities empty between about 800 and 950, as droughts strike and wars multiply; the share dips while the Andes' rises.
About 21 million, on a middle reading: central Mexico alone has been put at 25 million by Borah and Cook and at 6 to 12 million by their critics, the sharpest of the contact-population debates.
Smallpox in 1520 and the siege of Tenochtitlan (ev.smallpox-americas): perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), perhaps the deadliest single epidemic in Mexico's history; whether it was an introduced Salmonella or a native haemorrhagic fever is debated.
The second cocoliztli (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576) kills perhaps two million.
Perhaps one in ten of central Mexico's people of 1519 remain; New Spain's whole population is about three million, Spaniards, Africans and mixed included.
Flat through the Mexican Revolution (ev.am.mexican-revolution): perhaps one to two million die or flee in 1910 to 1920, and Mexico's people barely grow.
Monte Verde, about 14,500 years ago.
The largest share of the hemisphere's foragers: the Andes, the Amazon and the pampas, with squash, gourds and later potatoes and manioc taken into cultivation.
Caral and the monumental sites of the Peruvian coast.
Moche and Nasca on the coast, Tiwanaku by Lake Titicaca.
Wari and Tiwanaku, and the earthwork towns of Amazonia and the Llanos de Mojos; Amazonia's numbers are among the most debated (AbsenceEvidence#10a3).
About 22 million on a middle reading: the Inca realm perhaps 10 to 14 million, Amazonia and the rest of the continent the remainder, with estimates for Amazonia from 1 to 10 million.
Smallpox reaches the Andes ahead of the Spaniards, about 1525 to 1528, and kills the Inca Huayna Capac; the civil war that follows is fought among the survivors (ev.am.inca-fall).
The nadir: the Andes' people perhaps a sixth of 1520's, Brazil's coastal peoples largely gone, and about a million Europeans and Africans.
The Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870) kills perhaps half of Paraguay's people, invisible at this scale beside Brazil's and Argentina's growth.
Mass immigration from Italy and Spain to Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil.
South America's peak share; Brazil's fertility falls below replacement in the early 2000s (ev.lac.fertility-transition).
Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few thousand years of entering the hemisphere.
About 45 million, nine in ten of the hemisphere's people, on a middle reading of a debate that runs from under 10 to over 100 million for the Americas as a whole.
The nadir: perhaps ten million, Indigenous, African, European and mixed.
Northern America has passed it, about 1875: for the first time since the first Americans, most of the hemisphere's people live north of Mexico.
Back ahead of Northern America about 1955: deaths fall fast while births stay near six per woman.
The peak share: from here births below the world's average and emigration north bring it down.
Zero on the usual account; the White Sands footprints in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would make it a small positive share. Their dating is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
People south of the ice in the far north-west and the Pacific coast (Paisley Caves, Cooper's Ferry) and in the east (Page-Ladson), soon after the ice-free corridor and the coast open.
The Clovis hunters spread across the continent within a few centuries.
Archaic foragers; from here the farming centres of Mesoamerica and the Andes grow faster, and Northern America's part of the hemisphere falls for six thousand years.
Maize farming spreads through the eastern woodlands and the Mississippian towns begin.
Cahokia empties and the Great Drought (1276 to 1299) drives the Ancestral Puebloans from the Four Corners.

Perhaps 4 to 5 million north of Mexico on middle estimates; the range runs from about 2 million (Ubelaker) to 18 million (Dobyns), with Thornton's 7 million between, a debate this value does not settle.
The Native nations' losses begin in earnest after de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the first coastal epidemics; the settlers are not yet a thousand.
The epidemics among the north-eastern nations of 1616 to 1640 and the Huron losses of the 1630s (ev.nam.northeast-epidemics) (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The low point: about a million Native people and a quarter of a million colonists and enslaved Africans.
The British colonies double every 25 years or so, the fastest growth then known, as Franklin and Malthus both noted.
Immigration is cut by the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, and the share rises more slowly.
Northern America's peak share, with the baby boom; from here births fall below the world's and the share declines.
Immigration keeps the decline slow: about one in seven of its people was born abroad.
The White Sands footprints (about 21,000–23,000 years ago) would make this a small positive share; their dating is debated.
Monte Verde in Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
People are south of the ice by now (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago); the Americas' isolation from Afro-Eurasia begins as Beringia floods (ev.americas-isolation).
The first Americans, a few tens of thousands, south of the ice (ev.americas-isolation).
Untouched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Afro-Eurasia's falls.
About 50 million; estimates range from 8 to over 100.
Before smallpox reaches the mainland: the Caribbean's Taíno are already mostly dead of war, forced labour and earlier disease.
Mid-epidemic: smallpox is killing central Mexico during the siege of Tenochtitlan.
After the smallpox epidemic of 1520: perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (ev.smallpox-americas).
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa (ev.am.inca-fall) as smallpox runs ahead of the conquest; VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and forced labour.

On the eve of the cocoliztli of 1545: the losses of the conquest decades are already deep, but the largest single blow is still to come, so the share stands above the straight line from 1533 to 1550 that the series had drawn.

After the cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), which on the high estimates killed most of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people: the share falls by about a point in three years. The size of the step depends on the disputed counts of New Spain's people before it.
VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and enslavement: the share halves in fifty years.
Before the second cocoliztli: above the straight line from 1550 to 1600, because the epidemic of 1576 to 1580 concentrates much of the half-century's fall.

After the cocoliztli of 1576 to 1580 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576), which killed perhaps two million, about half of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people; the decline continues to the nadir of about 1650 with later epidemics in the Andes and Brazil.
The nadir, about 12 million.
Mass European migration.

The share's 150-year rise has ended: from about 1965 Latin America's fertility falls (ev.lac.fertility-transition), and from 1980 the Americas' share declines, as births fall faster there than in Africa and South Asia.

changes.value: Review pass, coverage: the Americas' shares before 1492 gain values at the Events bound to them (Clovis and the megafauna's end, the first farmers of Mexico, the Andes and Amazonia, the Formative, Classic and Postclassic eras), and nine other places and measures gain values at the Events they passed over: Western Asia's Middle Bronze Age, Northern Africa, Eastern and Southern Asia in the Hellenistic and Mauryan centuries, Oceania's Lapita and ancestral Polynesian centuries, Southern Europe's eleventh century, Europe in the 1490s, Eastern and Western Africa's medieval kingdoms, Eastern Europe in 1941, politics in the Scramble's years and the largest polity when India passes China. All are interpolated with their neighbours' bands; the one turn of leader (India over China, April 2023) is noted.

points.note: Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.
New Kingdom Egypt and the Shang each rule a few million as the Bronze Age collapse begins.
Before the Achaemenid empire: Assyria, Egypt and the Zhou each rule a few million.
Cyrus takes the Median kingdom (ev.as.achaemenid); Lydia and Babylon fall to him within twelve years.
Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace: the Achaemenid empire holds perhaps a fifth of humanity (ev.as.achaemenid).
The Achaemenid empire.
Qin unifies China (ev.as.qin) as the Maurya empire declines after Ashoka: each holds perhaps a sixth to a fifth of humanity.
Han China.
Rome, about 65 million of 245.
Rome, with the Han breaking up.
Rome's western half has fallen (ev.eu.rome-fall) and China is divided between north and south: no polity holds more than about a seventh of humanity.
Sui China, whose census of 609 counts about 46 million.
Tang China.
The Northern Song, perhaps 80 million of 295 million, before the Jin take the north (ev.as.song).
Southern Song after losing the north to the Jin.
The Southern Song, with the Jin close behind.
Yuan China after the fall of the Song.
Revised from 28: Yuan China holds about the same quarter of humanity as at 1279; the 28 was the coarse fill's value and rose with no cause.
Ming China, about 80 million of 350 million; the 1393 census count of 60 million is taken as an undercount.
Qing China at its population peak.
Qing China and the British Empire about equal.
India passes China as the most populous state about April 2023, on the UN's estimate (ev.as.india-most-populous): the largest polity changes, but its share holds near 17.7% across the change.
Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils yet found are in Northern Africa.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and Northern Africa's people shrink to the Nile and the coasts.
The Last Interglacial's monsoon greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes; people spread into it from the south and east (the green Sahara corridors).
The green Sahara at its widest: Northern Africa's share peaks before the drier phases after 115,000 years ago shrink it again.
The glacial maximum: the Sahara at its driest; people hold on along the Nile and the Maghreb's coasts (the Iberomaurusians).
The African Humid Period greens the Sahara with lakes and grassland from about 12,500 years ago; hunters and then herders spread into it.
The Sahara dries after about 3500 BCE and its herders crowd into the Nile valley, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Roman Egypt, perhaps four to seven million, and Roman Africa's grain lands: Northern Africa holds about two fifths of the continent's people.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Egypt's people, and its returns keep Egypt's numbers down for two centuries.
The low point: Egypt perhaps four million, after plague's returns and famine; the Maghreb about six.
Egypt's people double in the nineteenth century, with cotton and the end of plague, to about ten million.
Egypt passes 118 million; with Sudan and the Maghreb the region holds a third of a billion.
Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, about 230,000 years ago.
The dispersal out of Africa probably leaves from Eastern Africa, across the Bab el-Mandeb or the Sinai.
Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands; Bantu-speaking farmers reach the Great Lakes.
Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili coast's towns at their height.
Eastern Africa has become Sub-Saharan Africa's largest part as the Atlantic trade drains the west; the Indian Ocean and Red Sea trades take fewer.
The east African slave trade to Zanzibar's clove plantations and the Gulf peaks in the 1860s and 1870s.
The rinderpest panzootic from 1887 kills most cattle, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) perhaps a third of its people.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985 kills perhaps 400,000 to a million, a dent the region's growth fills within a year.
The Rwandan genocide (1994) kills perhaps 500,000 to 800,000.
Ethiopia passes 130 million, Tanzania 70, Kenya 57: Eastern Africa now holds about one person in sixteen.
Pearl millet domesticated in the Sahel about 2500 BCE; yams and oil palm in the forest margins.
The Nok culture's iron and terracottas on the Jos plateau.
The empire of Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade; Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes.
The Mali empire at its height, Ife's and Benin's cities in the forest.

The Bights of Benin and Biafra and the Gold Coast lose tens of thousands a year to the Atlantic trade: on Manning's estimates Western Africa's numbers stand still from about 1700 to 1850, while the rest of the world's grow.
The Nigerian civil war (1967 to 1970): perhaps one to two million Biafrans die, most of hunger.
Nigeria, about 230 million, is half of the region; Niger's births are the world's highest, near seven per woman.
Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz by about 8000 BCE; teosinte becomes maize over the next millennia.
The Olmec centres of the Gulf coast.
Teotihuacan, perhaps 100,000 people, and the Classic Maya cities near their height.
The Classic Maya collapse (ev.am.maya-collapse): the southern lowland cities empty between about 800 and 950, as droughts strike and wars multiply; the share dips while the Andes' rises.
About 21 million, on a middle reading: central Mexico alone has been put at 25 million by Borah and Cook and at 6 to 12 million by their critics, the sharpest of the contact-population debates.
Smallpox in 1520 and the siege of Tenochtitlan (ev.smallpox-americas): perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), perhaps the deadliest single epidemic in Mexico's history; whether it was an introduced Salmonella or a native haemorrhagic fever is debated.
The second cocoliztli (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576) kills perhaps two million.
Perhaps one in ten of central Mexico's people of 1519 remain; New Spain's whole population is about three million, Spaniards, Africans and mixed included.
Flat through the Mexican Revolution (ev.am.mexican-revolution): perhaps one to two million die or flee in 1910 to 1920, and Mexico's people barely grow.
Monte Verde, about 14,500 years ago.
The largest share of the hemisphere's foragers: the Andes, the Amazon and the pampas, with squash, gourds and later potatoes and manioc taken into cultivation.
Caral and the monumental sites of the Peruvian coast.
