Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

points.note: The first Homo sapiens in Europe come in from the south-east: Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria about 46,000 years ago, Kostenki on the Don about 42,000.
The Gravettian mammoth hunters of Moravia and the Russian plain.
The glacial maximum empties the northern plain; people hold on in the Carpathian basin and the Ukrainian steppe.
The Cucuteni-Trypillia towns of Ukraine and Moldova, some of fifteen thousand people, the largest settlements in Europe.
Dacians, Thracians, Sarmatians, Balts and Slavs beyond Rome's frontier: about a fifth of Europe's people.
The Black Death strikes Eastern Europe less hard than the west and south; Poland is said to have escaped the worst of it.
Eastern Europe becomes Europe's largest part: Russia's peasants spread over the black-earth steppe and beyond the Volga.
Eastern Europe's peak share, more than a tenth of humanity, as the Russian Empire's births stay high while its deaths fall.
War, revolution, the civil war and the famine of 1921 cost the Russian lands perhaps 15 to 20 million lives between 1914 and 1922.
The Holodomor and the Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 kill perhaps five to seven million, about four million of them in Ukraine.
The Second World War's deadliest ground: the Soviet Union loses about 27 million and Poland about six, Jews and others murdered in the Holocaust among them (ev.eu.eastern-front, ev.eu.holocaust).
After the Soviet Union's end births collapse and deaths rise among Russian and Ukrainian men: the region's numbers fall in absolute terms from 1993.
Russia's war on Ukraine from 2022 kills and scatters Ukraine's people; how many left Eastern Europe and how many remain in Poland and the rest of it is uncertain, so the band is wider.
Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, may be an early Homo sapiens venture that left no descendants; counted as zero.
The glacial refuges of Iberia, Italy and the Balkans hold almost half of Europe's people at the glacial maximum.
Europe's first farmers arrive from Anatolia in Thessaly and Macedonia, about 6500 BCE, and spread along the Mediterranean coasts.
Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.
Greek cities and colonies, Etruscan and Latin Italy, Phoenician and Iberian Spain.
Augustan Italy, Iberia and Greece: perhaps 15 million, almost half of Europe's people, the Roman Empire's heart.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), which struck the Mediterranean hardest.
The western empire's fall: Italy's and Spain's cities shrink, and the Mediterranean loses its lead in Europe.
The Justinianic plague and the Gothic wars in Italy (535 to 554).
The Black Death kills perhaps half of Italy's and Spain's people in towns like Florence and Siena.
Plague in northern Italy (1629 to 1631) and Spain's seventeenth-century crisis.
Mass emigration from Italy, Spain and Portugal to the Americas holds the share nearly flat.
Italy and Spain now have the lowest births in the world, about 1.2 children per woman, and the Yugoslav wars (1991 to 1999) scatter the Balkans' people.
Neanderthals hold Europe; archaic humans are not counted, and Apidima's skull, if it is an early sapiens, left no lasting population.
Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) may be an early sapiens venture with no descendants; counted as zero.
Glacial maximum: retreat to southern refugia.
The Roman peak.
After the Antonine plague.
After the first wave of the Justinianic plague.
High-medieval growth: about 70 million.
The Black Death: from about 74 to 50 million.
Europe's peak share, a quarter of humanity.
Europe's war dead and the expulsions after it lower its share.

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.
Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The band now carries both; moving the value needs Asia's and Europe's shares rebalanced with it.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney (ev.oc.first-fleet); smallpox and the frontier wars begin to cut Aboriginal numbers while settlers are still few. The usual pre-contact estimates would put Oceania at 0.25 to 0.35% here; the band carries them.
Before gold is found: about 2.5 million people in Oceania, some 0.47 million of them settlers in Australia and New Zealand and about 2 million islanders and first peoples.
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) nearly double Australia's settlers in four years.
Corrected from 0.2, which left the gold rushes out: settlers reach about 1.1 million against roughly 2 million first peoples and islanders.
Corrected from 0.2: Otago's rush (1861) adds New Zealand's settlers to Australia's.
Corrected from 0.2: about 1.6 million settlers.
Corrected from 0.22: about 1.9 million settlers, while the first peoples keep falling (ev.oc.depopulation).

Corrected from 0.3: about 3.8 million settlers after the 1880s boom and Western Australia's rush, on the way to the 0.4% of 1900. The few hundredths of a point come from Asia's and Europe's shares, within their bands, and are not rebalanced here.

changes.value: Review pass, coverage and two corrections. Values at the Events the report found passed over: Asia through the Pacific war, South-eastern Asia's independence years, Europe in 1943, Sahul's first millennia, Egypt's first states, Benin and Songhay, Tang China before the An Lushan rebellion, Mughal India before Plassey, Western Asia before the sack of Baghdad, the Viking age, the Aegean of Thera, late Roman Gaul and the October War of 1973. Corrections: the Americas' shares at 1520 had smallpox killing central Mexico before it reached the mainland and South America falling with no cause, so they are moved after the epidemic's arrival (with Asia's share, so the five still sum to 100); and one-sided killing from 1972 was below even the lowest count of Burundi's killings of 1972 and left out Amin's in Uganda, so it is raised with War and Safety.

points.note: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils yet found are in Northern Africa.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and Northern Africa's people shrink to the Nile and the coasts.
The Last Interglacial's monsoon greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes; people spread into it from the south and east (the green Sahara corridors).
The green Sahara at its widest: Northern Africa's share peaks before the drier phases after 115,000 years ago shrink it again.
The glacial maximum: the Sahara at its driest; people hold on along the Nile and the Maghreb's coasts (the Iberomaurusians).
The African Humid Period greens the Sahara with lakes and grassland from about 12,500 years ago; hunters and then herders spread into it.
The Sahara dries after about 3500 BCE and its herders crowd into the Nile valley, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Interpolated: the Nile valley fills as herders leave the drying Sahara, and its first states form before Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Roman Egypt, perhaps four to seven million, and Roman Africa's grain lands: Northern Africa holds about two fifths of the continent's people.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Egypt's people, and its returns keep Egypt's numbers down for two centuries.
The low point: Egypt perhaps four million, after plague's returns and famine; the Maghreb about six.
Egypt's people double in the nineteenth century, with cotton and the end of plague, to about ten million.
Egypt passes 118 million; with Sudan and the Maghreb the region holds a third of a billion.
Pearl millet domesticated in the Sahel about 2500 BCE; yams and oil palm in the forest margins.
The Nok culture's iron and terracottas on the Jos plateau.
The empire of Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade; Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes.
The Mali empire at its height, Ife's and Benin's cities in the forest.
Interpolated: Benin under Ewuare and the rise of Songhay; Portuguese ships reach the coast from the 1440s, before the Atlantic slave trade grows.

The Bights of Benin and Biafra and the Gold Coast lose tens of thousands a year to the Atlantic trade: on Manning's estimates Western Africa's numbers stand still from about 1700 to 1850, while the rest of the world's grow.
The Nigerian civil war (1967 to 1970): perhaps one to two million Biafrans die, most of hunger.
Nigeria, about 230 million, is half of the region; Niger's births are the world's highest, near seven per woman.
The first islanders: Banwari Trace on Trinidad, then Cuba and Hispaniola by about 4000 BCE.
Saladoid farmers and potters move up the island chain from the Orinoco.
The Taíno and their neighbours, perhaps two and a half million on the middle estimates; Hispaniola alone has been put anywhere from a few hundred thousand to eight million.
War, forced labour and earlier disease have killed most of the Greater Antilles' Taíno before smallpox arrives in December 1518; Hispaniola's census of 1514 finds about 26,000 left.
Smallpox, from December 1518, kills perhaps a third to a half of the Taíno left in the Greater Antilles.
The low point: the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, a few Spanish towns and the first enslaved Africans, perhaps a third of a million.
Barbados's sugar boom of the 1640s begins the sugar islands' growth on enslaved Africans.
Saint-Domingue alone holds half a million enslaved people, the most valuable colony in the world.
The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) costs perhaps 150,000 to 350,000 lives.
The Caribbean's peak share: from here emigration to North America and Europe and early-falling births hold its growth below the world's.
Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz by about 8000 BCE; teosinte becomes maize over the next millennia.
The Olmec centres of the Gulf coast.
Teotihuacan, perhaps 100,000 people, and the Classic Maya cities near their height.
The Classic Maya collapse (ev.am.maya-collapse): the southern lowland cities empty between about 800 and 950, as droughts strike and wars multiply; the share dips while the Andes' rises.
About 21 million, on a middle reading: central Mexico alone has been put at 25 million by Borah and Cook and at 6 to 12 million by their critics, the sharpest of the contact-population debates.

Revised from 4.21: smallpox reaches the mainland only in spring 1520, so at the start of the year central Mexico's numbers are still near their 1518 level (Cholula's massacre in October 1519 kills some thousands); the losses come between here and 1521.
Mid-epidemic: about half of the epidemic's deaths in central Mexico.
Smallpox in 1520 and the siege of Tenochtitlan (ev.smallpox-americas): perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), perhaps the deadliest single epidemic in Mexico's history; whether it was an introduced Salmonella or a native haemorrhagic fever is debated.
The second cocoliztli (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576) kills perhaps two million.
Perhaps one in ten of central Mexico's people of 1519 remain; New Spain's whole population is about three million, Spaniards, Africans and mixed included.
Flat through the Mexican Revolution (ev.am.mexican-revolution): perhaps one to two million die or flee in 1910 to 1920, and Mexico's people barely grow.
Monte Verde, about 14,500 years ago.
The largest share of the hemisphere's foragers: the Andes, the Amazon and the pampas, with squash, gourds and later potatoes and manioc taken into cultivation.
Caral and the monumental sites of the Peruvian coast.
Moche and Nasca on the coast, Tiwanaku by Lake Titicaca.
Wari and Tiwanaku, and the earthwork towns of Amazonia and the Llanos de Mojos; Amazonia's numbers are among the most debated (AbsenceEvidence#10a3).
About 22 million on a middle reading: the Inca realm perhaps 10 to 14 million, Amazonia and the rest of the continent the remainder, with estimates for Amazonia from 1 to 10 million.
Revised from 4.47, which fell without a cause: smallpox reaches the Andes about 1525 to 1528, so South America's share holds until then.
Revised from 4.47 for the same reason.
Smallpox reaches the Andes ahead of the Spaniards, about 1525 to 1528, and kills the Inca Huayna Capac; the civil war that follows is fought among the survivors (ev.am.inca-fall).
The nadir: the Andes' people perhaps a sixth of 1520's, Brazil's coastal peoples largely gone, and about a million Europeans and Africans.
The Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870) kills perhaps half of Paraguay's people, invisible at this scale beside Brazil's and Argentina's growth.
Mass immigration from Italy and Spain to Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil.
South America's peak share; Brazil's fertility falls below replacement in the early 2000s (ev.lac.fertility-transition).
Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few thousand years of entering the hemisphere.
Foragers of Mesoamerica, the Andes and Amazonia multiply through the early Holocene as squash, manioc and other plants are first tended; nearly all of the rise from 9700 BCE comes before here.
About 45 million, nine in ten of the hemisphere's people, on a middle reading of a debate that runs from under 10 to over 100 million for the Americas as a whole.
Revised from 8.83 with Central and South America: smallpox has not yet reached the mainland.
Revised from 8.33 with South America's share.
The nadir: perhaps ten million, Indigenous, African, European and mixed.
Northern America has passed it, about 1875: for the first time since the first Americans, most of the hemisphere's people live north of Mexico.
Back ahead of Northern America about 1955: deaths fall fast while births stay near six per woman.
The peak share: from here births below the world's average and emigration north bring it down.
The White Sands footprints (about 21,000–23,000 years ago) would make this a small positive share; their dating is debated.
Monte Verde in Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
People are south of the ice by now (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago); the Americas' isolation from Afro-Eurasia begins as Beringia floods (ev.americas-isolation).
The first Americans, a few tens of thousands, south of the ice (ev.americas-isolation).
The Americas' foragers multiply through the early Holocene as squash and other plants are first tended; nearly all of the rise from 9700 BCE comes before here.
Untouched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Afro-Eurasia's falls.
About 50 million; estimates range from 8 to over 100.
Before smallpox reaches the mainland: the Caribbean's Taíno are already mostly dead of war, forced labour and earlier disease.
Cortés's company has landed (ev.spanish-conquest) and Tlaxcala has joined it (ev.cam.tlaxcala-alliance); smallpox is killing the Taíno of the Greater Antilles but has not reached the mainland.

Revised from 9.8, whose note put smallpox in central Mexico and the siege of Tenochtitlan at the start of 1520. Smallpox reaches the mainland with Narváez's ships in spring 1520 and the siege is fought from May to August 1521; at the start of 1520 only the Caribbean's Taíno have died of it (from December 1518).
Mid-epidemic: smallpox kills through central Mexico from about September to December 1520, after the Spanish have been driven from Tenochtitlan in June, and the city's ruler Cuitláhuac dies of it.

Revised from 9.3 with South America's share, which no longer falls before smallpox reaches the Andes (about 1525 to 1528). After the epidemic of 1520, perhaps a third of central Mexico has died within a year (ev.smallpox-americas).
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa (ev.am.inca-fall) as smallpox runs ahead of the conquest; VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and forced labour.

On the eve of the cocoliztli of 1545: the losses of the conquest decades are already deep, but the largest single blow is still to come, so the share stands above the straight line from 1533 to 1550 that the series had drawn.

After the cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), which on the high estimates killed most of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people: the share falls by about a point in three years. The size of the step depends on the disputed counts of New Spain's people before it.
VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and enslavement: the share halves in fifty years.
Before the second cocoliztli: above the straight line from 1550 to 1600, because the epidemic of 1576 to 1580 concentrates much of the half-century's fall.

After the cocoliztli of 1576 to 1580 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576), which killed perhaps two million, about half of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people; the decline continues to the nadir of about 1650 with later epidemics in the Andes and Brazil.
The nadir, about 12 million.
Mass European migration.

The share's 150-year rise has ended: from about 1965 Latin America's fertility falls (ev.lac.fertility-transition), and from 1980 the Americas' share declines, as births fall faster there than in Africa and South Asia.
Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.

Tang China at its height, just before the An Lushan rebellion (755 to 763). The register of 754 counts about 53 million and that of 764 about 17 million. Most historians read the fall as a collapse of registration, with real losses of some millions; a minority reading, popular in lists of the deadliest wars, takes it as some 36 million dead. This series takes the first reading, so the share stays on its line to 770; the second would put a fall of several points here (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

Japan surrenders; the August Revolution in Vietnam and Indonesia's proclamation open wars of independence (ev.sea.august-revolution, ev.as.indonesia-independence). The famines end and the region grows again at about 2% a year against the world's 1 to 1.5%, so the share climbs after four flat years.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
Interpolated: the Mughal empire has broken into successor states; the Company's victory at Plassey (1757) comes two years later.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.

Interpolated. The Mongols have beaten the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dağ (1243) and overrun Armenia and Georgia, but most of the fall to 1300 comes after this date, with the sack of Baghdad (1258) and the wars between the Ilkhans and the Mamluks. The value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Asia's subregions still sum to Asia; the band holds the later timing.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

points.note: The Denisovans and other archaic humans are not counted; Homo sapiens has not yet left Africa for good.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant to Homo sapiens, Skhul and Qafzeh soon after (ev.era.last-interglacial); Misliya's earlier venture left no lasting population.
Between the Last Interglacial values on either side: Homo sapiens in the Levant and Arabia, all of Asia's people in Western Asia.
Toba erupts in Sumatra (ev.toba); whether it thinned the few Homo sapiens then in Asia is debated.
Between Toba and the dispersal; set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's interpolated value.
Between -44000 and -37000, set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's, Europe's and Oceania's interpolated values.
Farming in south-west Asia and China multiplies Asia's numbers first.
The Mongol conquests begin (ev.mongol-conquests); China's losses to them and to the Yuan collapse carry Asia's share down toward 1400.
China's own losses in the Yuan collapse bring Asia's share down after 1353.
Revised from 60.8 with the Americas' share, which no longer falls before smallpox reaches the mainland, so the five shares still sum to 100.
Rises only because the Americas' share falls, mid-epidemic in central Mexico.
Revised from 61.3 with the Americas' share, so the five shares still sum to 100. Rises only because the Americas' share falls.
Asia's lowest share in two thousand years.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor and its conquest of South-east Asia (ev.sea.japanese-occupation, ev.oc.pacific-war): Asia's share holds near 55% through the war. China's war dead and the famines of Henan (1942 to 1943), Bengal (1943), Java and northern Vietnam (1944 to 1945) are set against Europe's heavier losses for its size and Southern and Western Asia's growth; the share moves by hundredths, not points.
India overtakes China as the most populous country (ev.as.india-most-populous); Asia's share keeps easing as Africa's grows.
Under the ice: Britain north of the Thames, Ireland and Scandinavia are covered or polar desert at the glacial maximum.
Hunters return to Britain and the Baltic as the ice retreats (the Creswellian and Hamburgian).
Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 6500 BCE.
Foragers still, while farmers fill the Balkans and the Danube valley: the north's share of Europe falls until farming arrives about 4000 BCE.
Roman Britain at its fullest, perhaps two to three million.
The Viking age: raids and settlement in Britain, Ireland and Normandy move people within the region and out of it more than they change its share.
England near its medieval peak, perhaps four and a half to five million before the famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death kills perhaps four in ten in England and Scandinavia.
Britain's industrial towns grow fastest in Europe; Ireland loses a million to the famine of 1845 to 1852 and as many to emigration, yet the subregion's share rises.
Northern Europe's peak share: from here falling births and the emigration of Britons, Irish and Scandinavians overseas hold it back.
Immigration keeps the British and Nordic numbers growing while their births are below replacement.
Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, may be an early Homo sapiens venture that left no descendants; counted as zero.
The glacial refuges of Iberia, Italy and the Balkans hold almost half of Europe's people at the glacial maximum.
Europe's first farmers arrive from Anatolia in Thessaly and Macedonia, about 6500 BCE, and spread along the Mediterranean coasts.

Minoan Crete at its height and the first Mycenaean shaft graves. The eruption of Thera is dated about 1600 BCE by radiocarbon and about 1500 BCE by the older archaeological chronology, a standing debate; it devastates Aegean coasts but leaves no mark on a share this coarse.
Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.
Greek cities and colonies, Etruscan and Latin Italy, Phoenician and Iberian Spain.
Augustan Italy, Iberia and Greece: perhaps 15 million, almost half of Europe's people, the Roman Empire's heart.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), which struck the Mediterranean hardest.
The western empire's fall: Italy's and Spain's cities shrink, and the Mediterranean loses its lead in Europe.
The Justinianic plague and the Gothic wars in Italy (535 to 554).
The Black Death kills perhaps half of Italy's and Spain's people in towns like Florence and Siena.
Plague in northern Italy (1629 to 1631) and Spain's seventeenth-century crisis.
Mass emigration from Italy, Spain and Portugal to the Americas holds the share nearly flat.
Italy and Spain now have the lowest births in the world, about 1.2 children per woman, and the Yugoslav wars (1991 to 1999) scatter the Balkans' people.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley may hold a brief Homo sapiens presence about 54,000 years ago, among Neanderthals; debated, and with no lasting population.
The Aurignacians of the Danube and the Swabian Jura, with the first figurines and flutes, and Chauvet's paintings about 36,000 years ago.
South-west France, the Franco-Cantabrian refuge, holds Western Europe's people at the glacial maximum; the north and the Alps are empty.
The Linear Pottery farmers spread from the Danube across the loess of Germany and northern France, about 5500 to 5000 BCE.
Celtic Gaul before Caesar's conquest, perhaps six to eight million.
Late Roman Gaul and the Rhineland, after the third-century crisis and before the Rhine frontier breaks at the end of 406.
The high-medieval clearing of forests in France and Germany: Western Europe becomes Europe's largest part.
France perhaps 17 to 20 million, the most populous kingdom in Christendom, before the great famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death (ev.black-death).
The Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648) costs Germany perhaps a third of its people, in some regions more than half, to war, plague and hunger.
France's births begin to fall a century before the rest of Europe's, and Western Europe's share eases from here.
The Western Front: France and Germany each lose more than a million and a half soldiers.
Some twelve million Germans expelled from the east arrive in the occupied zones, 1945 to 1950.
Immigration, the refugees of 2015 and of Ukraine since 2022 among them, keeps Germany's and France's numbers rising while their births stay low.
Neanderthals hold Europe; archaic humans are not counted, and Apidima's skull, if it is an early sapiens, left no lasting population.
Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) may be an early sapiens venture with no descendants; counted as zero.
Glacial maximum: retreat to southern refugia.
The Roman peak.
After the Antonine plague.
After the first wave of the Justinianic plague.
High-medieval growth: about 70 million.
The Black Death: from about 74 to 50 million.
Europe's peak share, a quarter of humanity.
The war's deadliest years in Europe, the Holocaust and the war in the east (ev.eu.holocaust, ev.eu.eastern-front): Europe's share falls by about a tenth of a point a year.
Europe's war dead and the expulsions after it lower its share.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
The postwar migration programmes, 'populate or perish', hold the share steady while the world grows fastest.
About 33 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.

Interpolated: Sahul's first people reach New Guinea's highlands (the Ivane valley) and Arnhem Land's ground-edge axes by about 49,000 years ago. When they first arrived is debated, about 65,000 years ago on Madjedebe's dates or about 50,000 on others; this series takes the later date, and the band carries both.
Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The dead are debated: about 270,000 violent deaths by a survey-based estimate (Obermeyer and others, 2008), 300,000 to 500,000 in many scholarly accounts, 1.5 million in Rummel's, 3 million in Bangladesh's official figure. Taken here as about 500,000, some 18 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over nine months, with the Vietnam war's 3. The parent's 1970 reading had left it out.

Estimates run from about 500,000 (Human Rights Watch) through 600,000 to 800,000 in most scholarly work to over a million in Rwanda's own count of victims; taken here as about 650,000 in a hundred days, some 43 per 100,000 a year of the world's people, with other wars at about 1.5. changes.value: Review pass, coverage: values at the last Events the report found passed over. Asia from the oil shock to the Khmer Rouge; South-eastern Asia through Japan's occupation, with its first postwar values lowered to the famine's timing; the Americas at Chile's coup; Latin America at the Haitian Revolution; Western Asia on the eve of the Armenian genocide; Europe at the postwar boom; Eastern Asia at the late Tang; Northern Africa at the Middle Kingdom; Southern Europe at Rome's and Athens' new constitutions; Western Europe in the wars of religion; Oceania and Australia in Sahul's first millennia and the mid-Holocene. Interpolated with their neighbours' bands unless a note gives the reason for a turn.

points.note: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils yet found are in Northern Africa.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and Northern Africa's people shrink to the Nile and the coasts.
The Last Interglacial's monsoon greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes; people spread into it from the south and east (the green Sahara corridors).
The green Sahara at its widest: Northern Africa's share peaks before the drier phases after 115,000 years ago shrink it again.
The glacial maximum: the Sahara at its driest; people hold on along the Nile and the Maghreb's coasts (the Iberomaurusians).
The African Humid Period greens the Sahara with lakes and grassland from about 12,500 years ago; hunters and then herders spread into it.
The Sahara dries after about 3500 BCE and its herders crowd into the Nile valley, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Interpolated: the Nile valley fills as herders leave the drying Sahara, and its first states form before Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.

The Middle Kingdom reunites Egypt after the First Intermediate Period, a century of divided rule that came with the low Nile floods of the 4.2-kiloyear drought. How many died in it is unknown, and the series keeps a straight line through it.
Roman Egypt, perhaps four to seven million, and Roman Africa's grain lands: Northern Africa holds about two fifths of the continent's people.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Egypt's people, and its returns keep Egypt's numbers down for two centuries.
The low point: Egypt perhaps four million, after plague's returns and famine; the Maghreb about six.
Egypt's people double in the nineteenth century, with cotton and the end of plague, to about ten million.
Egypt passes 118 million; with Sudan and the Maghreb the region holds a third of a billion.
Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few thousand years of entering the hemisphere.
Foragers of Mesoamerica, the Andes and Amazonia multiply through the early Holocene as squash, manioc and other plants are first tended; nearly all of the rise from 9700 BCE comes before here.
About 45 million, nine in ten of the hemisphere's people, on a middle reading of a debate that runs from under 10 to over 100 million for the Americas as a whole.
Revised from 8.83 with Central and South America: smallpox has not yet reached the mainland.
Revised from 8.33 with South America's share.
The nadir: perhaps ten million, Indigenous, African, European and mixed.

The Haitian Revolution begins (August 1791); perhaps a third of Saint-Domingue's half million enslaved people die in its wars to 1804. Latin America's share eases from 1780 to 1800 because Europe's and Asia's numbers grow faster, not because the region's fall.
Northern America has passed it, about 1875: for the first time since the first Americans, most of the hemisphere's people live north of Mexico.
Back ahead of Northern America about 1955: deaths fall fast while births stay near six per woman.
The peak share: from here births below the world's average and emigration north bring it down.
Zero on the usual account; the White Sands footprints in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would make it a small positive share. Their dating is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
People south of the ice in the far north-west and the Pacific coast (Paisley Caves, Cooper's Ferry) and in the east (Page-Ladson), soon after the ice-free corridor and the coast open.
The Clovis hunters spread across the continent within a few centuries.
Archaic foragers; from here the farming centres of Mesoamerica and the Andes grow faster, and Northern America's part of the hemisphere falls for six thousand years.
Maize farming spreads through the eastern woodlands and the Mississippian towns begin.
Cahokia empties and the Great Drought (1276 to 1299) drives the Ancestral Puebloans from the Four Corners.

Perhaps 4 to 5 million north of Mexico on middle estimates; the range runs from about 2 million (Ubelaker) to 18 million (Dobyns), with Thornton's 7 million between, a debate this value does not settle.
The Native nations' losses begin in earnest after de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the first coastal epidemics; the settlers are not yet a thousand.
The epidemics among the north-eastern nations of 1616 to 1640 and the Huron losses of the 1630s (ev.nam.northeast-epidemics) (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The low point: about a million Native people and a quarter of a million colonists and enslaved Africans.
The British colonies double every 25 years or so, the fastest growth then known, as Franklin and Malthus both noted.
Immigration is cut by the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, and the share rises more slowly.
Northern America's peak share, with the baby boom; from here births fall below the world's and the share declines.
Immigration keeps the decline slow: about one in seven of its people was born abroad.
The White Sands footprints (about 21,000–23,000 years ago) would make this a small positive share; their dating is debated.
Monte Verde in Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
People are south of the ice by now (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago); the Americas' isolation from Afro-Eurasia begins as Beringia floods (ev.americas-isolation).
The first Americans, a few tens of thousands, south of the ice (ev.americas-isolation).
The Americas' foragers multiply through the early Holocene as squash and other plants are first tended; nearly all of the rise from 9700 BCE comes before here.
Untouched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Afro-Eurasia's falls.
About 50 million; estimates range from 8 to over 100.
Before smallpox reaches the mainland: the Caribbean's Taíno are already mostly dead of war, forced labour and earlier disease.
Cortés's company has landed (ev.spanish-conquest) and Tlaxcala has joined it (ev.cam.tlaxcala-alliance); smallpox is killing the Taíno of the Greater Antilles but has not reached the mainland.

Revised from 9.8, whose note put smallpox in central Mexico and the siege of Tenochtitlan at the start of 1520. Smallpox reaches the mainland with Narváez's ships in spring 1520 and the siege is fought from May to August 1521; at the start of 1520 only the Caribbean's Taíno have died of it (from December 1518).
Mid-epidemic: smallpox kills through central Mexico from about September to December 1520, after the Spanish have been driven from Tenochtitlan in June, and the city's ruler Cuitláhuac dies of it.

Revised from 9.3 with South America's share, which no longer falls before smallpox reaches the Andes (about 1525 to 1528). After the epidemic of 1520, perhaps a third of central Mexico has died within a year (ev.smallpox-americas).
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa (ev.am.inca-fall) as smallpox runs ahead of the conquest; VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and forced labour.

On the eve of the cocoliztli of 1545: the losses of the conquest decades are already deep, but the largest single blow is still to come, so the share stands above the straight line from 1533 to 1550 that the series had drawn.

After the cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), which on the high estimates killed most of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people: the share falls by about a point in three years. The size of the step depends on the disputed counts of New Spain's people before it.
VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd with war and enslavement: the share halves in fifty years.
Before the second cocoliztli: above the straight line from 1550 to 1600, because the epidemic of 1576 to 1580 concentrates much of the half-century's fall.

After the cocoliztli of 1576 to 1580 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576), which killed perhaps two million, about half of central Mexico's remaining Indigenous people; the decline continues to the nadir of about 1650 with later epidemics in the Andes and Brazil.
The nadir, about 12 million.
Mass European migration.
Chile's coup and the oil shock: the Americas' share holds at 13.9%, Northern America's falling as fast as Latin America's rises.

The share's 150-year rise has ended: from about 1965 Latin America's fertility falls (ev.lac.fertility-transition), and from 1980 the Americas' share declines, as births fall faster there than in Africa and South Asia.
Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.

Tang China at its height, just before the An Lushan rebellion (755 to 763). The register of 754 counts about 53 million and that of 764 about 17 million. Most historians read the fall as a collapse of registration, with real losses of some millions; a minority reading, popular in lists of the deadliest wars, takes it as some 36 million dead. This series takes the first reading, so the share stays on its line to 770; the second would put a fall of several points here (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Interpolated: the late Tang loses its hold, Huang Chao's rebellion (875 to 884) sacks Guangzhou and Chang'an, and the dynasty ends in 907; the Five Dynasties follow in the north until the Song reunite China from 960.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Japan invades (ev.sea.japanese-occupation). The region has grown a little faster than the world since 1936; from here its growth stops for four years.

The famine in northern Vietnam begins. Its dead are debated: about two million in Vietnamese accounts, about one million in some others. Hunger and forced labour in Java kill on a similar scale on some estimates, and the battle of Manila (February to March 1945) kills about 100,000 civilians; most of these deaths fall in the next eight months.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

Revised from 6.37, recorded earlier in this pass: the famine in northern Vietnam peaks in spring 1945 and the battle of Manila is fought in February and March, so at Japan's surrender the share is still at its wartime level. Revised from 6.43 with the value at 1945.63.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.

Interpolated. The Mongols have beaten the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dağ (1243) and overrun Armenia and Georgia, but most of the fall to 1300 comes after this date, with the sack of Baghdad (1258) and the wars between the Ilkhans and the Mamluks. The value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Asia's subregions still sum to Asia; the band holds the later timing.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
On the eve of the Armenian genocide and Gallipoli. Most of Western Asia's wartime losses, from massacre, deportation, war and the famine in Lebanon and Syria, come after this date.
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

Rises only because the Americas' share falls, mid-epidemic in central Mexico.

Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, may be an early Homo sapiens venture that left no descendants; counted as zero.
The glacial refuges of Iberia, Italy and the Balkans hold almost half of Europe's people at the glacial maximum.
Europe's first farmers arrive from Anatolia in Thessaly and Macedonia, about 6500 BCE, and spread along the Mediterranean coasts.

Minoan Crete at its height and the first Mycenaean shaft graves. The eruption of Thera is dated about 1600 BCE by radiocarbon and about 1500 BCE by the older archaeological chronology, a standing debate; it devastates Aegean coasts but leaves no mark on a share this coarse.
Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.
Interpolated: Rome expels its kings (509 BCE) and Cleisthenes' reforms follow at Athens (508 BCE); Greek cities and colonies keep growing.
Greek cities and colonies, Etruscan and Latin Italy, Phoenician and Iberian Spain.
Augustan Italy, Iberia and Greece: perhaps 15 million, almost half of Europe's people, the Roman Empire's heart.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), which struck the Mediterranean hardest.
The western empire's fall: Italy's and Spain's cities shrink, and the Mediterranean loses its lead in Europe.
The Justinianic plague and the Gothic wars in Italy (535 to 554).
The Black Death kills perhaps half of Italy's and Spain's people in towns like Florence and Siena.
Plague in northern Italy (1629 to 1631) and Spain's seventeenth-century crisis.
Mass emigration from Italy, Spain and Portugal to the Americas holds the share nearly flat.
Italy and Spain now have the lowest births in the world, about 1.2 children per woman, and the Yugoslav wars (1991 to 1999) scatter the Balkans' people.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley may hold a brief Homo sapiens presence about 54,000 years ago, among Neanderthals; debated, and with no lasting population.
The Aurignacians of the Danube and the Swabian Jura, with the first figurines and flutes, and Chauvet's paintings about 36,000 years ago.
South-west France, the Franco-Cantabrian refuge, holds Western Europe's people at the glacial maximum; the north and the Alps are empty.
The Linear Pottery farmers spread from the Danube across the loess of Germany and northern France, about 5500 to 5000 BCE.
Celtic Gaul before Caesar's conquest, perhaps six to eight million.
Late Roman Gaul and the Rhineland, after the third-century crisis and before the Rhine frontier breaks at the end of 406.
The high-medieval clearing of forests in France and Germany: Western Europe becomes Europe's largest part.
France perhaps 17 to 20 million, the most populous kingdom in Christendom, before the great famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death (ev.black-death).
Interpolated: France's wars of religion (from 1562) and the Dutch revolt (from 1568) kill hundreds of thousands, yet Western Europe's numbers keep pace with the world's.
The Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648) costs Germany perhaps a third of its people, in some regions more than half, to war, plague and hunger.
France's births begin to fall a century before the rest of Europe's, and Western Europe's share eases from here.
The Western Front: France and Germany each lose more than a million and a half soldiers.
Some twelve million Germans expelled from the east arrive in the occupied zones, 1945 to 1950.
Immigration, the refugees of 2015 and of Ukraine since 2022 among them, keeps Germany's and France's numbers rising while their births stay low.
Neanderthals hold Europe; archaic humans are not counted, and Apidima's skull, if it is an early sapiens, left no lasting population.
Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) may be an early sapiens venture with no descendants; counted as zero.
Glacial maximum: retreat to southern refugia.
The Roman peak.
After the Antonine plague.
After the first wave of the Justinianic plague.
High-medieval growth: about 70 million.
The Black Death: from about 74 to 50 million.
Europe's peak share, a quarter of humanity.
The war's deadliest years in Europe, the Holocaust and the war in the east (ev.eu.holocaust, ev.eu.eastern-front): Europe's share falls by about a tenth of a point a year.
Europe's war dead and the expulsions after it lower its share.
The postwar boom begins. Europe's births rise in the baby boom, but deaths fall faster in Asia, Africa and Latin America, so Europe's share falls by about a quarter of a point a year.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.

Interpolated. From about 4000 BCE backed blades, seed-grinding and new sites spread across mainland Australia and Pama-Nyungan languages spread from the Gulf country. Many read these as signs of more people, but the share still falls because farmers elsewhere multiply faster.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
The postwar migration programmes, 'populate or perish', hold the share steady while the world grows fastest.
About 33 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.

Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). Before gold is found: about 2.5 million people in Oceania, some 0.47 million of them settlers in Australia and New Zealand and about 2 million islanders and first peoples.
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) nearly double Australia's settlers in four years.
Corrected from 0.2, which left the gold rushes out: settlers reach about 1.1 million against roughly 2 million first peoples and islanders.
Corrected from 0.2: Otago's rush (1861) adds New Zealand's settlers to Australia's.
Corrected from 0.2: about 1.6 million settlers.
Corrected from 0.22: about 1.9 million settlers, while the first peoples keep falling (ev.oc.depopulation).

Corrected from 0.3: about 3.8 million settlers after the 1880s boom and Western Australia's rush, on the way to the 0.4% of 1900. The few hundredths of a point come from Asia's and Europe's shares, within their bands, and are not rebalanced here.

The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Interpolated: the rice frontiers of the Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya and Mekong deltas open, and France begins its conquest of Indochina (1858); the region's growth outpaces the world's.
Japan invades (ev.sea.japanese-occupation). The region has grown a little faster than the world since 1936; from here its growth stops for four years.

The famine in northern Vietnam begins. Its dead are debated: about two million in Vietnamese accounts, about one million in some others. Hunger and forced labour in Java kill on a similar scale on some estimates, and the battle of Manila (February to March 1945) kills about 100,000 civilians; most of these deaths fall in the next eight months.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

Revised from 6.37, recorded earlier in this pass: the famine in northern Vietnam peaks in spring 1945 and the battle of Manila is fought in February and March, so at Japan's surrender the share is still at its wartime level. The August Revolution and Indonesia's proclamation open wars of independence (ev.sea.august-revolution, ev.as.indonesia-independence); the famines end, and the region grows again at about 2% a year against the world's 1 to 1.5%.
Revised from 6.43 with the value at 1945.63.

After the killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million dead, on estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, take about two hundredths of a point from the region's share, which its births keep rising.
Saigon falls and the Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh; the note at 1976 gives the scale of their effect on the share.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

Between Toba and the dispersal; set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's interpolated value.

Farming in south-west Asia and China multiplies Asia's numbers first.
