upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The people living in Africa (africa): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Africa (M49 002).
- Necessity pass: Without it the whole of humanity before about 130,000 years ago, and every change in Africa's people since, has no home.
- Independence pass: Africa's people grow and shrink apart from other regions' (its share falls from 100% to 8% and rises again to 19% after 1950). Shares of one pool must sum to 100, so a rise in one is a fall in the rest together, but no region's change forces the same change in any other: in numbers of people all can rise together.
- Universality pass: People live in Africa at every date of the range.

The people living in the Americas (americas): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in the Americas (M49 019).
- Necessity pass: The peopling of the hemisphere, the collapse after 1492 and the settler growth after 1800 need a home.
- Independence pass: The Americas' share collapsed after 1492 while Asia's rose, and grew from 1800 to 1960 while Africa's fell.
- Universality pass: The place is part of the Earth at every date; before people arrive, perhaps 23,000 and certainly 16,000 years ago, its share is zero, a value of the measure, not the absence of the part.

The people living in Asia (asia): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Asia (M49 142).
- Necessity pass: About three in five of all people since farming; without it most of humanity has no home.
- Independence pass: Asia's share fell from 1800 to 1930 while Europe's and the Americas' rose, and rose again after 1950.
- Universality pass: Zero before the first lasting presence in the Levant; a value, not an absence of the part.

The people living in Europe (europe): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Europe (M49 150, the whole Russian Federation included).
- Necessity pass: The Black Death, the rise of Europe's share to a quarter of humanity by 1900 and its fall to 9% need a home.
- Independence pass: Europe's share fell in 1347 to 1353 while Asia's held, and rose in the nineteenth century while Asia's fell.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches Europe about 45,000 years ago (the Neanderthals are not counted); a value, not an absence.

The people living in Oceania (oceania): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Oceania (M49 009).
- Necessity pass: The peopling of Sahul and of the remote Pacific, the depopulation after contact and the settler growth after 1788 need a home.
- Independence pass: Oceania's share moves with its own settlement and collapse, apart from the rest.
- Universality pass: Zero before Sahul is reached, 65,000 or about 50,000 years ago; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Antarctica (antarctica): dropped.
- What it covers: Permanent residents of Antarctica (M49 010), which belongs to no region.
- Necessity fail: No one has ever lived there permanently: the few thousand people at research stations live elsewhere and are counted where they usually live, so its share is zero at every date and no change has a home here that lacks one elsewhere.
- Independence pass: Would change apart from the others.
- Universality pass: The place exists at every date.

People by climate zone or biome (climate-zones): dropped.
- What it covers: The share of people living in the tropics, the arid belt, the temperate zones and the cold north.
- Necessity uncertain: It would show the move of people into the temperate and arid farming belts, but every change it holds already has a home in the regions.
- Independence fail: It partitions the same people along a second criterion; mixed with the regions it would put each person in two parts (MECE#ae19, dimensional error).
- Universality pass: Every date.

Completeness pass: The UN M49 standard divides the World (001) into Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania, with Antarctica (010) in none; every inhabited place on Earth lies in exactly one of the five, so every living person has exactly one home, and the shares sum to 100 at every date. People at sea or in transit are counted where they usually live. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The people living in Asia (concept.humanity.asia):
- What it is: The people living in Asia, divided by where in Asia they live.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of Asia's people that rise and fall apart, which Asia's one share hides: China's and Japan's in Eastern Asia against India's in Southern Asia, the early farmers of the Fertile Crescent against the late-growing islands and deltas of South-eastern Asia, and the steppe oases of Central Asia.
- The range it claims: Every date from 320,000 years ago to 2025, with places fixed by the UN M49 subregions of Asia (142) within 2026 borders: Iran counts in Southern Asia, the Caucasus and Cyprus in Western Asia, and Siberia, as part of the Russian Federation, in Europe.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The people living in Asia is a kind of Humanity: The people of Asia are one of the five parts of humanity by place, the most populous since the first farmers. Other kinds within it: the people living in Africa, the people living in the Americas, the people living in Europe, the people living in Oceania.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The people living in Asia is carved into 5 parts: The people living in Eastern Asia, The people living in Southern Asia, The people living in South-eastern Asia, The people living in Western Asia, The people living in Central Asia.

How the parts make the whole work: The five shares divide Asia's people at every date and sum to Asia's share of humanity, so Asia's one curve becomes the sum of curves that rise and fall apart: Western Asia's first lead and long relative fall, Eastern Asia's swings with China's dynasties (its peak near 39% of humanity in 1820 and its fall to 20% now as its births fell first), Southern Asia's steadier growth that overtakes it about 2001, South-eastern Asia's late rise from 3% to 8.5% since 1800, and Central Asia's small share cut by the Mongol sacks and the Kazakh famine. A conquest that crosses subregions, like the Mongols', has a part in each, and the parts split cleanly by where the dead and the survivors lived.

Routed elsewhere: The people living in North Asia (Siberia) to Europe (h.region-europe), Eastern Europe, under the M49 standard, China and India as parts of their own to parts of Eastern and Southern Asia, to be opened beneath them in a later pass.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The people living in Eastern Asia (eastern): part.
- What it covers: China, Japan, the two Koreas, Mongolia and Taiwan (M49 030).
- Necessity pass: China's rises and collapses (the Han census, the Song boom, the Mongol and Ming-Qing losses, the Taiping war, the famine of 1959 to 1961) and Japan's growth need a home of their own; inside Asia's one share they cancel against India's.
- Independence pass: Eastern Asia's share fell in the Ming-Qing transition while Southern Asia's rose, and rose under the Qing to 39% of humanity in 1820 while India's fell; its fertility fell from 1970 decades before India's.
- Universality pass: The place is part of Asia at every date; before Homo sapiens reaches it, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago (the Fuyan teeth of 80,000 years or more are debated), its share is zero, a value of the measure.

The people living in Southern Asia (southern): part.
- What it covers: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Iran, Afghanistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and the Maldives (M49 034).
- Necessity pass: The Harappan cities, the Gangetic states, Mughal India, the famines of 1876 to 1902 and 1943 and India's overtaking of China need a home.
- Independence pass: Southern Asia grew steadily through China's collapses, and its fertility transition lagged Eastern Asia's by decades, so its share overtook Eastern Asia's about 2001.
- Universality pass: Zero before the dispersal reaches it, about 70,000 to 60,000 years ago; the tools under the Toba ash at Jwalapuram are of debated makers.

The people living in South-eastern Asia (south-eastern): part.
- What it covers: Mainland South-east Asia from Myanmar to Vietnam, and the islands from Sumatra to the Philippines and Timor (M49 035).
- Necessity pass: Sundaland's foragers and its drowning, the late arrival of rice farming, and the region's fourfold rise from 3% of humanity in 1800 to 8.5% need a home.
- Independence pass: Its share rose through the nineteenth century, with Java's and the deltas' growth, while Eastern and Southern Asia's fell.
- Universality pass: Zero before the dispersal reaches it, perhaps 70,000 years ago at Lida Ajer.

The people living in Western Asia (western): part.
- What it covers: Anatolia, the Caucasus, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Arabia and Cyprus (M49 145).
- Necessity pass: The only part of Asia with Homo sapiens before 75,000 years ago (Misliya, Skhul and Qafzeh, Arabia), the first farmers and cities, and the long fall of its share from perhaps a quarter of humanity to 2% in 1900 need a home.
- Independence pass: Western Asia's share fell from the first millennium BCE to 1900, through the Mongol sack of Baghdad and the Black Death, while Eastern Asia's rose; since 1950 it has grown faster than Asia's.
- Universality pass: People live there at every date after about 130,000 years ago; before that its share is zero.

The people living in Central Asia (central): part.
- What it covers: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan (M49 143).
- Necessity pass: The oases of Sogdiana and Khwarazm, the Mongol and Timurid sacks, the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933 and the region's post-1950 growth need a home; in Asia's one share they are invisible.
- Independence pass: Central Asia's share fell after the Mongol conquest and in the Kazakh famine while the rest of Asia's did not.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches the steppe, about 45,000 years ago.

The people living in North Asia (Siberia) (north-asia): routed to Europe (h.region-europe), Eastern Europe, under the M49 standard.
- What it covers: Siberia and the Russian Far East.
- Necessity fail: Under M49 Siberia lies in the Russian Federation, which is wholly in Eastern Europe, so its people already have a home there; a part here would count them twice.
- Independence pass: Would change apart.
- Universality pass: Every date after people reach it.

China and India as parts of their own (countries): routed to parts of Eastern and Southern Asia, to be opened beneath them in a later pass.
- What it covers: The two most populous countries as parts beside the subregions.
- Necessity pass: Each has histories of its own.
- Independence fail: Each lies inside a subregion (Eastern and Southern Asia), so as a sibling of the subregions it would put its people in two parts; the countries are parts one level down.
- Universality pass: The land exists at every date, by 2026 borders.

Completeness pass: The M49 standard divides Asia (142) into Central (143), Eastern (030), South-eastern (035), Southern (034) and Western Asia (145); every place in Asia lies in exactly one, so the five shares sum to Asia's at every date. Checked against UN M49 Standard country or area codes for statistical use (United Nations Statistics Division): the composition of Asia (142), as recorded in structure/history-tree.mjs.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.asia","conceptId":"concept.humanity.asia","candidates":[{"key":"eastern","label":"The people living in Eastern Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"southern","label":"The people living in Southern Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"south-eastern","label":"The people living in South-eastern Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"western","label":"The people living in Western Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"central","label":"The people living in Central Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"north-asia","label":"The people living in North Asia (Siberia)","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Europe (h.region-europe), Eastern Europe, under the M49 standard"},{"key":"countries","label":"China and India as parts of their own","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"parts of Eastern and Southern Asia, to be opened beneath them in a later pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"UN M49 Standard country or area codes for statistical use (United Nations Statistics Division): the composition of Asia (142), as recorded in structure/history-tree.mjs"}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Humanity is carved into 2 parts: What matters to people, How people get it.

How the parts make the whole work: Humanity's numbers grow when its means let more people meet their ends, and fall when the means fail them, as in famine, war and plague. The means (what a population produces, trades, builds, connects and governs) are the levers; the ends (survival, sufficiency, belonging, understanding, standing, freedom, meaning, play and children) are what the levers are for, and the account's turning points are mostly moments when the two moved apart: output rose and lives did not improve in the agrarian empires, and lives improved faster than output after 1945. The seam between them, income, is recorded rather than merged. The rival carve of the same whole, the twelve dimensions of a way of living, stays a frontier alternative until the choice of tree is made.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: The twelve dimensions of a human way of living (necessity, independence).

Routed elsewhere: Humanity's numbers: births, deaths and moves to the parent's own measure (h.humanity), with births and deaths under h.wants (h.continuation, h.alive) and moves under the places carve (carve.concept.humanity.places).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

What matters to people (wants): part.
- What it covers: The conditions of a life that people seek for themselves and their children: to stay alive and well, to have enough, to belong, to understand, to stand well among others, to be free, to find meaning, to play, and to have children.
- Necessity pass: Without it life expectancy, poverty, literacy, freedom from bondage, worship and fertility have no home: they are what the account's numbers are ultimately about.
- Independence pass: The ends change apart from the means more often than the means-ends link suggests: life expectancy doubled in poor countries after 1945 at incomes Europe had in 1850, literacy spread in Protestant Europe under flat output, and heights fell in early industrial Britain and the United States while output per person rose. The coupling through income is a seam recorded here, not a merger.
- Universality pass: Every society has conditions its people seek; the measures under it are defined for every date, if only as guesses.

How people get it (means): part.
- What it covers: What a population does to secure those conditions: produce, exchange, settle, connect and govern; followed at its root as world output.
- Necessity pass: Without it farming, trade, cities, roads and states have no home.
- Independence pass: Output, trade and states grew in the agrarian empires while life expectancy, height and poverty stood still or worsened (MalthusianTrap#0f6b): the means change apart from the ends.
- Universality pass: Every society produces, exchanges, settles, moves and decides together, if only as a band.

Humanity's numbers: births, deaths and moves (numbers): routed to the parent's own measure (h.humanity), with births and deaths under h.wants (h.continuation, h.alive) and moves under the places carve (carve.concept.humanity.places).
- What it covers: How many people there are and how that changes.
- Necessity pass: Demographic history needs a home.
- Independence fail: Humanity's numbers are the parent's own measure, and births and deaths are already ends under what matters to people (continuation, staying alive); moves are carried by the shares by place. A third part would hold each twice.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The twelve dimensions of a human way of living (twelve-dimensions): frontier.
- What it covers: The structure construction's carve of the same whole (acut.way-of-living): provisioning, exchange, wealth, population, habitat, connection, society, politics, security, knowledge, beliefs and norms, arts and play.
- Necessity uncertain: It is not a part beside the ends and the means but a rival carve of the whole; whether the account's measures should hang on it is the open choice this pass does not make.
- Independence fail: It covers everything the ends and the means cover, along another criterion; as a sibling it would give every measure two homes (MECE#ae19, dimensional error).
- Universality pass: Judged for every society from 320,000 years ago to 2026 in the structure construction.

Completeness uncertain: Every one of the twelve dimensions of a way of living has a home in one of the two parts or below them, so no measure is left homeless. But checked against Michael Mann's four sources of social power (ideological, economic, military, political), a list made for another purpose, two sources have a home only as ends, not as means: military power appears only as its toll (safety, under staying alive), and ideological power only as worship (under meaning). The means of organized violence and the making of new knowledge have no home as means; the carve of how people get it is where they belong, and it is recorded next. Checked against Michael Mann's IEMP model of the sources of social power (The Sources of Social Power, 1986), as recalled; and the structure construction's twelve dimensions (structure/history-tree.mjs). Still without a home: the means of organized violence (armies, weapons, the organization of fighting) as a means rather than a toll; the making of new knowledge and technique as a means.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.ends-means","conceptId":"concept.humanity","candidates":[{"key":"wants","label":"What matters to people","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"means","label":"How people get it","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"numbers","label":"Humanity's numbers: births, deaths and moves","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"the parent's own measure (h.humanity), with births and deaths under h.wants (h.continuation, h.alive) and moves under the places carve (carve.concept.humanity.places)"},{"key":"twelve-dimensions","label":"The twelve dimensions of a human way of living","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Michael Mann's IEMP model of the sources of social power (The Sources of Social Power, 1986), as recalled; and the structure construction's twelve dimensions (structure/history-tree.mjs)","missing":["the means of organized violence (armies, weapons, the organization of fighting) as a means rather than a toll","the making of new knowledge and technique as a means"]}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The Earth as setting is carved into 5 parts: The air and the climate it holds, Land and sea, The plant cover, The wild animals, The Earth's stores.

How the parts make the whole work: The Earth's setting at any date is the joint state of its air, its seas and ice, its plants, its animals and its stores. The air and the orbit set the temperature (the parent's own measure), which moves the seas and the plant cover on slower clocks; plants and wild animals are what foragers live on and among, and the stores are what toolmakers and then industry dig up. For most of the span the setting changes on its own and humanity adapts to it; since farming, people clear the plants and kill the animals, and since 1850 they draw on the stores so fast that the air and the temperature follow. Each of those couplings is a seam between this part of History and humanity, recorded on the verdicts rather than merged.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Fresh water (independence), The nitrogen and phosphorus cycles (declared).

Routed elsewhere: The microbes people live among to deaths from infection, under staying alive (h.alive), carved in this pass, Domesticated plants and animals to land used for crops and pasture (h.farmland), under habitat.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The air and the climate it holds (climate): part.
- What it covers: The composition of the atmosphere and the temperature and rainfall it sets; followed by carbon dioxide beside the parent's own measure, global temperature.
- Necessity pass: The glacial cycles (carbon dioxide from 180 to 280 parts per million), the Holocene's stable warmth and the rise to 425 since 1850 need a home; they set what grows and where people can live.
- Independence pass: Carbon dioxide and temperature move together in the glacial cycles, but each also moves apart: orbital forcing warms first at the terminations, eruptions such as Toba and Tambora cool for years without changing carbon dioxide, and the industrial rise in carbon dioxide ran decades ahead of the warming. Sea level lags both by millennia.
- Universality pass: Every date has an atmosphere and a climate.

Land and sea (land-and-sea): part.
- What it covers: The extent of land, ice and sea, and the coastlines between them; followed by global mean sea level.
- Necessity pass: Beringia, Sundaland, Sahul and Doggerland exposed and drowned, the coasts every early crossing followed, need a home.
- Independence pass: Sea level rose 120 metres after the glacial maximum over ten thousand years while temperature had settled; it changes on its own slow clock.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The plant cover (vegetation): part.
- What it covers: The living world's plants, followed by the share of land under forest.
- Necessity pass: The spread of forest after the glacial, the green Sahara and its drying, and the clearing of forests by farmers need a home.
- Independence pass: Forest is cleared by people under an unchanged climate (Europe's high Middle Ages, the tropics since 1950) and returns where fields are abandoned, apart from carbon dioxide and sea level.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The wild animals (wild-animals): part.
- What it covers: The living world's wild animals, followed by the biomass of wild land mammals.
- Necessity pass: The extinction of the megafauna of Sahul, the Americas and northern Eurasia, the slaughter of the bison and of Africa's herds, and the collapse of wild mammals to a few per cent of humanity's biomass have no other home: forest measures plants only.
- Independence pass: The megafauna vanished from the Americas while forests spread; the bison were killed in fifteen years while the prairie stood; wild animals change apart from plants and climate.
- Universality pass: Every date has wild animals.

The Earth's stores (resources): part.
- What it covers: Stone, sand, clay, ores and fossil fuels: the stores laid down in the crust that people dig up; followed by how much of them people take each year.
- Necessity pass: Flint and ochre, copper and tin, the iron of the first millennium BCE, the coal of the Industrial Revolution and the concrete of the twentieth century have no home without the stores they come from.
- Independence pass: The draw on the stores changes apart from climate and from the living world: coal rose a hundredfold in a century while forest and sea level barely moved. It is coupled to carbon dioxide through fossil fuels, a seam recorded here.
- Universality pass: Every society takes stone for tools and ochre for colour; the draw is tiny for foragers, a value of the measure, not the absence of the part.

The microbes people live among (pathogens): routed to deaths from infection, under staying alive (h.alive), carved in this pass.
- What it covers: The pathogens and parasites of the living world.
- Necessity fail: What they do to people is followed as deaths from infection under staying alive; as a world measure of the living world no number can be stated for them.
- Independence pass: They change apart (new diseases, the Columbian exchange).
- Universality pass: Every date.

Domesticated plants and animals (domesticates): routed to land used for crops and pasture (h.farmland), under habitat.
- What it covers: Crops and livestock, the living world people have remade.
- Necessity pass: Domestication needs a home.
- Independence fail: Their extent is the land people use for crops and pasture, followed as h.farmland under habitat; as a part of the Earth's setting they would be counted twice.
- Universality fail: Absent before about 11,000 years ago except the dog.

Fresh water (freshwater): frontier.
- What it covers: Rivers, lakes, groundwater and rain.
- Necessity pass: The drying of the Sahara, the irrigation of Mesopotamia and the Aral Sea's loss need a home.
- Independence uncertain: Rainfall is part of climate; withdrawals are human use. Whether a separate part pays is not settled.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The nitrogen and phosphorus cycles (nutrient-cycles): frontier.
- What it covers: The flows of the nutrients that limit plant growth.
- Necessity pass: Industrial nitrogen fixation since 1913 feeds about half of humanity and has no home.
- Independence pass: Nitrogen fixed by people rose apart from carbon dioxide and forest.
- Universality pass: Every date.

Completeness uncertain: Against the four parts the structure construction carved for the Earth as setting (climate, land and sea, the living world, resources) every one now has a home: the living world as plants and wild animals. Against the planetary boundaries (Rockström and colleagues 2009, Richardson and colleagues 2023), a list made for another purpose, climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change and ocean acidification have homes, but freshwater change and the nitrogen and phosphorus flows have none, and aerosols, ozone and novel entities only through temperature. Those are kept as frontier alternatives for a later pass. Checked against The planetary boundaries framework (Rockström et al. 2009; Richardson et al. 2023), as recalled; and the structure construction's carve of the Earth as setting (structure/history-tree.mjs). {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving What matters to people (concept.humanity.wants):
- What it is: What matters to people: the conditions of a life that people seek for themselves and their children.
- What the carve is for: To follow how far humanity's people secure each of those conditions, so that every change history records in how people live (how long, how well fed, with whom, knowing what, ranked how, free or bound, believing what, with how much leisure, with how many children) has one home; the parent's own measure reads which of them people put first.
- The range it claims: Every human society from 320,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures of the living population.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. What matters to people is a kind of The ends a population lives for: For people the ends are learned and chosen as well as given by the body: meaning, standing, freedom and understanding beside survival and offspring. Other kinds within it: the ends of an animal population: survival and offspring, the ends of an institution: what its charter or its members say it is for.

How the parts make the whole work: The nine parts are the conditions of a life people seek: to live and be well, to have enough, to belong, to understand, to stand well among others, to be free, to find meaning, to play, and to raise children. A society secures each to some degree, and each moves on its own clock. The parent's own measure, the share of people whose first want is survival, reads which condition people put first: while staying alive and having enough are insecure they come first for most people, and as they are secured the other ends move up (Inglehart's account, as recalled), so the parent falls as staying alive and sustenance rise. The development index is kept where it is as a summary view over three of these and output per person, not as a part.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Living with other species and the natural world (necessity, independence).

Merged: Creation into play.
Routed elsewhere: The development index to a view over h.alive, h.understanding and h.provisioning; kept where it is as a summary index, not as a dimension.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Staying alive and well (alive): part.
- What it covers: How long people live and how well their bodies grow and work; followed by life expectancy at birth.
- Necessity pass: Plagues, famines, the doubling of life expectancy after 1900 and the toll of violence need a home.
- Independence pass: Life expectancy doubled in poor countries after 1945 with little change in poverty, freedom or worship.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Sustenance and comfort (sustenance): part.
- What it covers: Having enough food, warmth and shelter, and the toil it costs; followed by the share living in extreme poverty.
- Necessity pass: Hunger, the escape from mass poverty after 1820 and above all after 1980 need a home.
- Independence pass: Poverty fell in East Asia after 1980 while worship, household size and freedom changed little; the coupling with life expectancy through food is a seam.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Belonging (belonging): part.
- What it covers: Living with and being cared for by others, kin above all; followed by household size, with women's age at first marriage beneath it.
- Necessity pass: The European marriage pattern, the shrinking of households and single living after 1950 need a home.
- Independence pass: Households shrank in rich countries after 1950 without a change in poverty or freedom.
- Universality pass: Every society lives in households and kin groups.

Understanding (understanding): part.
- What it covers: Knowing and being able to learn; followed by adult literacy, with years of schooling beneath it.
- Necessity pass: Writing, printing and mass schooling, and the spread of literacy from about 12% of adults in 1820 to 87%, need a home.
- Independence pass: Literacy spread in Protestant Europe and in Japan under flat incomes, and apart from life expectancy.
- Universality pass: Every society knows and teaches; literacy is zero before writing, a value of the measure.

Standing among others (standing): part.
- What it covers: Where people stand relative to each other; followed by income inequality among all people, with hereditary rank beneath it.
- Necessity pass: Estates, castes and classes, the great divergence between countries and its partial reversal need a home.
- Independence pass: Inequality between all people rose from 1820 to 1970 while poverty fell, and fell after 2000 while freedom and worship changed little.
- Universality pass: Every society ranks, if only by prestige; equality is a value of the measure.

Freedom and power (freedom): part.
- What it covers: Being free rather than held, and having a voice; followed by the share held in bondage, with the share living in democracies beneath it.
- Necessity pass: Slavery, serfdom and their abolition, and the spread of the vote, need a home.
- Independence pass: Serfdom ended in Russia in 1861 while rank, poverty and worship stood; voice spread after 1990 without a change in household size.
- Universality pass: Every society: that no one is held is a value of it.

Meaning (meaning): part.
- What it covers: What people hold sacred and live by; followed by the share taking part in regular worship, with the religious traditions people belong to beneath it.
- Necessity pass: The axial-age religions, conversion and secularization need a home.
- Independence pass: Worship fell in Europe after 1960 while life expectancy, freedom and literacy rose; conversions changed traditions without changing poverty.
- Universality pass: Every society, on the positive inference the structure construction recorded for the sacred: rites are found in every living human lineage.

Beauty and play (play): part.
- What it covers: Time and means for leisure, play and the arts; followed by hours of leisure a day, with the share reached by mass media beneath it.
- Necessity pass: The loss of leisure with farming and industry, its return after 1870, and mass entertainment need a home.
- Independence pass: Leisure fell with the industrious revolution while output per person rose, and rose after 1870 apart from worship and freedom.
- Universality pass: Every society plays, sings and tells stories.

Continuation (continuation): part.
- What it covers: Having children and raising them; followed by children per woman.
- Necessity pass: The fertility transition, the baby boom and below-replacement births need a home.
- Independence pass: Births fell after deaths, decades apart (DemographicTransition#6e31), and fell in Iran and Bangladesh at incomes where they stayed high elsewhere.
- Universality pass: Every society.

The development index (ends-index): routed to a view over h.alive, h.understanding and h.provisioning; kept where it is as a summary index, not as a dimension.
- What it covers: A composite of life expectancy, adult literacy and income per person.
- Necessity fail: No change has a home here that lacks one in staying alive, understanding or output per person: it is their geometric mean.
- Independence fail: It is computed from three other measures and cannot change unless they do.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Creation (creation): merged into play.
- What it covers: Making things for their form or meaning: ornament, image, music, story.
- Necessity pass: Art history needs a home.
- Independence fail: Making and taking part in the arts share time and occasions with play; the structure construction carves them as one dimension, arts and play.
- Universality pass: Every society, on the inference recorded for arts and play.

Living with other species and the natural world (other-species): frontier.
- What it covers: Nussbaum's capability of living with concern for animals, plants and nature.
- Necessity uncertain: A real end in many traditions, but no world measure of it can be stated that is not a measure of the Earth's living world itself.
- Independence uncertain: Not settled.
- Universality pass: Every society relates to other species.

Completeness uncertain: Checked against two outside lists made for other purposes. Max-Neef's nine fundamental needs: subsistence (sustenance), protection (staying alive), affection (belonging), understanding, participation (freedom, with voice beneath it), leisure and creation (play), identity (meaning) and freedom all have homes. Nussbaum's ten central capabilities: life, bodily health and bodily integrity (staying alive, with safety beneath it), senses, imagination and thought (understanding and play), emotions and affiliation (belonging and standing), practical reason (meaning), play, and political control (freedom) have homes; control over one's material environment, holding property, has a home only as standing, and concern for other species has none. Continuation is on neither list but is what every population's future rests on. Checked against Martha Nussbaum's central human capabilities (Creating Capabilities, 2011) and Manfred Max-Neef's fundamental human needs (Human Scale Development, 1991), as recalled. Still without a home: property: holding assets on an equal basis, followed only through standing; concern for other species and the natural world.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants","candidates":[{"key":"alive","label":"Staying alive and well","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"sustenance","label":"Sustenance and comfort","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"belonging","label":"Belonging","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"understanding","label":"Understanding","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"standing","label":"Standing among others","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"freedom","label":"Freedom and power","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"meaning","label":"Meaning","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"play","label":"Beauty and play","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"continuation","label":"Continuation","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"ends-index","label":"The development index","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"a view over h.alive, h.understanding and h.provisioning; kept where it is as a summary index, not as a dimension"},{"key":"creation","label":"Creation","outcome":"merged","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","mergedInto":"play"},{"key":"other-species","label":"Living with other species and the natural world","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Martha Nussbaum's central human capabilities (Creating Capabilities, 2011) and Manfred Max-Neef's fundamental human needs (Human Scale Development, 1991), as recalled","missing":["property: holding assets on an equal basis, followed only through standing","concern for other species and the natural world"]}}}

- What it is: How people get what matters to them: what a population does to secure the conditions of its members' lives.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"How people get it is carved into 6 parts: Provisioning, Exchange, Habitat, Connection, Politics, Force.

How the parts make the whole work: A population's means are the joint state of what it produces, how its goods pass, where it settles, how far and fast it reaches, how it decides and rules, and what force it keeps. World output, the parent's own measure, is what production yields once the other means have done their work: trade lets each place make what it makes best, cities and roads let work be divided further, states keep the peace that markets and roads need and take a share, and force defends or takes what the rest produce. Each moves on its own clock; the seams (states keep armies, cities need roads and trade) are recorded on the verdicts rather than merged.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Know-how (independence), Wealth (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Work to provisioning (h.food-work) for the division of work, and sustenance (h.toil) for working time.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Provisioning (provisioning): part.
- What it covers: Producing food, energy and things; followed by output per person.
- Necessity pass: Foraging, farming and industry, and output per person's long flat stretch and modern rise, need a home.
- Independence pass: Output per person rose in the industrial revolution without a matching change in trade's share or in states' reach, and states spread for millennia at flat output.
- Universality pass: Every society produces.

Exchange (exchange): part.
- What it covers: Passing goods between people beyond the household; followed by trade as a share of world output.
- Necessity pass: Long-distance trade, the first and second globalizations and their collapse in 1914 to 1945 need a home.
- Independence pass: Trade's share fell from 1914 to 1945 while output and cities kept growing.
- Universality pass: Every society exchanges, if only by sharing and gift.

Habitat (habitat): part.
- What it covers: Where and how densely people settle and what land they take; followed by the share living in towns and cities.
- Necessity pass: Sedentism, cities and urbanization need a home.
- Independence pass: The urban share stood near 10% for two thousand years while output and states grew.
- Universality pass: Every society settles somewhere, in camps at least.

Connection (connection): part.
- What it covers: Carrying people, goods and word across space; followed by the fastest regular passenger speed, with the share online beneath it.
- Necessity pass: Horses, ships, railways, aircraft, the telegraph and the internet need a home.
- Independence pass: The telegraph and the jet changed connection apart from what was traded and how people were governed.
- Universality pass: Every society moves people, goods and word, on foot and by voice at least.

Politics (politics): part.
- What it covers: Deciding and acting together, and ruling; followed by the share of people living under a state.
- Necessity pass: States, empires and their reach need a home.
- Independence pass: States spread across Africa and the Americas apart from output per person and trade.
- Universality pass: Every society decides together, bands included; living under no state is a value of the measure.

Force (force): part.
- What it covers: The means of organized violence a population keeps: who is kept under arms, how they are organized and with what weapons; followed by how many people are kept under arms.
- Necessity pass: Military history has no home without it: the Warring States' mass armies, the Roman legions, the military revolution, the levée en masse, the conscript armies of 1914 and 1939 and the demobilization after the Cold War. Safety and war hold only what violence costs, not the means kept for it; the carve of humanity's ends and means found it missing.
- Independence pass: Armies grow and shrink apart from who rules and how much is produced: mobilization quadrupled the share under arms in 1914 to 1918 and again in 1939 to 1945 under unchanged regimes, and armies were cut by a third after 1990 while output grew. Coupled to politics, since states keep armies; recorded as a seam.
- Universality pass: Every society meets the possibility of violence from outsiders and has some means to fight; where no one is kept under arms, zero is a value of the measure, as in most bands.

Know-how (know-how): frontier.
- What it covers: The techniques a population commands and its capacity to make new ones.
- Necessity pass: Invention and the growth of useful knowledge drive most of the means.
- Independence fail: A technique is the means by which another part is realized (ploughs in provisioning, ships in connection, guns in force), as the structure construction found when it rejected technology as a dimension; the making of new knowledge is a part of knowledge, not of the means.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Wealth (wealth): frontier.
- What it covers: The assets a population holds and who holds them: land, herds, buildings, capital.
- Necessity pass: Property, enclosure and the accumulation of capital need a home.
- Independence uncertain: Its distribution is followed as standing under what matters to people; its size is not followed at all, and no world measure across the span has been settled.
- Universality pass: Every society holds things.

Work (work): routed to provisioning (h.food-work) for the division of work, and sustenance (h.toil) for working time.
- What it covers: How labour is divided, directed and how much of life it takes.
- Necessity pass: Labour history needs a home.
- Independence fail: Who works at getting food is followed under provisioning (h.food-work) and how long people work under sustenance (h.toil); a part here would hold both twice.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Completeness uncertain: Against Michael Mann's four sources of social power, a list made for another purpose: economic power has homes in provisioning and exchange, political power in politics, and military power, missing until now, in force. Ideological power, the capacity of shared beliefs and their organizations to make people act together, has a home only as an end (meaning), not as a means. Against the structure construction's twelve dimensions, wealth's holdings and the making of knowledge have no home as means; both are kept as frontier alternatives. Checked against Michael Mann's IEMP model of the sources of social power (The Sources of Social Power, 1986), as recalled; the structure construction's twelve dimensions (structure/history-tree.mjs). Still without a home: ideological organization as a means (churches, parties, movements); the size of wealth held; the making of new knowledge.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means","candidates":[{"key":"provisioning","label":"Provisioning","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"exchange","label":"Exchange","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"habitat","label":"Habitat","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"connection","label":"Connection","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"politics","label":"Politics","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"force","label":"Force","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"know-how","label":"Know-how","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"wealth","label":"Wealth","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"},{"key":"work","label":"Work","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"provisioning (h.food-work) for the division of work, and sustenance (h.toil) for working time"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Michael Mann's IEMP model of the sources of social power (The Sources of Social Power, 1986), as recalled; the structure construction's twelve dimensions (structure/history-tree.mjs)","missing":["ideological organization as a means (churches, parties, movements)","the size of wealth held","the making of new knowledge"]}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The people living in the Americas (concept.humanity.americas):
- What it is: The people living in the Americas, divided by where in the Americas they live.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of the Americas' people that rise and fall apart, which one hemispheric share hides: the Indigenous societies of Mesoamerica and the Andes that held most of the hemisphere's people until 1492 and suffered most of its collapse, against Northern America, settled by Europeans and enslaved Africans, which overtook them in the nineteenth century.
- The range it claims: Every date from 320,000 years ago to 2025, with places fixed by the UN M49 standard within 2026 borders: Latin America and the Caribbean (419) and Northern America (021, Canada, the United States, Greenland, Bermuda and Saint Pierre and Miquelon).

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The people living in the Americas is a kind of A human population: The people of the Americas are the human population of one of humanity's five parts by place, isolated from Afro-Eurasia from the flooding of Beringia until 1492. Other kinds within it: the people living in Africa, the people living in Asia, the people living in Europe, the people living in Oceania.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The people living in the Americas is carved into 2 parts: The people living in Latin America and the Caribbean, The people living in Northern America.

How the parts make the whole work: The two shares divide the Americas' people at every date and sum to the hemisphere's share. Latin America and the Caribbean held nine in ten of the hemisphere's people from the first farmers to 1492, so the collapse after contact is mostly its collapse; Northern America, emptied by epidemics and frontier war, was refilled by settlers and enslaved Africans and overtook it about 1870, and Latin America's later and faster growth carried it back ahead about 1955. A migration between them is a departure from one part and an arrival in the other, and splits cleanly.

Routed elsewhere: Northern, Central and South America and the Caribbean as four parts at once to two levels, as the M49 standard nests them: Latin America and the Caribbean here, and its three subregions in its own carve (carve.concept.humanity.americas.latin-america).
Dropped: Anglo America and Iberian America.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The people living in Latin America and the Caribbean (latin-america): part.
- What it covers: Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America (M49 419).
- Necessity pass: Mesoamerica's and the Andes' civilizations, nine in ten of the hemisphere's people before 1492, the collapse after it and the region's fast growth after 1900 need a home.
- Independence pass: Its share collapsed after 1492 while Northern America's held, and rose after 1900 while Northern America's peaked and fell; its fertility fell later and faster.
- Universality pass: The place exists at every date; before people arrive its share is zero.

The people living in Northern America (northern-america): part.
- What it covers: Canada, the United States, Greenland, Bermuda and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (M49 021).
- Necessity pass: The first Americans south of the ice, the Mississippian towns, the Native nations' losses, and the settler growth that made the United States more than half the hemisphere by 1880 need a home.
- Independence pass: Northern America's share rose eightfold from 1800 to 1950 with immigration while Latin America's barely moved, and fell after 1950 while Latin America's rose.
- Universality pass: Zero before people arrive, perhaps 23,000 and certainly 16,000 years ago.

Northern, Central and South America and the Caribbean as four parts at once (four-subregions): routed to two levels, as the M49 standard nests them: Latin America and the Caribbean here, and its three subregions in its own carve (carve.concept.humanity.americas.latin-america).
- What it covers: The four M49 subregions without the intermediate region.
- Necessity pass: Each has histories of its own.
- Independence pass: They change apart.
- Universality pass: Every date.

Anglo America and Iberian America (anglo-iberian): dropped.
- What it covers: A division by colonizing power.
- Necessity uncertain: It names a real divide after 1500, but before 1492 it divides nothing.
- Independence pass: Would change apart.
- Universality fail: A division by colonizers is a kind of history that exists only after 1492 and leaves out the French, Dutch and Indigenous Americas; it is not a division of the land every date shares.

Completeness pass: The M49 standard divides the Americas (019) into Latin America and the Caribbean (419) and Northern America (021); every place in the hemisphere lies in exactly one, so the two shares sum to the Americas' share at every date. Hawai'i, by 2026 borders, counts in Northern America. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The people living in Central America (central): part.
- What it covers: Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama (M49 013): Mesoamerica and the isthmus.
- Necessity pass: Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan and the Aztecs, central Mexico's catastrophe of 1520 to 1600, and modern Mexico's growth need a home.
- Independence pass: Central America's share fell in the Classic Maya collapse while South America's held, and its Indigenous people fell earliest and furthest after 1520, a generation before the Andes'.
- Universality pass: Zero before people arrive, about 15,000 years ago; a value, not an absence.

The people living in the Caribbean (caribbean): part.
- What it covers: The islands of the Caribbean Sea, from Cuba and Hispaniola to Trinidad (M49 029).
- Necessity pass: The Taíno, their near-extinction within forty years of 1492, the sugar islands of enslaved Africans and the Haitian Revolution need a home.
- Independence pass: The Caribbean's share rose fourfold from 1650 to 1800 with the slave trade while Central and South America's barely moved.
- Universality pass: Zero before the first islanders reach Trinidad and then Cuba and Hispaniola, about 7,000 to 6,000 years ago.

The people living in South America (south): part.
- What it covers: The continent from Colombia and Venezuela to Patagonia, with its islands (M49 005).
- Necessity pass: Monte Verde, the Andean civilizations and the Inca, Amazonia's towns, Brazil's sugar and slavery, and the continent's growth to over 5% of humanity need a home.
- Independence pass: South America's share rose after the Classic Maya collapse while Central America's fell, and its Indigenous losses came a generation later and less completely than Mexico's.
- Universality pass: Zero before people arrive, about 15,000 years ago.

Mesoamerica, the Andes and the lowlands (mesoamerica-andes): dropped.
- What it covers: A division by culture area.
- Necessity pass: Culture areas carry most pre-1492 history.
- Independence pass: They change apart.
- Universality fail: Culture areas are kinds of society with shifting edges, defined for some eras; the M49 subregions are fixed parts of the land at every date.

Completeness pass: The M49 standard divides Latin America and the Caribbean (419) into the Caribbean (029), Central America (013) and South America (005); every place lies in exactly one, so the three shares sum to the region's share at every date. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The people living in Europe (concept.humanity.europe):
- What it is: The people living in Europe, divided by where in Europe they live.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of Europe's people that rise and fall apart, which one share hides: the Mediterranean's lead in antiquity, Western Europe's in the Middle Ages, the North Sea's rise with industry and emigration, and the East's growth with Russia's across Siberia and its losses in the twentieth century's famines and wars.
- The range it claims: Every date from 320,000 years ago to 2025, with places fixed by the UN M49 subregions of Europe (150) within 2026 borders: the whole Russian Federation, Siberia included, counts in Eastern Europe; the Baltic states in Northern Europe; the former Yugoslavia in Southern Europe.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The people living in Europe is a kind of A human population: The people of Europe are the human population of one of humanity's five parts by place, the last of the continents Homo sapiens shared with Neanderthals. Other kinds within it: the people living in Africa, the people living in the Americas, the people living in Asia, the people living in Oceania.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The people living in Europe is carved into 4 parts: The people living in Eastern Europe, The people living in Northern Europe, The people living in Southern Europe, The people living in Western Europe.

How the parts make the whole work: The four shares divide Europe's people at every date and sum to Europe's share. Southern Europe led while the Mediterranean was the centre of Europe's farming and empires, about four in ten of Europe's people under Rome; Western Europe led from the Carolingians to about 1750, with France the most populous kingdom; Northern Europe rose with Britain's industry and then sent its people overseas; Eastern Europe, with Russia's frontier reaching the Pacific, became the largest part from the eighteenth century and bore the heaviest losses of the twentieth. A forced migration such as the expulsions after 1945 is a departure from one part and an arrival in another, and splits cleanly.

Dropped: European Russia apart from Siberia.

The people living in Eastern Europe (eastern): part.
- What it covers: Belarus, Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, the Russian Federation, Slovakia and Ukraine (M49 151).
- Necessity pass: The first Homo sapiens in Europe (Bacho Kiro, Kostenki), the Cucuteni-Trypillia towns, the steppe's herders, Russia's expansion to the Pacific and the losses of the Holodomor and the Second World War need a home.
- Independence pass: Eastern Europe's share rose from 1700 to 1914 with Russia's frontier growth while Western Europe's fell, and fell after 1990 while the West's held.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches it, about 46,000 years ago; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Northern Europe (northern): part.
- What it covers: The British Isles, the Nordic countries, Iceland and the Baltic states (M49 154).
- Necessity pass: The ice sheet's retreat, Britain's industrial growth, Ireland's famine and the great emigration need a home.
- Independence pass: Northern Europe was empty at the glacial maximum while the south held people, and its share rose with Britain's industry while Southern Europe's fell.
- Universality pass: Zero under the ice; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Southern Europe (southern): part.
- What it covers: Iberia, Italy, Greece, Malta and the western Balkans (M49 039).
- Necessity pass: The glacial refuges, Europe's first farmers in Greece, the Greek and Roman world, and the Mediterranean's relative decline need a home.
- Independence pass: Southern Europe held almost half of Europe's people under Rome and lost ground to the north and west after it.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens arrives, about 45,000 years ago.

The people living in Western Europe (western): part.
- What it covers: France, Germany, the Low Countries, Switzerland, Austria and the microstates (M49 155).
- Necessity pass: The cave art of the Dordogne, Gaul and the Frankish heartland, France as Europe's most populous kingdom, the Thirty Years War's losses and Germany's industrial growth need a home.
- Independence pass: Western Europe lost perhaps a third of Germany's people in 1618 to 1648 while the east and north grew, and France's early fertility decline slowed it after 1800 apart from the others.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens arrives; a brief presence at Grotte Mandrin about 54,000 years ago is debated.

European Russia apart from Siberia (european-russia): dropped.
- What it covers: A division at the Urals.
- Necessity uncertain: The Urals line matters to some histories.
- Independence pass: Would change apart.
- Universality pass: Every date.

1. The people living in Africa is a kind of A human population: The people of Africa are the human population of the continent where Homo sapiens arose and lived alone for some two hundred thousand years. Other kinds within it: the people living in the Americas, the people living in Asia, the people living in Europe, the people living in Oceania.

The people living in Northern Africa (northern): part.
- What it covers: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Sudan, Tunisia and Western Sahara (M49 015).
- Necessity pass: Jebel Irhoud, the green Sahara, Egypt and Kush, Carthage and Roman Africa, the Black Death's toll in Egypt and the region's twentieth-century growth need a home.
- Independence pass: Northern Africa held perhaps two fifths of Africa's people in antiquity and lost its lead after the Black Death, while the lands south of the Sahara grew; the Atlantic slave trade struck the south, not the north.
- Universality pass: People live there at every date of the range; its share swings with the Sahara's wet and dry phases.

The people living in Sub-Saharan Africa (sub-saharan): part.
- What it covers: Africa south of Northern Africa (M49 202), divided into Eastern, Middle, Southern and Western Africa.
- Necessity pass: Most of humanity for most of its first two hundred thousand years, the Bantu expansion, the slave trades, conquest and colonial rule, and the fastest growth of the late twentieth century need a home.
- Independence pass: Its share fell from 1750 to 1900 with the slave trades and conquest while Northern Africa's held, and it has risen fastest of any region since 1950.
- Universality pass: People live there at every date.

Northern, Eastern, Middle, Southern and Western Africa as five parts at once (five-at-once): routed to two levels, as the M49 standard nests them: Sub-Saharan Africa here, and its four intermediate regions in its own carve (carve.concept.humanity.africa.sub-saharan).
- What it covers: The five regions without the intermediate grouping.
- Necessity pass: Each has histories of its own.
- Independence pass: They change apart.
- Universality pass: Every date.

Africa by language family (language-families): dropped.
- What it covers: Afroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Nilo-Saharan and Khoisan speakers.
- Necessity uncertain: Language families carry the expansions of farmers and herders.
- Independence pass: They change apart.
- Universality fail: Language families are kinds whose speakers move and whose dates of origin lie inside the range; they are not fixed parts of the land, and they would divide the same people along a second criterion (MECE#ae19).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The people living in Australia and New Zealand (australia-nz): part.
- What it covers: Australia, New Zealand and Norfolk Island (M49 053).
- Necessity pass: Aboriginal Australia over fifty thousand years, MƒÅori Aotearoa from about 1280, the frontier wars and smallpox, and settler growth from a few thousand in 1788 to 33 million need a home.
- Independence pass: Its share rose from a quarter to seven tenths of Oceania's people between 1850 and 1950 with settlers and gold, while the islands' numbers fell.
- Universality pass: Zero before people reach Sahul, about 50,000 or 65,000 years ago; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Melanesia (melanesia): part.
- What it covers: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji (M49 054).
- Necessity pass: New Guinea's independent invention of farming at Kuk, the highland valleys' dense populations found only in 1933, Lapita and Fiji need a home.
- Independence pass: Melanesia held most of Oceania's people from farming's start until the 1860s, and its share fell while Australia's rose; since 1950 it has grown faster than Australia and New Zealand.
- Universality pass: Zero before people reach Sahul; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Micronesia (micronesia): part.
- What it covers: The Marianas, the Carolines, Palau, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Nauru (M49 057).
- Necessity pass: The crossing to the Marianas about 1500 BCE, Nan Madol, the Spanish Chamorro wars and the Pacific war need a home.
- Independence pass: Micronesia's numbers fell with the Chamorro wars and epidemics of the 1670s to 1690s while Melanesia's did not.
- Universality pass: Zero before the first voyagers, about 3,500 years ago.

- What it covers: Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, French Polynesia, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Wallis and Futuna, American Samoa and Pitcairn (M49 061).

- What it covers: Australia, New Zealand and Norfolk Island (M49 053).

- Universality pass: Zero before people reach Sahul, about 50,000 or 65,000 years ago; a value, not an absence.

The people living in Melanesia (melanesia): part.
- What it covers: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji (M49 054).
- Necessity pass: New Guinea's independent invention of farming at Kuk, the highland valleys' dense populations found only in 1933, Lapita and Fiji need a home.
- Independence pass: Melanesia held most of Oceania's people from farming's start until the 1860s, and its share fell while Australia's rose; since 1950 it has grown faster than Australia and New Zealand.
- Universality pass: Zero before people reach Sahul; a value, not an absence.

- Independence pass: Micronesia's numbers fell with the Chamorro wars and epidemics of the 1670s to 1690s while Melanesia's did not.
- Universality pass: Zero before the first voyagers, about 3,500 years ago.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Staying alive and well is carved into 3 parts: Surviving childhood, Surviving adulthood, The body's growth and condition.

How the parts make the whole work: Life expectancy at birth, the parent's own measure, is made of the survival of children and the survival of those who reach adulthood: for most of history about half of everyone born died before fifteen, so the low averages hide adults who often lived into their fifties and sixties. The body's growth reflects the food and illness of childhood that both survival measures respond to. A plague that kills children and adults alike has a part in each, split by the ages of the dead.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Mental health (declared).

Routed elsewhere: Safety from violence to the carve of what ends people's lives (carve.concept.causes-of-death), as one cause beside infection, birth, hunger, chronic disease and injury.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Surviving childhood (childhood): part.
- What it covers: How many children die before their fifth birthday; followed by child mortality.
- Necessity pass: Most of the twentieth century's gain in life expectancy at birth, and most deaths in every society before it, are children's.
- Independence pass: Child mortality fell from 1950 to 2025 by four fifths while adult survival rose by a third; the 1918 influenza and AIDS struck adults and spared children by comparison.
- Universality pass: Every society loses children.

Surviving adulthood (adulthood): part.
- What it covers: How long those who reach fifteen go on to live; followed by life expectancy at age fifteen.
- Necessity pass: Plagues that kill adults, war, the 1918 influenza, AIDS and the late gains of old age have no home in child mortality, and life expectancy at birth mixes them with children's deaths so that a fall in child deaths reads like longer adult lives.
- Independence pass: Adult survival barely moved from the agrarian empires to 1900 while child mortality fell a little, and rose fastest after 1950 for different reasons (antibiotics, then the decline of heart disease); it fell in 1918 and in southern Africa's AIDS years while child mortality kept falling.
- Universality pass: Every society has adults who die at some age.

The body's growth and condition (growth): part.
- What it covers: How well bodies grow and stay well, reflecting food and disease in childhood; followed by adult male height.
- Necessity pass: Farming's shrinking of bodies, the early industrial height puzzle and the modern rise in stature have no home in survival.
- Independence pass: Height fell in early industrial Britain and the United States while life expectancy held or rose, and rose in the twentieth century faster in some places than survival.
- Universality pass: Every body grows to some height.

Safety from violence (violence): routed to the carve of what ends people's lives (carve.concept.causes-of-death), as one cause beside infection, birth, hunger, chronic disease and injury.
- What it covers: Deaths from homicide and war.
- Necessity pass: Needed, but as a cause of death, not an age or a condition.
- Independence fail: Violent deaths are part of adult and child mortality; in this carve by age they would be counted twice.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Mental health (mind): frontier.
- What it covers: Depression, anxiety, psychosis and their toll.
- Necessity pass: Part of being well.
- Independence pass: Changes apart from survival.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Completeness uncertain: Against the WHO's summary measures of population health, a list made for another purpose: mortality has homes by age (childhood, adulthood) and, in the other carve, by cause; the body's growth is followed by stature; but the years lived in ill health and disability (the disability-adjusted measures) have no world series here, and mental health is kept as a frontier alternative. Checked against The World Health Organization's summary measures of population health (life expectancy, healthy life expectancy, disability-adjusted life years), as recalled. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"What ends people's lives is carved into 6 parts: Infection, Birth, Hunger, Violence, Injury, Chronic disease.

How the parts make the whole work: The six rates sum to the crude death rate, and with the ages at which people die they give life expectancy. For three hundred thousand years about two thirds of deaths were infections, with births, hunger, accidents and violence taking most of the rest and chronic disease little, because few lived long enough; farming and cities raised the infections' share with crowd diseases (the first epidemiological transition), and plague years doubled the death rate. After 1850 infection, birth and hunger deaths fell by nine tenths while chronic disease deaths stayed nearly level per head, so they became three quarters of all deaths: the epidemiological transition, which drives the rise in life expectancy in the parent.

Dropped: Ill-defined causes.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Infection (infection): part.
- What it covers: Infectious and parasitic disease: plague, smallpox, cholera, typhus, tuberculosis, malaria, measles, pneumonia, diarrhoea, HIV and COVID-19, by underlying cause, apart from the infections of mothers and newborns and the excess deaths of famines.
- Necessity pass: The plagues, the virgin-soil epidemics, the crowd diseases of farming and cities and their retreat with sanitation, vaccines and antibiotics are most of mortality's history.
- Independence pass: Infection deaths fell by nine tenths after 1900 while chronic disease deaths rose; plagues spike them while violence and hunger stand.
- Universality pass: Every society dies of infections.

Birth (birth): part.
- What it covers: Deaths of mothers from pregnancy and childbirth, and of newborns in their first four weeks.
- Necessity pass: Childbed fever, obstetric care, midwifery and neonatal survival have a history of their own.
- Independence pass: Maternal deaths fell with antisepsis and obstetrics apart from infection elsewhere, and neonatal deaths fell more slowly than the deaths of older children.
- Universality pass: Every society bears children.

Hunger (hunger): part.
- What it covers: Deaths whose cause is lack of food: starvation, the excess deaths of famines whatever their proximate disease, and nutritional deficiency.
- Necessity pass: The great famines (Ireland, India 1876 to 1902, China 1876 to 1879 and 1959 to 1961, the Soviet famines, Bengal) and their near-disappearance after 1980 need a home.
- Independence pass: Famines come and go with harvests, wars and policy apart from the infection and chronic disease that kill in ordinary years.
- Universality pass: Every society can go hungry.

Violence (violence): part.
- What it covers: Homicide and war: deaths at the hands of others.
- Necessity pass: Homicide, feud and war.
- Independence pass: War deaths spike in 1618 to 1648, 1850 to 1864 and 1914 to 1945 apart from the other causes.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Injury (injury): part.
- What it covers: Accidents and self-harm: falls, drowning, burns, animals, work, transport and suicide.
- Necessity pass: Hunting accidents, mines and factories, road deaths and suicide need a home.
- Independence pass: Road deaths rose with motor vehicles while infection fell; suicide follows its own course.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Chronic disease (chronic): part.
- What it covers: Heart disease, stroke, cancers, chronic lung and kidney disease, diabetes, dementia and the frailty of old age.
- Necessity pass: The diseases that kill three quarters of people now, and tobacco's twentieth-century toll, need a home.
- Independence pass: Chronic deaths rose as people lived long enough to die of them while infection fell, and fell with less smoking and better blood pressure after 1970.
- Universality pass: Every society has old people who die.

Ill-defined causes (unknown): dropped.
- What it covers: Deaths whose cause was never known or recorded.
- Necessity fail: Not a cause but a gap in the record; each such death had one of the causes above.
- Independence pass: Changes with record-keeping.
- Universality pass: Every society.
