upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Findings of the tree pass so far, at model r125 (b75dd90e). Every value is recalled, tagged sketch or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. The regions beneath the M49 areas (24 processes, all summing to their parents at every date given). What the one-number shares hid:
- Eastern Asia's share peaks at 39% of humanity in 1820 under the Qing and falls to 20% now; Southern Asia's overtakes it about 2001, two decades before India passes China, because Eastern Asia's births fell first.
- South-eastern Asia's share falls for eight thousand years, from Sundaland's foragers to 2% of humanity in 1 CE (farming came late), and then quadruples after 1850 with Java's and the deltas' growth.
- Western Asia's share falls from perhaps a sixth of humanity about 2200 BCE to 1.6% in 1920, through Iraq's decay, the Mongols, the Black Death and Timur, and has doubled since.
- Northern America overtakes Latin America and the Caribbean about 1875 and Latin America overtakes it again about 1955. The Caribbean empties within forty years of 1492 and refills with enslaved Africans after 1650. Central America's collapse runs a generation ahead of the Andes'.
- Western Europe is Europe's largest part from the high Middle Ages to about 1750; Eastern Europe, with Russia's frontier, from then on, peaking at more than a tenth of humanity in 1910.
- Western and Middle Africa stand still from about 1700 to 1850 (the Atlantic slave trade, on Manning's estimates) while Eastern Africa becomes the largest part; Middle Africa falls to less than half of its 1750 share by 1950 (the slave trade, then the Congo Free State).
- Oceania: Melanesia holds most of the region's people from farming until about 1868, when Australia and New Zealand pass it. The children's sums expose a tension in the parent: Oceania's 0.2% for 1500 to 1800 (about 0.9 to 2 million) is below the sum of the usual pre-contact estimates (about 2.5 to 3 million). The parent stands as it is; Oceania's own pass should look at it.

2. The Earth. Wild land mammals fall from about 22 Mt C before the megafauna extinctions to about 13 after them and 3 now, against about 60 for humans and 100 for livestock (Bar-On and colleagues): the end-Pleistocene losses and the twentieth century's are of the same size. Minerals and fuels taken per person rise from a few kilograms for foragers to 0.3 tonnes in Rome and 1 in 1900, and to 10 now; the step from 2000 to 2014 is China's building boom.

3. Force (people under arms per 1,000) has two humps that the toll of war alone does not show: the Warring States' and Rome's mass armies, then the world wars (22 per 1,000 in 1916, 30 in 1944), and a halving since 1990.

4. Staying alive. Dividing deaths by cause shows the epidemiological transition: infection about two thirds of deaths for three hundred thousand years, rising with farming's crowd diseases, doubling the death rate in plague years, and falling by nine tenths after 1900; chronic disease passes infection about 1967. Opening adult survival exposes a contradiction in the existing values: the model's forager life expectancy (30) with child mortality of 45% implies that adults of fifteen live another 45 years, against 37 to 43 in the ethnographic comparisons (Gurven and Kaplan, as recalled), whose foragers lose a quarter to a third of children before five. The likely error is the forager child mortality; it is left as it stands in this pass, which keeps the existing measures, and named here for the next.

5. Method. Three of the carves first recorded a part as a kind in their climb (Asia under humanity, the Earth under History, staying alive under what matters to people): SpecializationEdge#4d20's 'part filed as kind'. Each was corrected in the next model revision by relabelling the relation as a part relation, which the notes stay anchored to, and adding the right genus (a human population, the setting of a lifecycle, a condition of a life). A climb names what a thing is a kind of, never what it is a part of. And the graph was not rebound after the value revisions r101, r102, r106, r109, r112, r114, r117, r120, r124 and r125 at the time they were made; each carve that followed rebound it across them, and from r125 every revision is rebound as it is made."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Meaning (concept.humanity.wants.meaning):
- What it is: Meaning: a population's holding, together, an account of what the world is and what a life is for, and living by it. The first pass measured it by one sign, the share taking part in regular worship, and filed eight religious traditions beneath it without recording why those are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of meaning that change apart, which the worship share alone hides: which tradition people belong to (and the spread of the faiths open to every people, the largest religious change in the record), what they believe the world's powers to be (above all whether gods or a cosmic law judge conduct, the change of the first millennium BCE), and how far they practise it (which fell by half since 1750 while affiliation fell far less).
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, foragers with local spirits and trance as much as the people of world faiths and the unaffiliated of today; measured for all living people.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Meaning is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Meaning is the condition of holding with others an account of what the world is and what a life is for, and of living by it; the other conditions are of the body (staying alive), of material comfort, of company, of offspring, of knowledge, of rank, of power over one's own life, and of beauty and play. Other kinds within it: Staying alive and well, Sustenance and comfort, Belonging, Continuation, Understanding, Standing among others, Freedom and power, Beauty and play.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Meaning is carved into 2 parts: Tradition, Belief.

How the parts make the whole work: Meaning as this account follows it is held in a tradition, believed, and practised. Tradition is the community that hands meaning on; its kinds are the eight existing shares, and its own measure reads the axis along which it changed most: from traditions bound to one people to faiths open to every people, none in 500 BCE, about a third of humanity by 1500 and three fifths now, spread by missions, conquest and conversion across lines of descent (Sideinherit#45d5) and lately by births. Belief is what people hold the world's powers to be, read by whether gods or a cosmic law judge conduct: few foragers, a minority in the first states, a majority after the first-millennium-BCE teachings of karma, Heaven's mandate and one judging god, falling again where unbelief is taught or chosen. Practice, the taking part in rites, is the parent's own measure. The three change apart: conversion moved tradition for two thousand years while practice held near 80%; since 1750 practice fell by half while affiliation fell far less; belief rose before most of the conversions and falls where affiliation stays. Moral rules and sacred buildings are routed to where they act; the experience of the sacred and religious institutions stay frontier. The eight shares stay filed under h.meaning as kinds of tradition; filing them under h.meaning.tradition is left for the pass that decides re-hanging.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Local and folk traditions (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Hindu (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Buddhist (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Chinese traditions (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Christian (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Muslim (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), Jewish and other (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition), No religion (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.tradition).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Experience of the sacred (necessity), Religious specialists and institutions (necessity, independence).

Merged: Secular meaning into tradition.
Routed elsewhere: Practice to h.meaning's own measure, the share taking part in regular worship, which already reads practice; a part with the same measure would count it twice, Moral rules to Where the rules rule: hereditary rank (h.rank), bondage (h.freedom), marriage (h.marriage), homicide (h.homicide); whether conduct is held to be judged is read in belief, Sacred buildings and objects to Beauty and play (h.play) for what they make, the built habitat for where they stand, practice for their use.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Tradition (tradition): part.
- What it covers: Which tradition of belief and rite people belong to, by birth or conversion: the community that hands meaning on. Its main axis in history is whether the tradition is bound to one people or open to converts from every people.
- Necessity pass: Without a tradition there is no shared content for meaning to hold: no myths, rites or teachings handed on. The largest religious change in the record, the spread of Buddhism, Christianity and Islam from nothing in 500 BCE to about a third of humanity by 1500 and three fifths now, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Affiliation changes by conversion and by differing birth rates without forcing belief or practice to change: Western Europe after 1960 kept most of its Christian affiliation while worship halved; the Muslim share grows from 14% in 1950 to about 24% now mainly by births, not by any change in what Muslims believe or practise.
- Universality pass: Every population belongs to some tradition, even if a local one or, since the nineteenth century, none; the measure's zero holds for every population before 500 BCE.

Local and folk traditions (local): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: Traditions bound to one people or place: the spirits, ancestors and rites of foragers, farmers and herders outside the scriptural faiths.
- Necessity pass: All of humanity's meaning before 1200 BCE, and a fifth of it in 1600.
- Independence pass: Shrinks by conversion and by the deaths of its peoples (the Americas after 1492) apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: One answer to which tradition, not a part every population contains: the people of Iceland or Egypt in 1500 hold none of it.

Hindu (hindu): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: The Brahmanical and Hindu traditions of South Asia and their diaspora.
- Necessity pass: About a sixth of humanity since the Mauryas.
- Independence pass: Moves with South Asia's share of people more than by conversion.
- Universality fail: Exists only from the Vedic period, and only in some populations.

Buddhist (buddhist): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: The traditions descended from the Buddha's teaching.
- Necessity pass: The first faith open to every people, at its height about an eighth of humanity.
- Independence pass: Spreads across Asia and contracts in India apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: Exists only from about 500 BCE.

Chinese traditions (chinese): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: Chinese folk religion, ancestor rites and the Confucian and Daoist traditions, counted together.
- Necessity pass: About a fifth of humanity for two thousand years.
- Independence pass: Falls by a half in the twentieth century under state atheism apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: Exists only in some populations, from the Shang.

Christian (christian): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: All Christian churches.
- Necessity pass: The largest tradition since about 1500.
- Independence pass: Grows by conversion in the Americas, Africa and Oceania apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: Exists only from about 30 CE.

Muslim (muslim): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: All Muslim communities.
- Necessity pass: A tenth of humanity by 1500 and a quarter now.
- Independence pass: Grows by conquest and conversion, later by births, apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: Exists only from 610.

Jewish and other (jewish-other): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: Judaism, Zoroastrianism, Jainism, Sikhism, Manichaeism and smaller scriptural traditions, counted together.
- Necessity pass: Holds the traditions whose ideas shaped the larger ones, and the Holocaust's victims.
- Independence pass: Moves apart from the others.
- Universality fail: Exists only from the first millennium BCE.

No religion (none): a kind of tradition.
- What it covers: People who belong to no tradition, including those whose meaning rests on a secular philosophy or ideology.
- Necessity pass: A tenth or more of humanity since 1950.
- Independence pass: Rises with state atheism and secularization apart from the other kinds.
- Universality fail: Near zero before the nineteenth century.

Belief (belief): part.
- What it covers: What people hold the world's powers and order to be: spirits, ancestors, gods, a cosmic law, or none. Its main axis in history is whether those powers watch and judge human conduct.
- Necessity pass: The change from local spirits indifferent to most conduct to gods and laws that judge it, which the Axial Age and Big Gods debates are about, has no home in affiliation or practice alone.
- Independence pass: It changes apart from affiliation: Hindu, Jewish and Zoroastrian belief judges conduct without seeking converts, and unbelief within a tradition (Europe, East Asia) lowers belief while affiliation stays. Coupling with tradition is real but low.
- Universality pass: Every population holds some account of the world's powers; the measure's low values hold for foragers whose spirits do not judge conduct.

Practice (practice): routed to h.meaning's own measure, the share taking part in regular worship, which already reads practice; a part with the same measure would count it twice.
- What it covers: Taking part together in rites: worship, prayer, sacrifice, festivals and rites of passage.
- Necessity pass: The fall of practice since 1750, from 80% to 39%, while affiliation fell far less, is the clearest secular change in the record.
- Independence pass: Practice falls in Western Europe after 1960 while affiliation and much belief stay.
- Universality pass: Every population has rites.

Moral rules (ethics): routed to Where the rules rule: hereditary rank (h.rank), bondage (h.freedom), marriage (h.marriage), homicide (h.homicide); whether conduct is held to be judged is read in belief.
- What it covers: The rules of conduct a tradition teaches: on killing, sex, marriage, property, rank and care of the poor.
- Necessity pass: Traditions bind conduct.
- Independence uncertain: A rule is read only in what it changes, and those changes already have homes.
- Universality pass: Every tradition has rules.

Experience of the sacred (experience): frontier.
- What it covers: Personal experience of the sacred: trance, possession, visions, mystical states, prayer felt as answered.
- Necessity uncertain: Central for foragers' trance and for mystics, but no world measure can be read across the span; surveys of religious experience begin in the twentieth century.
- Independence pass: Pentecostal and charismatic growth since 1970 raised it without changing affiliation.
- Universality pass: Every population has some.

Religious specialists and institutions (specialists): frontier.
- What it covers: People set apart to mediate the sacred and the bodies that keep them: shamans, priests, monks, clergy, temples, churches, the sangha and the ulama, and their land and revenue.
- Necessity uncertain: Meaning works with part-time shamans alone; the full-time clergy and temple economies that held a third of medieval Europe's land, Tibet's monasteries or the waqf are kinds tied to surplus. Worth opening if a series of full-time religious specialists per 1,000 people can be read.
- Independence uncertain: Full-time specialists move with surplus and state revenue (h.revenue).
- Universality pass: Every population has someone who mediates the sacred, if only part-time.

Sacred buildings and objects (material): routed to Beauty and play (h.play) for what they make, the built habitat for where they stand, practice for their use.
- What it covers: Temples, shrines, images and the art made for worship.
- Necessity fail: Meaning works without buildings; they serve practice.
- Independence fail: They change with practice and wealth.
- Universality fail: Mobile foragers build none.

Secular meaning (secular): merged into tradition.
- What it covers: Philosophies and ideologies that give a life its meaning without a tradition of the sacred: humanism, nationalism, communism.
- Necessity pass: Many of the unaffiliated hold one.
- Independence fail: It is one answer to which tradition, counted with No religion; whether ideologies are functional equivalents of religion is a debate (Durkheim's and Gentile's political religions against those who keep the categories apart) this carve does not settle.
- Universality fail: Only in some populations, and mainly since the eighteenth century.

Completeness uncertain: Ritual is practice (read by the parent's measure); narrative and doctrine are belief; the community Durkheim names is tradition; ethics and material are routed to where they act. Two of Smart's seven have no measured home, so completeness is uncertain, not failed. Checked against Ninian Smart's seven dimensions of religion (ritual, narrative and mythic, experiential and emotional, social and institutional, ethical and legal, doctrinal and philosophical, material) and Durkheim's definition of religion (beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, uniting their adherents into one moral community).. Still without a home: Experiential: the experience of the sacred has no world measure (frontier); Institutional: full-time religious specialists and religious institutions (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.meaning","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.meaning","candidates":[{"key":"tradition","label":"Tradition","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"local","label":"Local and folk traditions","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"hindu","label":"Hindu","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"buddhist","label":"Buddhist","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"chinese","label":"Chinese traditions","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"christian","label":"Christian","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"muslim","label":"Muslim","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"jewish-other","label":"Jewish and other","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"none","label":"No religion","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"tradition"},{"key":"belief","label":"Belief","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"practice","label":"Practice","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.meaning's own measure, the share taking part in regular worship, which already reads practice; a part with the same measure would count it twice"},{"key":"ethics","label":"Moral rules","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Where the rules rule: hereditary rank (h.rank), bondage (h.freedom), marriage (h.marriage), homicide (h.homicide); whether conduct is held to be judged is read in belief"},{"key":"experience","label":"Experience of the sacred","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"specialists","label":"Religious specialists and institutions","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"},{"key":"material","label":"Sacred buildings and objects","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Beauty and play (h.play) for what they make, the built habitat for where they stand, practice for their use"},{"key":"secular","label":"Secular meaning","outcome":"merged","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","mergedInto":"tradition"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Ninian Smart's seven dimensions of religion (ritual, narrative and mythic, experiential and emotional, social and institutional, ethical and legal, doctrinal and philosophical, material) and Durkheim's definition of religion (beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, uniting their adherents into one moral community).","missing":["Experiential: the experience of the sacred has no world measure (frontier)","Institutional: full-time religious specialists and religious institutions (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Sustenance and comfort (concept.humanity.wants.sustenance):
- What it is: Sustenance and comfort: having enough to eat, to keep warm, lit and dry, to be housed, at a cost in work a person can bear. The first pass measured it by the share in extreme poverty and filed food, energy and toil beneath it without recording why those are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of material sufficiency that change apart, which the poverty share mixes into one money line: food per person (flat near 2,000 kcal until 1800, then up by half), energy for warmth, light and work (up sixteenfold), room to live in, and the hours of work they cost (up in the first farming and again in the industrious revolution, down after 1870).
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, foragers as much as farmers and city dwellers; measured for all living people or all workers.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Sustenance and comfort is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Sustenance is the material condition: enough food, warmth, room and goods for the body's daily needs and comfort, at a bearable cost in work; staying alive is the outcome in years and deaths, and the others are of company, knowledge, rank, power, meaning and play. Other kinds within it: Staying alive and well, Belonging, Continuation, Understanding, Standing among others, Freedom and power, Meaning, Beauty and play.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Sustenance and comfort is carved into 4 parts: Food, Energy for warmth, light and work, Shelter, Toil.

How the parts make the whole work: Sustenance as this account follows it is food, warmth and shelter, bought with toil. Food is energy into the body and stayed near 2,000 kcal a person from the first farmers to 1800, the Malthusian ceiling (MalthusianTrap#0f6b), before rising by half. Warmth is energy around the body, fire, fuel, light and power, and rose sixteenfold, mostly after 1820. Shelter is the room a person lives in, read by dwelling floor per person, opened here: small for foragers, larger for farmers, crowded in the first industrial cities and rising fast since 1950. Toil is what the three cost: more hours with farming (DensityRatchet#2ace) and in the industrious revolution, fewer after 1870. They change apart, so the poverty share, a money line across all of them, hides which improved when. Clothing and household goods stay frontier; water and the security of subsistence are routed to staying alive.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Clothing (necessity, universality), Household goods (necessity).

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Food (food): part.
- What it covers: The food energy available to eat, per person per day.
- Necessity pass: Without food there is no life; its level per person is the first test of the Malthusian account (MalthusianTrap#0f6b), flat until about 1800 and up by half since.
- Independence pass: Food per person rose with the Green Revolution after 1965 while hours worked fell and housing barely changed; it held flat through the energy rise of 1820 to 1900.
- Universality pass: Every population eats.

Energy for warmth, light and work (warmth): part.
- What it covers: The energy a population uses per person beyond the body's own: fire for warmth and cooking, light, animals' and machines' work, with food counted in.
- Necessity pass: Warmth, cooked food and light are what fire and fuel give; without them the shift from 5 to 80 GJ a person, the largest material change in the record, has no home here.
- Independence pass: Energy per person rose 1820 to 1900 while food per person barely moved. The existing measure counts food energy in (3 to 4 GJ a year), which couples it to food mostly before industry; a later pass could subtract it. Whether energy belongs to comfort or to the means (Morris's energy capture, Smil's prime movers) is debated; it is kept here as the first pass filed it.
- Universality pass: Every population has used fire since well before 300,000 years ago, with the earliest dates for its control still debated.

Shelter (shelter): part.
- What it covers: The room people have to live in under a roof: dwellings and the floor space they give each person.
- Necessity pass: Crowding and housing are what poverty is lived in; the industrial slums of the nineteenth century and the housing booms of the twentieth have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Room per person fell in industrial cities in the nineteenth century while food and energy rose; it rose fivefold in Chinese cities after 1978 apart from food.
- Universality pass: Every population shelters, if only in brush huts, windbreaks or caves.

Toil (toil): part.
- What it covers: What sustenance costs in work: the hours a worker works in a year.
- Necessity pass: Comfort bought with exhausting work is not the same comfort; the forager leisure debate (Sahlins's original affluent society against its critics), farming's longer days (DensityRatchet#2ace) and the industrious revolution have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Hours rose 1650 to 1850 while food per person barely changed, and fell 1870 to 1980 while food and energy rose. It mirrors leisure (h.play under Beauty and play), which is filed apart.
- Universality pass: Every population works.

Clothing (clothing): frontier.
- What it covers: What people wear: skins, woven cloth, garments.
- Necessity uncertain: Cheap cotton cloth is central to the industrial revolution, but clothing's comfort is mostly warmth, and a world series of textile fibre per person exists only from about 1900; worth opening if it can be read further back.
- Independence pass: Cloth per person rose with the cotton revolution apart from food.
- Universality uncertain: Some tropical foragers wore little; body lice genetics place clothing perhaps 170,000 years ago, inside the range.

Household goods (goods): frontier.
- What it covers: The things a household owns and uses: pots, tools, furniture, linen, and later clocks, radios, phones.
- Necessity uncertain: The consumer revolution and the industrious revolution are about them, but no world measure reads them across the span; probate inventories and household surveys cover some places and times.
- Independence pass: Goods per household rose in eighteenth-century England and the Dutch Republic apart from food.
- Universality pass: Every household owns something.

Water and sanitation (water): routed to Staying alive (h.alive.infection) for its effect on health, and the built habitat for piped water and sewers, which only towns had before 1900.
- What it covers: Clean water to drink and wash, and the removal of waste.
- Necessity pass: Carrying water is daily toil and dirty water kills.
- Independence uncertain: Its history is read in infection deaths and in city building.
- Universality pass: Every population needs water.

Security of subsistence (secure): routed to Hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger), which read the famines that break subsistence.
- What it covers: How reliably food and warmth come: the risk of dearth and famine.
- Necessity pass: Famine is the failure of sustenance.
- Independence fail: It is read in the deaths it causes.
- Universality pass: Every population faces dearth.

Completeness uncertain: Food, shelter and fuel and electricity (warmth) have homes; water and sanitation are routed to staying alive and the habitat; transport, health and education have homes under connection, staying alive and understanding. Clothing and household goods have none measured, so completeness is uncertain. Checked against The ILO's basic needs list (1976: food, shelter, clothing, household equipment, and essential services of water, sanitation, transport, health and education) and the living-standard indicators of the Multidimensional Poverty Index (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets).. Still without a home: Clothing (frontier); Household goods and assets (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.sustenance","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.sustenance","candidates":[{"key":"food","label":"Food","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"warmth","label":"Energy for warmth, light and work","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"shelter","label":"Shelter","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"toil","label":"Toil","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"clothing","label":"Clothing","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"goods","label":"Household goods","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"water","label":"Water and sanitation","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Staying alive (h.alive.infection) for its effect on health, and the built habitat for piped water and sewers, which only towns had before 1900"},{"key":"secure","label":"Security of subsistence","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger), which read the famines that break subsistence"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The ILO's basic needs list (1976: food, shelter, clothing, household equipment, and essential services of water, sanitation, transport, health and education) and the living-standard indicators of the Multidimensional Poverty Index (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets).","missing":["Clothing (frontier)","Household goods and assets (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Habitat (concept.humanity.means.habitat):
- What it is: Habitat as a means: the places a population makes to live in and the land it turns to its use, from camps to megacities and from hunting grounds to fields and pastures. The first pass measured it by the share living in towns and cities and filed the largest city and farmland beneath it without recording why those are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of how people occupy the Earth that change apart, which the urban share hides: whether people have fixed homes at all (settling down came five thousand years before towns, and the steppe nomads stayed mobile beside empires), whether they live in towns, how large the greatest cities grow, and how much land they turn into fields and pasture.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, mobile foragers and herders as much as villagers and city dwellers; measured for all living people or all ice-free land.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Habitat is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Habitat is the means made of place: the settlements people build and the land they turn to their use. The other means are getting and making things, moving people, goods and words, trading, ruling, and fighting. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Connection, Exchange, Politics, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Habitat is carved into 3 parts: Settling down, The greatest settlement, Farmland.

How the parts make the whole work: Habitat as this account follows it is how a population occupies the Earth: whether it has fixed homes (settling down), whether those homes are in towns (the parent's own measure), how large its greatest settlement grows, and how much land it turns into fields and pasture. The four change apart and in order: people settled long before towns (the Natufians, then the first farmers), towns long before most people lived in them, the largest city reached a million under Rome and again under the Tang and the Song while the urban share stayed near 5%, and farmland spread fastest on nineteenth-century frontiers that had few towns. Mobile peoples, from foragers to the steppe nomads who conquered settled empires, shrink from all of humanity to under 1%, mostly before 1000 BCE and again when states forced herders to settle. Built land and works stay frontier until an independent reading exists; roads go to connection and housing to shelter.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Built land and works (necessity, universality).

Routed elsewhere: Living in towns to h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already, Roads, canals and ports to Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move, Housing to Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has.

Routing sample: 11 case(s); 3 with no home among the parts (China's urban share rising from under a fifth in 1978 to about two thirds by 2023; Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris with boulevards, sewers and water mains, 1853 to 1870; {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Settling down (mobile): part.
- What it covers: Whether people have a fixed home: mobile foragers and pastoral nomads move with the seasons; farmers, townspeople and sedentary foragers stay.
- Necessity pass: Settling down is the first and largest change in habitat, beginning with the Natufians about 12,500 BCE, five thousand years before towns; and the mounted nomads of the steppe, Arabia and the Sahara, who stayed mobile beside the settled empires and conquered many of them, have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It changes apart from the urban share (sedentism without towns for five millennia) and from farmland (pastoral nomads use vast pastures while staying mobile). It moves with the foraging share under provisioning before 3000 BCE, but differs from it by sedentary foragers and by pastoral nomads, who are most of the mobile after 1000 BCE.
- Universality pass: Every population either moves its homes or does not; the measure is 100% for the deep past and under 1% now.

Living in towns (towns): routed to h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already.
- What it covers: Whether people live in towns and cities or in the countryside.
- Necessity pass: Urbanization is habitat's main modern change.
- Independence pass: The urban share rose from 7% to 58% after 1800 while the largest city and farmland changed by other amounts.
- Universality pass: Every population lives somewhere on the scale from camp to city; zero for foragers.

The greatest settlement (largest-city): part.
- What it covers: How large the greatest settlement on Earth grows: the reach of what a place can gather and feed.
- Necessity pass: The scale of the greatest city is the classic reading of organization (Morris's social development index takes it as one of four traits), from Uruk to Rome, Chang'an, Baghdad, Hangzhou, London and Tokyo.
- Independence pass: Rome reached a million when the urban share was about 5%; the largest city fell by more than half after 200 while the urban share barely moved; it flattened after 1990 while the urban share kept rising.
- Universality pass: Every population has a largest settlement, if only a camp of a few dozen.

Farmland (farmland): part.
- What it covers: The land a population turns into fields and pasture.
- Necessity pass: Clearing land for fields and pasture is the largest human transformation of the Earth's surface, from nothing to over a third of ice-free land.
- Independence pass: Farmland stopped growing after about 2000 while the urban share and the largest city kept rising; it grew fastest 1850 to 1950, on the frontiers of the Americas, Russia and Australia, where few towns rose. It is also a change in the Earth's land cover, read beside forest under the Earth's setting.
- Universality pass: Every population uses land; the measure is zero for foragers.

Built land and works (built): frontier.
- What it covers: Land covered by buildings, streets and works: built-up area, and the water, sewer and power networks of settlements.
- Necessity uncertain: Sprawl and infrastructure are a large modern change, but before satellite mapping (from 1975) the world's built-up area is reconstructed from urban population times assumed densities, so a series would only restate the urban share; open it when an independent reading exists.
- Independence pass: Urban densities have fallen for two centuries (Angel's Planet of Cities), so built land grows apart from the urban share.
- Universality uncertain: Mobile foragers build almost nothing that lasts.

Roads, canals and ports (roads): routed to Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move.
- What it covers: The networks that tie settlements together.
- Necessity pass: They tie the habitat together.
- Independence fail: Their history is the history of moving people and goods.
- Universality uncertain: Foragers' paths are networks too.

Housing (housing): routed to Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has.
- What it covers: The dwellings in settlements.
- Necessity pass: Settlements are made of dwellings.
- Independence uncertain: Read as comfort, not as a means.
- Universality pass: Every population shelters.

Completeness uncertain: Settlement pattern is read by settling down and the urban share; housing is routed to shelter; streets and traffic to connection; cropland and pasture to farmland. Built-up area and utilities have no independent world reading before 1975, so completeness is uncertain. Checked against The Outline of Cultural Materials, sections 31 (land use) and 36 (settlements: settlement patterns, housing, streets and traffic, sanitation, public utilities, commercial and public facilities, urban and rural life), and the land-use classes of the HYDE reconstructions (cropland, pasture, built-up area).. Still without a home: Built-up land and public works (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat","candidates":[{"key":"mobile","label":"Settling down","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"towns","label":"Living in towns","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already"},{"key":"largest-city","label":"The greatest settlement","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"farmland","label":"Farmland","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"built","label":"Built land and works","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"roads","label":"Roads, canals and ports","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"uncertain","routedTo":"Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move"},{"key":"housing","label":"Housing","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The Outline of Cultural Materials, sections 31 (land use) and 36 (settlements: settlement patterns, housing, streets and traffic, sanitation, public utilities, commercial and public facilities, urban and rural life), and the land-use classes of the HYDE reconstructions (cropland, pasture, built-up area).","missing":["Built-up land and public works (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Politics (concept.humanity.means.politics):
- What it is: Politics as a means: making and enforcing decisions binding on a population, and taking from it what rule needs, from a band's consensus to empires and modern states. The first pass measured it by the share living under a state and filed state revenue and the largest polity beneath it without recording why those are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of rule that change apart, which the state share hides: how much rulers take and can do (capacity), how far one rule reaches over humanity (scale), and, routed elsewhere, who has a say (voice) and how rule is fought over (war); so that the rise of states, empires and their fragmentation, fiscal-military and welfare states, and colonial rule each have a home.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, bands and chiefdoms as much as states and empires; measured for all living people or all output.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Politics is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Politics is the means of ruling: decisions binding on a population and the taking that pays for them. The other means are getting and making things, place, moving people, goods and words, trading, and fighting. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Habitat, Connection, Exchange, Force.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Politics is carved into 2 parts: Capacity, Scale of rule.

How the parts make the whole work: Politics as this account follows it is the reach of the state (the parent's own measure), its capacity (what rulers take, read by revenue as a share of output) and its scale (how much of humanity the largest rule holds). The three change apart: states spread over humanity for five thousand years, the largest empire reached a fifth to a quarter of humanity under the Achaemenids, Han and Rome and again under the Ming and Qing and never more, and capacity stayed near 5% of output until the fiscal-military and welfare states tripled it in the twentieth century. Voice is routed to Freedom and power, fighting over rule to war and force; empire over other peoples is a kind of scale whose colonial form deserves its own series in a later pass; law and the form of rule stay frontier.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Rule over other peoples (a kind of concept.humanity.means.politics.scale).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Law and justice (independence), Form of rule (necessity).

Merged: Number of polities into scale.
Routed elsewhere: Reach of the state to h.politics's own measure, the share living under a state, which reads it already, Voice to Freedom and power (h.voice), the share living in democracies with broad suffrage, where the first pass filed it, Fighting over rule to War (h.war) under safety for its dead and Force (h.means.force) for the people under arms.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Reach of the state (reach): routed to h.politics's own measure, the share living under a state, which reads it already.
- What it covers: Whether people live under a state at all: rule by a permanent centre with officials, tribute or taxes, as against bands, tribes and chiefdoms.
- Necessity pass: The spread of the state from nothing in 3500 BCE to everyone by 1990 is politics' longest change.
- Independence pass: It reached 99% by 1945 while capacity kept rising and scale fell.
- Universality pass: Every population lives under a state or does not; zero for foragers.

Capacity (capacity): part.
- What it covers: How much rulers take from what a population makes, and so what they can do: armies, officials, works and, later, schools, pensions and health care.
- Necessity pass: The fiscal-military states of early modern Europe, Song China's commercial taxes and the twentieth century's rise from about 10% to 30% of output, the welfare state, have no home without it (Tilly's coercion and capital; Brewer's sinews of power).
- Independence pass: Revenue tripled between 1910 and 1950 while the state share barely moved and the largest polity's share fell.
- Universality pass: Every population sustains its rule somehow; for bands and most chiefdoms the measure is near zero.

Scale of rule (scale): part.
- What it covers: How far one rule reaches over humanity: the size of the largest polities, from Akkad to the Achaemenids, Han and Rome, the Mongols, Ming and Qing China and the British Empire.
- Necessity pass: The rise and fall of empires, unifications and fragmentations, is what a political history of the world most often narrates; without scale it has no home.
- Independence pass: The largest polity fell from about a quarter to a seventh of humanity after 400 while the state share held; it shrank after 1820 while capacity rose.
- Universality pass: Every population has a largest unit of rule, if only a band of a few dozen.

Rule over other peoples (empire): a kind of scale.
- What it covers: Empire: rule by one people's centre over conquered or colonized peoples who have no part in it; above all the overseas colonial empires of 1500 to 1975, which at their height around 1920 held about a third of humanity, and the land empires before them.
- Necessity pass: Colonial rule and decolonization (1945 to 1975) are among the largest political changes of the modern world.
- Independence pass: Decolonization ended colonial rule for about a third of humanity without changing the state share and while revenue rose.
- Universality fail: Only where a state rules other peoples, so a kind of scale. A series of the share of people under colonial rule from 1500 is worth opening in a later pass; before 1500 the line between a conquest state and alien rule (the Mongols, the Qing, the Mughals) is a debate a single number would hide.

Number of polities (fragmentation): merged into scale.
- What it covers: How many independent polities share humanity: from hundreds of thousands of bands to about 200 states.
- Necessity pass: Unification and fragmentation are what scale reads.
- Independence fail: It is the other side of the size distribution that the largest polity reads; a second reading of scale, not a separate part.
- Universality pass: Every population lives in some number of polities.

Voice (voice): routed to Freedom and power (h.voice), the share living in democracies with broad suffrage, where the first pass filed it.
- What it covers: Who has a say in rule: councils, assemblies, elections, suffrage.
- Necessity pass: Democratization is a central political change.
- Independence pass: Voice spread after 1945 apart from capacity and scale.
- Universality pass: Every population decides somehow.

Law and justice (law): frontier.
- What it covers: The rules rule follows and how disputes and crimes are judged: codes, courts, the rule of law and its absence.
- Necessity pass: Fukuyama counts the rule of law among the three components of political order; law codes from Ur-Nammu to the Tang Code and the Code Napoleon have no other home.
- Independence uncertain: A world measure exists only from 1789 (V-Dem's rule of law index); before that, a share living under written law would mostly restate the state share.
- Universality pass: Every population has norms and ways of judging.

Form of rule (form): frontier.
- What it covers: Who rules and how they are chosen and constrained: chiefs, kings, emperors, oligarchies, republics, party states.
- Necessity uncertain: Monarchy's decline after 1789 and the party states of the twentieth century are large changes, but they are categories competing for one pool, better followed as a Cut of regime types (life_series_record) than as a number.
- Independence pass: Monarchies fell after 1917 apart from capacity.
- Universality pass: Every population has some form of rule.

Fighting over rule (fighting): routed to War (h.war) under safety for its dead and Force (h.means.force) for the people under arms.
- What it covers: Wars, rebellions and coups fought over who rules.
- Necessity pass: Much rule is won by force.
- Independence fail: Its history is the history of war and force, which have homes.
- Universality pass: Every population fights.

Completeness uncertain: The state is read by reach, capacity and scale; accountable government by voice, routed to Freedom and power; polities by scale, government by capacity, membership and participation by voice. The rule of law and the form of rule have no measured home, so completeness is uncertain. Checked against Fukuyama's three components of political order (the state, the rule of law, accountable government), Mann's political power within the IEMP model, and the structure construction's own politics node (polities, rule, government, law and justice, membership and participation) in structure/history-tree.mjs.. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Provisioning (concept.humanity.means.provisioning):
- What it is: Provisioning: getting and making what a population uses, measured as output per person, from foragers' food and tools to farms, workshops, factories and services. The first pass measured it by output per person and filed the foraging share and the share of workers getting food beneath it without recording why those are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of output that change apart, which output per person sums into one number: food-getting, which stayed most of output until the nineteenth century and has barely grown per person since; making, which rose fifteenfold per person with industry; and services, which became two thirds of output; so that the agricultural, industrial and service transformations each have a home.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, foragers as much as farmers and industrial and service economies; measured as output per person of the world in 2011 dollars.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Provisioning is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Provisioning is the means of getting and making things and doing services for use; the other means are place, moving people, goods and words, trading, ruling and fighting. Other kinds within it: Habitat, Connection, Exchange, Politics, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Food-getting (food): part.
- What it covers: Getting food and other living materials from plants and animals: foraging, hunting, fishing, farming, herding and forestry.
- Necessity pass: Food-getting was four fifths of output for foragers and half or more until about 1820; the agricultural revolutions and the shrinking of farming in the last two centuries have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Food-getting per person barely grew between 1900 and 1990 while making tripled and services rose sixfold.
- Universality pass: Every population gets food.

Making (making): part.
- What it covers: Making things: tools, clothing, buildings, pots and metal, and later mining, manufacturing, construction and power.
- Necessity pass: The industrial revolution, the largest change in what people make, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Making per person rose eightfold from 1820 to 1950 while food-getting per person rose a fifth; in rich countries its share fell after 1970 while services kept rising.
- Universality pass: Every population makes tools, clothing and shelters.

Services (services): part.
- What it covers: Doing things for others: trade, transport, housing, government, religion, healing, teaching, finance, entertainment and care, as far as output counts it.
- Necessity pass: Services are two thirds of output now; merchants, priests, officials and servants were a fifth to a quarter of agrarian output.
- Independence pass: Services per person doubled between 1990 and 2025 while making rose by less than that and food-getting by a third.
- Universality pass: Every population heals, teaches, rules and exchanges; foragers' services are mostly unpaid and barely counted, so the measure is small for them.

Foraging (foraging): a kind of food.
- What it covers: Getting food by gathering, hunting and fishing wild resources, read by the share of people living by it.
- Necessity pass: All of humanity's food-getting before 10,000 BCE.
- Independence pass: It shrinks as farming spreads, apart from making and services.
- Universality fail: One way of getting food among foraging, farming and herding; a population of farmers contains no foragers, so it is a kind of food-getting, not a part of provisioning.

Share of workers getting food (food-work): merged into food.
- What it covers: The share of all workers whose work is getting food: food-getting read by labour rather than output.
- Necessity pass: The fall of farm labour from three quarters to a quarter of workers is the structural transformation.
- Independence fail: It is a second reading of food-getting, by labour instead of output; the gap between the two (a quarter of workers make a twentieth of output) is farming's lower output per worker.
- Universality pass: Every population divides its work.

Unpaid household work (household): frontier.
- What it covers: Cooking, cleaning, caring for children and the old, fetching water and fuel, done in the household and not counted as output.
- Necessity uncertain: Perhaps a third or more of all work in every era, mostly women's; output measures leave it out, so it would be a part of provisioning only if output were redefined to count it.
- Independence pass: Household appliances and piped water cut its hours after 1920 apart from output.
- Universality pass: Every household does it.

Tools and capital (tools): routed to The means' frontier parts know-how and wealth in the carve carve.concept.humanity.means, which hold what produces output rather than output itself.
- What it covers: The tools, machines, buildings and animals that output is made with.
- Necessity pass: Output per worker rises with capital.
- Independence uncertain: A stock, not a flow of output.
- Universality pass: Every population has tools.

Energy used (energy): routed to Energy for warmth, light and work (h.warmth) under Sustenance and comfort.
- What it covers: The energy that drives provisioning.
- Necessity pass: Output follows energy capture.
- Independence fail: Already followed as h.warmth.
- Universality pass: Every population uses energy.

Completeness pass: Every ISIC section falls in exactly one of food-getting (A), making (B to F) or services (G to U), and the three sum to output; the only work without a home is the unpaid work output does not count, which is a question about the parent's measure, not a missing part of it. Checked against The International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) sections, grouped into Clark's and Kuznets's three sectors (agriculture; industry; services), as the national accounts of every country divide value added.. Still without a home: Unpaid household work, which output leaves out by definition (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.provisioning","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.provisioning","candidates":[{"key":"food","label":"Food-getting","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"making","label":"Making","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"services","label":"Services","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"foraging","label":"Foraging","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"food"},{"key":"food-work","label":"Share of workers getting food","outcome":"merged","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","mergedInto":"food"},{"key":"household","label":"Unpaid household work","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"tools","label":"Tools and capital","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The means' frontier parts know-how and wealth in the carve carve.concept.humanity.means, which hold what produces output rather than output itself"},{"key":"energy","label":"Energy used","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Energy for warmth, light and work (h.warmth) under Sustenance and comfort"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) sections, grouped into Clark's and Kuznets's three sectors (agriculture; industry; services), as the national accounts of every country divide value added.","missing":["Unpaid household work, which output leaves out by definition (frontier)"]}}}

1. Violence is a kind of A cause of death: Violence is death caused deliberately by other people; the other causes are infection, death around birth, hunger, unintended injury and self-harm, and chronic disease. Other kinds within it: Infection, Birth, Hunger, Injury, Chronic disease.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Violence is carved into 2 parts: Homicide, War and massacre.

How the parts make the whole work: Violent death as this account follows it is homicide and war, which the parent sums. They change apart: homicide falls slowly over centuries, as states disarm and courts take over (Elias's civilizing process, as Eisner and Pinker read it), and rises where states lose hold; war comes in rare enormous peaks, the Mongol conquests, the seventeenth-century crisis, the Taiping war and the world wars, between long stretches of a few per 100,000. Terrorism is a small modern kind of war; self-harm is routed to injury and deliberate starvation to hunger, where the famine counts its dead. Executions are a part by the tests but the parent's measure leaves them out, so they stay frontier until the measure is widened; violence that does not kill stays frontier for want of a world measure.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Terrorism (a kind of concept.causes-of-death.violence.war).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Execution (universality), Violence that does not kill (necessity).

Routed elsewhere: Self-harm to Injury (h.alive.injury), which counts suicide with unintended injuries, Killing by deliberate starvation to Hunger (h.alive.hunger), which counts the excess deaths of famines whatever caused them; whether a famine made or worsened by policy, such as the Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933, counts as killing is debated.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Homicide (homicide): part.
- What it covers: Killing between persons outside organized group fighting: murder, manslaughter, feud, killings in quarrels and robbery.
- Necessity pass: The long fall of homicide in Europe from 20 to 40 per 100,000 in the late Middle Ages to about 1 by 1900 (Eisner's series), and its rises in the Americas, have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Homicide fell steadily through the centuries while war deaths spiked and fell; Latin America's homicide rose after 1980 while war deaths were at their lowest.
- Universality pass: Every population has killings between persons.

War and massacre (war): part.
- What it covers: Organized killing: fighting between polities, fighting within a polity over who rules it, and one-sided killing of the unarmed by organized groups, as the existing values count them (the Holocaust, the killings in Indonesia in 1965 and the Khmer Rouge's are in it).
- Necessity pass: The world wars, the Taiping war and the Mongol conquests are the largest peaks of violent death.
- Independence pass: War deaths peak and fall in years and decades apart from homicide's slow trend.
- Universality pass: Every population fights other groups, from forager raids to world wars.

Execution (execution): frontier.
- What it covers: Killing by a group's own rule: judicial executions, and among foragers the collective killing of a dangerous member.
- Necessity pass: Executions reached perhaps 10 per 100,000 a year in sixteenth-century England and fell to a few hundredths now; Boehm and Wrangham argue collective execution shaped human evolution.
- Independence pass: Executions fell in Europe after 1750 on their own timetable, with the abolition movement.
- Universality uncertain: Found among foragers and states alike, but the parent's measure, homicide plus war, leaves it out: opening it means widening an existing measure, which this pass does not do. The Global Burden of Disease counts 'executions and police conflict' as a cause of its own.

Terrorism (terror): a kind of war.
- What it covers: Killing by small organized groups to frighten a wider public.
- Necessity pass: Political violence of the last century and a half.
- Independence pass: Rises and falls with its own waves (Rapoport's four).
- Universality fail: A modern form of organized killing, so a kind of war, and a small one: under a tenth of a death per 100,000 a year for the world.

Self-harm (self-harm): routed to Injury (h.alive.injury), which counts suicide with unintended injuries.
- What it covers: Killing oneself.
- Necessity pass: A large cause of death.
- Independence pass: Moves apart from homicide.
- Universality pass: Found in every population.

Killing by deliberate starvation (starving): routed to Hunger (h.alive.hunger), which counts the excess deaths of famines whatever caused them; whether a famine made or worsened by policy, such as the Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933, counts as killing is debated.
- What it covers: Famine made or used as a weapon: sieges, blockades, requisitioning.
- Necessity pass: Many of the deadliest episodes of organized violence killed by hunger.
- Independence uncertain: Its deaths are famine deaths.
- Universality pass: Sieges are as old as walls.

Violence that does not kill (harm): frontier.
- What it covers: Assault, rape, torture, beating of children and wives.
- Necessity uncertain: Most violence does not kill, but no world measure reads it across the span; surveys of victimization begin in the late twentieth century.
- Independence pass: The legal acceptance of beating wives and children fell after 1850 apart from homicide.
- Universality pass: Every population has it.

Completeness uncertain: Assault and interpersonal violence are homicide; operations of war and conflict and terrorism are war; self-harm is routed to injury. Legal intervention and executions have no home in homicide plus war, so completeness is uncertain. Checked against The external causes of the International Classification of Diseases (assault; legal intervention; operations of war; intentional self-harm) and the injury causes of the Global Burden of Disease (interpersonal violence; conflict and terrorism; executions and police conflict; self-harm).. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving War and massacre (concept.causes-of-death.violence.war):
- What it is: War and massacre: deaths in organized killing, which the account follows as one number, h.war, averaged to the next date. The deepen check names it second: nine Events move it, and over half its values are sketched or wider than themselves.
- What the carve is for: To follow the kinds of organized killing that change apart, which one number hides: fighting between polities, which made the world wars and collapsed after 1945 (the Long Peace); fighting within a polity over who rules it, which made the Taiping war and most war deaths since 1945; and the one-sided killing of the unarmed, which made the Holocaust, Indonesia 1965, the Khmer Rouge and Rwanda.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, forager raids as much as world wars; measured as deaths per 100,000 living people a year for the world, averaged to the next date as the parent is.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. War and massacre is a kind of A form of deliberate killing: War is killing by organized groups acting as groups, against other groups or the unarmed; homicide is killing by persons, and execution killing by a group's rule of one of its own. Other kinds within it: Homicide, Execution.
2. A form of deliberate killing is a kind of A cause of death: Deliberate killing is death caused on purpose by other people; the other causes are infection, death around birth, hunger, unintended injury and self-harm, and chronic disease. Other kinds within it: Infection, Birth, Hunger, Injury, Chronic disease.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"War and massacre is carved into 3 parts: Fighting between polities, Fighting within a polity, One-sided killing.

How the parts make the whole work: War as this account follows it is fighting between polities, fighting within a polity and one-sided killing of the unarmed, which sum to the parent at every date. They change apart. Between polities: forager and farmer raids, then conquest wars, the Mongols, the seventeenth-century wars and the world wars, then near zero after 1945. Within polities: rare among bands, enormous in the collapses of Chinese dynasties (the Yellow Turbans, An Lushan, the Ming fall, the Taiping), and the larger kind since 1945. One-sided: massacres in every era, with the twentieth century's genocides as its peaks, often apart from any fighting. Splitting the parent's values exposes two questions it leaves open: its pre-modern peaks seem to include war's famine and disease deaths, which belong to hunger and infection, and it counts some one-sided killings but not others, such as China's campaigns of 1950 to 1953 and the Cultural Revolution's killings. This pass adds two well-dated genocides it lacked, Bangladesh 1971 and Rwanda 1994, as earlier passes added Indonesia and Cambodia.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Colonial wars (a kind of concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.between), Terrorism (a kind of concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.within).

Routed elsewhere: Deaths from war's famine and disease to Hunger (h.alive.hunger) and infection (h.alive.infection), where the causes-of-death carve counts each death once by its underlying cause. The parent's values for the Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War (1618 to 1650) and the Taiping war (1850 to 1864) appear to include those wars' famine and disease deaths, which would count them twice; a later pass should decide.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Fighting between polities (between): part.
- What it covers: Killing in fighting between independent polities: raids between bands and villages, wars between chiefdoms, states and empires, and conquests of other peoples, colonial wars included.
- Necessity pass: The world wars, the Mongol conquests and the wars of unification are the largest peaks of organized killing; the Long Peace between great powers after 1945 has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Deaths between polities collapsed after 1945 to a fraction of a death per 100,000 while killing within polities went on at one to three.
- Universality pass: Every population lives beside others it may fight, from forager raids on.

Fighting within a polity (within): part.
- What it covers: Killing in fighting within a polity over who rules it or whether it holds together: civil wars, rebellions, revolutions, wars of secession and independence, warlord wars, and fighting between armed groups inside a state.
- Necessity pass: The Yellow Turban and An Lushan risings, the Taiping war, the Russian and Chinese civil wars, and most war deaths since 1945 have no home without it.
- Independence pass: The Taiping war's peak in the 1850s and 1860s came while fighting between polities was low; since 1945 civil wars carry most war deaths.
- Universality pass: Every polity can split and fight within itself; among bands, where killings within the group are homicide, the measure is zero.

One-sided killing (one-sided): part.
- What it covers: Killing of the unarmed by organized groups: massacres of camps, villages and cities, genocide, politicide and campaigns of mass execution, whoever does it and whether or not a war is being fought.
- Necessity pass: The Mongols' city massacres, the Armenian genocide, the Holocaust, Indonesia 1965, the Khmer Rouge and Rwanda are among the deadliest episodes of organized killing, and the debate over whether states' killing of their own people outweighs war (Rummel's democide) has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Indonesia's killings of 1965 and Rwanda's of 1994 came with little fighting; the Khmer Rouge's after their civil war ended.
- Universality pass: Massacres of whole camps are found among foragers (Nataruk, about 8000 BCE) and in every era since.

Deaths from war's famine and disease (war-famine): routed to Hunger (h.alive.hunger) and infection (h.alive.infection), where the causes-of-death carve counts each death once by its underlying cause. The parent's values for the Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War (1618 to 1650) and the Taiping war (1850 to 1864) appear to include those wars' famine and disease deaths, which would count them twice; a later pass should decide.
- What it covers: People who die of famine and epidemics that a war brings, rather than by violence.
- Necessity pass: In many pre-modern wars most of the dead died this way.
- Independence fail: Their deaths are famine and infection deaths.
- Universality pass: Every war that burns crops and moves armies brings them.

Colonial wars (colonial): a kind of between.
- What it covers: Wars of conquest and resistance between a colonial power and peoples outside its own state.
- Necessity pass: The conquests of the Americas, India, Africa and Australia.
- Independence pass: They follow empire's timetable.
- Universality fail: Only where empires rule overseas; a kind of fighting between polities.

Terrorism (terror): a kind of within.
- What it covers: Killing by small organized groups to frighten a wider public, mostly inside one state.
- Necessity pass: Political violence of the last century and a half.
- Independence pass: Its own waves.
- Universality fail: A modern form; a kind of fighting within polities, and a small one.

Completeness pass: Interstate and extrasystemic or extra-state wars are fighting between polities; intrastate, internationalized intrastate, intra-state and non-state conflicts are fighting within a polity; one-sided violence is one-sided killing. Every category has one home. Checked against The Uppsala Conflict Data Program's categories of organized violence (state-based conflict: interstate, intrastate, internationalized intrastate and extrasystemic; non-state conflict; one-sided violence) and the Correlates of War's kinds of war (inter-state, extra-state, intra-state, non-state)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.causes-of-death.violence.war","conceptId":"concept.causes-of-death.violence.war","candidates":[{"key":"between","label":"Fighting between polities","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"within","label":"Fighting within a polity","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"one-sided","label":"One-sided killing","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"war-famine","label":"Deaths from war's famine and disease","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Hunger (h.alive.hunger) and infection (h.alive.infection), where the causes-of-death carve counts each death once by its underlying cause. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Core people and subject peoples (core-subjects): dropped.
- What it covers: The largest polity's own people against the conquered or colonized peoples it rules: Britain's 45 million against the Raj's 300 million in 1920.
- Necessity fail: Only empires have subject peoples; for Ming or Qing China, the largest polity for most of five centuries, the division hardly applies or is the debate over whether the Qing was alien rule. The colonial form is recorded as a kind of scale, empire, in carve.concept.humanity.means.politics, worth its own series.
- Independence pass: Colonial subjects came and went with conquest and decolonization.
- Universality fail: Absent from most largest polities.

Which polity is largest (which): dropped.
- What it covers: The Achaemenids, Han, Rome, Tang, Song, the Mongols, Ming and Qing China, the British Empire, China and India.
- Necessity fail: The identity of the largest polity is a sequence of kinds, already told by the Events that move the share; it is not a part that sums to it.
- Independence pass: Each rises and falls on its own.
- Universality fail: Each exists only in some centuries.

The rest of the size distribution (distribution): dropped.
- What it covers: How the rest of humanity is divided among polities: the share in the five largest, or the effective number of polities.
- Necessity fail: A second reading of scale beside the largest polity's share, a sibling measure, not a part of it.
- Independence uncertain: Moves with the largest share in unifications and against it in fragmentations.
- Universality pass: Every date has a distribution of polity sizes.

Territory held (territory): dropped.
- What it covers: The share of the Earth's land under the largest polity: the Mongols and the British Empire held about a sixth to a quarter.
- Necessity fail: A second reading of scale by land instead of people, not a part of the people's share.
- Independence pass: Land and people diverge: Russia's land against India's people.
- Universality pass: Every polity holds land.

Completeness uncertain: No set of parts sums to the largest polity's share; the candidates are kinds (which polity, empire) or sibling readings of scale (the size distribution, territory).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.politics.scale","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics.scale","candidates":[{"key":"core-subjects","label":"Core people and subject peoples","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"},{"key":"which","label":"Which polity is largest","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"},{"key":"distribution","label":"The rest of the size distribution","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"},{"key":"territory","label":"Territory held","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain"}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The plant cover is carved into 4 parts: Tropical forest, Subtropical forest, Temperate forest, Boreal forest.

How the parts make the whole work: Forest as this account follows it is four forests by climate, whose shares of land sum to the forest share. In the deep past all four follow the ice: at glacial maxima the boreal forest shrinks to refugia and the temperate forest moves south, while the tropical forest contracts less and gains the drowned shelves of Sunda. In the Holocene people take over: subtropical and temperate forests are cleared first by dense farming societies (the Mediterranean, China, India, Europe), the tropical forests regrow briefly after the Great Dying in the Americas and are cleared fastest after 1950, temperate forests turn back up after about 1930 (the forest transition), and the boreal forest is the least touched. China's planting since 1978 has two homes because it spans the temperate and subtropical domains, as the domains divide its land. Open covers and the planted-primary axis stay frontier.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Open covers (universality), Planted and primary forest (necessity, universality).
