upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Tropical forest (tropical): part.
- What it covers: Forest in the tropical climatic domain: the rainforests of Amazonia, the Congo basin and South-east Asia, and the tropical dry forests.
- Necessity pass: Nearly half of all forest, and most of the clearing since 1950.
- Independence pass: Tropical forest fell fastest after 1950 while temperate forest grew back.
- Universality pass: Present at every date, smaller in glacial dry spells.

Subtropical forest (subtropical): part.
- What it covers: Forest in the subtropical domain: the Mediterranean, southern China, northern India, the south-eastern United States, southern Brazil and eastern Australia.
- Necessity pass: The forests of the Mediterranean and of southern China and northern India were among the first cleared by dense farming societies.
- Independence pass: Cleared over three millennia apart from the boreal and tropical forests.
- Universality pass: Present at every date.

Temperate forest (temperate): part.
- What it covers: Forest in the temperate domain: Europe's broadleaf forests, northern China, Korea and Japan, eastern North America, Chile and New Zealand.
- Necessity pass: Farmers cleared about half of it before 1900, and its regrowth since, the forest transition, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: It has grown back since about 1930 while tropical forest shrank.
- Universality pass: Present at every date, pushed south into refugia at glacial maxima.

Boreal forest (boreal): part.
- What it covers: Forest in the boreal domain: the conifer forests of Siberia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska.
- Necessity pass: The forest that the glacial cycles move most, and over a quarter of all forest now.
- Independence pass: It follows the ice, shrinking to small refugia at glacial maxima, while people barely touched it until logging and fire after 1900.
- Universality pass: Present at every date, if only south of the ice.

Open covers (open): frontier.
- What it covers: The land's other plant covers: grassland, savanna, shrubland, tundra and desert scrub.
- Necessity pass: The prairies, pampas and steppes turned into farmland, and the greening and drying of the Sahara, belong to the plant cover.
- Independence pass: Grasslands were converted on their own timetable.
- Universality uncertain: A part of the plant cover, but not of the forest share that measures it here; a measure of natural open cover would need its own series from the land-use reconstructions, which a later pass could open.

Planted and primary forest (planted): frontier.
- What it covers: A second axis across the domains: primary forest, naturally regenerating forest and planted forest.
- Necessity uncertain: Planted forest is about 7% of forest now and much of the temperate regrowth; primary forest's loss matters more for the living world than the area alone.
- Independence pass: Planting rose after 1950 apart from clearing.
- Universality uncertain: It crosses the domains instead of dividing forest beside them, and it is measured only from 1990.

Completeness pass: Every forest falls in exactly one climatic domain, and the four shares sum to the forest share. Checked against The climatic domains of the global ecological zones used by FAO's Global Forest Resources Assessments (tropical, subtropical, temperate, boreal), which divide all forest on Earth.. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Voice is carved into 2 parts: Inclusiveness, Contestation.

How the parts make the whole work: Voice as this account follows it is inclusiveness and contestation, Dahl's two dimensions; the parent, democracy with broad suffrage, is where both are high. They change apart: contestation came first and narrowly, in Greek democracies, the Roman Republic, the elective monarchy of Poland-Lithuania and Britain after 1688, among small electorates; inclusiveness came later and fast, with manhood suffrage after 1848, women's suffrage after 1893, and formal universal suffrage spread by one-party states and new nations after 1945, so that by the 1960s nearly all adults could vote while only about a third of humanity chose its rulers in competitive elections. India's first election in 1951 to 1952 moves both at once, which is why it has two homes; the Emergency of 1975 to 1977 moves only contestation. Civil liberties stay frontier; the voice of band councils is outside the parent's measure, a debate recorded rather than a zero claimed.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Civil liberties (necessity, independence).

Routed elsewhere: Say in band and village councils to Outside the parent's measure, which counts bands and tribes at zero; the egalitarian decision-making of foragers (Boehm's reverse dominance hierarchy) is a debate about whether voice is lost or gained with the state, recorded here so the zero is read as a definition, not a finding.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Inclusiveness (suffrage): part.
- What it covers: How many may vote: the share of adults with the legal right to vote for their country's assembly or head of state, directly or through electors, whether or not the elections are free.
- Necessity pass: The widening of the franchise, from propertied men to all men (France 1848, Germany 1871) and to women (New Zealand 1893 to Switzerland 1971), is the main story of democratization in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
- Independence pass: Formal suffrage became nearly universal by the 1960s, through one-party states as much as democracies, while contestation stayed near a third of humanity; and Britain had competitive elections from 1688 with a few percent of adults voting.
- Universality pass: Every population either has a franchise or does not; zero for bands and most states before the eighteenth century.

Contestation (contest): part.
- What it covers: Whether rulers are chosen in competitive elections, whoever may vote: the share of people living in a polity whose government is chosen by elections whose outcome is uncertain.
- Necessity pass: Competitive oligarchy, the Roman Republic, the elective monarchy of Poland-Lithuania, Britain after 1688, the early American republic, has no home without it; nor has the difference between elections that choose rulers and those that only ratify them.
- Independence pass: It rose and fell with republics and parliaments while suffrage stayed narrow, and stayed near a third of humanity from 1950 to 1985 while formal suffrage spread to nearly everyone.
- Universality pass: Every population either chooses its rulers in competitive elections or does not; zero for bands, chiefdoms and most states.

Civil liberties (liberties): frontier.
- What it covers: Freedom to speak, publish, assemble and worship without punishment, which competitive elections need.
- Necessity uncertain: Dahl counts them among the guarantees of polyarchy, but as a part of voice they mostly restate contestation; as a part of freedom they may stand alone.
- Independence uncertain: Liberal non-democracies (Britain before 1867) had them without broad suffrage, but since 1945 they move with contestation.
- Universality pass: Every population has or lacks them.

Say in band and village councils (consensus): routed to Outside the parent's measure, which counts bands and tribes at zero; the egalitarian decision-making of foragers (Boehm's reverse dominance hierarchy) is a debate about whether voice is lost or gained with the state, recorded here so the zero is read as a definition, not a finding.
- What it covers: The voice adults have in bands and villages without a state.
- Necessity pass: Most of human history's voice was of this kind.
- Independence pass: It shrinks with chiefdoms and states.
- Universality fail: Only in stateless populations.

Completeness pass: Suffrage is inclusiveness; clean and competitive elections with elected officials are contestation; freedom of association and of expression are the guarantees contestation needs, recorded as a frontier. A democracy with broad suffrage, the parent, is where both parts are high. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Food is carved into 3 parts: Staples, Animal foods, Other foods.

How the parts make the whole work: Food as this account follows it is staples, animal foods and other foods, which sum to the total at every date. Their mix changed twice. With farming the world's diet narrowed: staples rose from perhaps two fifths of foragers' energy to three quarters, and animal foods fell from about a third to a tenth, the first nutrition transition, read in early farmers' shorter stature. Since 1950 the total rose by a third while staples per person stayed flat: the gain went to animal foods and above all to oils, sugar and other foods (Popkin's nutrition transition). The world mix is built from the model's own foraging share and a forager mix and a farmer mix, so before 1800 it is a sketch whose bands carry the debate over how much meat foragers ate. Diet quality and who gets the food are routed to height, hunger and poverty.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Cereals (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.sustenance.food.staples).

Routed elsewhere: Diet quality to The body's growth and condition (h.health, adult height) and hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger), which read what poor diets do, Who gets the food to Hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger) and the share in extreme poverty (h.sustenance); the distribution of food within the world is a question for a later pass.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Staples (staples): part.
- What it covers: The starchy and protein plant foods eaten as the bulk of a diet: cereals, roots and tubers, pulses, and for foragers wild seeds, tubers and staple nuts.
- Necessity pass: Farming made grain, rice, maize and roots three quarters of the diet; the Columbian exchange's maize and potatoes and the Green Revolution's wheats and rices have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Staples per person have barely changed since 1960 while animal foods and oils and sugar rose.
- Universality pass: Every population eats some starchy plant food, foragers' tubers and seeds included.

Animal foods (animal): part.
- What it covers: Meat, fish, eggs, milk and animal fats.
- Necessity pass: Hunting fed foragers; farming cut meat to a tenth of the diet; dairying, the post-plague meat of late medieval Europe and the meat boom of the last fifty years have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Animal foods fell as a share with farming while total food held, and rose with incomes after 1950 while staples stayed flat.
- Universality pass: Every population eats some.

Other foods (other): part.
- What it covers: Sugars and honey, vegetable oils, fruit and vegetables, other nuts, spices and alcoholic drinks.
- Necessity pass: Sugar from the slave plantations and vegetable oils since 1960 are the two largest new sources of calories in the modern world; honey and fruit were a large share of some foragers' diets.
- Independence pass: Other foods rose by more than half per person from 1960 to 2025 while staples did not change.
- Universality pass: Every population eats fruit or honey, if not sugar and oil.

Cereals (cereals): a kind of staples.
- What it covers: Wheat, rice, maize, barley, millet, sorghum.
- Necessity pass: About half of all calories now.
- Independence pass: Cereals replaced roots and wild seeds.
- Universality fail: Domesticated cereals exist only from about 9500 BCE, wild grains only in some places before; a kind of staple.

Diet quality (quality): routed to The body's growth and condition (h.health, adult height) and hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger), which read what poor diets do.
- What it covers: Protein, vitamins and minerals; the variety of the diet.
- Necessity pass: Farmers' narrow grain diets stunted them.
- Independence uncertain: Read in stature and deaths.
- Universality pass: Every diet has a quality.

Who gets the food (access): routed to Hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger) and the share in extreme poverty (h.sustenance); the distribution of food within the world is a question for a later pass.
- What it covers: How evenly the food available is shared: the gap between supply and what the poor eat.
- Necessity pass: Famines happen with food in the market (Sen's entitlements).
- Independence pass: Distribution changes apart from supply.
- Universality pass: Every population shares food somehow.

Completeness pass: Cereals, starchy roots and pulses are staples; meat, offals, animal fats, eggs, milk, fish and seafood and other aquatic products are animal foods; sweeteners, nuts, oils, vegetables, fruits, stimulants, spices and alcohol are other foods. Every group has one home, and the three sum to the total. Checked against The commodity groups of FAO's food balance sheets (cereals, starchy roots, sugars and sweeteners, pulses, nuts, oil crops and vegetable oils, vegetables, fruits, stimulants, spices, alcoholic beverages, meat, offals, animal fats, eggs, milk, fish and seafood, other aquatic products)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.sustenance.food","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.sustenance.food","candidates":[{"key":"staples","label":"Staples","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"animal","label":"Animal foods","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"other","label":"Other foods","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"cereals","label":"Cereals","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"staples"},{"key":"quality","label":"Diet quality","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The body's growth and condition (h.health, adult height) and hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger), which read what poor diets do"},{"key":"access","label":"Who gets the food","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Hunger deaths (h.alive.hunger) and the share in extreme poverty (h.sustenance); the distribution of food within the world is a question for a later pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The commodity groups of FAO's food balance sheets (cereals, starchy roots, sugars and sweeteners, pulses, nuts, oil crops and vegetable oils, vegetables, fruits, stimulants, spices, alcoholic beverages, meat, offals, animal fats, eggs, milk, fish and seafood, other aquatic products)."}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The greatest settlement (concept.humanity.means.habitat.largest-city):
- What it is: The greatest settlement, measured as the people living in the largest city on Earth (h.largest-city). The deepen check names it next: four Events move it, one at the top of an importance scale, and half its values are sketched.
- What the carve is for: To decide whether the largest city's size is made of parts that change apart and are worth following, or stays one number.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, from the largest forager camp to Tokyo.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The greatest settlement is a kind of A dimension of how a population settles: The greatest settlement is the upper end of the size distribution of settlements; the other dimensions are whether people have fixed homes, whether they live in towns, and how much land they turn to use. Which city is largest (which): dropped.
- What it covers: Uruk, Babylon, Rome, Chang'an, Baghdad, Kaifeng, Hangzhou, Nanjing, Beijing, London, New York, Tokyo.
- Necessity fail: A sequence of kinds, each the largest for a time, told by the Events that move the number; not a part that sums to it.
- Independence pass: Each rises and falls on its own.
- Universality fail: Each exists only in some centuries.

Core and suburbs (core-ring): dropped.
- What it covers: The city proper against its suburbs and commuter ring.
- Necessity fail: Where a city's edge is drawn is a choice of definition (city proper, built-up area, metropolitan region), fixed here as the built-up area; splitting by it would follow the definition, not a change in the world.
- Independence uncertain: Suburbs grow faster than cores after 1900, but both are read in the built-up area.
- Universality fail: Suburbs in the modern sense are recent.

The other great cities (distribution): dropped.
- What it covers: How many people live in great cities at all: the share of humanity in cities of a million or more, from Rome alone to some six hundred cities now.
- Necessity fail: A sibling reading of the settlement pattern beside the largest city, not a part of it; worth opening as its own process under habitat in a later pass, since it rose from about a tenth of a percent in 1800 to about a quarter of humanity now while the largest city grew far less.
- Independence pass: The number of million-cities rose fastest after 1950 while the largest city's growth slowed.
- Universality pass: Every date has a distribution of settlement sizes.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Fewer than two candidates passed, so Freedom and power has no carve in the model yet (passed: Voice). The verdicts are kept here for the next attempt.

How the parts make the whole work: Freedom as this account follows it is freedom of the person, read by the parent's own measure (the share held in bondage), and voice, a say in rule. They change apart and in sequence: bondage peaked about 1500 to 1700 and fell with the abolitions and emancipations of 1794 to 1888 while almost no one had a vote; voice rose after 1918 and above all after 1945, when bondage was already low, with the totalitarian camps of the 1930s and 1940s raising bondage in between. Freedom of movement is merged into freedom of the person; civil liberties and women's legal autonomy are parts by necessity but stay frontier until a world series can be read.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Civil liberties (independence, universality), Women's legal autonomy (universality).

Merged: Freedom of movement into person.
Routed elsewhere: Freedom of the person to h.freedom's own measure, the share held in bondage, which reads it already: slavery, serfdom and forced labour are its kinds.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Freedom of the person (person): routed to h.freedom's own measure, the share held in bondage, which reads it already: slavery, serfdom and forced labour are its kinds.
- What it covers: Not being owned, bound to a master or to the land, or forced to work.
- Necessity pass: Slavery and serfdom held up to a tenth of humanity for three thousand years; their abolition is among the largest changes in freedom.
- Independence pass: Bondage fell from about 9% to 3% between 1780 and 1870 while voice was near zero.
- Universality pass: Every population either holds people in bondage or does not.

Voice (voice): part.
- What it covers: A say in who rules: living in a democracy with broad suffrage.
- Necessity pass: The spread of democracy, from a few percent of humanity in 1918 to about half by 2000, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Voice spread after 1945 when bondage was already low; the Soviet and Nazi camps raised bondage in the 1930s and 1940s apart from voice.
- Universality pass: Every population has or lacks a say in rule; zero for bands by the measure, which counts states.

Civil liberties (liberties): frontier.
- What it covers: Freedom of belief, speech, press and assembly.
- Necessity pass: Religious toleration, the free press and their suppression under twentieth-century dictatorships are large changes in freedom.
- Independence uncertain: They came before broad suffrage in nineteenth-century Britain, but move with contestation since 1945.
- Universality uncertain: Every population has some freedom of belief and speech, but no world measure reads it before V-Dem's from 1789; a later pass could open it with a defined threshold.

Women's legal autonomy (women): frontier.
- What it covers: Whether women may own property, contract, divorce, choose a spouse and work without a husband's or father's consent.
- Necessity pass: Half of humanity's freedom; coverture, the married women's property acts, and the laws that bound women to husbands' consent until the 1960s and 1970s have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Its history runs apart from bondage and voice: married women held property under Islamic and Roman law while they could not under English common law until 1870 to 1882.
- Universality uncertain: Every population has rules for women's autonomy, but no world series reads them before the World Bank's index from 1970; its non-monotonic history (higher under some ancient and Islamic laws than in early modern Christian Europe) makes a sketch risky without sources.

Freedom of movement (movement): merged into person.
- What it covers: Being free to leave one's land, town or country.
- Necessity pass: Serfs were bound to the land; passports and residence permits bind many now.
- Independence fail: Where it is lost by status (serfdom), it is bondage; where by state rules (China's household registration), it is a matter of law and rule.
- Universality pass: Every population moves or is kept from moving.

Completeness uncertain: Freedom from slavery and servitude is the parent's own measure, with movement merged into it; a part in government is voice. The civil liberties and women's legal autonomy have no measured home, so completeness is uncertain. Checked against The freedoms of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (freedom from slavery and servitude, movement, thought, conscience and religion, opinion and expression, assembly and association, a part in government) and Sen's instrumental freedoms (political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees, protective security).. Still without a home: Civil liberties: thought, conscience, religion, expression and assembly (frontier); Women's legal autonomy (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.freedom","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.freedom","candidates":[{"key":"person","label":"Freedom of the person","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.freedom's own measure, the share held in bondage, which reads it already: slavery, serfdom and forced labour are its kinds"},{"key":"voice","label":"Voice","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"liberties","label":"Civil liberties","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"women","label":"Women's legal autonomy","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"movement","label":"Freedom of movement","outcome":"merged","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","mergedInto":"person"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The freedoms of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (freedom from slavery and servitude, movement, thought, conscience and religion, opinion and expression, assembly and association, a part in government) and Sen's instrumental freedoms (political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees, protective security).","missing":["Civil liberties: thought, conscience, religion, expression and assembly (frontier)","Women's legal autonomy (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Standing among others (concept.humanity.wants.standing):
- What it is: Standing among others: where people stand against each other, in what they have and in the ranks they are born into. The first pass measured it by income inequality between all people (Gini) and filed hereditary rank beneath it, as its only child, without recording why.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of inequality that change apart, which the income Gini hides: hereditary rank, which rose with chiefdoms and states and fell with revolutions and reforms after 1789; and the concentration of wealth, which accumulates over generations, was levelled by plague, war, revolution and state collapse (Scheidel's four horsemen) and rose again, apart from incomes.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025; measured for all living people.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Standing among others is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Standing is the condition of where one stands against others, in what one has and in the rank one is born to; the other conditions are of the body, of material comfort, of company, of offspring, of knowledge, of freedom, of meaning and of beauty and play. Other kinds within it: Staying alive and well, Sustenance and comfort, Belonging, Continuation, Understanding, Freedom and power, Meaning, Beauty and play.

How the parts make the whole work: Standing as this account follows it is income (the parent's own measure), hereditary rank and wealth. They change apart: rank rose with chiefdoms and states to about half of humanity and fell after 1789; wealth concentrated from foragers' fairly even holdings to the richest tenth owning most of everything in agrarian empires, was levelled by plague, war, revolution and collapse (Scheidel), and rose again after 1980; income inequality between all people rose from about 1820 to 2000 mainly between countries and has fallen since. Women's standing and esteem stay frontier.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Women's standing (universality), Esteem (necessity).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Income (income): routed to h.standing's own measure, income inequality between all people (Gini), which reads it already.
- What it covers: How unequal yearly incomes are.
- Necessity pass: The divergence between rich and poor countries after 1820 and its partial reversal after 1990 (Milanovic) are its history.
- Independence pass: World income inequality fell after 2000 while wealth concentration held.
- Universality pass: Every population divides what it gets.

Hereditary rank (rank): part.
- What it covers: Living under ranks or castes one is born into: nobles and commoners, castes, estates.
- Necessity pass: Aristocracy and caste, from chiefdoms to the old regimes ended after 1789 and India's constitution of 1950, have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Rank fell from about two fifths to a few percent between 1789 and 1990 while income inequality between all people rose.
- Universality pass: Every population has or lacks inherited rank; near zero for mobile foragers.

Wealth (wealth): part.
- What it covers: How concentrated what people own is: land, herds, houses, slaves, capital.
- Necessity pass: Inherited wealth is how inequality outlasts a generation; its rise with farming and herds (Kohler, Borgerhoff Mulder), its levelling by the Black Death, the world wars and communist revolutions, and its return since 1980 have no home in incomes alone.
- Independence pass: Wealth is far more concentrated than income at every date with records, and moves on its own clock: the Black Death levelled it while incomes rose, and it rose after 1980 while world income inequality fell.
- Universality pass: Every population owns something; foragers' material and relational wealth is shared more evenly.

Women's standing (gender): frontier.
- What it covers: How women stand against men: in income, property, office and esteem.
- Necessity pass: Half of humanity's standing.
- Independence pass: Moves apart from rank and wealth.
- Universality uncertain: Every population ranks women and men somehow, but no world measure reads it before the 1990s; recorded with women's legal autonomy under freedom as a frontier.

Esteem (esteem): frontier.
- What it covers: How people feel they stand: respect, recognition, status in their own eyes.
- Necessity uncertain: Status anxiety matters to people, but it is a reading of persons with no world series.
- Independence pass: Not tied to income alone.
- Universality pass: Every population has it.

Completeness uncertain: Class is read by income (the parent) and wealth; status by hereditary rank; party, power in rule, by voice under freedom. Gender and esteem have no measured home. Checked against Weber's three dimensions of stratification (class, status, party) and the World Inequality Database's income and wealth series.. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Connection (concept.humanity.means.connection):
- What it is: Connection as a means: moving people, goods and words between places. The first pass measured it by the fastest regular passenger speed and filed the share of people online beneath it, as its only child, without recording why.
- What the carve is for: To follow the three things connection carries, which change apart and which passenger speed alone hides: people, whose fastest regular speed rose from a walking pace to jet speed; goods, whose tonnage moved per person rose a thousandfold, mostly by sea; and words, whose speed jumped from a horse's to near the speed of light with the telegraph, a century before people flew.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, from foragers carrying their goods and news on foot to container ships and fibre networks; measured for the world.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Connection is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Connection is the means of moving people, goods and words between places; the other means are getting and making things, place, trading, ruling and fighting. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Habitat, Exchange, Politics, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Connection is carved into 2 parts: Moving goods, Moving words.

How the parts make the whole work: Connection as this account follows it is moving people (the parent's own measure, passenger speed), moving goods (freight per person) and moving words (message speed). They change apart and on different clocks: for millennia all three moved at the pace of feet, animals and sails, news a little faster through relay posts; the semaphore and the telegraph freed words from travel between 1794 and 1866, so that message speed reached its limit a century before people flew; railways and steamships multiplied freight from the 1830s, and bulk and container shipping kept it growing after passenger speed stopped rising. The railway moves people and goods at once, which is why it has two homes; it changed both, as a carrier, not as one part. Being online is a kind of moving words; migration stays frontier.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Being online (a kind of concept.humanity.means.connection.news).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Moving home (universality).

Routed elsewhere: Moving people to h.connection's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed, which reads it already, Mass media to Beauty and play (h.media), where the first pass filed the share reached by print, radio, television or internet.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Moving people (people): routed to h.connection's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed, which reads it already.
- What it covers: How fast and far people travel.
- Necessity pass: Horses, sailing ships, railways and airliners.
- Independence pass: Passenger speed barely moved from the horse to 1830, while news speed jumped with the semaphore and telegraph.
- Universality pass: Every population travels.

Moving goods (goods): part.
- What it covers: How much freight a population moves and how far: by porters, pack animals, carts, boats, ships, railways, trucks and pipelines.
- Necessity pass: Bulk shipping made distant grain, coal and ore cheap; the steamship, the railway and the container ship have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Freight per person doubled between 1970 and 2025 while the fastest passenger speed fell back from Concorde's to a jet's; it grew a hundredfold from 1820 to 1970 while news speed had already reached its limit.
- Universality pass: Every population carries goods, foragers on their backs.

Moving words (news): part.
- What it covers: How fast messages travel between distant places: runners, mounted relays, signal fires and semaphores, telegraph, radio, cable and fibre.
- Necessity pass: The telegraph decoupled news from travel in the 1840s; empire, markets and war changed with it (Standage's Victorian Internet). The Persian and Mongol relay posts have no other home.
- Independence pass: Message speed rose a thousandfold with the semaphore and telegraph (1794 to 1866) while passenger speed rose fivefold.
- Universality pass: Every population passes news.

Being online (online): a kind of news.
- What it covers: Using the internet.
- Necessity pass: Two thirds of humanity now.
- Independence pass: Spread after 1995 apart from freight and travel.
- Universality fail: Exists only since the 1970s and for the public since 1991: a kind of moving words, which reads who can send and receive rather than how fast.

Moving home (migration): frontier.
- What it covers: People moving to live elsewhere: migration within and between countries, forced and free.
- Necessity pass: The Atlantic slave trade, the European and Asian mass migrations of 1850 to 1914 and today's migrants have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Migration waves follow wages and wars, not speed.
- Universality uncertain: Every population moves, but a world measure (the share living outside their country of birth, about 3.6% now) needs countries; before them the measure has no clear meaning. A later pass could open it from 1500.

Mass media (broadcast): routed to Beauty and play (h.media), where the first pass filed the share reached by print, radio, television or internet.
- What it covers: Words sent to many at once.
- Necessity pass: Print and broadcasting.
- Independence uncertain: Reach, not speed.
- Universality fail: Only since print.

Completeness uncertain: Passengers are the parent's measure, freight is goods, messages are news; travel and transportation and communication have homes. Migration, people moving to live elsewhere, has none measured. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Carbon dioxide in the air (concept.dim.earth.climate.co2):
- What it is: Carbon dioxide in the air, the measure the Earth carve gave to the air and its climate (h.co2, ppm). The deepen check names it: six Events move it, two at the top of an importance scale. This carve divides the measured gas by where it comes from; dividing the air and its climate into gases and aerosols is a different carve, left for a later pass.
- What the carve is for: To separate what the carbon cycle holds on its own, which swung between about 180 and 280 ppm with the ice ages, from what people have added by clearing land and burning fuel, so that the Anthropocene question (when did people start to change the air?) has a home: from about 1850 by every account, from the first farmers by Ruddiman's early anthropogenic hypothesis.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025; measured in ppm for the whole atmosphere, the two parts summing to the observed concentration.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Carbon dioxide in the air is a kind of A condition of the Earth as setting: Carbon dioxide in the air is the main long-lived greenhouse gas, the carbon the air holds between the oceans, the living world and the rocks; the other conditions are the plant cover, land and sea, the wild animals and the stores in the rocks. Other kinds within it: The plant cover, Land and sea, The wild animals, The Earth's stores.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Carbon dioxide in the air is carved into 2 parts: The carbon cycle's own level, Added by people.

How the parts make the whole work: Carbon dioxide in the air as this account follows it is the carbon cycle's own level plus what people have added, which sum to the observed concentration at every date. For 290,000 years the first is all there is, swinging with the ice ages. From the first farmers a human addition may begin: a few ppm by most carbon-cycle accounts, about 35 by Ruddiman's, a debate the bands carry with a midpoint of about 12 ppm by 1750. It dips about 1610 as the Americas' fields return to forest, and from 1800 it grows from about 17 to about 160 ppm, first from clearing land, then mostly from fossil fuel, while the natural level holds. Fossil fuel and land clearing are kinds of the addition; methane, nitrous oxide and aerosols belong to a carve of the air that remains open.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): From fossil fuels (a kind of concept.dim.earth.climate.co2.human), From clearing land (a kind of concept.dim.earth.climate.co2.human).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Other greenhouse gases and aerosols (universality).

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The carbon cycle's own level (natural): part.
- What it covers: The carbon dioxide the oceans, the living world and the rocks would hold in the air without people: the glacial and interglacial swings, and the Holocene's own course.
- Necessity pass: The ice ages' swings of about a hundred ppm, the largest changes in the record before 1850, have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It swung with the orbital cycles for 300,000 years with nothing added; since 1850 it has barely moved while the added part grew from 20 to about 160 ppm.
- Universality pass: Present at every date.

Added by people (human): part.
- What it covers: The carbon dioxide in the air that people's clearing of forests and burning of wood, coal, oil and gas have added and the oceans and land have not yet taken back.
- Necessity pass: The rise from about 280 to 427 ppm since 1750, the cause of modern warming, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: It grew from about 20 to 160 ppm since 1850 while the natural level held; it dipped about 1610 when forests regrew on the Americas' abandoned fields, apart from the ocean's own response to the Little Ice Age.
- Universality pass: Every date has a human addition, zero before farming.

From fossil fuels (fossil): a kind of human.
- What it covers: Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and gas, and from making cement.
- Necessity pass: About two thirds of the addition since 1850.
- Independence pass: It took off with coal after 1800 and oil after 1950, apart from clearing.
- Universality fail: Negligible before Song China's coal and Britain's after 1600; a kind of human addition.

From clearing land (land): a kind of human.
- What it covers: Carbon dioxide from clearing and burning forests and draining soils for fields and pasture.
- Necessity pass: All of the addition before 1800 by any account, and about a third since.
- Independence pass: It follows farmland and deforestation, not fuel.
- Universality fail: Absent before farming; a kind of human addition.

Other greenhouse gases and aerosols (other-gases): frontier.
- What it covers: Methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and the dust and sulfate that cool.
- Necessity pass: Methane from rice paddies and cattle is the other half of Ruddiman's hypothesis; sulfate aerosols masked part of the warming after 1950.
- Independence pass: Methane rose about 3000 BCE while carbon dioxide's rise was slower.
- Universality uncertain: Parts of the air and its climate, not of carbon dioxide: they belong to a carve of the air that this pass leaves open.

Completeness pass: The observed concentration is by definition the carbon cycle's own level plus the human addition still in the air; the two sum to it at every date. Checked against The Global Carbon Budget's accounting, in which the rise of atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1750 is the sum of fossil and land-use emissions less what the ocean and land sinks take up, against a natural baseline..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.dim.earth.climate.co2","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.climate.co2","candidates":[{"key":"natural","label":"The carbon cycle's own level","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"human","label":"Added by people","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"fossil","label":"From fossil fuels","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"human"},{"key":"land","label":"From clearing land","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"human"},{"key":"other-gases","label":"Other greenhouse gases and aerosols","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The Global Carbon Budget's accounting, in which the rise of atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1750 is the sum of fossil and land-use emissions less what the ocean and land sinks take up, against a natural baseline."}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Findings of the tree pass from model r126 to r157 (bb3c3d17), after claude.finding.tree-pass-1. Every value is recalled, tagged sketch or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Divisions carved (13 recorded cuts): meaning, sustenance, habitat, politics, provisioning, violence (safety), war, the plant cover (forest), voice, food, standing, connection and carbon dioxide. Kept whole with the reason recorded: the largest polity and the largest city (order statistics with kinds but no parts). Tried and not recorded: freedom, where only voice passed as a measured part (below).

2. What the 24 new parts show:
- Meaning. The faiths open to every people go from nothing in 500 BCE to about 36% of humanity by 1500 and 61% now, mostly by conversion until 1900 and by births since. Belief that gods or a cosmic law judge conduct rises most between 800 and 500 BCE (the Axial Age, debated as break or slope, and as cause or effect of large societies), peaks near 80% about 1900, falls to about 66% under state atheism by 1970. Practice (the parent) fell by half since 1750 while affiliation fell far less.
- Shelter: about 3 m² a person for foragers, 7 to 9 for farmers, dips in the industrial cities of the 1850s and in 1944, then rises from 9 to 23 since 1950.
- Settling down: the mobile share falls from all of humanity at the Natufians (about 12,500 BCE) fastest from 9500 to 7900 BCE; pastoral nomads are about a third of the mobile after 1000 BCE; the Soviet forced settlement of the 1930s; about 0.3% now.
- Output by sector: food-getting about four fifths of foragers' output and half in 1820, about 5% now; making passes food-getting about 1910; services pass it about 1900, reach half of output by 1970 and two thirds now; making stalls from 1985 to 1995 (deindustrialization, the Soviet collapse) until China.
- War: deaths in fighting between polities collapse after 1945 while fighting within polities becomes the larger kind; one-sided killing peaks with the Mongols, in 1941 to 1944, in 1965, 1975 to 1979 and 1994. Bangladesh 1971 and Rwanda 1994 were missing from war and safety and are now in both.
- Forest: the boreal forest moves most with the ice (about 4% of land at the glacial maximum, 10% in the Last Interglacial); temperate forest is cleared first and bottoms out about 1950 to 1976 for the world, rising since 1980 with China's planting; tropical forest regrows after the Great Dying and falls fastest after 1950.
- Voice: contestation came first and narrowly (Greek democracies, the Roman Republic, Poland-Lithuania, Britain after 1688), inclusiveness later and fast; by the 1960s three quarters of adults could vote while a third of humanity chose its rulers in competitive elections; India's Emergency moves only contestation.
- Food: staples per person flat since 1960; animal foods fell from about a third of foragers' energy to a tenth with farming and rise again since 1950; oils, sugar and other foods carry most of the gain since 1960 (Popkin's nutrition transition).
- Wealth: the richest tenth's share rises from about a quarter among foragers to half in the Bronze Age and two thirds in Rome and Han China, is levelled by the Black Death, peaks near 87% in 1910, is levelled by the world wars and revolutions to about 71% from 1950 to 1980, and returns to about 76% now (Scheidel's levellers).
- Connection: freight per person from about 3 tonne-km a year for foragers to 40 in 1800, 800 in 1900, 7,000 in 1970 and about 16,700 now; message speed from a runner's pace to the semaphore (1794) and telegraph (1840s), at the limit of light in fibre by about 1996.
- Carbon dioxide: the human addition is about 12 ppm by 1750 (a midpoint between Ruddiman's early anthropogenic hypothesis, about 35, and most carbon-cycle modellers, a few), dips about 1610 with the Americas' regrowth, and is about 160 ppm of the 427 now.

3. What dividing exposed in existing values:
- War: the parent's peaks for 1618 to 1650 and 1850 to 1864 appear to include those wars' famine and disease deaths, which the causes-of-death carve counts under hunger and infection; and the parent counts some one-sided killings (the Holocaust, Indonesia 1965, the Khmer Rouge, now Bangladesh and Rwanda) but not China's campaigns of 1950 to 1953 or the Cultural Revolution's killings, and whether it counts the Soviet Great Terror is unrecorded.
- Energy for warmth (h.warmth) counts food energy, which food also counts.
- Parts made as shares of a parent (output's sectors, the forests, the food sources, the parts of war and carbon dioxide) sum exactly but inherit the parent's errors.
- The carbon cycle's own level after 1800 is a counterfactual held constant.
- The forest carve's synthesis says temperate forest turns up 'after about 1930'; for the world the values bottom out later, about 1950 to 1976, as their note says; a re-carve should align the wording.

4. Method. A carve records a cut only when at least two candidates pass as parts with measures. Where a parent's measure is itself one aspect of the concept (freedom read by bondage, connection by passenger speed, standing by income, worship for meaning), that aspect is routed to the parent's measure and two other parts must pass; for freedom only voice did, so its carve is kept as notes, not a cut. Kinds and second readings filed under a parent (the eight religious shares, foraging, the food-work share, being online, the development index) stay flagged as untested parts until they are re-filed, which this pass did not do."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"plan","text":"Continuing on 2026-10-15 at graph r148 (c7f3d7c2), bound to model r157 (bb3c3d17), the only head the saved-work listing shows, read back through life_construction_replay (all 149 graph revisions at outline level; the Americas, Oceania and South-eastern Asia and tree passes at reasoning level, every carve's frame, tests and synthesis in full) and life_model_outline. The engine reports 0.13.0; the repository pins 0.12.0, and construction/MANIFEST.json still holds the construction as imported at graph r22 (model r57).

This pass checks the work added since the placement pass of 2026-10-14 before it is published: the Americas pass (model r64 to r77), the Oceania and South-eastern Asia pass (r78 to r95) and the tree pass (r96 to r157). It is a self-review by the same kind of model that wrote the records, so its checks have Self assurance, not Independent (EpistemicCascade#00ae), and every figure it checks against is recalled from one training foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca); none becomes a source by being checked here.

What the reading found, to be corrected each with a note saying what was wrong, what showed it and how to check the correction (Coursecandor#639e), keeping what the old record got right (Revisance#73f1):
1. Event texts: Uruguay's coup dated 1976 (it was June 1973); the Bourbon reforms credited with New Granada's viceroyalty (founded 1717 and re-established 1739, before Charles III); manioc domesticated 'by about 6800 BCE' (Lombardo and colleagues date it about 10,350 years ago, 6800 BCE being maize's 6,850 years ago misread); the Windrush's 'about 500 Caribbean migrants' (an old count; the ship's list shows about 800 of its 1,027 passengers from the Caribbean); Tambora's toll double-counting its direct deaths; the Louisiana Purchase made 'having lost Saint-Domingue' (in April 1803 the army was dying but the colony not yet lost); Colombia's toll given as 450,000 alone where two counts disagree; the westerly-wind window for East Polynesia (1140 to 1260) given as what ended the long pause though the model's own Society Islands settlement (1025 to 1120) comes before it.
2. Causes: East Polynesia's settlement re-read for that chronology, with the drought rival stated; the Myanmar coup question has lost its own reason to a reading's.
3. Importance: the Americas' top level holds eleven Events for ten.
4. Values and carves: war deaths (h.war) count the famine and disease deaths of the great wars, as the tolls usually cited do, while hunger (h.alive.hunger) also counts the same famines in 1618 to 1650 and 1941 to 1945, so the causes-of-death carve's rule that each death is counted once is broken there; the forager child mortality is inconsistent with life expectancy and adult survival by about a year and a half; Oceania's share for 1500 to 1800 sits below the usual pre-contact counts with too narrow a band; the forest carve dates the temperate forest's turn to about 1930 where its values turn about 1950 to 1976; Pinatubo's dip is a little small.
5. Coverage: 105 processes pass over the model's own Events; the new parts lack the dates the placement pass gave their parents, and the regional passes' Events crowd stretches such as 1941 to 1946.

Order: Event texts, causes, importance, value corrections and carve re-records, then the coverage fill window by window from the densest stretches, the graph rebound after every model revision, and one closing note."}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"revision","text":"The review of the Americas, Oceania and South-eastern Asia and tree passes, against recalled knowledge only: a self-review with Self assurance, not Independent (EpistemicCascade#00ae), every figure resting on one training foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca). Each change keeps the old record in the history, says what was wrong and what showed it, and gives a check (Coursecandor#639e); what the old record got right is kept (Revisance#73f1).

What was read. Every one of the about 390 Events the two regional passes added, by name, dates and description (in full where a figure or claim needed it); their located_in bindings for the multi-region cases (Hawai'i, Rapa Nui, the Peruvian raids, Hokule'a, the galleons, the boat people); all 20 cause questions and their 65 readings; the importance levels on the Americas' scale; the values the two passes recorded; all 28 carves of the tree pass with their frames, verdicts and syntheses, and the values of their 57 parts against their wholes at key dates.

Wrong, and corrected:
1. Event texts (r158). Uruguay's coup was in June 1973, not 1976 (ev.am.dictatorships). New Granada's viceroyalty was Philip V's (1717, 1739), not Charles III's (ev.lac.bourbon-reforms). Manioc in the Llanos de Moxos dates to about 10,350 years ago, about 8400 BCE, not 6800 BCE, which is maize's 6,850 years ago misread (ev.sam.manioc, interval opened to -8400). The Windrush carried about 800 Caribbean passengers of 1,027, not 'about 500' (ev.car.windrush). Tambora's direct deaths were added twice to a total that includes them (ev.sea.tambora). France had not lost Saint-Domingue when it sold Louisiana in April 1803 (ev.am.louisiana). Colombia's dead have two counts, about 260,000 documented and about 450,000 estimated, not one (ev.sam.colombia-conflict). The westerly winds were said to explain why East Polynesia was settled when it was, though the model's own Society Islands settlement (1025 to 1120) precedes their window (ev.pol.voyaging-winds).
2. Causes (r159). East Polynesia's settlement: the winds re-read from 0.45 to 0.8 without them, a difference of 0.1 instead of 0.45; the question now lists every rival, drought among them. Myanmar's coup had lost its question's reason; restored. The Haitian Revolution's question now states the historians' debate it left implicit.
3. Importance (r160). The Americas' top level held eleven Events: Columbus's landfall comes down beneath the Columbian exchange, which carries it; nine Events come down from the second level, which now holds 102 (BaseRateInclude#1e63).
4. Values (r161). Hunger counted the famines of the Ming-Qing and Thirty Years wars (1618 to 1650) and of the Second World War (1941 to 1945) that war's toll (h.war) has always counted, so the six causes of death counted those deaths twice; hunger is lowered at 1650, 1941.5 and 1945 and given 1618. Forager and early farmer child mortality (45 to 47%) did not fit life expectancy (30) and adult survival (41 more years at fifteen): the three are tied, and child mortality is now 42% for foragers, rising to 45% by 1200 BCE; from 90 BCE on the earlier values already fit within a point. Oceania's share before 1850 keeps its 0.2% but its band now reaches the usual pre-contact counts (0.4 to 0.7% in 1500), which are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b); Australia and New Zealand's 1788 note no longer claims more people than its value holds. Pinatubo's dip is 0.2 degrees, not 0.15.
5. Carves (r162). The causes-of-death carve said each death is counted by its underlying cause; the values count war's famines and epidemics in war's toll, as the usual tolls of the great wars do, and the carve, its hunger, infection and violence parts and the war carve's routing now say so, with the alternative rule (direct conflict deaths only, as the Uppsala data and the Global Burden of Disease count them) stated with what it would move. The forest carve said temperate forest has grown back since about 1930; that holds for western Europe and eastern North America, while this account's world values turn about 1950 to 1976, and the lens now says both.

Checked and standing: the other Events of the two passes (dates, tolls and claims as usually stated, debated ones already marked); the other 17 cause questions; the M49 carves of the regions, whose parts sum to their wholes; the causes of death summing to crude death rates consistent with life expectancy (1900: 3,200; 1950: 1,950; 2019: 725, against the Global Burden of Disease's about 730 as recalled); output's sectors (about 4% food-getting, a quarter making, two thirds services now); wild mammals (about 3 Mt C now against about 60 for people and 100 for livestock); freight (about 16,700 tonne-km a person now); the richest tenth's wealth (about 76%). The East Polynesia question still reads Lapita and Ancestral Polynesian society as large differences (0.85 each) although both were present through the pause; the earlier passes' rule was to leave such shared conditions unread or small, so this is a method question for the next pass rather than a factual error, and it is left as recorded."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Role: reviewer and continuing modeler. This pass checked the work added since the first pass of 2026-10-14 before it is published, corrected what was wrong, and brought the coverage report back to done. It ends at model revision 182 (a82f1a8b) and graph revision 171. The notes of this pass, at the records they concern, give the detail; this note is the map for the next pass.

WHAT IT DID
1. Checks of the Events, causes, importance judgments and carves added for the Americas, Oceania and South-eastern Asia and by the tree pass. It corrected Event texts and weighed causes (one cause record, malformed, was sent again well-formed), judged the Americas' importance, and corrected abstract cuts. Each carve's parts were read against the whole they divide. Every change carries a note saying what was wrong.
2. Value corrections, each with its note:
- War, 1800 to 1820, raised for the Napoleonic wars (18 to 1808, then 40), with its parts and Safety.
- The Korean War's deaths concentrated in 1950 to 1954, and the reading at -490 split at -200.
- Comet 1's service and grounding (1952 to 1956), and Concorde's grounding in late 2001.
- Provisioning's peak in 1929 and trough in 1932, with the sector split (industry falls about a third).
- India's 1951-52 election in the democracy share, and the end of the Emergency in 1977.
- China's 1953-54 elections in suffrage.
- The Holocaust's timing in h.religion-6, at 1943.2.
- Pinatubo's cooling at 1992.
- The Americas' shares at 1520. Smallpox had been placed in central Mexico before it reached the mainland, and South America's share fell with no cause. Both are moved after the epidemic's arrival, and Asia's share is revised so that the five shares still sum to 100.
- One-sided killing from 1971.96 to 1976. The value was below even the lowest count of Burundi's killings of 1972 and left out Amin's in Uganda; it is raised, with War and Safety.
- South-eastern Asia's first postwar values, lowered to the timing of the famine.
- Reasons added to the out-of-Africa dispersal's moves in Asia's, South-eastern Asia's and Africa's shares; those values are unchanged.
3. Debates stated with their alternatives rather than one side (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): the An Lushan registers; the contact population of the Americas and of central Mexico; Sahul's first arrival; the tolls of the Vietnam famine and of Java under occupation; Bangladesh in 1971 and Indonesia in 1965-66; the date of the dispersal; Thera's date; India's toll from COVID-19; Oceania's early-modern level.
4. Coverage. The measures passing over their own Events went from 105 to 0, and the report said done at r180: every level of the schedule filled, no process empty, none passing over its Events, none flat, no contradictions or residuals. New values sit at the Events that move each measure. Where a cluster of Events would not visibly move a share, the value is interpolated and its note says why. The last rounds read each place's Events against its values directly, rather than waiting for the report to name gaps one at a time.
5. The graph was rebound to the model after every revision.
Sema patterns used: EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b, Coursecandor#639e, Revisance#73f1, ContrastClass#7398, BaseRateInclude#1e63, EvidenceDependence#23ca, EpistemicCascade#00ae, DecompositionGate#1b2d, Synthesis#4f1f.

WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN
- Publication is not ready. construction/history-numbers.construction.json and construction/MANIFEST.json still describe head graph 9403f66d and model r57, exported with 0.12.0. README.md still says 52 processes pass over their Events, and METHOD.md has not been updated. The store is at r182 on engine 0.13.0. Export with life_construction_export, check the import in a fresh engine, then update the manifest, the README's status and METHOD.md. This is the first job of the next pass, because nothing of this pass is published until it is done.
- Some losses are spread by interpolation. Several shares stay on the straight line between their neighbours so that subregions sum to regions and regions to 100, although the loss came at a known time: the Great Leap Forward's famine in Eastern Asia (shown only faintly, 1958 to 1961), Western Asia before 1258, Western Europe before the Thirty Years' War, and Asia across the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879. Each needs its region family and the world shares revised together. It can wait for a pass that revises them together, because the bands already hold the truer timing.
- Oceania's early-modern level is open: 0.2% here against the usual estimates of 0.25 to 0.7% for 1500 to 1800. The band carries the debate; moving the value needs Asia's and Europe's shares rebalanced with it.
- Open war counts. China's campaigns, the Cultural Revolution and the Great Terror are still to be checked. Amin's killings are counted from 1971.96 to 1976 but not yet at 1971.23 or 1979.02. The Napoleonic revision should be checked against the cause questions that cite war deaths.
- Importance judgments have not been calibrated across regions.
- Carves and method: the East Polynesia method question; the 12 parts never tested in their carve (h.internet, h.food-work, h.foraging, h.ends, and the eight religions under h.meaning); and the freedom carve.
- World kcal around 1961 sits near the edge of its band.
- Nothing is tagged source. Every figure named beside a source is recalled, not checked; a source pass should check the largest figures first.
- A binding to check: the Pacific islands' COVID-19 border closures are counted among Asia's Events.
- The report's own suggestions: carve h.religion-6 or keep it whole, then sea level and no religion; open the coarsest stretches (carbon dioxide and the Earth's stores, 1950 to 1960); and weigh four cause questions with unweighed causes, among them the Roman Empire, the Antarctic Treaty and the rise of Christianity."}
upsertNodes.title: Closing note of the review pass: what it did and what it leaves open
